Interface with BOJ-NET for funds settlement and JGB transfers


IRS Clearing Platform
Accepts trade registrations from trade matching platforms (e.g., MarkitWire/DTCC, Tradeweb) and trade execution platforms (SEFs)


VaR Margin Software (VMA)
Proprietary margin calculation engine; currently v3.0, upgrading to v4.0 in April 2026; clearing participants can run the same software for pre-trade margin estimation


PTS Connectivity
Connected to multiple PTS venues (Japannext, Chi-X Japan) for clearing of off-exchange equity trades


FIX Protocol
Used for certain connectivity with PTS and international participants [unverified]





5.2 Resilience

Business Continuity Planning (BCP): JSCC maintains comprehensive BCP arrangements including a secondary operations site (backup center) geographically separated from the primary site.
RPO/RTO: Recovery Time Objective of 2 hours for critical systems [unverified]; Recovery Point Objective targets zero data loss.
System Availability: JSCC’s systems are designed for high availability consistent with PFMI Principle 17 requirements.
Cyber Security: JSCC participates in JPX group-wide cyber security initiatives and information sharing arrangements.
Collateral Tokenization Pilot: JSCC participated in a DTCC industry sandbox initiative exploring how CCPs could use tokenization technology to optimize collateral management processes for clearing members and buy-side firms, including margin call automation. [Source: Risk.net]

title: Japan Securities Clearing Corporation (JSCC)
text:
6. Regulatory Framework

6.1 Supervising Authority







Authority
Role




JFSA (Japan Financial Services Agency)
Primary regulator and supervisor; licenses JSCC as a Financial Instruments Clearing Organization under the FIEA; conducts inspections; issues business improvement orders


Bank of Japan (BOJ)
Oversight of JSCC, particularly for IRS clearing and systemically important payment/settlement systems; conducts joint inspections with JFSA


Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
Supervisory role for commodity derivatives clearing (joint supervision with JFSA following TOCOM integration) [unverified]





6.2 Key Regulations







Regulation
Description




Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA)
Primary law governing JSCC’s CCP activities; Article 2, Paragraph 29 defines “Financial Instruments Obligation Assumption Services”


Cabinet Office Ordinance on Financial Instruments Clearing Organizations
Detailed rules for CCP operations, risk management, capital requirements


JSCC Business Rules
JSCC’s own rulebook governing clearing qualification, margin, default management, settlement, and fees for each clearing business


Commodity Derivatives Act
Governs commodity derivatives clearing (applicable post-TOCOM integration)


Act on Book-Entry Transfer of Company Bonds, Shares, etc.
Governs book-entry transfer and settlement finality for securities





6.3 PFMI Compliance

JSCC publishes comprehensive PFMI (Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures) self-assessment disclosures, most recently updated March 31, 2025.
The disclosure covers all 24 PFMI principles applicable to CCPs.
JSCC also publishes quarterly CPMI-IOSCO Public Quantitative Disclosures (PQD), providing over 200 quantitative data fields covering margin, default resources, credit risk, collateral, liquidity risk, and back-testing.
The PQD data is available on the JSCC Quantitative Disclosure page and is also aggregated by CCP Global.

[Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure (March 2025)]


6.4 Reporting Requirements

Trade Reporting: OTC derivative transactions (IRS, CDS) must be reported to a licensed trade repository under JFSA rules, consistent with G20 commitments.
Clearing Obligation: Japan mandates clearing for certain OTC derivatives – specifically, JPY-denominated plain vanilla IRS and iTraxx Japan CDS indices – at a licensed CCP (JSCC is the only eligible CCP).
PQD Disclosure: Quarterly public quantitative disclosure following CPMI-IOSCO standards.
Annual Reporting: JSCC submits annual reports and financial statements to JFSA.

title: Japan Securities Clearing Corporation (JSCC)
text:
7. Interoperability

7.1 CCP Interoperability Arrangements

JSCC does not currently operate any CCP interoperability arrangements (CCP links) with other CCPs.
As the sole CCP for Japanese exchange-traded products and the dominant CCP for JPY OTC derivatives, there has been limited demand for interoperability.


Comparison with KRX: Like KRX, JSCC operates as a domestic monopoly CCP without interoperability links. This contrasts with European CCPs (e.g., LCH EquityClear, Eurex Clearing, Cboe Clear Europe) which operate interoperable clearing arrangements for cash equities.

title: Japan Securities Clearing Corporation (JSCC)
text:
9. Recent Developments

2024

Record IRS clearing volume: JSCC cleared ¥8.3 quadrillion (US$56.3 trillion) in JPY IRS in 2024, doubling the 2023 record. Monthly clearing volume surpassed ¥1,000 trillion for the first time in December 2024. This growth was driven by Japan’s changing interest-rate environment as the BOJ exited its ultra-loose monetary policy. [Source: Risk.net]
Cross-margin enhancement: March 2024 – 3-month TONA futures included in IRS cross-margin functionality, enabling estimated 50-60% margin reduction for combined portfolios.
Asia Risk Award: Won “Clearing House of the Year” at Asia Risk Awards 2024 for VaR migration and cross-margin innovation.
CFTC engagement: Intensified discussions with CFTC regarding US customer access to JSCC’s IRS clearing service.



2025

CFTC breakthrough (September 2025): CFTC issued amended exempt DCO order and no-action letter (Letter No. 25-32) permitting US customers (eligible contract participants) to clear JPY IRS at JSCC through non-US clearing member affiliates of CFTC-registered FCMs. This was a landmark achievement removing a long-standing impediment. [Source: CFTC]
Initial margin reform proposals: JSCC consulted with clearing members on further refinements to initial margin and clearing fund calculation methods for listed derivatives. [Source: FIA]



2026

Listed Derivatives April 2026 Project (go-live April 13, 2026): Major system upgrade including VaR Margin Software upgrade from v3.0 to v4.0, improved VaR margin calculation methodology, new commodity products (Pocket Gold 100 Futures, Pocket Platinum 100 Futures), and enhanced margin offsets across asset classes. [Source: JSCC News]
Default fund consolidation review: JSCC is considering reorganizing its 10 separate default funds within the listed derivatives segment into a consolidated structure, as part of a broader review of membership and default management. [Source: Risk.net]
Collateral tokenization: JSCC continues to participate in DTCC-led industry sandbox exploring tokenization of collateral for margin optimization.

title: HKEX Clearing – HKSCC / HKCC / SEOCH
text:
2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services

HKSCC – Securities Clearing
HKSCC provides clearing, settlement, depository, and nominee services for securities listed on SEHK through CCASS. Two primary clearing modes exist:







Mode
Description




CNS (Continuous Net Settlement)
HKSCC acts as the CCP via novation, becoming the settlement counterparty to both buyer and seller. Positions in the same security are continuously netted, reducing settlement obligations. This is the default mode for Exchange Trades.


Isolated Trades (IT)
Trade-for-trade settlement without HKSCC acting as CCP. Used for specific trade types where netting is not appropriate.



HKSCC also clears and settles non-exchange transactions including: Settlement Instructions (SI) for broker-custodian deliveries, Stock Borrowing and Lending transactions, Clearing Agency Transactions (options exercise settlements from SEOCH), and Investor Settlement Instructions (ISI).
China Connect Securities: HKSCC clears northbound Stock Connect trades as a participant of ChinaClear, and clears southbound trades as the host CCP with ChinaClear as its Clearing Agency Participant.
[Source: HKEX Clearing Services – Securities Overview; HKSCC PFMI Disclosure]


HKCC – Derivatives (Futures) Clearing
HKCC acts as the CCP for all derivatives contracts traded on Hong Kong Futures Exchange (HKFE), guaranteeing settlement of transactions effected by its Clearing Participants. Products cleared include:







Product Category
Examples




Equity Index Futures & Options
Hang Seng Index, Hang Seng China Enterprises Index, Hang Seng TECH Index, Mini-Hang Seng Index


Single Stock Futures
Various Hong Kong-listed equities


Currency Futures & Options
USD/CNH, EUR/CNH, JPY/USD, AUD/USD


Interest Rate Futures
HIBOR futures


Commodity Futures
London Metal Mini Futures (Gold, Silver, Copper, Zinc, Nickel, Aluminium)



Trade details are electronically and automatically transmitted to HKCC once validly concluded on the exchange.
[Source: HKEX Listed Derivatives Clearing Overview; HKEX Product Information]


SEOCH – Stock Options Clearing
SEOCH acts as the CCP for stock options contracts traded on SEHK. It guarantees settlement of all transactions between its Clearing Participants. SEOCH clears Hong Kong dollar (HKD) and Renminbi (RMB) denominated stock options on major Hong Kong-listed stocks.
Both HKCC and SEOCH share the DCASS infrastructure and are operationally integrated, though they maintain separate legal identities, separate Reserve Funds, and distinct rulebooks.
[Source: HKEX Listed Derivatives Clearing Services]



2.2 Novation Process
HKSCC (Securities): Upon acceptance of an Exchange Trade for CNS settlement, HKSCC interposes itself as the CCP through novation. The original bilateral obligation between the buying and selling brokers is replaced by two separate obligations: one between HKSCC and the buyer, and one between HKSCC and the seller. This process is continuous – as new trades are matched and accepted, they are netted against existing CNS positions in the same security.
HKCC and SEOCH (Derivatives): Upon registration of a trade, HKCC/SEOCH novates the contract, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. The original contract between the two exchange participants is extinguished and replaced by two new contracts with the clearing house.
[Source: HKSCC Operational Procedures Section 9; HKCC Rules and Procedures]


2.3 Netting
HKSCC: Multilateral netting is applied daily under the CNS system. All CNS transactions in the same security are netted to produce a single net long or net short position per security per participant. Money obligations across all securities are then aggregated to determine a single net payment or receipt per participant per settlement day.
HKCC / SEOCH: Both clearing houses provide multilateral netting of obligations. Positions within each participant’s account are netted, and margin is calculated on a portfolio basis (net margining for house accounts; gross or net for client accounts depending on account type). Variation margin (mark-to-market) produces a single net pay/collect per settlement cycle.
[Source: HKSCC Operational Procedures; HKCC Rules]


2.4 Clearing Membership

Per bilateral agreement with HKSCC

Per HKSCC rules

Per HKSCC rules

Key Financial Requirements

title: HKEX Clearing – HKSCC / HKCC / SEOCH
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework

HKSCC – Securities Margin
HKSCC employs a two-tier margin framework based on the Hang Seng Composite Index classification:









Tier
Securities Covered
Methodology
Margin Rate




Tier P
Constituents of Hang Seng Composite LargeCap or MidCap Index; all equity ETPs and structured products with these underlyings
Value-at-Risk (VaR) based portfolio margining
Minimum 3.2% (effective August 14, 2023)


Tier N
All non-Tier P instruments and related products
Flat-rate margin by sub-group
Group 1: 12% (eff. June 13, 2022); Group 2: 30% (eff. Dec 16, 2022); Group 3: 55% (eff. Oct 27, 2025)



HKSCC additionally imposes: - Mark-to-market margin: Daily mark-to-market of all CNS positions to reflect current market value - Concentration margin / margin add-ons: Discretionary additional margin on Clearing Participants with elevated or concentrated risk exposures - Dynamic Contributions: Risk-based contributions to the Guarantee Fund, calculated based on each participant’s Expected Uncollateralised Loss (EUL) over the most recent 60 business days
[Source: HKEX – HKSCC Margin page; HKSCC Initial Margin Calculation Guide]


HKCC & SEOCH – Derivatives Margin (PRiME)
Both HKCC and SEOCH use the Portfolio Risk Margining System (PRiME), a SPAN 1-compatible margining algorithm, implemented in DCASS:







Aspect
Details




Methodology
PRiME evaluates the maximum potential loss of a portfolio of futures and options over a one-day holding period under 16 simulated scenarios at a defined confidence level


Risk Array
Represents how each derivative instrument will gain or lose value across defined price and volatility movements


Confidence Level
Calibrated to provide adequate coverage; reviewed regularly


Clearing House Margin
Calculated using the PRiME algorithm directly


Client Margin
Clearing House Risk Margin x Client Margin Multiplier (1.33x, effective March 20, 2017)


Margining Basis
House accounts: net margined; Omnibus Client, Sink, and Daily accounts: gross margined


SEOCH Premium Margin
For premium-paid options in SEOCH, Mark-to-Market Margin is added to the PRiME margin to achieve total margin requirements



HKCC also applies: - Additional Margin for concentrated positions exceeding 30% of aggregate losses in stress scenarios - Capital-based position limits (CBPLs) linking allowable positions to each participant’s liquid capital
Comparison with KRX: KRX uses a SPAN-based margin system for derivatives (KOSPI 200 futures/options, etc.), similar in concept to HKEX’s PRiME. Both apply portfolio-based margining with scenario analysis. KRX additionally applies a net option value-based margin approach for certain products. The client margin multiplier differs – HKEX uses 1.33x while KRX applies different scaling depending on the product.
[Source: HKEX PRiME Margining Guide v1.5 (October 2023); HKEX Margin page – Listed Derivatives]



3.2 Margin Call Schedule








Entity
Timing
Details




HKSCC
End-of-day (T)
Provisional clearing statements issued around 18:00-20:00 on trade date; final clearing statements after 14:00 on T+1; margin and Marks payable on settlement date


HKCC
End-of-day + Intraday
Daily end-of-day mark-to-market and margin recalculation; intraday variation adjustments and additional margin calls may be issued during volatile market conditions


SEOCH
End-of-day + Intraday
Each day after close of trading, SEOCH marks positions to market with the fixing price of each option series; intraday margin calls may be triggered during extreme movements



Margin may be provided in cash (HKD, USD, RMB) or in acceptable forms of collateral as specified by each clearing house. CCMS (Common Collateral Management System) manages collateral holdings and obligations across all three clearing houses.
[Source: HKEX Clearing FAQs – Derivatives; HKSCC Operational Procedures]


3.3 Default Waterfall

HKSCC Default Waterfall (Securities)
Upon declaration of a Clearing Participant as defaulter, HKSCC applies the following resources sequentially, per Rule 2507 of the General Rules of HKSCC:








Layer
Resource
Description




1
Defaulting CP’s margin, Marks, and collateral
All margin deposits, Marks (mark-to-market payments), collateral, admission fees, Mainland Settlement Deposit, and Mainland Security Deposit held by HKSCC


2
Defaulting CP’s Guarantee Fund contributions
Both Basic Contribution and Dynamic Contribution of the defaulter


3
HKSCC’s own contribution (Skin-in-the-Game)
Clearing house resources appropriated to the Guarantee Fund, equivalent to 10% of the Guarantee Fund size


4
Non-defaulting CPs’ Dynamic Contributions
Pro-rata allocation of Dynamic Contributions from non-defaulting Relevant Clearing Participants


5
Non-defaulting CPs’ Basic Contributions
Pro-rata allocation of Basic Contributions from non-defaulting Relevant Clearing Participants



Guarantee Fund Threshold: HKD 7.3 billion (effective June 13, 2022). When daily risk exposure exceeds 90% of the aggregate Guarantee Fund plus available credits, additional contributions are required from participants.
Guarantee Fund Risk Collateral (GFRC): When the Guarantee Fund threshold is breached, HKSCC collects GFRC in the amount of Expected Uncollateralised Loss (EUL) of the CP group in excess of 50% of the Guarantee Fund threshold. Each participant receives a HKD 1 million Dynamic Contribution Credit.
Minimum aggregate Basic Contributions: HKD 100 million.
Key protection: Customer segregated margin deposits held by the clearing house for one participant cannot be used to cover either a house or customer default of another participant.
[Source: HKEX – HKSCC Default Fund page; HKEX – HKSCC Default Management page; HKSCC General Rules Chapter 25]


HKCC Default Waterfall (Derivatives)








Layer
Resource
Description




1
Defaulting CP’s margin deposits
All margin collateral of the defaulting participant


2
Defaulting CP’s Participant Deposit
Basic deposit to the Reserve Fund


3
Defaulting CP’s Additional Deposit (HPAD)
Risk-based additional deposit to the Reserve Fund


4
HKCC’s own contribution (Skin-in-the-Game)
Clearing house resources equal to 10% of the Reserve Fund size


5
Non-defaulting CPs’ Reserve Fund contributions
Applied “in layers” from non-defaulting participants’ deposits and additional deposits



Reserve Fund Threshold: HKD 7.3 billion (effective June 1, 2018).
Reserve Fund composition: Participant Deposits (HK$1.5M per CP, HK$7.5M per GCP) + HKCC Participant Additional Deposits (HPAD) + interest income + HKCC’s own resources (10% of fund size).
HPAD formula: Level of HPAD = (Projected Loss from stress testing – Defaulting CP Groups’ Margin and collateral) x 1.15 – Basic Elements of Reserve Fund – Clearing House contributions. As of August 2024, total HPAD requirement was HK$2,863 million.
Stress test assumptions for fund sizing: - Price movements: +/-20% for key markets; equity products range -56% to +96% - Volatility assumptions: -24% to +47% for options; equity products range -35% to +91% - Counterparty default: largest plus second-largest CP group simultaneous default (Cover 2 standard)
[Source: HKEX – HKCC Default Fund page; HKCC Reserve Fund Chapter 4; HKCC Rules and Procedures]


SEOCH Default Waterfall (Stock Options)
The SEOCH default waterfall follows a structure parallel to HKCC:



Layer
Resource




1
Defaulting CP’s margin deposits


2
Defaulting CP’s Initial Contribution to Reserve Fund


3
Defaulting CP’s Variable Contributions


4
SEOCH’s own contribution (10% of Reserve Fund size)


5
Non-defaulting CPs’ Reserve Fund contributions (in layers)



Reserve Fund Threshold: HKD 3.6 billion (effective April 1, 2026).
Variable Contribution formula: Same as HKCC – (Projected Loss – Defaulting CP Groups’ Margin) x 1.15 – Basic Elements – Clearing House contributions.
Stress test assumptions for fund sizing: - Market movement: -48% to +96% - Implied volatility: -90% to +175% - Counterparty default: largest plus second-largest CP group simultaneous default (Cover 2 standard)
Key distinction: Participant contribution shares are based on that participant’s share of the average total margin requirement and net premium paid over the most recent 60 business days.
[Source: HKEX – SEOCH Default Fund page; SEOCH Rules]



3.4 Default Fund / Guarantee Fund Summary










Fund
Entity
Threshold
HKEX Contribution
Coverage Standard




Guarantee Fund
HKSCC
HKD 7.3 billion
10% of fund size
Cover 2 (simultaneous default of two largest CP groups)


Reserve Fund
HKCC
HKD 7.3 billion
10% of fund size
Cover 2


Reserve Fund
SEOCH
HKD 3.6 billion
10% of fund size
Cover 2



All three funds are reviewed and recalculated monthly (on the first trading/business day of each month). Contributions are adjusted when existing amounts fall below required levels or when daily risk exposure exceeds 90% of total fund resources plus available credits.
Comparison with KRX: KRX as CCP maintains a Joint Compensation Fund for derivatives clearing, with contributions from members and KRX’s own capital. Both HKEX and KRX follow the Cover 2 standard. KRX’s fund structure is somewhat simpler as it operates as a single integrated CCP across equity and derivatives markets, whereas HKEX maintains three separate clearing houses with distinct funds.
[Source: HKEX Default Fund pages for HKSCC, HKCC, SEOCH]


3.5 Stress Testing & Back-testing








Practice
HKSCC
HKCC / SEOCH




Stress Testing

Aspect

4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle








Market
Settlement Cycle
Details




Securities (SEHK)
T+2
Standard settlement for all SEHK Exchange Trades via CNS. Both securities and money settlement finalised on T+2.


Stock Connect – Northbound
T+0 (securities) / T+1 (money)
A-share trades settle with securities on trade day and cash on T+1, reflecting mainland China settlement conventions


Stock Connect – Southbound
T+2
Follows Hong Kong T+2 settlement cycle


Derivatives (HKCC)
Daily
Variation margin (mark-to-market) settled daily; physical delivery contracts per contract specifications


Stock Options (SEOCH)
T+1 (premium); T+2 (exercise)
Premium settlement on T+1; exercise and assignment settled via CCASS on T+2



T+1 Settlement Transition: In July 2025, HKEX published a discussion paper on accelerating settlement from T+2 to T+1 for the cash market, with a feedback deadline of September 1, 2025. HKEX has confirmed its post-trade systems will be technically ready to support T+1 by end of 2025. The proposal covers all listed products (equities, ETFs, structured products, REITs, bonds) but excludes Northbound Stock Connect trades. No firm implementation date has been announced; this will be a multi-year journey with phased consultation and industry-wide testing.
Comparison with KRX: KRX operates on T+2 for equities (aligned with Hong Kong), T+1 for government bonds, and T+0 for general bonds. Both exchanges are studying T+1 settlement in the context of global trends (US, India already on T+1; Europe/UK targeting 2027).
[Source: HKEX Settlement page; HKEX Accelerated Settlement Discussion Paper (July 2025); Broadridge – Hong Kong T+1 Settlement Discussion]


4.2 DVP Model
HKSCC (Securities):
HKSCC operates a DVP settlement model within CCASS:

CNS settlement is always effected on a DVP basis
Securities are allocated and put “on hold” during the settlement day until good and irrevocable payment is made
Cash settlement is effected through electronic payment instructions sent by CCASS to participants’ designated banks via the Hong Kong Interbank Clearing Limited (HKICL) using the CHATS (Clearing House Automated Transfer System) real-time gross settlement system
Upon receipt of good and irrevocable intra-day payments from long CPs (or ChinaClear), HKSCC releases the corresponding allocated shares, achieving intra-day finality
Short CPs receive good and irrevocable payments in the end-of-day money settlement process

The model functions as a DVP Model 2 variant – securities settlement on a net basis with money settlement through RTGS (CHATS).
HKCC / SEOCH (Derivatives): As cash-settled derivatives, settlement is effected through daily variation margin payments. Physical delivery contracts (where applicable) settle through the relevant depository systems.
[Source: HKSCC Operational Procedures Section 13; BIS Red Book – Hong Kong; Clearstream Market Profile – Hong Kong]


4.3 Settlement Finality








Aspect
HKSCC
HKCC / SEOCH




Legal Basis
SFO Part III, Division 3 confers statutory finality on “market contracts” with an RCH

Achieved intra-day upon release of allocated shares after good and irrevocable payment received

Money Finality (standard)
Same-day value but not final until 09:30 on SD+1 (no returned unpaid items) or 10:00 on SD+1 (returned items)
Daily settlement finality upon completion of settlement cycle


Intra-day Finality
Achievable for long CPs upon receipt of good and irrevocable payments via CHATS
N/A


Protection
SFO protections ensure settlement finality is not disturbed by insolvency proceedings against a participant
Same



[Source: Lexology – T+2 finality arrangement for CCASS; BIS Red Book – Hong Kong; SFO Part III]


4.4 CSD / Settlement Infrastructure – CCASS
CCASS (Central Clearing and Settlement System) is the core infrastructure operated by HKSCC, functioning as CSD, SSS, and clearing system:







Component
Description




Depository
Immobilised depository for all eligible securities; securities held in fungible book-entry form in HKSCC Nominees Limited (the nominee holding company)


Clearing
Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) engine; automated matching and netting of Exchange Trades


Settlement
Automated securities and money settlement; settlement instructions for non-exchange transactions


Connectivity
Accessible via CCASS terminals, CCASS/IP (internet-based), and host-to-host interfaces via SDNet/2


Eligible Securities
All securities listed on SEHK (equities, ETFs, warrants, debt securities, structured products); China Connect Securities


Operational Hours
Settlement processing on business days; provisional clearing statements ~18:00-20:00 on T; final clearing statements after 14:00 on T+1



CCASS/3 is the current generation of the system, upgraded from earlier versions to support higher capacity and additional functionality including Stock Connect processing.
[Source: HKEX CCASS FAQ; HKEX Settlement and Depository pages; HKSCC Operational Procedures Section 9]

T+2 (following Hong Kong convention)

6. Regulatory Framework

6.1 Primary Regulation







Aspect
Details




Primary Regulator
Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) of Hong Kong


Primary Legislation
Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO), enacted 2003


Key Provisions
Part III, Division 3 of SFO sets out framework for Recognised Clearing Houses (RCHs): recognition, duties, statutory protections, settlement finality


RCH Status
HKSCC, HKCC, SEOCH, and OTC Clear are all recognised clearing houses under SFO


Exchange Controller
HKEX is the sole Recognised Exchange Controller under SFO Section 59(1), and is the sole shareholder of all three clearing houses


PFMI Compliance
SFC requires all RCHs to observe and apply the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI)


Oversight Coordination
SFC coordinates with HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority), which oversees the payment and settlement infrastructure including CHATS; HKMA designated as the resolution authority for systemically important FMIs under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance (FIRO) [unverified]





6.2 Self-Regulatory Functions
HKEX and its clearing subsidiaries exercise certain self-regulatory functions including: - Participant admission and ongoing compliance monitoring - Rulebook enforcement and disciplinary proceedings - Market surveillance (in coordination with SFC) - Financial resource monitoring of participants
The SFC retains ultimate supervisory authority and can direct HKEX entities to take specific actions in the public interest.
[Source: SFC website; SFO Cap. 571; HKEX Introduction to Regulatory Framework page]

text:
7. Interoperability

7.1 Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong & Shenzhen-Hong Kong)
See Section 4.5 for detailed clearing and settlement arrangements. Stock Connect represents the most significant cross-border interoperability arrangement, linking HKSCC with ChinaClear (CSDC) for mutual market access between Hong Kong and mainland China equity markets.


7.2 Bond Connect
Northbound Bond Connect (since July 2017) and Southbound Bond Connect (since October 2024) link international investors with China’s interbank bond market. Settlement and custody involve CMU (HKMA’s Central Moneymarkets Unit), ChinaClear, and Shanghai Clearing House.


7.3 Swap Connect
Launched May 2023, linking OTC Clear and Shanghai Clearing House for interest rate swap clearing. See Section 4.5 for details.


7.4 ETF Connect
Launched July 2022, extending Stock Connect to include eligible ETFs traded on both SEHK and mainland exchanges.


7.5 Other CSD Linkages
HKSCC maintains Clearing Agency Participant arrangements with external clearing organisations to facilitate cross-border settlement. Clearstream and Euroclear maintain access to the Hong Kong market through their relationships with local custodians and CMU.
Comparison with KRX: KRX/KSD does not have an equivalent to Stock Connect. Cross-border access to the Korean market is primarily through the QFII-like Foreign Investor Registration system. KSD maintains CSD linkages with other Asian CSDs (e.g., through ASEAN CSD linkages) and Euroclear/Clearstream, but these are more conventional custodian/depository relationships rather than the direct CCP-CCP clearing links that characterise Stock Connect.
[Source: HKEX Stock Connect pages; HKEX Bond Connect pages; Clearstream Market Infrastructure – Hong Kong]

2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services



Service

Pan-European clearing across 52 venues and segments covering approximately 95% of all European equity trades
1.2 billion client trades cleared in 2024 (+5% YoY); EUR 49.3 billion average daily CCP protection value [Source: Cboe Clear Europe Annual Report 2024]

Options and Futures on European equities
Clearing for Cboe Europe Derivatives (CEDX), a pan-European equity derivatives exchange launched 2021
210,000 lots cleared in 2024 (up from 94,000 in 2023) [Source: Cboe Clear Europe Annual Report 2024]

Launched March 2025; nine initial participants including Bank of America and State Street; settlement across 19 European CSDs [Source: PR Newswire]



Covered Markets (Securities from 20+ European markets): Including but not limited to Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, and Poland. [Source: Cboe Clear - Markets]


2.2 Novation Process

Open Offer Model: Cboe Clear Europe interposes itself as the central counterparty through novation at the point of trade registration. The original bilateral obligation between buyer and seller is replaced by two new obligations – one between the CCP and each counterparty.
Real-time Processing: Transactions are fed to the risk management system as soon as they are received from the trading platform. Margin and P&L are recalculated in real-time.
Trade Registration: Trades are accepted and novated upon receipt from connected trading venues, subject to risk validation checks.

[Source: CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework - EuroCCP Sept 2020]


2.3 Netting
Multilateral Netting: - Cboe Clear Europe performs multilateral netting across all cleared positions per clearing participant, reducing gross settlement obligations to net amounts per ISIN per CSD. - Netting Efficiency: In 2024, netting eliminated 70.29% (EUR 34.6 billion) of the average daily value that would otherwise require settlement. This means that of the EUR 49.3 billion average daily CCP protection value, only approximately EUR 14.7 billion required actual settlement each day. - Cross-venue Netting: A key benefit of Cboe Clear Europe is that positions from multiple trading venues can be netted together into a single settlement obligation per ISIN, significantly reducing settlement volume and costs.
[Source: Cboe Clear Europe Annual Report 2024]

3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
Cboe Clear Europe uses a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) based margin model, as required under EMIR.
Securities Margin Model Parameters:







Parameter
Value




Model Type
Historical simulation CVaR


Confidence Level
99% (with CVaR capturing tail risk beyond 99th percentile)


Margin Period of Risk (MPOR)
2 business days (for cash equities); 3 business days (for certain products) [unverified – MPOR may differ by service]


Lookback Window
700 historical scenarios (approximately 2.8 years of data)


Minimum Data Requirement
At least 12 months, capturing a full range of market conditions including stress periods (per EMIR requirement)


Anti-Procyclicality Measure
Stressed Historical Simulation (StressHS) margin, per EMIR RTS Article 28(1)(b)


Recalculation Frequency
At least every 5 minutes in real-time



[Source: Cboe Clear Europe Margin Model Description - Securities; ECB Occasional Paper on CCP IM Models]
Margin Components:







Component
Description




Initial Margin (IM)
Potential future exposure based on CVaR model; covers worst-case losses over MPOR at 99% confidence


Variation Margin (VM)
Mark-to-market / current exposure reflecting unrealized P&L


Total Margin
Max [0; (Initial Margin - Variation Margin)]; i.e., if VM gains exceed IM, no additional margin is required


Add-ons
Additional margin to cover risks not captured by core IM model (e.g., concentration risk, liquidity risk, wrong-way risk)



Cross-Product Margining: - Cboe Clear Europe offers cross-product margining across cash equities, derivatives, and SFT positions, recognizing offsets where correlations justify reduced margin.
[Source: CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework - EuroCCP Sept 2020]
Real-Time Risk Management (RTRM): - The risk management system (COH/RTRM – Collateral Haircut / Real Time Risk Management) calculates margin requirements for Clearing Participants and Co-CCPs. - Prices are updated instantaneously upon receipt from data providers (Refinitiv). - P&L in portfolios is recalculated in real-time.


3.2 Margin Call Schedule








Margin Call
Timing
Description




End-of-Day Margin
After market close
Full recalculation based on closing prices


Intraday Margin
Throughout trading hours
Triggered when real-time monitoring detects that margin is insufficient; recalculated at least every 5 minutes


Interoperability Fund
Before 09:00 CET
Daily determination of required Interoperability Fund Deposits; if additional deposit required, notification by email before 09:00 CET, account debited via Direct Debit before 09:30 CET



[Source: Cboe Clear Europe - Risk Management]


3.3 Default Waterfall
The default waterfall defines the sequence in which financial resources are applied in the event of a clearing participant default:



Layer
Resource
Description




1
Defaulting Member’s Margin
Initial margin and variation margin of the defaulting participant are applied first


2
Defaulting Member’s Default Fund Contribution
The defaulting participant’s share of the Clearing Fund


3
CCP Skin-in-the-Game (First Tranche)
Cboe Clear Europe’s own dedicated financial resources, amounting to 25% of minimum required capital. As of mid-2021 this was approximately EUR 6.8 million [Source: Cboe Insights - Dedicated Own Resources July 2021]


4
Non-Defaulting Members’ Default Fund Contributions
Clearing Fund contributions of surviving (non-defaulting) clearing participants are mutualized


5
CCP Additional Dedicated Resources (Second Tranche)
Additional dedicated own financial resources of Cboe Clear Europe, introduced per EU R&R Regulation Article 9(14)


6
Recovery Tools
Calls beyond the default waterfall – including loss allocation to non-defaulting members, additional assessment powers, and other recovery measures




Note on Sizing: The exact current size of the Clearing Fund and CCP dedicated resources fluctuates. The 2021 disclosure indicated EUR 6.8 million in CCP skin-in-the-game (25% of minimum capital). The total Clearing Fund size varies based on stress-test outcomes and participant composition. For current figures, refer to the latest PQD disclosures. [Source: Cboe Clear Public Disclosures]

[Source: Cboe Clear Europe Clearing Rule Book, Article 9.1.2]


3.4 Default Fund / Guarantee Fund
Clearing Fund (Default Fund): - All clearing participants contribute to the Clearing Fund based on their risk profile and stress-test outcomes. - The fund is sized to cover the default of the largest member (Cover 1) or the two largest members (Cover 2) under extreme but plausible stress scenarios, as required by EMIR. - Contributions are recalculated periodically and can be called for replenishment after a default event. - Separate fund arrangements exist for the Interoperability Fund (for co-CCP exposures).
Interoperability Fund: - A dedicated fund to cover exposures arising from interoperable CCP arrangements (with LCH Ltd and SIX x-clear AG). - Daily recalculation of required deposits.
[Source: CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework - EuroCCP Sept 2020]


3.5 Stress Testing & Back-Testing
Stress Testing: - Cboe Clear Europe conducts regular stress tests to assess the adequacy of financial resources under extreme but plausible market conditions, as required by EMIR Article 49. - Participates in ESMA’s EU-wide CCP stress tests. In ESMA’s 5th CCP Stress Test (2024), the European clearing system was found to be resilient overall. [Source: ESMA 5th CCP Stress Test Report] - Stress scenarios include historical scenarios (e.g., 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19 March 2020) and hypothetical extreme scenarios.
Back-Testing: - Daily back-testing of margin model adequacy to verify that collected margins would have been sufficient to cover actual observed losses. - EMIR requires CCPs to evaluate whether initial margin covered potential losses assuming a clearing member defaults on a specific historical day. - Results are reported to DNB/AFM and disclosed in CPMI-IOSCO PQD reports.
Anti-Procyclicality: - The Stressed Historical Simulation (StressHS) margin add-on ensures that margin levels do not decline excessively during calm market periods, maintaining a buffer that reduces sudden spikes during stress.
[Source: Cboe Clear Europe Margin Model Description; ESMA Opinion on CCP Backtesting]


3.6 Recovery & Resolution
Recovery Plan: - Cboe Clear Europe maintains a recovery plan and a plan for orderly wind-down, as required under the EU CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (CCP R&R). - Recovery tools include: - Calls for losses beyond the default waterfall (assessment powers on non-defaulting members) - Calls for additional liquidity resources - Calls for replenishment of the Clearing Fund - Variation Margin Gains Haircutting (VMGH) as an ultimate tool - Partial or full tear-up of contracts
Resolution: - The resolution authority for Cboe Clear Europe is the Single Resolution Board (SRB) or DNB [unverified – the specific resolution authority designation may depend on evolving EU CCP R&R framework implementation]. - Resolution tools mirror those available under the EU CCP R&R Regulation, including write-down of equity, position transfer, bridge CCP, and orderly wind-down.
[Source: CPMI-IOSCO Disclosure Framework - EuroCCP Sept 2020]

4. Settlement

[Source: BNP Paribas - T+1 in Europe]


4.2 DVP Model

Cboe Clear Europe uses Delivery-versus-Payment (DVP) settlement, ensuring that the transfer of securities occurs simultaneously with the transfer of cash, eliminating principal risk.
Settlement instructions are submitted by Cboe Clear Europe to the relevant CSD on behalf of clearing participants (via CSD Power of Attorney model).



4.3 Settlement Finality

Settlement finality is governed by the EU Settlement Finality Directive (SFD), as implemented in Dutch law and the laws of each CSD’s jurisdiction.
Once settlement instructions are entered into the relevant CSD settlement system and become irrevocable, they cannot be unwound, even in the event of insolvency of a participant.
Cboe Clear Europe is designated as a system under the SFD in the Netherlands.

[Source: Cboe Clear - Regulation Settlement]


4.4 CSD / Settlement Infrastructure

Cboe Clear Europe does not operate its own CSD. It relies on national CSDs for settlement of securities.
Settlement is performed through the domestic CSD of the relevant market, ensuring that securities remain in the home market’s settlement infrastructure.
The CSD participant (clearing participant or its settlement agent) grants Cboe Clear Europe a CSD Power of Attorney (PoA) to submit settlement instructions on their behalf.

SFT Clearing Service (launched March 2025): - Cboe Clear Europe introduced centrally cleared Securities Financing Transactions, a first for pan-European equity SFTs. - The service covers matching, CCP clearing, settlement, and post-trade lifecycle management for securities lending/borrowing in European cash equities and ETFs. - Participant categories: Principal lenders, Special Participant lenders (UCITS and non-UCITS), and borrowers. - Special Participant model: Beneficial owners (e.g., UCITS funds) can participate without paying margin or contributing to the default fund, with Required Value (RQV) models developed on a case-by-case basis [unverified – specific terms may vary]. - Cross-product margining: SFT positions can be margined together with cash equities and derivatives positions. - Initial launch participants: Nine firms including Bank of America and State Street.

text:
7. Interoperability

Overview
CCP interoperability is a defining feature of Cboe Clear Europe and a core element of its competitive strategy. Under interoperability, trading firms – rather than the trading venue – choose which CCP clears their transactions. This “user choice” model promotes competition, lowers post-trade costs, and allows participants to consolidate clearing at a single CCP across multiple venues.


Interoperable CCP Partners








Co-CCP
Scope
Markets




LCH Ltd (EquityClear)
Full interoperability
Cboe Europe (CXE/BXE), Aquis Exchange, Turquoise, SIX Swiss Exchange, and others


SIX x-clear AG
Full interoperability
Cboe Europe, SIX Swiss Exchange, Aquis Exchange, and others





How Interoperability Works

A trade is executed on an interoperable venue (e.g., Cboe Europe).
The buyer and seller may each choose a different CCP (e.g., buyer chooses Cboe Clear Europe, seller chooses LCH Ltd).
Each CCP novates the leg facing its own clearing participant.
The two CCPs face each other for the inter-CCP leg, managing the resulting exposure through the Interoperability Fund and margin arrangements between the Co-CCPs.
Settlement occurs through the normal CSD channels.



Preferred Clearing
In addition to full interoperability, Cboe Clear Europe offers a Preferred Clearing model for certain venues where full interoperability is not available (e.g., Euronext Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin, Lisbon, Milan, Paris). Under Preferred Clearing, Cboe Clear Europe acts as an alternative CCP to the venue’s primary CCP.

Euronext Oslo: Cleared via the full interoperable model.
Euronext (other markets): Via Preferred Clearing arrangement.

[Source: Cboe - Preferred Clearing; Cboe - Interoperability]


Regulatory Framework for Interoperability

EMIR Title V establishes the regulatory framework for CCP interoperability arrangements.
Interoperable links require regulatory approval and must meet specific risk management standards.
The European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) published a report in January 2019 examining the risks and benefits of CCP interoperability arrangements in Europe. [Source: ESRB Report on CCP Interoperability]



Cboe’s Advocacy for Interoperability
Cboe has been a vocal advocate for clearing competition and interoperability in Europe, arguing that Europe benefits from multiple competing CCPs rather than a single monopoly CCP. Cboe contends that interoperability has substantially lowered post-trade costs in European cash equity markets. [Source: Cboe Insights - Europe Needs Clearing Competition]

2.2 Novation Process
NSCC (CNS System): - NSCC interposes itself as CCP through novation – upon trade comparison and recording, NSCC becomes the legal counterparty to both buyer and seller. - The Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) system is NSCC’s core netting and settlement engine. All compared trades in CNS-eligible securities are netted by CUSIP into a single net long (buy) or net short (sell) position per participant per settlement date. - NSCC guarantees completion of settlement for trades accepted into the CNS system.
FICC (GSD and MBSD): - FICC similarly novates trades, becoming the CCP to each Netting Member. - GSD uses a real-time trade comparison system and nets trades for settlement. - MBSD provides Electronic Pool Notification (EPN) and processes TBA (To-Be-Announced) trades.
Sources: NSCC Disclosure Framework (dtcc.com); CNS overview (dtcclearning.com)


2.3 Netting
NSCC: - Multilateral netting through CNS reduces the value of payments that need to be exchanged by an average of 98% each day. - Each security is netted to one position per participant, dramatically reducing the number of settlement obligations.
FICC-GSD: - Multilateral netting of U.S. government securities trades among Netting Members. - Netting efficiency is critical given daily volumes exceeding $10 trillion.
FICC-MBSD: - Nets TBA and specified pool MBS trades, producing net delivery obligations.

title: Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework

NSCC Margin (Required Fund Deposit)
Each NSCC Member’s Required Fund Deposit serves as margin. The deposit consists of multiple components:








Component
Methodology
Details




Volatility Charge (VaR Charge)
Parametric Value-at-Risk
Calculated as the greatest of: (1) the larger of two VaR model calculations, (2) a gap risk measure based on the largest non-index position exceeding a concentration threshold, or (3) a portfolio margin floor based on long/short market values. VaR is designed to cover potential losses at a 99% confidence level over a 3-day liquidation period (MPOR). Uses a lookback period of historical price data.


Mark-to-Market Charge
Current market value
Reflects unrealized gains/losses on net unsettled positions (Regular MTM and ID Net MTM)


Margin Requirement Differential (MRD)
Supplemental
Addresses differences between NSCC margin and exchange/OCC margin for certain positions


Margin Liquidity Adjustment (MLA)
Liquidity-based
Addresses liquidity risk for less liquid securities


Excess Capital Premium
Capital-based
Additional charge for members whose exposure is large relative to their capital


Special Charges
Various
Including municipal bond haircut charge, anti-cicyclical charges

3.4 Default Fund / Guarantee Fund
NSCC Clearing Fund: - Total size (daily average 2024): ~$11.24 billion - Post-T+1 average: ~$9.8 billion - Methodology for sizing: Risk-based; each member’s Required Fund Deposit calculated based on VaR Charge, MTM, and supplemental components. Aggregate fund designed to cover the default of the member (including affiliates) presenting the largest exposure (Cover 1 standard). - Contribution methodology: Each member contributes proportionally based on their calculated Required Fund Deposit. - Eligible collateral: Cash, U.S. Treasury securities, and certain other eligible securities (subject to haircuts). - Review frequency: Daily recalculation of Required Fund Deposits; periodic model validation and stress testing.
FICC Clearing Funds (GSD and MBSD separate): - Methodology: Risk-based margining using VaR methodology; designed to cover liquidation of a defaulting member’s portfolio over a 3-day liquidation period. - GSD minimum Required Fund Deposit: $1,000,000 per Netting Member. - MBSD: Separate clearing fund with similar methodology. - Maintenance fee: 0.25% per annum of average cash deposit balance (charged monthly). - Review frequency: Daily recalculation; model validation as required by Rule 17Ad-22(e).
CCLF (Committed Liquidity Clearing Facility): - Both GSD and MBSD maintain CCLF to address liquidity needs in a default scenario. - Members must attest that they understand their CCLF obligations and incorporate them into liquidity planning. - CCLF sized based on the largest liquidity need from the default of the member (including affiliates) presenting the greatest liquidity exposure over a specified lookback period, plus a buffer.
Sources: NSCC Financial Statements; GSD Clearing Fund Methodology Overview (dtcc.com); SR-FICC-2024-003 (federalregister.gov)


3.5 Stress Testing & Back-testing
Stress Testing: - NSCC, FICC, and DTC conduct daily stress testing of their margin and clearing fund adequacy. - Scenarios include historical stress events, hypothetical scenarios, and combined scenarios. - Cover 1 standard: Each CCP’s pre-funded resources (including margin and clearing fund) must be sufficient to cover the default of the single member (and its affiliates) presenting the largest aggregate exposure under extreme but plausible market conditions. - NSCC stress tests cover equity market crashes, interest rate shocks, credit events, and combined scenarios. - FICC stress tests cover interest rate and yield curve movements, spread widening, and prepayment risk for MBS.
Back-testing: - Daily back-testing of margin model coverage. - NSCC Q4 2024 PQD: 12-month backtesting coverage level of 99.9%; largest deficiency in Q4 2024 was $129.6 million on December 11, 2024. - Results reviewed by risk management and reported to the Board Risk Committee. - Model performance metrics trigger reviews and potential recalibration when coverage drops below target thresholds.
Model Validation: - Independent model validation conducted at least annually, as required by SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(6). - External validation by independent parties.
Sources: CPMI-IOSCO PQD Q4 2024; NSCC Disclosure Framework; SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)


3.6 Recovery & Resolution
Recovery & Wind-Down (R&W) Plan: - DTC, NSCC, and FICC each maintain a comprehensive Recovery & Wind-Down Plan, managed by DTCC’s Office of Recovery & Resolution Planning (R&R Team). - Plans are reviewed and overseen by the DTCC Executive Committee and Board. - Most recent review completed in 2024; amended in April-June 2025 to comply with SEC Rule 17ad-26 (compliance date: December 15, 2025).
Recovery Scenarios: 1. Uncovered credit losses – losses exceeding defaulter’s margin and clearing fund contribution 2. Uncovered liquidity shortfalls – inability to meet payment obligations despite available resources 3. General business losses – including multi-member default, significant internal operational incident, and third-party failure scenarios

4.2 DVP Model
DTC Settlement: - BIS DVP Model 2: Gross securities transfers (individual security-by-security delivery) with net funds settlement. - Securities deliveries are processed on a gross (trade-by-trade) basis throughout the day. - Money settlement is netted – each participant has a single net debit or credit position settled at end of day. - DTC operates two main settlement cycles: - Night Cycle: Pre-positioning of deliveries for next-day settlement - Day Cycle: Real-time delivery processing during business hours with continuous net settlement recalculation - End-of-Day Net Settlement: Net money obligations settled through the Federal Reserve’s National Settlement Service (NSS) or through DTC’s settlement banks.
NSCC/CNS Settlement: - CNS produces net delivery obligations per security per participant. - Net long positions receive securities from NSCC’s account at DTC. - Net short positions deliver securities to NSCC’s account at DTC. - Money settlement is netted and settled through DTC’s end-of-day process.
FICC-GSD Settlement: - Net settlement obligations delivered through the Fedwire Securities Service (for Fed-eligible securities) or through DTC (for DTC-eligible securities).


4.3 Settlement Finality
Legal Basis: - New York contract law, New York Uniform Commercial Code (Articles 8 and 9), and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. - Protected in insolvency by: Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDIA), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act (FDICIA), U.S. Bankruptcy Code, Securities Investor Protection Act (SIPA), and Title II of Dodd-Frank.
Point of Finality: - DTC securities transfers: Final and irrevocable as to the delivering party once the transfer has passed DTC’s risk controls and securities have been debited from the delivering party’s account (intraday finality for deliveries). - DTC money settlement: Net money settlement is final at end of day upon completion through the Federal Reserve’s NSS. - NSS funds transfers: Immediately final when effected. - NSCC: Settlement finality achieved when obligations are discharged through DTC’s settlement system. - FICC-GSD: Settlement finality for government securities achieved upon completion of Fedwire delivery or DTC book-entry transfer.
Irrevocability: - Once a securities transfer passes DTC risk management controls and is completed, it cannot be unilaterally revoked.
Sources: DTC Disclosure Framework (dtcc.com); DTC Settlement Service Guide; IMF FSAP Assessment (imf.org); NSCC Disclosure Framework


4.4 CSD / Settlement Infrastructure
DTC as CSD: - DTC is the sole CSD for the U.S. securities markets, holding a natural monopoly position. - Immobilization model: Physical securities certificates are deposited at DTC (or its nominee, Cede & Co.) and ownership is transferred via book-entry. - Dematerialization: Increasingly, securities are issued in book-entry-only form. - Securities accounts: DTC maintains securities accounts for each Participant. - Cash settlement: Primarily through the Federal Reserve’s National Settlement Service (NSS) (central bank money) for end-of-day net settlement. DTC also uses commercial bank settlement for certain transactions.
Registered Holder: - DTC’s nominee, Cede & Co., is the registered holder of securities deposited at DTC. - Beneficial ownership is tracked through the DTC participant accounts and their customer records.

Note: DTC does not have formal CCP interoperability links in the European sense, but maintains operational connections for cross-border settlement.


4.6 Securities Lending & Borrowing

Facility available: Yes
SL&B (Stock Loan/Borrow) Program: NSCC operates an automated stock borrow program within the CNS system.

When a member has a fail-to-deliver obligation, the CNS system may automatically borrow securities from members with available lending positions to facilitate settlement.
The stock borrow program reduces CNS fails by sourcing securities from willing lenders.

DTC Lending Services: DTC provides book-entry transfer infrastructure for bilateral securities lending transactions between participants.

text:
9. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2022: Project Ion DLT-based bilateral settlement platform went live in parallel production, processing 100,000+ equity transactions per day on distributed ledger technology.
2023: NSCC adopted Intraday Volatility Charge (replacing Intraday Backtesting Charge) and enhanced Gap Risk Measure and VaR Charge calculations (SR-NSCC-2023-003, SR-NSCC-2023-013).
2023: DTCC acquired Securrency, rebranded as DTCC Digital Assets, for institutional-grade digital asset infrastructure.
2024 (May 28): Successful transition to T+1 settlement cycle for equities, corporate bonds, municipal bonds, and UITs. Results:

Affirmation rate improved from 73% (Jan 2024) to ~95% by 9:00 PM ET cutoff
CNS fail rate: 2.12% (July 2024), consistent with prior T+2 levels
NSCC Clearing Fund reduced by ~$3 billion (23%), freeing ~$750 billion annually for broker-dealers

2025 (April): DTCC unveiled tokenized collateral management platform on AppChain (Hyperledger Besu-based).
2025 (November): ISO 20022 Corporate Actions messaging converted to SR2025 version.
2025 (November): SEC approved DTC/FICC/NSCC rule changes for managing Participant System Disruptions.



New Services

FICC ACS Triparty Service: Approved by SEC; launched December 2025 for cleared triparty repo through agent clearing framework.
FICC Sponsored GC CIL (Collateral-in-Lieu) Service: New service within Sponsored General Collateral offering.
FICC Securities Financing Transaction (SFT) Clearing Service: Proposed to expand FICC’s repo clearing capabilities in preparation for Treasury clearing mandate.
DTC Tokenization Services: SEC No-Action Letter (December 2025) authorizing DTC to offer tokenization of DTC-custodied assets on approved blockchains (Canton Network); first U.S. CSD to tokenize security entitlements on public/private-permissioned blockchains.
DTCC Digital Launchpad: Collaborative ecosystem for testing and co-creating digital asset solutions with market participants and technology providers.
DTCC Digital Assets Solutions: New business line launched in 2026 following SEC authorization, building on DTCC ComposerX, LaunchPad, and Collateral AppChain.
Fnality Integration: Fnality International’s digital payment rail integrated with DTCC Digital Launchpad for atomic settlement and real-time payment.



Regulatory Changes

SEC Rule 17ad-26 (Recovery & Wind-Down): DTC/NSCC/FICC amended R&W Plans; compliance date December 15, 2025; SEC approved June 2025.
Treasury Clearing Mandate: SEC adopted rules requiring expanded central clearing of U.S. Treasury cash transactions (compliance: December 31, 2026) and repo transactions (compliance: June 30, 2027). FICC-GSD is the primary CCP; CME Securities Clearing Inc. approved as second CCP.
FICC GSD Minimum Margin Amount: SEC approved FICC’s adoption of a minimum margin floor for GSD positions (November 2024).
FICC Volatility Event Charge: SEC approved new charge for GSD to address elevated volatility periods (April 2025).
NSCC Intraday Margin Enhancement: Proposed rule change (April 2025) with Amendment No. 1 approved June 2025 for enhanced intraday margin collection.
NSCC CNS Fails Charge Amendment: Proposed rule change (September 2025) to amend the CNS Fails Charge in NSCC Rules.



Strategic Initiatives

Treasury Clearing Expansion: Major strategic priority – preparing FICC-GSD infrastructure and membership access models for the SEC’s Treasury clearing mandate. FICC expanding Sponsored Member access, Agent Clearing Service (ACS), and triparty repo clearing to accommodate expected volume growth.
Digital Asset Strategy: Multi-pronged approach including tokenization of DTC-custodied assets on Canton Network, Digital Launchpad for industry collaboration, and ComposerX platform. DTCC joined Canton Foundation as co-chair alongside Euroclear.
Cloud Migration: Ongoing initiative to modernize infrastructure with cloud-based services while maintaining core mainframe reliability for critical settlement systems.
Global T+1 Leadership: DTCC actively engaging with international markets (EU, UK, APAC) to share lessons from U.S. T+1 transition and support global settlement acceleration.

2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services
CME Clearing acts as the central counterparty (CCP) for all trades executed on or submitted through CME Group’s four exchanges and OTC platforms. It clears the following product categories:








Product Category
Exchange / Platform
Examples




Interest Rate Derivatives
CME, CBOT
SOFR futures, U.S. Treasury futures & options, Eurodollar futures (legacy)


Equity Index Derivatives
CME
E-mini S&P 500, E-mini Nasdaq-100, Micro E-mini, Nikkei 225 futures


Foreign Exchange
CME
EUR/USD, JPY/USD, and 40+ FX pairs in futures & options


Agricultural Commodities
CBOT, CME
Corn, Soybeans, Wheat, Live Cattle, Lean Hogs, Dairy


Energy Products
NYMEX
WTI Crude Oil, Henry Hub Natural Gas, Refined Products


Metals
COMEX, NYMEX
Gold, Silver, Copper, Platinum, Palladium, Aluminum


OTC Interest Rate Swaps
CME ClearPort
SOFR swaps, USD IRS, cross-currency swaps, swaptions


OTC FX
CME ClearPort
OTC FX forwards and swaps (select currency pairs)


Cryptocurrency
CME
Bitcoin futures & options, Ether futures & options





2.2 Novation Process
Upon acceptance of a trade for clearing, CME Clearing interposes itself as the legal counterparty to both sides of every transaction through the process of novation. The original bilateral contract between buyer and seller is extinguished and replaced by two new contracts: one between CME Clearing and the buyer, and one between CME Clearing and the seller. This ensures that each clearing member only faces CME Clearing as its counterparty, eliminating bilateral counterparty credit risk.


2.3 Netting
CME Clearing provides multilateral netting across all products within each clearing member’s account. Variation margin (settlement variation) is netted across all positions within a given account, resulting in a single net pay or collect amount per settlement cycle. For performance bonds (initial margin), CME applies portfolio-based margining via SPAN / SPAN 2 that recognises offsets between correlated positions.


2.4 Clearing Membership Tiers & Requirements
CME, CBOT, NYMEX, and COMEX clearing memberships are entirely separate from one another. A firm must hold the appropriate division-specific clearing membership to clear products traded on that exchange.
Membership Categories:
Each exchange division recognises multiple categories of clearing members (CME Rulebook Chapter 9; NYMEX Rulebook Chapter 9):

title: CME Clearing
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework: SPAN
CME Clearing developed the SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk) methodology, which has become the global standard for portfolio-based margin calculation, adopted by over 50 exchanges and clearing organisations worldwide (SPAN Methodology Overview).
How SPAN Works:
SPAN evaluates overall portfolio risk by calculating the worst reasonable loss that a portfolio of derivative and physical instruments might incur over a specified time period (typically one trading day for exchange-traded products, five days for OTC).
16 Risk Scenarios:
SPAN constructs 16 hypothetical risk scenarios based on two key parameters: - Price Scanning Range – calibrated to the distribution of price movements under normal market conditions (typically a 1-day, 99% confidence interval) - Volatility Scanning Range – calibrated to the distribution of implied volatility movements
The 16 scenarios represent combinations of: - Price changes at fractions of the price scanning range (0, 1/3, 2/3, 1x, 2x, and 3x – with 3x given reduced weight) - Volatility changes (up and down by the volatility scanning range)
Five Components of SPAN Risk:







Component
Description




Scanning Risk
The largest loss from the 16 risk scenarios for a given combined commodity group


Intra-Commodity Spread Charge
Captures basis risk between different expiration months within the same commodity (calendar spread risk)


Inter-Commodity Spread Credit
Recognises risk-reducing offsets between correlated commodity groups (e.g., WTI vs. Brent crude)


Delivery Month Charge
Additional charge for positions approaching physical delivery


Short Option Minimum
Floor margin requirement for deep out-of-the-money short options to capture tail risk



SPAN Margin Calculation:
Performance Bond = MAX(Scanning Risk + Intra-Commodity Spread Charge + Delivery Month Charge
                       - Inter-Commodity Spread Credit,
                       Short Option Minimum)
Source: CME SPAN Methodology


3.2 SPAN 2 Transition
CME is transitioning to SPAN 2, a next-generation VaR-based (Historical Value-at-Risk) margin framework. Key differences from legacy SPAN:








Feature
SPAN (Legacy)
SPAN 2




Methodology
16 parametric scenarios
Thousands of HVaR scenarios from historical data


Risk Symmetry
Same margin for long and short positions
Asymmetric – long and short margins differ based on historical risk profiles


Offset Calculation
Explicit inter-commodity spread credits
Offsets inherent in VaR calculation via portfolio covariance


Tail Risk
Short option minimum
Expected Shortfall (ES) component capturing tail losses beyond VaR threshold


Additional Factors
N/A
Seasonality, options term structure, liquidity/concentration costs



SPAN 2 Rollout Schedule (phased):







Asset Class
Go-Live Date




Energy Products
September 8, 2023 (completed)


Equity Products
October 18, 2024 (primary) / November 15, 2024 (backup)


Interest Rate & FX Products
Second half of 2024


Agricultural & Remaining Products
Second half of 2025



During the multi-year transition, both SPAN and SPAN 2 run in parallel. Cross-model offsets between SPAN- and SPAN 2-margined products are supported via covariance. Legacy SPAN will continue to be supported for the foreseeable future.
Source: SPAN 2 Framework Rollout; SPAN 2 Methodology


3.3 Comparison: SPAN vs. PRISMA vs. STANS









Feature
CME SPAN / SPAN 2
Eurex PRISMA
OCC STANS




Operator
CME Clearing
Eurex Clearing
Options Clearing Corporation


Methodology
Parametric scenarios (SPAN) / HVaR + ES (SPAN 2)
Filtered Historical Simulation VaR + stress add-ons
Monte Carlo simulation


Confidence Level
99%+ (SPAN); 99.7%+ (SPAN 2) [unverified]
99.7% (2-day MPOR)
99% (2-day MPOR)


Portfolio Scope
Futures, options, OTC swaps
Listed + OTC derivatives
Equity options, futures


Cross-Product Offsets
SPAN credits / VaR covariance (SPAN 2)
Full portfolio-based
Full portfolio-based

1 day (ETD), 5 days (OTC IRS)

2 days





3.4 Margin Call Schedule
CME Clearing recalculates performance bond (margin) requirements at least once daily, but typically twice daily for exchange-traded derivatives:








Cycle
Timing
Description




End-of-Day (EOD)
After market close (~4:00 PM CT)
Full recalculation of all positions against settlement prices; settlement variation pays/collects calculated


Intraday
Mid-morning (~10:00-11:00 AM CT)
Intraday mark-to-market; additional performance bond calls issued if needed


Ad-hoc / Extraordinary
As needed
CME Clearing has authority to issue additional margin calls at any time based on market conditions



For OTC IRS and FX swaps, settlement variation is calculated at least once daily at end-of-day.
USD settlement cycles run twice daily (EOD and intraday) through CME’s settlement banks. CME has authority to run additional cycles if market conditions warrant.
Source: CME PFMI Disclosure, November 2023


3.5 Default Waterfall
CME Clearing maintains two distinct financial safeguards waterfalls, each with its own guaranty fund:

Base Products Waterfall – covering futures, options, and OTC FX across CME, CBOT, NYMEX, and COMEX
IRS Products Waterfall – covering OTC interest rate swaps and swaptions

Base Products Default Waterfall (sequential application):








Layer
Resource
Approximate Size




1
Defaulting Clearing Member’s Performance Bonds (initial margin)
Varies by portfolio


2
Defaulting Clearing Member’s Guaranty Fund Contribution
Pro-rata share


3
CME Clearing’s Own Contribution (Skin-in-the-Game / SITG)
$100 million (pre-funded)


4
Non-Defaulting Clearing Members’ Guaranty Fund Contributions
Mutualized pool (sized to Cover 2 standard)


5
Assessment Powers
Up to 2.75x each non-defaulting member’s guaranty fund contribution per single default event


6
Recovery Tools
Voluntary contributions, variation margin haircutting, mandatory tear-ups



IRS Products Default Waterfall (sequential application):








Layer
Resource
Approximate Size




1
Defaulting IRS Clearing Member’s Performance Bonds
Varies by portfolio


2
Defaulting IRS Clearing Member’s Guaranty Fund Contribution
Pro-rata share


3
CME Clearing’s Own Contribution (SITG)
$150 million (pre-funded)


4
Non-Defaulting IRS Clearing Members’ Guaranty Fund Contributions
Mutualized pool (sized to Cover 2 standard)


5
Assessment Powers
Capped assessment on non-defaulting IRS clearing members


6
Recovery Tools
Gains haircutting, mandatory tear-ups, voluntary contributions, voluntary tear-ups



Guaranty Fund Sizing:

Each guaranty fund is sized to cover the default of the two clearing members (and their affiliates) with the largest anticipated stress shortfalls – the “Cover 2” standard.
As of December 31, 2024, guaranty fund contributions available to collateralise facilities totalled approximately $10.1 billion (CME Inc. Financial Statements 2024).
CME Clearing maintained approximately $87.4 billion in cash within accounts at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago as of December 31, 2024 (representing performance bond and guaranty fund deposits).
A guaranty fund buffer is maintained above the Cover 2 minimum to mitigate potential breaches.

Source: CME Clearing Financial Safeguards Waterfalls; Financial Safeguards System; CME Rulebook Chapter 8


3.6 Stress Testing & Back-Testing



Practice
Details




Stress Testing Frequency
Daily


Scenario Types
Historical scenarios and hypothetical (extreme but plausible) market conditions


Confidence Level
At least 99.9%


Cover Standard
Cover 2 – sized to withstand simultaneous default of the two clearing members with the largest stress shortfalls


Reverse Stress Testing
Conducted routinely; results reviewed at least monthly to identify conditions that could exhaust guaranty fund resources


Backtesting
Performance bond adequacy backtested against actual market movements; reported quarterly via PQD


Independent Validation
Annual validation by independent experts


Regulatory Examination
CFTC and Federal Reserve Board conduct annual examinations of risk management practices


CFTC Supervisory Stress Tests
CFTC conducts periodic supervisory stress tests of major DCOs including CME (CFTC Stress Test Report 2019)



Source: CME Clearing Stress Testing Practices


3.7 Recovery & Resolution Tools
CME Clearing has adopted specific recovery tools, particularly for the IRS waterfall, to address “end of waterfall” scenarios (CME Advisory 19-365):







Tool
Description




Variation Margin Gains Haircutting (VMGH)
Pro-rata reduction in amounts owed to non-defaulting members with net gains for the relevant settlement cycle


Mandatory Tear-Up
Forced termination of contracts to re-establish a matched book; designed to localise impact to affected markets


Voluntary Contributions
IRS clearing members (and customers) may voluntarily contribute resources; only effective if aggregate contributions are sufficient to fully cover losses


Voluntary Tear-Up
Clearing members (and customers) may voluntarily terminate positions


Assessment Powers
Capped additional contributions from non-defaulting members (up to 2.75x guaranty fund contribution for Base products)



Resolution Authority: The FDIC is the designated resolution authority for SIFMUs under Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act, though Title VIII provides a framework for the Federal Reserve to provide emergency lending to SIFMUs in extremis.


3.8 Cross-Margining Programs
See Section 7 (Interoperability) for details on CME-OCC and CME-FICC cross-margining arrangements.

title: CME Clearing
text:
4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle








Product Type
Settlement Cycle
Details




Futures (Variation Margin)
Daily (T+0 or T+1 intraday)
Settlement variation (mark-to-market pays/collects) calculated and settled at least twice daily (EOD and intraday)


Options on Futures
Daily premium settlement; exercise/assignment T+1
Premium paid/received next business day; exercise results in futures position


OTC IRS
Daily (variation margin)
At least once daily at end-of-day


Physical Delivery (Futures)
Delivery period varies by contract
Delivery occurs during designated delivery months per contract specifications





4.2 DVP Model
For physically-delivered securities (e.g., U.S. Treasury futures expiry):

Settlement occurs on a DVP Model 1 (gross, real-time) basis
Delivery of U.S. Treasury securities occurs via book-entry transfer in Fedwire Securities between banks that are members of the Federal Reserve System
Transfer of funds is conditional on delivery of the securities (true DVP)
Clearing participants must make funds available to designated settlement banks the day prior to delivery

Source: RBA Assessment – Standard 11: Exchange-of-Value Settlements


4.3 Settlement Finality
Settlement finality is achieved when the settlement variation payment is debited/credited through the settlement bank accounts. Under CME rules, once a settlement cycle is completed and payments are effected, the transfers are final and irrevocable. CME Clearing’s status as a SIFMU provides additional legal certainty under Title VIII of Dodd-Frank, which provides protections against potential legal challenges to netting and settlement finality.


4.4 Cash Settlement Process
For cash-settled contracts (e.g., E-mini S&P 500, Eurodollar/SOFR futures), final settlement prices are determined by reference to an external index or fixing rate on the last trading day. The cash settlement amount is calculated as the difference between the final settlement price and the prior day’s settlement price, and is collected/paid through the standard variation margin settlement cycle.


4.5 Settlement Banks
CME Clearing uses the following concentration banks for settlement:







Bank
Currencies




BMO Harris Bank
USD, MXN


JPMorgan Chase (London)
AUD, NOK, CHF, GBP, NZD, SEK, TRY, SGD, HKD, ZAR


Citibank (London)
EUR, CNH, DKK, PLN, CZK, HUF


Citibank (Canada)
CAD



CME Clearing holds accounts at each settlement bank, and clearing members must maintain demand deposit cash accounts at one or more approved settlement banks. CME runs two USD settlement cycles daily (EOD and intraday).
Source: Custodian and Settlement Banks

text:
7. Interoperability

7.1 CME-OCC Cross-Margining Program



Item
Details




Established
1989 – one of the earliest cross-margining arrangements globally


Participants
OCC (Options Clearing Corporation) and CME Clearing


Purpose
Combine hedged positions in equity index options (cleared by OCC) with equity index futures (cleared by CME) into a single portfolio for margin purposes


Margin Model
Combined positions margined using OCC’s STANS (System for Theoretical Analysis and Numerical Simulations) portfolio methodology


Eligibility
Open to clearing members and their affiliates, market makers, and futures locals. Not generally available to retail customers due to differing securities vs. futures customer protection requirements


Key Benefit
SPX options (OCC) combined with E-mini S&P 500 futures (CME) for portfolio-level margin offsets


Milestone
20th anniversary of partnership celebrated in 2019 (CME-OCC 20 Years)



Source: OCC Cross-Margin Programs


7.2 CME-FICC Cross-Margining Arrangement







Item
Details




Launched
January 2024 (proprietary/house accounts)


Participants
FICC (Fixed Income Clearing Corporation, a DTCC subsidiary) and CME Clearing


Purpose
Capital efficiencies for clearing members trading and clearing both U.S. Treasury securities (FICC) and Interest Rate futures (CME)


Eligible Products
FICC-cleared U.S. Treasury Notes and Bonds (>1 year maturity) from buy/sell or repo/reverse repo transactions, paired with CME Treasury futures


Margin Methodology
Both CCPs calculate margins on combined portfolios using their respective models; the more conservative result is applied with a joint margin savings percentage


Customer Extension
Proposed rule change filed May 2025 to extend program to end-user customers of dually-registered broker-dealers/FCMs; target go-live December 2025, subject to regulatory approval


Significance
A critical element for the upcoming SEC U.S. Treasury clearing mandate (effective December 31, 2026 for cash; June 30, 2027 for repo)



Source: CME-FICC Cross-Margining FAQ; DTCC-CME Cross-Margining Forum, April 2025


7.3 Mutualization Across CME/CBOT/NYMEX/COMEX
All four exchange divisions share the Base Products financial safeguards waterfall. This means: - A single Base guaranty fund covers futures, options, and OTC FX across all four divisions - Clearing member default losses in any division can draw on the common Base guaranty fund - IRS products have their own separate guaranty fund and waterfall - This structure creates mutualization of default risk across all Base product clearing members regardless of which division they clear on


7.4 Global CCP Links
CME Clearing does not operate formal interoperability links (shared CCP clearing arrangements) with other global CCPs in the European sense (e.g., EuroCCP-LCH interoperability). Instead, CME maintains its position as a standalone CCP with: - Cross-margining agreements (OCC, FICC) - QCCP recognition in multiple jurisdictions - Global client access via its clearing member network

title: CME Clearing
text:
8. Fees

8.1 Fee Structure Overview

title: CME Clearing
text:
9. Recent Developments

9.1 SPAN 2 Rollout (2023-2025)
The next-generation SPAN 2 margin framework has been rolling out in a phased, multi-year approach: - Energy products went live September 2023 - Equity products went live October/November 2024 - Interest rate and FX products (including cleared swaps) targeted for second half of 2024 - Agricultural and remaining products targeted for second half of 2025 - Both SPAN and SPAN 2 run in parallel during the transition
Source: SPAN 2 Framework Rollout


9.2 Google Cloud Partnership

June 2024: Announced new private Google Cloud region and co-location facility in Aurora, IL for ultra-low-latency trading infrastructure
March 2025: Piloting tokenisation technology using Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL) for wholesale payments and asset tokenisation; Phase 1 completed, Phase 2 (settlement) underway with 2026 target for market solutions
Long-term: 10-year strategic partnership to migrate all CME Group technology to Google Cloud



9.3 CME Securities Clearing & Treasury Clearing

December 2025: SEC approved registration of CME Securities Clearing Inc. as a clearing agency for U.S. Treasury cash and repo securities
Q2 2026: Target launch for CME Securities Clearing operations
This positions CME as a direct competitor to FICC (DTCC) in the U.S. Treasury clearing space, in advance of the SEC’s clearing mandate:

Cash Treasury transactions: clearing mandate effective December 31, 2026
Repo transactions: clearing mandate effective June 30, 2027

CME Securities Clearing will integrate with existing CME Group clearing services and extend cross-margining with FICC

2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services (brief)
CDS operates three distinct financial market infrastructure functions [Source: CDS About]:







Function
Description




Central Securities Depository (CSD)
Safekeeping of almost CAD 4 trillion in securities on deposit; record-keeping for depository-eligible domestic and international securities


Securities Settlement System (SSS)
DVP settlement of exchange-traded and OTC equity, debt, and money market transactions through CDSX


Central Counterparty (CCP)
CNS (Continuous Net Settlement) service for eligible exchange-traded equity transactions; CDS interposes itself as counterparty through novation






Product Class
CCP Clearing (CNS)
Settlement (CDSX)




Equities

Yes

No CCP service
