title: Asia-Pacific Derivatives Regulation
text:
5. Summary & Outlook

5.1 Convergence Trends
All four jurisdictions are converging on several fronts: 1. Trade reporting harmonization: All adopted CPMI-IOSCO CDE, UTI, and UPI standards during 2024-2025. 2. OTC clearing mandates: All have mandatory IRS clearing, though scope and thresholds vary. 3. IOSCO participation: All are full MMOU and APRC Supervisory MMoU signatories. 4. Cross-border CCP recognition: Mutual recognition frameworks are well-established with major Western counterparts (CFTC, ESMA).


5.2 Divergence Points

Regulatory architecture: Ranges from fully integrated (Singapore/MAS) to split-function (Korea/FSC+FSS) to split-by-entity (Hong Kong/SFC+HKMA).
Position limit authority: Statutory (Hong Kong) vs. exchange-level (Japan, Singapore, Korea).
Foreign investor access: Korea’s IRC system remains more restrictive than the other three.
Exchange structure: KRX’s monopoly quasi-public model differs from the publicly listed exchange groups in the other three jurisdictions.



5.3 Key Watchpoints (2026-2027)

Japan: FIEA 2024 amendments taking effect May 2026; continued TONA futures market development
Hong Kong: Southbound Swap Connect development; Clearing Rules calculation period amendments (proposed effective March 2027); ODP platform rollout
Singapore: Continued expansion of FX futures product suite; potential updates to mandatory clearing thresholds
Korea: Potential KRX IPO implications for regulatory structure; ongoing derivatives market reforms; foreign investor access modernization

title: Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Order Matching

Matching Method: Computerized centralized matching using price-time priority
Priority Rules: Price priority first (higher bids and lower offers matched first), then time priority (earlier orders at the same price have priority)
Matching Engine: Orders enter the mainframe for centralized matching; concluded deals feedback delivered to trading terminals



3.2 Auction Mechanisms

Call Auction (Opening): Used at the start of each session to determine the opening price. Orders accumulated during the pre-opening period are matched at a single price that maximizes volume.
Continuous Auction: After the opening, incoming orders are continuously matched against resting orders on the book.



3.3 Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Order to buy or sell at a specified price or better


Market Order
Order executed at the best available price; unfilled portion cancelled





3.4 Settlement Price

The daily settlement price is typically the volume-weighted average price of all trades during the trading day (or a specified calculation window)
Used for daily mark-to-market margin calculations



3.5 Spread Trading

Calendar spread (inter-month spread) trading is supported for selected products
Cross-commodity spreads may be available for related products [unverified]

[Source: SHFE, “Application Report on Remote Trading Seat”, https://www.shfe.com.cn/upload/20131120/1384924405429.doc] [Source: SHFE, “Rules”, https://www.shfe.com.cn/eng/services/Rules/SHFERules/]

Expansion Mechanism: - If a contract settles at its price limit for consecutive trading days, SHFE may expand the price limit range and increase margin requirements - SHFE can also implement ad hoc adjustments before holidays or during extreme market conditions - In January 2026, SHFE significantly tightened rules amid precious metals surge — expanded daily price limits for gold, silver, copper, and aluminum while raising margin requirements


8.2 Trading Margin Requirements
SHFE uses a fixed-percentage margin system. Margins are calculated as a percentage of contract value.

Margin Adjustment Rules: - Margins increase as a contract approaches its delivery month (stepped increases) - Margins increase when open interest exceeds specified thresholds - SHFE raises margins before long holidays (Spring Festival, National Day, Labor Day) - The exchange can raise margins at any time based on market conditions


8.3 Position Limits

SHFE imposes speculative position limits specifying the maximum long or short position each member or client may hold
Position limits differ by product and are expressed as maximum lots
Daily opening position limits apply to certain products (e.g., silver and tin have reduced daily opening position limits)
Hedging positions can be approved for higher limits upon application
Large trader reporting requirements apply when positions exceed specified thresholds



8.4 Risk Management Framework
SHFE applies a comprehensive risk management regime including:

Alerts issued when abnormal trading patterns are detected





8.5 Forced Liquidation

If a member’s margin falls below the required level and is not replenished by the next trading day’s opening, SHFE may forcibly close positions
Positions may also be forcibly liquidated if position limits are exceeded
The exchange can invoke emergency measures including trading suspension during extreme conditions

text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority







Regulator
Role




China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC)
Primary regulator; oversees all futures and derivatives exchanges in China; approves new product listings





9.2 Key Regulations

Regulations on the Administration of Futures Trading (State Council): Primary national regulation governing futures markets in China
Futures and Derivatives Law (2022): China’s first comprehensive law on futures and derivatives, effective August 1, 2022; provides legal foundation for market development, investor protection, and cross-border activities
SHFE Trading Rules: Exchange-level rules governing trading conduct, order management, price limits, and market operations
SHFE Clearing Rules: Rules governing margin, settlement, delivery, and default management
SHFE Risk Management Rules: Rules on margins, price limits, position limits, large trader reporting, and forced liquidation
INE Business Rules: Separate but aligned rules for Shanghai International Energy Exchange operations and international participant access



9.3 Market Surveillance

SHFE conducts real-time market surveillance monitoring for abnormal trading patterns, market manipulation, and insider trading
Coordinates with CSRC on enforcement actions
Reports large positions and unusual trading activity
Daily opening position limits enforced for certain products to control speculative activity



9.4 Internationalization via INE
The Shanghai International Energy Exchange (INE), established in 2013 as a subsidiary of SHFE, serves as the platform for internationalized commodity products:







Feature
Description




Purpose
Provide a regulated venue for overseas investors to trade Chinese commodity futures


Currency
All contracts denominated and settled in RMB


Access Channels
Direct overseas participation through overseas intermediaries, or via QFII/RQFII channels


Products Open to Foreign Traders
Crude Oil (SC), Low Sulfur Fuel Oil (LU), TSR 20 Rubber (NR), Bonded Copper (BC), Containerized Freight Index (SCFIS)


Bonded Delivery
Physical delivery through bonded warehouses in Shanghai Free Trade Zone and other designated zones


Significance
Crude oil futures (SC, launched March 2018) was the first commodity futures in mainland China open to overseas investors





9.5 Self-Regulatory Organization

SHFE functions as a self-regulatory organization (SRO) under CSRC supervision
Operates 224 delivery warehouses across China
Member firms include futures commission merchants (FCMs) and non-futures-company members
SHFE sets and enforces its own trading rules, clearing rules, and membership requirements

title: Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE)
text:
Margin Framework

Margin Methodology
SHFE uses a fixed-percentage margin system (not SPAN or VaR). Trading margins are calculated as a percentage of contract value, with the percentage varying by product, delivery month proximity, position size, and market conditions.


Margin Calculation

Initial Margin = Contract Price x Contract Size x Margin Rate
Example: Copper at CNY 70,000/ton, 5 tons/lot, 8% margin = CNY 28,000 per lot



Margin Escalation Rules







Condition
Effect




Approaching Delivery Month
Margin rate increases in stepped increments as the contract nears the delivery month


High Open Interest
When total open interest exceeds specified thresholds, margin rate increases


Consecutive Limit Moves
If a contract settles at its price limit for consecutive days, margin increases


Holiday Periods
SHFE routinely raises margins before long holidays (Spring Festival, National Day, Labor Day)


Exchange Discretion
SHFE can adjust margins at any time; in January 2026, margins for copper raised from 7% to 8% (general) and 11% (speculative) amid precious metals surge





Variation Margin

Settled daily (mark-to-market) based on the daily settlement price
Gains credited and losses debited to the member’s margin account daily
If margin falls below the maintenance level, a margin call is issued; failure to replenish by the next trading day’s opening may result in forced liquidation



Delivery Margin

During the delivery month, margin requirements increase significantly
Both buyers and sellers must deposit delivery margins
Physical delivery through SHFE-designated warehouses (224 warehouses across China)



INE Margin Specifics

INE products (crude oil, bonded copper, etc.) follow the same fixed-percentage methodology
Overseas participants can use foreign currency (USD) as margin collateral, subject to haircuts [unverified — specific haircut rates]
INE margin requirements are generally higher than domestic SHFE products due to the international nature of the contracts

title: Osaka Exchange (OSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (Itayose): At the start of each session (day and night), orders are matched via a single-price auction (Itayose method). All accumulated orders during the pre-opening period are matched at a single equilibrium price that maximizes volume.
Closing Auction: At the end of each session, a closing auction determines the settlement price. For certain products, closing prices are determined by the Itayose method.



3.2 Continuous Trading (Zaraba)
After the opening auction, trading proceeds via continuous matching (Zaraba method): - Incoming orders are matched against the order book on a price-time priority basis - If no match is available, the order rests in the book at its limit price - Market orders have highest priority and are matched at the best available price


3.3 Price Discovery

Special Quotation (SQ): For final settlement of index futures and options, a Special Quotation value is calculated based on the opening prices of each component stock on the business day following the last trading day. This SQ value serves as the final settlement price.
Theoretical Opening Price (TOP): During pre-opening periods, a theoretical opening price is disseminated indicating likely opening level.



3.4 Order Priority

Price Priority: Better-priced orders (higher bids, lower offers) have priority
Time Priority: Among orders at the same price, earlier orders have priority

[Source: JPX, “Trading | Derivatives”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/derivatives/rules/]

title: Osaka Exchange (OSE)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits (Static Circuit Breakers)
OSE applies daily price limit ranges to futures and options contracts. These limits are calculated by multiplying a base price by predetermined rates and are recalculated quarterly (March, June, September, December).
Expansion Mechanism: - If a futures contract hits its price limit, trading in all related contracts (same underlying index) is temporarily halted for approximately 10 minutes - After the halt, trading resumes with expanded price limits (1st expansion) - If limits are hit again, a further expansion (2nd expansion) is applied
Example (Nikkei 225 Futures): Under normal conditions, the initial price limit is approximately 8% of the base price. After the 1st expansion, the limit widens further. [unverified — exact percentages vary by period]


8.2 Immediately Executable Price Range (Dynamic Circuit Breakers)
A dynamic circuit breaker mechanism (Immediately Executable Price Range rule) prevents sudden large price moves within continuous trading: - If an incoming order would result in execution at a price outside the “immediately executable price range” from the last traded price, a temporary trading halt is triggered - This functions similarly to a volatility interruption mechanism - Trading resumes after a brief cooling-off period with a single-price auction


8.3 Pre-Trade Risk Controls

TradeGuard: Mandatory pre-trade risk check system implemented in J-GATE 3.0 for all trading participants

Maximum order size limits
Maximum position limits
Order price reasonability checks
Configured by each trading participant with exchange-mandated minimums




8.4 Kill Switch

Trading participants can use TradeGuard or manual procedures to cancel all resting orders and prevent new order entry
OSE can also intervene to halt a participant’s trading in emergency situations

[Source: JPX, “Price Limits / Circuit Breaker Rule | Derivatives”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/derivatives/rules/price-limit-cb/] [Source: JPX, “Immediately Executable Price Range Rule”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/derivatives/rules/price-range/]

text:
11. Recent Developments

11.1 System Upgrades

J-GATE 4.0 Announced (2025): OSE selected Nasdaq’s Eqlipse Trading platform and Nasdaq Market Surveillance technology for the next-generation derivatives system. J-GATE 4.0 is scheduled for launch around the latter half of 2028 and will deliver sub-40 microsecond latency, enhanced scalability, and AI-powered market surveillance.
J-GATE 3.0 Continuing Enhancements: Ongoing updates to the current Genium INET-based platform for stability and performance.



11.2 New Products & Volumes

3-Month TONA Futures Growth (2024–2025): Following the BOJ’s exit from negative interest rates (March 2024) and subsequent rate hikes (July 2024, January 2025), demand for JPY interest rate hedging has surged. Open interest surpassed 100,000 contracts in March 2025. OSE introduced Pack and Bundle trading for TONA Futures.
Nikkei 225 micro Futures Success: Launched May 2022 to attract retail investors; achieved record trading volumes in 2025.
Nikkei 225 mini Options: Launched May 2023 with weekly expirations, enabling more granular risk management.
20-Year JGB Futures: Set annual volume record in 2025 (196,682 contracts), driven by increased yield curve trading.
Record Overall Volumes: CY2024 total of 464 million contracts (record); night session ratio at 40.5%.



11.3 Regulatory Changes

JSCC Margin Migration to VaR (November 2023): JSCC transitioned from SPAN-based margining to a VaR (Value-at-Risk) methodology using Historical Simulation (HS-VaR) for all listed derivatives. The VaR method uses 1,250+ historical data points vs. SPAN’s 16 simplified scenarios, providing more accurate risk-based margin calculations at a 99% confidence level.
Securities Options Revitalization: Regulatory improvements in 2024–2025 to promote Japan’s single stock options market, including relaxed position limits and enhanced market maker programs.



11.4 Strategic Initiatives

Cryptocurrency Derivatives Exploration: OSE CEO Ryosuke Yokoyama has signaled plans to explore crypto futures, options, and crypto ETFs as part of JPX’s medium-term strategy to diversify into new asset classes.
Holiday Trading Expansion: Continuing to expand the derivatives holiday trading calendar to maximize global accessibility.
CME Group Partnership: Ongoing cross-listing and mutual offset arrangement for Nikkei 225 products.
Global Access Promotion: Leveraging FBOT status and extending night session hours to attract international institutional participation.

[Source: Nasdaq, “Japan’s Osaka Exchange Adopts Nasdaq Eqlipse Trading and Surveillance Technology”, https://ir.nasdaq.com/news-releases/news-release-details/japans-osaka-exchange-adopts-nasdaq-eqlipse-trading-and] [Source: JPX, “JGB and JPY Interest Rate Derivatives Reach Annual Record Highs in 2025”, January 2026, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/news/2041/20260113-01.html] [Source: CoinGape, “Osaka Exchange Could Bring Crypto Futures and Options to Japanese Markets Soon”, https://coingape.com/osaka-exchange-could-bring-crypto-futures-and-options-to-japanese-markets-soon/] [Source: The TRADE, “Japan’s equity derivatives market set to grow in 2025”, https://www.thetradenews.com/thought-leadership/japans-equity-derivatives-market-set-to-grow-in-2025/]

D3. Margin Framework

JSCC VaR-Based Margining (Since November 2023)







Item
Details




Clearing House
Japan Securities Clearing Corporation (JSCC) — CCP for all OSE listed derivatives


Methodology
Value-at-Risk (VaR) — replaced SPAN on November 6, 2023


VaR Approach
Historical Simulation (HS-VaR): portfolio P&L calculated using 1,250+ historical scenarios; Alternative Simulation (AS-VaR) used for products with insufficient history


Confidence Level
At least 99% of potential future exposures


Lookback Period
At least 1,250 trading days (~5 years) of historical data


Margin Types
Initial margin (upfront deposit) + Variation margin (daily mark-to-market settlement)


Eligible Collateral
Cash (JPY), government bonds, listed equities, and other approved securities


Margin Call Process
Intraday margin calls possible during extreme volatility; regular margin calls at end of day


Portfolio Margining
Cross-margining across correlated positions (e.g., Nikkei 225 futures and options)



Comparison with Previous SPAN Method: - VaR uses 1,250+ historical scenarios vs. SPAN’s 16 simplified scenarios - VaR provides more accurate risk-based margins, especially for complex portfolios - VaR can result in lower margins for hedged positions and higher margins for concentrated risk



D4. Position Limits

Position limits apply to speculative positions in selected products
Hedge exemptions available upon application with documented hedging rationale
Large position reporting thresholds trigger reporting obligations to OSE and JFSA
Specific position limit levels vary by product and are set by OSE Business Regulations [unverified — exact limits not publicly summarized in a single source]



D5. J-NET Trading (Off-Auction Facility)







Item
Details




Description
Off-auction (negotiated) trading facility for derivatives, independent of the central order book


Eligible Products
All futures and options listed on OSE


Mechanism
Participants negotiate bilaterally and submit matched orders to J-NET; executed when price, volume, and counterparty details match


Price Constraints
Must be within specified price bands relative to the auction market


Trading Hours
Available during both day and night sessions; also available on holiday trading days


Flexible Contracts
J-NET supports flexible terms (e.g., non-standard expiration dates, settlement methods) for certain products


Reporting
J-NET trade prices (open, high, low, close) and volumes published daily


Use Cases
Block trading, basis trades, portfolio rebalancing, and other off-exchange negotiated transactions



[Source: JPX, “J-NET Trading | Derivatives”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/derivatives/rules/j-net/index.html] [Source: JPX, “Outline of J-NET Trading Rules”, November 2025, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/derivatives/rules/outline/dreu250000001ove-att/dreu250000001oxp.pdf]


D6. Delivery & Settlement

Cash-Settled Products (Majority)

Equity Index Futures/Options: Settled against the Special Quotation (SQ) value, calculated from the opening prices of all component stocks on the business day after the last trading day
Mini/Micro Futures: Cash-settled using the same SQ methodology
Commodity Futures (some): Cash-settled based on reference prices



Physically-Delivered Products

10-Year JGB Futures: Physical delivery of eligible JGB issues; delivery month is the contract month; the deliverable basket consists of JGBs with remaining maturity of 7–11 years (approximate); conversion factor system used
20-Year JGB Futures: Physical delivery of eligible JGBs with remaining maturity of 15–21 years (approximate) [unverified]
Gold/Platinum/Silver Futures: Physical delivery through designated warehouses



Central Counterparty

JSCC (Japan Securities Clearing Corporation) acts as the CCP for all OSE listed derivatives
JSCC interposes itself between buyer and seller, guaranteeing settlement
JSCC also clears OTC JPY interest rate swaps (separate clearing service; annual clearing value reached approximately JPY 12,202 trillion in 2025, a record)
JSCC maintains a default fund (clearing fund) contributed by all clearing members

[Source: JSCC, “Margin on Futures and Options”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/jscc/en/cash/futures/marginsystem/margin.html] [Source: JSCC, “Margin Calculation Method (VaR Method)”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/jscc/en/cash/futures/marginsystem/VaR.html] [Source: JPX, “JGB and JPY Interest Rate Derivatives Reach Annual Record Highs in 2025”, January 2026, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/news/2041/20260113-01.html]

Country / City

Ownership Structure
Wholly-owned subsidiary of TMX Group Limited (TSX: X)


Parent Company / Group

Regulatory Authority
Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF, Quebec) as lead regulator; Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO) for market integrity oversight


President & CEO
Luc Fortin (since August 2016)


Clearing House
Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corporation (CDCC), wholly-owned subsidiary of MX


Average Daily Volume (2025)
~937,000 contracts/day combined (~520K IRD + ~417K EQD); record year with ~20% YoY growth in both segments


Key Product Areas
Interest rate derivatives (CORRA futures, Government of Canada bond futures), equity index derivatives, equity options, ETF options



[Source: Wikipedia, “Montreal Exchange”; TMX Group website; MX website (m-x.ca); MX Q4 2025 Highlights report]

Key Historical Milestones

1832: Informal stock exchange established at Exchange Coffee House in Montreal — one of Canada’s earliest financial markets
1874: Formally incorporated as the Montreal Stock Exchange by Lorn MacDougall and partners
1903: Purpose-built exchange building opened, designed by George B. Post (architect of the NYSE building)
1926: Montreal Curb Market created for speculative and junior stocks
1953: Curb Market renamed to Canadian Stock Exchange
1965: Moved into Tour de la Bourse (Stock Exchange Tower), Montreal’s third-tallest building
1974: Canadian Stock Exchange merged with Montreal Stock Exchange
1975: First exchange in Canada to list stock options
1982: Renamed from “Montreal Stock Exchange” to “Montreal Exchange” to reflect expanded financial instruments
1989 (September): Launched Ten-Year Government of Canada Bond Futures (CGB)
1999: Following restructuring agreement among Canadian exchanges, MX became Canada’s sole derivatives exchange; equity trading transferred to Toronto Stock Exchange
2001: Completed migration from open outcry to fully automated electronic trading — first traditional exchange in North America to achieve this
2004 (February): Became sole provider of electronic trading systems for Boston Options Exchange (BOX); held 31.4% stake, increasing to over 51% by 2009
2006 (July): Established Montreal Climate Exchange (joint venture with Chicago Climate Exchange) — first regulated environmental market in Canada
2007 (December): TSX Group announced acquisition of MX for C$1.31 billion
2008 (May 1): Acquisition completed; combined entity renamed TMX Group Inc.
2013: Upgraded SOLA trading platform with ~300% improvement in trading response time and doubled messaging capacity to 100,000 quotes/second
2020: Launched Three-Month CORRA Futures (CRA) market-making program
2023 (January): Launched One-Month CORRA Futures (COA)
2024 (April 26): Open BAX positions converted to CRA contracts on a 1:1 basis following CDOR cessation
2024 (June 28): CDOR permanently ceased publication; BAX contracts formally discontinued
2025: Record year across both interest rate and equity derivatives; ETF options ADV +80% YoY
2025 (June): Announced FTSE Canada Bank Credit Index Futures (CBC) — first-of-its-kind credit derivatives product for Canadian market, planned Q1 2026 launch

[Source: Wikipedia, “Montreal Exchange”; MX website; TMX press releases 2007–2025; Finextra, “Montreal Exchange upgrades Sola derivatives trading platform”, 2013; MX Q4 2025 Highlights; Mondovisione, “Montréal Exchange To Launch FTSE Canada Bank Credit Index Futures”, June 2025]

8. Risk Controls & Market Integrity

8.1 Exchange-Level Controls

25 contracts minimum display for most futures; 50 contracts for CGB





8.2 Circuit Breaker Coordination
MX derivatives circuit breakers are coordinated with the underlying equity market: - Trading halts in equity options are invoked when the underlying stock or ETF is halted on TSX (Single Stock Circuit Breaker / SSCB) - Index derivatives follow equity market-wide circuit breaker levels set by CIRO/exchanges - After a halt, re-opening follows an auction-like process


8.3 Clearing-Level Risk Controls (CDCC)
See Section 11 (Margin Framework) for detailed CDCC risk management methodology.
[Source: MX website, “Exchange Market Thresholds and Controls”; MX Share Futures specifications; MX Equity Options Reference Manual]

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Regulatory Structure
MX operates within a multi-layered Canadian regulatory framework:







Regulator / Body
Role




Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF)
Lead regulator; recognized exchange and self-regulatory organization (SRO) status granted by AMF under Quebec’s Derivatives Act (CQLR, Chapter I-14.01)


MX Regulatory Division (MX-R)
Independent unit within MX; performs surveillance, compliance, and enforcement for MX derivative markets


Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO)
National SRO formed January 2023 (from merger of IIROC and MFDA); oversees market integrity; performs cross-asset surveillance between MX-listed derivatives and underlying securities


Bank of Canada
Oversees systemic risk; supervises CDCC as a designated systemically important financial market infrastructure


Canadian Securities Administrators (CSA)
Umbrella organization of provincial/territorial regulators; harmonizes regulation across Canada





9.2 Self-Regulatory Functions
As a recognized SRO, MX is required by the AMF to maintain the Regulatory Division (MX-R), which: - Monitors trading activity in real time - Investigates potential market abuses (manipulation, insider trading, front-running) - Enforces MX rules against approved participants and market makers - Conducts compliance examinations - Publishes regulatory notices and circulars


9.3 Rule-Making Process

MX rule amendments are self-certified under the self-certification process established in the Derivatives Act
Significant rule changes are subject to AMF review and public comment
CIRO’s Universal Market Integrity Rules (UMIR) apply to cross-market trading activity



9.4 Key Regulatory Developments

2023: CIRO formed from IIROC-MFDA merger (effective January 1, 2023; renamed CIRO on June 1, 2023)
2024: T+1 settlement implemented across Canadian markets (May 27, 2024)
2024: CDOR cessation and BAX-to-CRA transition completed under ISDA framework

[Source: AMF website, “Self-Regulatory Organizations”; MX Regulatory Division website (reg.m-x.ca); CIRO website, “About CIRO”; MX “Accessing the Montréal Exchange” document]

title: Montreal Exchange (MX)
text:
12. Margin Framework (CDCC)

12.1 Overview
The Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corporation (CDCC) is the central counterparty (CCP) for all exchange-traded derivatives on MX and for a growing range of OTC customized financial instruments.







Item
Details




Full Name
Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corporation


Ownership
Wholly-owned subsidiary of Bourse de Montréal Inc.


Headquarters
100 Adelaide Street West, 3rd Floor, Toronto, Ontario


Designation
Recognized as a clearing house by AMF; designated as a systemically important financial market infrastructure by the Bank of Canada


Margin Methodology
SPAN-based (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk), adopted 1997





12.2 Margin Methodology
Initial Margin (SPAN-Based): - CDCC adopted SPAN in 1997 as the core framework for calculating initial margin requirements - Risk parameters are calibrated on a daily basis, including Margin Interval and Intra-Commodity Spreads - Incorporates historical volatility of daily price returns - Volatility estimator uses a confidence level exceeding 99% - Variable Margin Period of Risk (MPOR) applied depending on product liquidity
Anti-Procyclicality Measures: - Stress Risk component calculated via Stress Value at Risk (SVaR) with a 25% weighting factor - Volatility floor calculated as the average of the daily volatility estimator observed over the last 10 years - These measures prevent margin requirements from dropping too low during periods of calm and spiking excessively during stress
Margin Relief (Inter-Commodity Spreads): - Currently available for a limited list of futures products exhibiting high correlation: - Index Futures combinations - Short-Term Interest Rate (STIR) Futures combinations - Canadian clients may use the CDCC SPAN file as an alternative to other margin files
Additional Capital Margin: - Measures credit exposure of clearing members - Requires collection of a minimum of 50% of the excess when a clearing member’s Base Initial Margin exceeds their capital amount


12.3 Variation Margin

Mark-to-market settlement performed daily
Futures: daily settlement price used for P&L calculation; variation margin collected/paid daily
Options: premium-style margining for equity and ETF options



12.4 Default Management
CDCC maintains a default waterfall including: 1. Defaulting member’s margin and collateral 2. Defaulting member’s contribution to the clearing fund 3. CDCC’s own dedicated resources (skin-in-the-game) 4. Non-defaulting members’ clearing fund contributions 5. Additional assessments
[Source: CDCC website, “Margining”, “Risk Management”; CDCC Operations Manual (August 2025); OSC, “Canadian Derivatives Clearing Corporation” RFC document, February 2023; CDCC Notice 154-22; Bank of Canada, “Stress testing central counterparties for resolution planning”, March 2025]

Key Historical Milestones

1870: New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE) founded – predecessor of ICE Futures U.S.
1882: Coffee Exchange of the City of New York founded
1980: International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) founded in London as an open-outcry energy exchange
1998: New York Board of Trade (NYBOT) formed by the merger of NYCE and the Coffee, Sugar & Cocoa Exchange (CSCE)
2000: Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) founded in Atlanta, Georgia, by Jeffrey Sprecher as an electronic over-the-counter (OTC) energy marketplace
2001: ICE acquires the International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) in London, entering the exchange-traded futures market
2005 (April 7): IPE fully transitions from open-outcry to electronic trading; renamed ICE Futures (later ICE Futures Europe)
2005: ICE goes public on the NYSE (ticker: ICE)
2007: ICE acquires the New York Board of Trade (NYBOT); renamed ICE Futures U.S.
2007: ICE acquires ChemConnect (chemical marketplace) and Winnipeg Commodity Exchange (now ICE Futures Canada)
2008: ICE Clear Europe established as a central counterparty clearing house in London
2010: ICE acquires the Climate Exchange (including European Climate Exchange and Chicago Climate Exchange)
2012 (December): ICE announces acquisition of NYSE Euronext for $8.2 billion
2013 (November 13): ICE completes acquisition of NYSE Euronext (~$11 billion total value); acquires LIFFE (London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange) and NYSE
2014 (June): ICE spins off continental European Euronext exchanges via IPO; retains LIFFE operations, integrating them into ICE Futures Europe
2016: ICE launches ICE Benchmark Administration (IBA), becoming administrator of LIBOR, ICE Swap Rate, and other benchmarks
2018: ICE acquires MERSCORP Holdings (mortgage electronic registry); launches Bakkt digital asset platform
2020: ICE acquires Ellie Mae (mortgage technology) for $11 billion; acquires Simplifile
2022: ICE acquires Black Knight (mortgage technology) for $13.1 billion
2025: Record derivatives volumes (2.4 billion contracts); launch of EUA 2 (EU Carbon Allowance 2) futures; launch of battery materials futures (lithium, cobalt, spodumene); ICE invests up to $2 billion in Polymarket
2026 (ongoing): Launch of regulated cryptocurrency futures based on CoinDesk Indices (seven new contracts); strategic investment in OKX ($200 million); datacenter DR migration from Atlanta to Mahwah

[Source: ICE, “Our History”, https://www.ice.com/about/history] [Source: Wikipedia, “Intercontinental Exchange”, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_Exchange] [Source: ICE press releases, 2025-2026]

title: ICE Futures (Intercontinental Exchange Futures)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Continuous Trading
ICE’s derivatives markets operate on a continuous electronic order-matching basis during regular trading hours:

Price-Time Priority: Orders are matched on a strict price-time priority basis – best price first, then earliest timestamp at the same price
Central Limit Order Book (CLOB): All orders enter a central limit order book; visible (displayed) and non-displayed portions handled according to order type
Anonymous Trading: Counterparty identities are not disclosed on the order book; all trades are cleared through ICE’s clearing houses



3.2 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (selected products): Pre-open period where orders accumulate without matching, followed by a single-price uncrossing auction
Closing/Settlement Period: Products such as Brent crude use a weighted average of trades during a defined settlement window (e.g., Brent settlement based on VWAP during a 2-minute window at 19:28 London time)
Intraday Auctions: Not a standard feature for most ICE products [unverified]



3.3 Spread Trading

Calendar Spreads: Directly tradable as instruments; separate order book for spread markets
Inter-Commodity Spreads: Supported for related products (e.g., Brent/WTI spread, crack spreads)
Strategy Trading: Complex multi-leg strategies can be submitted as a single order



3.4 Implied Pricing

Implied-in and Implied-out: ICE supports implied pricing for spread markets, deriving synthetic prices from outright and spread orders to enhance liquidity [unverified]

[Source: ICE, “ICE Futures Europe Trading Procedures”, https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/contractregs/185_XX_TRADING_PROCEDURES.pdf]

title: ICE Futures (Intercontinental Exchange Futures)
text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Order to buy/sell at a specified price or better


Market Order
Order to buy/sell at the best available price; immediate execution


Stop Order
Triggered when market price reaches the stop price; becomes a market order


Stop Limit Order
Triggered at stop price; becomes a limit order at the specified limit price





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Iceberg / Reserve Order
Only a portion of the order is displayed; remainder hidden and replenished


Market-if-Touched (MIT)
Converts to a market order when a specified price is touched


Discretionary Order
Limit order with a hidden discretionary range for price improvement [unverified]





4.3 Time-in-Force Conditions







Condition
Description




Day
Valid for the current trading session only


Good Till Cancelled (GTC)
Remains active until filled or cancelled


Good Till Date (GTD)
Remains active until a specified date


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be filled entirely and immediately or cancelled


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Any portion not immediately filled is cancelled





4.4 Order Modification & Cancellation

Orders can be modified (price, quantity) or cancelled at any time during the trading session
Modifications that change price lose time priority
Quantity reductions retain time priority
Mass Cancellation: Participants can cancel all orders via a single “cancel all” message (kill switch functionality)

[Source: ICE, “ICE Futures U.S. Trading Rules”, https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/rulebooks/futures_us/4_Trading.pdf]

title: ICE Futures (Intercontinental Exchange Futures)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Interval Price Limits (IPL) – Circuit Breaker
ICE uses Interval Price Limits (IPLs) as a temporary circuit breaker mechanism on its electronic platform:

If an order crosses the IPL level for a particular futures contract, a market hold (trading halt) is triggered for a pre-set period
IPLs slow the rate of price movement in a given direction, preventing aberrant price spikes
All IPL parameters (price bands, hold duration) may be adjusted by the exchange based on prevailing market conditions
After the hold period expires, trading resumes and new IPLs are recalculated



8.2 Daily Price Limits (DPL)

ICE Futures U.S. applies Daily Price Limits to selected contracts:

Cotton No. 2 – DPL with expandable limits (~50% wider than standard)
FCOJ-A – DPL with expandable limits
Canola (ICE Futures Canada) – DPL

Most energy and interest rate products do not have daily price limits



8.3 Reasonability Limits

Hard Limits: Pre-determined price parameters that reject orders outside the specified range on entry (buy orders above the upper limit and sell orders below the lower limit are rejected)
No Cancellation Ranges: Soft limits where trades executed within the specified range will not normally be adjusted or cancelled by the exchange



8.4 Pre-Trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Size: Configurable per product/participant
Maximum Position Size: Monitored in real-time
Credit Controls: Clearing member-level risk limits enforced at the matching engine level
Cancel-on-Disconnect: Automatic cancellation of resting orders if a participant’s connection drops [unverified]
Kill Switch: Mass cancellation functionality allowing participants or clearing members to cancel all resting orders immediately



8.5 Position Limits
ICE Futures U.S.: - Exchange-established speculative position limits per CFTC Part 150 and exchange rules - Position limits apply on both an intraday and end-of-day basis - Hedge exemptions available upon application - Aggregation of positions under common ownership or control required - Violations constitute breach of Exchange Rule 6.13 or 6.20
ICE Futures Europe: - Position management controls under UK FCA rules and EU/UK MiFID II framework - Position limits and accountability levels set per contract - ESMA opinions on position limits for significant contracts (e.g., Dutch TTF)
[Source: ICE, “ICE’s supervision of markets and price controls”, https://www.ice.com/insights/exchanges/why-financial-participants-matter-to-the-commodity-markets/ice-supervision-of-markets] [Source: ICE, “Guidance on Position Limits”, September 2025, https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/futures_us/ICE_Futures_US_PositionLimitGuidance.pdf]

B. Margin Framework

ICE Risk Model (IRM) – Legacy

Methodology: Scenario-based margining (similar in concept to SPAN); evaluates portfolio risk across a range of price and volatility scenarios
Application: Used across most ICE clearing houses for futures and options initial margin calculation



ICE Risk Model 2 (IRM 2) – New Standard

Methodology: Filtered Historical Simulation Value at Risk (FHS VaR)
Confidence Level: 99% (calibrated to cover expected close-out cost under normal market conditions)
Key Features:

Full portfolio-based margining with diversification benefits
Responsive to changing market conditions via GARCH-type volatility filtering
Replaces scenario-based approach with empirically-driven risk measurement

Rollout Status:

January 2022: Launched for equity index futures (ICE Clear U.S.)
2025: Extended to energy futures and options (1,000+ contracts including oil, natural gas, LNG, power, emissions, freight)
Further asset class expansion ongoing




Variation Margin

Collected/paid daily based on mark-to-market changes
Intraday margin calls may be issued during periods of high volatility



Margin Call Process

Initial margin posted by clearing members on behalf of their clients
Intraday margin calls if positions move adversely beyond threshold
Clearing members responsible for collecting from end-clients

[Source: ICE, “Clearing Margin Models”, https://www.ice.com/clearing/margin-models] [Source: ICE, “ICE Risk Model 2”, https://www.ice.com/clearing/margin-models/irm-2] [Source: ICE, “ICE Clear Europe Risk Management”, https://www.ice.com/clear-europe/risk-management]



C. Block Trading and EFP/EFS Rules

Block Trades

Privately negotiated transactions executed apart from the public auction market
Must meet minimum quantity thresholds (vary by product)
Must be executed at a price that is fair and reasonable in light of transaction size and comparable market prices
Submitted via the ICE Block system
Reported to the exchange and cleared through the relevant clearing house



Exchange for Physical (EFP)

Two-legged transaction: one leg is a futures position, the other is a corresponding physical commodity position
Both parties must have a bona fide physical position
Must be submitted via ICE Block system



Exchange for Swap (EFS)

Two-legged transaction: one leg is a futures position, the other is a corresponding OTC swap/derivative position
Related position must bear genuine economic risk



Exchange for Risk (EFR) / Exchange of Futures for Related Positions (EFRP)

Umbrella category covering EFP, EFS, and EOO (Exchange of Options for Options)
Key Requirements:

Genuine economic risk must be present
“Transitory” EFRPs (where execution of one is contingent on another between same parties to offset related positions) are prohibited
Registration may be refused if ICE is not satisfied with the commercial rationale
EFRP transactions must be submitted via ICE Block system


[Source: ICE, “ICE Futures Europe EFP, EFS, Soft Commodity EFRP and Basis Trade Policy”, https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/futures/IFEU_EFP_EFS_Policy.pdf] [Source: ICE, “EFRP FAQs”, February 2026, https://www.ice.com/publicdocs/futures_us/EFRP_FAQ.pdf]

title: Euronext Derivatives
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Euronext derivatives markets employ the following auction types within the Optiq platform:

Opening Auction: Orders collected during a call phase; indicative prices displayed. Uncrossing occurs at the price maximizing executable volume. Applies to all derivatives products at market open
Closing Auction: Determines official closing/settlement prices; similar call-and-uncross mechanics
Volatility Interruption (Circuit Breaker Auction): Triggered when potential trade price breaches dynamic or static price collars. Trading enters a reservation period (auction call phase) allowing orderly price discovery before resumption
Intraday Auctions: Scheduled auctions for specific products to provide additional price discovery points [unverified for derivatives – primarily used in cash equities]



3.2 Continuous Trading

Central Limit Order Book (CLOB): Fully electronic order-driven market for all derivatives products
Continuous matching: Orders matched throughout the trading session at the best available price
Market makers: Supplement order book liquidity via continuous quotes; market is order-driven, not quote-driven
Request for Cross (RFC): Facility allowing members to cross client orders on-exchange with pre-arranged counterparties, subject to price improvement rules and minimum exposure to the order book



3.3 Price Discovery

Primary price discovery through opening auction and continuous order book
Auction uncrossing: Maximum executable volume, then minimum surplus, then reference price as tiebreaker
Settlement prices: For index futures, calculated using averaging methodology near close (e.g., CAC 40: arithmetic mean of all index values between 15:40 and 16:00 CET on expiry day, rounded to two decimal places)
Indicative prices: Displayed during auction call phases



3.4 Order Priority Rules

Price-time priority: Standard priority for all Euronext derivatives products – best price first, then earliest timestamp at the same price
Market orders have priority over limit orders at any price level
Visible over hidden: At the same price, visible quantities take priority over iceberg reserve quantities
Pro-rata allocation: Not standard on Euronext derivatives; price-time priority is the default matching algorithm [unverified – specific products may have alternative allocation]

Order Type

Triggered when a specified price is reached; released as a limit order at the specified limit price





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description

Only a portion of total order volume is visible in the order book


Market-to-Limit (MTL)
Market order that, after partial execution, converts remaining quantity to a limit order at the last executed price

Opening-Auction-Only

Closing-Auction-Only
Active only during the closing auction

Description




Day

5. Trading System Technology – Optiq

5.1 Overview







Item

Architecture
Modular, partition-based architecture with Order Entry Gateway (OEG) and Matching Engine (ME) components

5.2 Architecture

Modular service structure: Flexible, modular design allowing independent scaling of components
Harmonised messaging: Unified cash and derivatives messaging model on a single platform
Order Entry Gateway (OEG): Entry point for order submission; supports SBE and FIX 5.0 protocols
Matching Engine (ME): Core matching component processing orders with price-time priority
Market Data Gateway (MDG): Disseminates real-time market data via SBE over UDP multicast
Kafka-based persistence: Confluent Platform/Apache Kafka underpins the persistence layer, providing reliable message streaming and replay capabilities

Date

5.4 Performance Highlights
Since going live for derivatives, Optiq has processed more than 14 billion messages and 18.8 million trades. The platform achieved a tenfold reduction in latency compared to the legacy LIFFE CONNECT system and unlimited overall capacity scaling.

title: Euronext Derivatives
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Trading Safeguards Philosophy
Euronext’s approach is to only halt trading under extreme circumstances, relying on a comprehensive set of trading safeguards rather than circuit breakers alone. The philosophy is to detect unusual events and prevent disorderly markets while maximizing continuous trading.


8.2 Price Collar Mechanisms

Dynamic Collar: Based on the dynamic reference price (last traded price); defines a permitted price range around the most recent trade. The dynamic reference price updates after each trade
Static Collar: Based on the static reference price (typically the previous day’s closing price or opening auction price); defines a wider permitted price range. The static reference remains fixed unless manually changed by Euronext Market Operations
Reservation Period: When the potential trade price breaches a collar, trading enters a reservation period (volatility interruption) – effectively an intraday auction. This gives market participants time to review orders before trading resumes
Trade Price Validation (TPV): Additional safeguard layer for derivatives markets; validates trade prices before execution to prevent aberrant trades



8.3 Pre-Trade Risk Controls – Euronext RiskGuard
Euronext RiskGuard is a pre-trade risk management service for derivatives (and cash) markets, available via FIX 5.0 API and web-based GUI:







Control
Description




Order Size Limit
Maximum number of contracts per order; applies to new orders, revisions, and quotes; orders exceeding the limit are rejected


Max Order Quantity
Per-contract limits for buy and/or sell orders, configurable per member or trader group


Daily Maximum Exposure Position
Position monitoring with email alerts when limits are approached or breached


Kill Switch
Clearing Members can immediately halt all trading activity for a trading firm; all open orders and quotes are pulled; new orders rejected until explicitly reinstated by the Clearing Member


Self-Trade Prevention (STP)
Prevents unintended matching of orders from the same member/trader



Scope: RiskGuard controls apply to financial and commodity derivatives markets. Delta-neutral trades, RFCs, and wholesale trades are excluded from certain controls.
[Source: Euronext, “Trading safeguards on the Euronext markets”, https://www.euronext.com/en/trading/market-quality/trading-safeguards-euronext-markets] [Source: Euronext, “Euronext RiskGuard Service General Overview”, February 2019, https://www.euronext.com/sites/default/files/2019-04/euronext_riskguard_service_general_overview_feb_2019_0.pdf] [Source: Euronext, “Euronext RiskGuard”, https://www.euronext.com/en/trading/trading-services/riskguard]

9.2 Key Regulations

MiFID II / MiFIR: Euronext derivatives markets are Regulated Markets under MiFID II. Key implications include:

Pre- and post-trade transparency requirements for derivatives
Position limits on commodity derivatives (set by national competent authorities with ESMA coordination)
Transaction reporting obligations
Algorithmic trading requirements (including market-making obligations during stressed conditions)
Best execution obligations

EMIR (European Market Infrastructure Regulation): Governs CCP supervision (Euronext Clearing supervised by CONSOB with ESMA coordination); mandates central clearing for certain OTC derivatives classes
MAR (Market Abuse Regulation): Prohibits insider trading and market manipulation; Euronext operates market surveillance systems
Benchmark Regulation (BMR): Applies to indices used as derivatives underlyings



9.3 Surveillance & Reporting

Euronext operates real-time market surveillance across all markets
Transaction reporting to national competent authorities via Euronext ARM (Approved Reporting Mechanism) service
Trade reporting for MiFID II post-trade transparency via Euronext APA (Approved Publication Arrangement)
Suspicious transaction and order reports (STORs) submitted to regulators



9.4 Cross-Border Coordination

The College of Regulators ensures consistent rule application across Euronext’s seven markets
Euronext Rule Book (Harmonised Rules) applies uniformly; supplemented by market-specific rules for each national market
Single operational framework across markets facilitates cross-border trading and clearing

11. Recent Developments

11.1 Euronext Clearing Migration (2023-2024)
The most transformative recent development was the migration of derivatives clearing from LCH SA to Euronext Clearing (formerly CC&G):

November 2023: Cash equity clearing migrated to Euronext Clearing
July 15, 2024: Commodity derivatives clearing migrated
September 9, 2024: All Euronext financial derivatives (including CAC 40, AEX futures, index options, single name options) migrated to Euronext Clearing – completing the full transition from LCH SA
Key benefit: ~20% margin efficiencies through VaR-based methodology and unified equity/derivatives default fund enabling cross-margining
Strategic significance: Euronext now controls end-to-end trading and clearing infrastructure, internalizing clearing revenue

[Source: Euronext, “Successful expansion of Euronext Clearing to all Euronext financial derivatives”, September 2024, https://www.euronext.com/en/about/media/euronext-press-releases/successful-expansion-euronext-clearing-all-euronext-financial] [Source: FOW, “Euronext reflects on landmark clearing migration from LCH”, https://www.fow.com/insights/3702151-analysis-euronext-reflects-on-landmark-clearing-migration-from-lch]


11.2 Borsa Italiana Derivatives Migration to Optiq (2024)

On April 3, 2024, Borsa Italiana’s derivatives markets (IDEM) completed migration to Optiq – the third and final phase of the Borsa Italiana platform migration
Achieved less than 3 years after the acquisition of Borsa Italiana Group
All Euronext derivatives now trade on a single unified platform (Optiq)

[Source: Euronext, “Successful completion of the migration of Borsa Italiana to the Optiq trading platform”, https://www.euronext.com/en/about/media/euronext-press-releases/successful-completion-migration-borsa-italiana-optiqr-trading]


11.3 New Product Launches

September 2025: Launch of fixed income derivatives – first-ever mini cash-settled futures on European government bonds (BTP 10Y/30Y, OAT, Bund, Bono) on Euronext Derivatives Milan
May 2025: Mini single stock options on French and Dutch underlyings
September 2025: First-ever mini cash-settled futures
March 2026: Mini ETF options
Ongoing: Quarterly product releases adding new single stock options from Germany, Ireland, Portugal, and other markets
Retail derivatives strategy: Euronext aims to become the European retail exchange for derivatives, targeting retail investor participation

[Source: Euronext, “Euronext launches an innovative suite of fixed income derivatives”, February 2025, https://www.euronext.com/en/about/media/euronext-press-releases/euronext-launches-innovative-suite-fixed-income-derivatives] [Source: Markets Media, “Euronext Aims to Become European Retail Exchange for Derivatives”, https://www.marketsmedia.com/euronext-aims-to-become-european-retail-exchange-for-derivatives/]


11.4 Strategic Initiatives

Euronext Clearing expansion: Post-migration focus on leveraging cross-margining and attracting new clearing members
Fixed income derivatives growth: Multi-year initiative to build a European government bond derivatives franchise
Repo expansion: First phase of multi-year Repo Expansion Initiative extending Italian repo offering across Europe
Nasdaq Nordic power futures acquisition: Reinforcing leadership in European energy markets
Technology platform licensing: Optiq offered as a technology solution for other exchanges and venue operators

D3. Margin Framework

Euronext Clearing Margin Methodology
Following the migration from LCH SA (completed September 2024), all Euronext derivatives are cleared through Euronext Clearing (formerly CC&G), which employs a VaR-based margin methodology:







Item
Details




Methodology
Dynamic (auto-updating) VaR-like portfolio margining


Risk Measure
Historical Simulation Expected Shortfall (ES) based on cash flow mapping on sovereign zero curves


Confidence Level
99.0% for most products [unverified – standard EMIR requirement]


Lookback Period
Based on historical market data [specific period not publicly disclosed]


Update Frequency
Dynamic/auto-updating based on market conditions


Procyclicality
EMIR-compliant measures to prevent excessive procyclical margin increases





Margin Add-Ons
Euronext Clearing applies additional margin add-ons to address portfolio-specific risks beyond mid-price risk:

Idiosyncratic risk: Risk specific to individual securities
Liquidity risk: Accounts for varying liquidity across products
Concentration risk: Additional margins for large concentrated positions
Settlement risk: Risk related to settlement timing
Repo risk: For positions involving repo transactions



Methodology Timeline







Date
Change




Pre-October 2023
MARS (SPAN-like methodology) used for Italian equity and derivatives


June 2022
VaR-based methodology goes live for Italian, Portuguese, Spanish, Irish government bonds


October 2023
VaR-based methodology goes live for Italian equity, ETF, and equity derivatives (replacing MARS/SPAN-like model)


September 2024
VaR-based methodology extended to all Euronext financial derivatives following migration from LCH SA





Cross-Margining

Unified default fund: Single equity and derivatives default fund facilitating cross-margining between cash and derivatives positions
Margin efficiency: ~20% margin reduction achieved through portfolio margining across equity and derivatives products within the same default fund

[Source: Euronext, “Euronext Clearing introduces an innovative VaR-based margin methodology”, https://www.euronext.com/en/about/media/euronext-press-releases/euronext-clearing-introduces-innovative-var-based-margin] [Source: Euronext, “Risk Management Methodologies”, https://www.euronext.com/en/post-trade/euronext-clearing/risk-management/methodologies] [Source: Euronext, “Model Validation”, May 2024, https://www.euronext.com/sites/default/files/2024-05/Euronext_Clearing_Model%20Validation_May24.pdf]



D4. Position Limits

MiFID II Position Limits: National competent authorities (coordinated by ESMA) set position limits on commodity derivatives
Milling Wheat position limits: ESMA publishes opinions on position limits for the EBM (Milling Wheat No. 2) contract; limits are set by the AMF as the relevant national authority for the Paris MATIF market
Accountability levels: Position reporting thresholds apply to all derivatives; large position holders must report to the exchange and relevant regulator
Hedge exemptions: Available for bona fide hedgers who apply to the national competent authority
Financial derivatives: Position limits for equity/index derivatives are generally less restrictive than for commodity derivatives; specific limits vary by product [unverified]

[Source: ESMA, “Opinion on position limits on Milling Wheat No. 2 contract”, https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/library/amf_milling_wheat_ebmobm.pdf]


D5. Block Trading / EFP / EFS / Wholesale Trading
Euronext operates several off-book and wholesale trading facilities for derivatives:







Facility
Description




TCS (Trade Confirmation System)
Publication of regulated market trades including negotiated deals, block trades, and VWAP trades; used for post-trade registration and reporting


Block Execution Service (BES)
Enables trading members to report off-book wholesale trades to the exchange for registration


EFP (Exchange for Physical)
Simultaneous exchange of a futures position for a basket of underlying shares weighted according to the index; can be entered directly on the Optiq order book via the AMR (Automated Market Reference) strategy


EFS (Exchange for Swaps)
Exchange of futures for swap positions; eliminates execution risk associated with trading in the Central Order Book


RFC (Request for Cross)
Facility for crossing client orders on-exchange with pre-arranged counterparties; subject to price improvement rules (the cross must be at a price equal to or better than the best bid/offer in the order book)


Auto-match RFC
Automated matching of RFC orders, introduced March 2024



Key Rules: - All wholesale trades must be reported through TCS and are subject to post-trade transparency requirements under MiFID II - Minimum block trade sizes apply per product (defined in Euronext Trading Procedures) - EFP/EFS transactions must involve a genuine related position in the underlying or swap
[Source: Euronext, “Wholesale trading & RFC”, https://www.euronext.com/en/for-investors/financial-derivatives/wholesale-trading] [Source: Euronext, “Euronext Derivatives Markets: Trading Procedures”, https://www.euronext.com/sites/default/files/2025-02/trading_procedures_for_derivatives_-_dsp_fair_value_and_deferred_publication.pdf]

title: Euronext Derivatives
text:
Summary
Euronext Derivatives is a pan-European derivatives exchange operating across seven markets (Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin, Lisbon, Milan, Oslo, Paris) on the unified Optiq trading platform. Its product range spans equity index futures/options, single stock derivatives, commodity futures/options (notably Milling Wheat as a European benchmark), dividend derivatives, total return futures, and newly launched fixed income derivatives.
The period 2023-2024 marked a transformative era with two landmark migrations: (1) Borsa Italiana’s derivatives markets moved to the Optiq platform (April 2024), and (2) all derivatives clearing migrated from LCH SA to Euronext Clearing (completed September 2024). These changes gave Euronext full vertical control over its trading and clearing stack, enabling ~20% margin efficiencies through VaR-based portfolio margining and a unified default fund.
Optiq delivers ~15 microsecond order roundtrip latency with 1M+ messages/second capacity, using SBE and FIX 5.0 protocols from the Bergamo, Italy data center. The exchange continues to expand its product offering with fixed income derivatives (launched September 2025), mini options, and a retail derivatives strategy.

Key Historical Milestones

2005: Tatweer (a Dubai Holding subsidiary) and NYMEX signed a Joint Venture Agreement to launch a commodities exchange in the Middle East
2007 (1 June): Dubai Mercantile Exchange launched with the Oman Crude Oil Futures Contract (OQD) as its flagship product, aiming to establish a transparent crude oil benchmark for the East of Suez market
2007: DME Oman represented approximately 8% of Middle Eastern crude heading to the Asian market at launch
2008: Global financial institutions — Concord Energy, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, Shell, and Vitol — became shareholders of DME; NYMEX was acquired by CME Group, bringing DME into CME Group’s orbit
2009 (February): DME futures contracts migrated from NYMEX ACCESS to the CME Globex electronic trading platform, enabling all three global crude benchmarks (WTI, Brent, DME Oman) to be traded on the same platform
2012 (February): CME Group’s NYMEX division doubled its holding to approximately 50%; Oman Investment Fund held ~29%; Dubai Holding ~9%; institutional investors ~12%
2016: Oman’s Ministry of Oil & Gas adopted DME Oman as the official selling price (OSP) benchmark for Oman crude exports
2018: Dubai’s Supreme Council of Energy adopted DME Oman as the pricing benchmark for Dubai crude OSP
2024 (January): Saudi Tadawul Group (STG) acquired a 32.6% strategic stake in DME Holdings, becoming joint largest shareholder alongside CME Group
2024 (2 September): Official rebranding from Dubai Mercantile Exchange to Gulf Mercantile Exchange (GME)
2024: DME Oman represents 36% of Middle Eastern crude heading to the Asian market (up from 8% in 2007)

[Source: Wikipedia — Dubai Mercantile Exchange; Wikipedia — DME Oman Crude Oil Futures Contract; MarketsWiki — Dubai Mercantile Exchange; Logistics Middle East — Gulf Mercantile Exchange launched; PR Newswire — Saudi Tadawul Group acquires strategic stake]


Strategic Importance
DME Oman is the world’s third major crude oil benchmark alongside ICE Brent (European benchmark) and NYMEX WTI (North American benchmark). Its strategic significance includes:

Asian Sour Crude Pricing: DME Oman is the explicit and sole benchmark for Oman and Dubai crude oil Official Selling Prices (OSPs), which serve as the historically established price markers for Middle Eastern crude oil exports to Asia
Physical Delivery: The contract is the largest physically delivered crude oil contract in the world, providing physical underpinning to price discovery
Geographical Advantage: The export port Mina al Fahal (operated by Petroleum Development Oman) is located in the Gulf of Oman, past the Strait of Hormuz — avoiding geopolitical chokepoint risk
Market Share Growth: From 8% of Middle Eastern crude to Asia in 2007 to 36% by 2024

[Source: GME — About GME; Oxford Energy — Prospects of the DME Oman Crude Oil Futures Contract; Ursa Space — DME Oman crude in the spotlight]

text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Trading Platform — CME Globex
DME/GME products are listed and executed on the CME Globex electronic matching engine, the same platform used for NYMEX WTI and other CME Group energy products. This provides several advantages:

Single Platform Access: Traders can access all three global crude benchmarks (WTI, Brent, DME Oman) on the same electronic platform
Matching Algorithm: Price-time priority (FIFO) — standard CME Globex matching logic
Order Types: Full suite of CME Globex order types available, including limit, market, stop, stop-limit, market-if-touched, and iceberg orders
Spread Trading: Inter-commodity spreads available between OQD and other CME Group energy contracts (e.g., WTI-Oman spread)



3.2 Trade at Marker (TAM)
GME offers a Trade at Marker (TAM) facility: - Allows market participants to execute trades at the daily Oman Marker Price - Marker Window: 16:25 – 16:30 Singapore Time on each trading day - The marker price is determined from trades executed on the nearby contract month (M1) during the Marker Window


3.3 Clearing — CME Clearing

All GME products are cleared by CME Clearing (formerly NYMEX Clearing)
Novation: CME Clearing becomes the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer
Netting: Positions netted at the clearing level across CME Group products
Settlement Banks: Global network of CME Group-approved settlement banks



3.4 Physical Delivery

The Oman Crude Oil Futures Contract is physically delivered
Delivery point: FOB (Free on Board) at the export terminal Mina al Fahal, Muscat, Oman
Front month is always two months forward (e.g., the March contract is the front month during January trading)
Physical delivery underpins the contract’s credibility as a benchmark — unlike financially settled contracts

[Source: CME Group — GME Strategic Partnership; Wikipedia — DME Oman Crude Oil Futures Contract; GME — OQD Contract Summary; Rigzone — DME’s Contracts Migrate to CME Group Trading Platform]

U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC); each sub-exchange (CME, CBOT, NYMEX, COMEX) is a separately registered Designated Contract Market (DCM) and Self-Regulatory Organization (SRO)

Total Listed Instruments
Thousands of futures and options contracts across 7 asset classes on 4 exchanges


Clearing House
CME Clearing — one of the world’s largest central counterparties (CCPs)




Key Historical Milestones

1848: Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) founded — world’s oldest futures exchange; initially traded grain forward contracts
1865: CBOT introduces standardized futures contracts with margin requirements
1882: New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) founded as the Butter and Cheese Exchange of New York
1898: Chicago Butter and Egg Board founded (predecessor of CME)
1919: Reorganized as the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME)
1933: Commodity Exchange Inc. (COMEX) formed in New York through merger of four commodity exchanges
1961: CME introduces first frozen pork belly futures
1972: CME creates the International Monetary Market (IMM) — the world’s first financial futures contracts (seven foreign currencies)
1981: CME introduces Eurodollar futures — first cash-settled futures contract
1982: CME introduces S&P 500 index futures
1987: CME Globex electronic trading system proposed by Leo Melamed and Jack Sandner
1992: CME Globex launched — first global electronic futures trading platform
1994: COMEX and NYMEX merge, with COMEX continuing as a division of NYMEX
2000: CME demutualizes (first U.S. exchange to do so)
2002: CME Holdings goes public on NYSE (December 6)
2007: CME merges with CBOT to form CME Group Inc. (~$8 billion deal, July 12)
2008: CME Group acquires NYMEX Holdings (including COMEX) for ~$8.9 billion (August 22)
2012: CME Group acquires Kansas City Board of Trade for $126 million
2017: Launch of Bitcoin futures on CME

2025: Record annual ADV of 28.1 million contracts; SPAN 2 margin framework rollout for energy and equity contracts; November 2025 — 10-hour outage due to cooling system failure at Aurora data center

title: CME Group
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Types
Opening Auction: - Pre-open period allows order entry and cancellation but no matching - At market open (5:00 PM CT Sunday), accumulated orders are matched using an opening price determination algorithm - The Globex system calculates a single opening price that maximizes matched volume
Closing / Settlement: - Daily settlement prices are determined during defined settlement windows (e.g., 3:14:00–3:15:00 CT for equity indexes, 13:14:00–13:15:00 CT for agriculture) - Settlement committee procedures may be used for illiquid or disrupted markets


3.2 Continuous Trading

Primary trading mechanism: continuous electronic matching on CME Globex
Orders are matched in real-time according to price priority and the applicable matching algorithm
Supports outright orders, spreads (calendar, inter-commodity, butterfly, condor), and implied trading



3.3 Price Discovery

Implied Pricing: CME Globex generates implied orders from combinations of outright and spread orders, enhancing liquidity and tightening bid-ask spreads across related contracts
Implied In: Prices implied from component orders into a spread
Implied Out: Prices implied from a spread and one leg into the other leg



3.4 Order Priority Rules / Matching Algorithms
CME Globex supports multiple matching algorithms, assigned per product:








Algorithm
Description
Example Products




FIFO (Price-Time)
Strict price and time priority; earliest order at best price filled first. Default algorithm.
E-mini S&P 500 futures, crude oil futures, Brent Oil


Pro-Rata
At each price level, incoming quantity is allocated proportionally to resting order sizes. Minimum allocation thresholds apply.
Certain FX futures (EUR/USD, NZD/USD), Eurodollar successors


Split FIFO/Pro-Rata
Configurable split (e.g., 40% FIFO / 60% Pro-Rata). Combines time priority and size incentives.
Grain & oilseed futures and spreads (40/60 split), livestock spreads


Threshold Pro-Rata
Pro-rata allocation only above a quantity threshold; below threshold, FIFO applies
Selected interest rate products


FIFO with LMM
LMM receives a configurable percentage of the aggressor order first; remainder allocated FIFO
Select options markets


Configurable
Exchange can tune parameters: FIFO %, Pro-Rata %, LMM %, top-order priority
Various — parameters differ by product



Key Rules: - Price priority is absolute — better-priced orders always fill first - Within the same price, the selected algorithm (FIFO, Pro-Rata, or hybrid) determines allocation - Minimum allocation sizes prevent excessively small fills - Lead Market Makers may receive priority allocation in options markets
[Source: CME Group, “Matching Algorithm Overview”; Databento, “CME matching algorithms explained”]

4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit
Buy/sell at a specified price or better; unfilled quantity rests on the book


Market with Protection
Executes immediately within a pre-defined “protected range” from the current best price; prevents extreme fills. Replaces traditional market orders on Globex.


Market-Limit
Executes at the best available price; any unfilled quantity converts to a limit order at the execution price


Stop with Protection
Triggered when the stop price trades; once triggered, becomes a market-with-protection order within the protected range


Stop-Limit
Triggered when the stop price trades; once triggered, becomes a limit order at the specified limit price





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Spread Orders
Submit orders for defined spread strategies (calendar, inter-commodity, butterfly, condor, crack, crush, etc.)


One Cancels Other (OCO)
Two orders linked; execution of one cancels the other (ISV-managed, not native Globex)


Bracket Orders
Profit target + stop loss enclosing a position (ISV-managed)


Trailing Stop
Stop price adjusts automatically as the market moves favorably (ISV-managed)


Mass Quote
Allows market makers to submit multiple two-sided quotes in a single message





4.3 Time-in-Force (TIF) Conditions







TIF
Description




Day
Valid for the current trading session only; cancelled at session end


Good Till Cancel (GTC)
Remains active until filled or explicitly cancelled


Good Till Date (GTD)
Remains active until a specified date


Fill and Kill (FAK)
Executes immediately for any available quantity; unfilled portion is cancelled


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be filled in its entirety immediately or cancelled entirely





4.4 Order Modification & Cancellation

Orders can be modified (price, quantity) or cancelled at any time during the trading session via iLink 3
Mass Cancel: Functionality to cancel all working orders for a session, product group, or specific instrument
Cancel on Disconnect: Optional feature that automatically cancels all working orders if the iLink session is disconnected
Self-Trade Prevention (STP): Configurable to prevent matching of orders from the same firm/account

[Source: CME Group, “Futures Order Types”; CME Group Client Systems Wiki, “iLink Order Types”; “Order Types for Futures and Options”]

title: CME Group
text:
5. Trading System Technology — CME Globex

5.1 System Overview







Item
Details




Platform Name
CME Globex


First Launched
1992


Current Architecture
Distributed matching engine architecture with product-level partitioning


Primary Data Center
CyrusOne Aurora facility, Aurora, Illinois (35 miles from Chicago HQ)


Backup / DR Site
CME New York Data Center (NYDC) — geographically disparate


Market Data Throughput
Regularly exceeds 1 Gbps; 10 Gbps connections required for MDP 3.0 multicast (effective March 2026, 1 Gbps no longer supported for multicast)


Order Entry Protocol
iLink 3 (FIX Simple Binary Encoding / FIXP session layer)


Market Data Protocol
MDP 3.0 (FIX SBE-encoded, UDP multicast and TCP unicast)





5.2 Architecture

Matching Engines: Product-partitioned matching engines running on dedicated hardware
Message Bus: High-speed internal messaging infrastructure connecting order entry gateways, matching engines, and market data dissemination
Deterministic Processing: Designed for low-latency, deterministic order processing
Capacity: Handles peak throughput of millions of messages per second across all product groups



5.3 Latency

CME Globex processes trades in sub-millisecond timeframes for most products
Latency is measured gate-to-gate (from order receipt at the gateway to acknowledgment back to the client)
Co-located participants achieve the lowest latency due to proximity to matching engines
Exact median latency figures are not publicly disclosed but are estimated in the low-microsecond range for co-located participants [unverified]



5.4 Protocol History & Evolution







Year
Milestone




1992
CME Globex launched — first global electronic futures platform


1998
Partnership with MATIF (later Euronext)


2004
In-house Globex platform developed (replacing Reuters technology)


2012
iLink 2 (FIX 4.2-based) becomes primary order entry protocol


2019
MDP 3.0 market data platform deployed (replacing legacy MDP/FIX FAST)


2020
iLink 3 (FIX SBE binary) launched — mandatory migration by 2023


2026
iLink SBE schema version 9 effective January 2026; Google Cloud migration begins mid-2026





5.5 Technology Stack

Order Entry: iLink 3 — binary FIX protocol using Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) for order submission; FIXP session layer protocol for session management
Market Data: MDP 3.0 — SBE-encoded messages over UDP multicast (primary) and TCP unicast (conflated)
Drop Copy / Trade Notification: CME STP (Straight Through Processing) FIX API
Reference Data: CME SmartStream
Risk Management GUI: Globex Credit Controls (GC2), Account Management Service (AMS)



5.6 Google Cloud Migration (2026–2028)
CME Group has entered a 10-year strategic partnership with Google Cloud to migrate the entire Globex platform:

Private Google Cloud Chicago Region: A dedicated, private cloud region with co-location facility purpose-built for CME Group’s listed derivatives markets
Timeline: Sandbox environment available mid-2026 (private zones in Dallas region); production market migration from Aurora to private Google Cloud Chicago region beginning mid-2026 with phased approach; full migration targeted by 2028
Connectivity: Co-location facilities will be maintained for ultra-low latency access; existing connectivity methods (GLink, EConnect) to be supported in new environment
Benefits: Enhanced scalability, reduced technical debt, AI-powered analytics, improved disaster recovery via multi-region cloud deployments
Impact on Clients: All Globex clients and vendors must plan for onboarding to the new environment; CME Group is publishing detailed migration roadmaps

[Source: CME Group Client Systems Wiki, “CME Globex on Google Cloud”; A-Team Insight, “Inside CME Group’s Strategic Migration”; Google Cloud Blog]


5.7 Disaster Recovery & Business Continuity

Primary DC: CyrusOne Aurora, Aurora, IL (~428,000 sq ft; 92 MW redundant power)
DR Site: CME New York Data Center (NYDC) — geographically disparate backup
Recovery Model: Real-time data replication between primary and backup environments
RTO: 2-hour Recovery Time Objective for critical services (e.g., EBS Market, eFix)
Market Data Redundancy: Dual feeds (Feed A and Feed B) available from both Aurora and NYDC
DR Testing: Annual DR test scripts published and executed (e.g., CoreSite DR test)
Operational Support: 24/7 follow-the-sun production support model

Notable Incident — November 2025 Outage: On November 28, 2025, a cooling system failure at the CyrusOne Aurora data center caused a 10-hour trading halt — the longest in recent CME history. Temperatures inside the facility exceeded 100 deg F (38 deg C) when multiple chillers failed simultaneously and backup systems failed to engage independently. The incident affected global markets from Tokyo to London across all asset classes. CyrusOne subsequently installed additional redundancy to cooling systems. This event has accelerated CME Group’s cloud migration planning.
[Source: Fortune, “Worldwide markets roiled by data-center snafu”; Bloomberg, “CME Data Center Bolsters Backup Cooling After 10-Hour Outage”]
