Exempt from proxy solicitation rules (Regulation 14A)
Full proxy rules apply


Section 16 reporting
Exempt from insider reporting (Forms 3, 4, 5) and short-swing profit disgorgement
Full Section 16 obligations


Regulation FD
Exempt from selective disclosure rules
Full Regulation FD applies


Corporate governance
May follow home country practices for most listing standards (with disclosure of differences)
Must comply with exchange listing standards


Tender offers
Can use Tier I or Tier II exemptions from US tender offer rules based on US shareholder participation
Full tender offer rules apply



2025 Concept Release on FPI Definition: In 2025, the SEC issued a Concept Release seeking public comment on potential changes to the FPI definition. Key proposals under consideration: - Conditioning FPI eligibility on the issuer being subject to the oversight of a jurisdiction that has signed the IOSCO Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU) or the Enhanced MMoU (130+ jurisdictions are signatories) - Potential tightening of the residency test - Addressing the growth of foreign companies with predominantly US investor bases
[Source: SEC, “Concept Release on Foreign Private Issuer Eligibility”, Release No. 33-11376, 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]


7.2 American Depositary Receipts (ADR) / American Depositary Shares (ADS)
ADRs are negotiable certificates issued by US depositary banks representing shares in a non-US company. They enable US investors to invest in foreign companies through US markets.

SEC Cross-Border Enforcement Powers (Dodd-Frank Enhanced): - Section 929I of the Dodd-Frank Act expanded SEC subpoena powers for cross-border investigations - SEC can bring enforcement actions against foreign entities and individuals with US market connections - SEC regularly cooperates with foreign regulators on insider trading, market manipulation, and accounting fraud investigations


7.4 Regulation S
Regulation S provides a safe harbor from Securities Act registration requirements for offers and sales of securities that occur outside the United States: - Issuer Safe Harbor: Offers and sales must be made in an “offshore transaction” with no “directed selling efforts” in the US - Distribution Compliance Period: Equity securities of US reporting issuers are subject to a 6-month distribution compliance period (1 year for non-reporting issuers) during which flow-back to the US is restricted - Category 1/2/3: Securities are classified based on the likelihood of flow-back to the US, with progressively stricter requirements

8. Recent Changes (2021-2026)

8.1 T+1 Settlement (May 28, 2024)
On February 15, 2023, the SEC adopted rule amendments to shorten the standard settlement cycle for most broker-dealer transactions from T+2 (two business days) to T+1 (one business day). The new cycle took effect on May 28, 2024.
[Source: SEC, “Shortening the Securities Transaction Settlement Cycle”, Press Release 2024-62, May 2024, accessed 2026-04-06]
Key Details:







Item
Description




Effective date
May 28, 2024


Previous cycle
T+2 (since September 5, 2017; before that, T+3)


New cycle
T+1


Applicable transactions
Most secondary market transactions in equities, corporate bonds, unit investment trusts, municipal securities, and financial instruments involving these


Exceptions
Some transactions (e.g., certain firm commitment offerings, securities lending transactions) have different settlement conventions


Goal
Reduce credit, market, and liquidity risks from unsettled trades; reduce margin requirements at clearing agencies



Impact: - DTCC (Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation) modified its systems and processes to support T+1 - Margin requirements at NSCC reduced by an estimated 41% [unverified] - International investors (especially in Asian time zones) faced operational challenges due to compressed timelines for FX settlement and securities delivery - Same-day affirmation rates increased significantly - Discussion of further shortening to T+0 has emerged but no formal proposals as of April 2026


8.2 Tick Size and Access Fee Reform (2024 — Compliance Delayed to November 2026)
On September 18, 2024, the SEC unanimously adopted amendments to Regulation NMS Rules 610 and 612.
[Source: SEC, “SEC Adopts Rules to Amend Minimum Pricing Increments and Access Fee Caps”, Press Release 2024-137, September 2024, accessed 2026-04-06]

Implementation Timeline: - September 18, 2024: Rules adopted - October 14, 2025: D.C. Circuit upholds the rules, denying industry petition for review - October 31, 2025: SEC issues exemptive order delaying tick size and access fee compliance from November 3, 2025 to first business day of November 2026 - May 2026: Round lot/odd-lot definition compliance date (not delayed) - November 2026: Tick size and access fee compliance date
[Source: Sidley Austin, “D.C. Circuit Upholds SEC Tick Size/Fee-Cap Rule”, October 2025, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: SEC, “SEC Issues Exemptive Order Regarding Compliance with Certain Rules Under Regulation NMS”, Press Release 2025-130, October 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.3 Best Execution and PFOF Proposals — Withdrawn (June 2025)
The SEC, under Chair Gary Gensler, proposed four major equity market structure reforms in December 2022 and early 2023:








Proposal
Description
Status (as of April 2026)




Regulation Best Execution (Rules 1100-1102)
Federal best execution standard; heightened obligations for conflicted transactions (PFOF, principal trading)
Withdrawn (June 12, 2025)


Order Competition Rule (Rule 615)
Required certain retail orders to be exposed to order-by-order competition in qualified auctions
Withdrawn (June 12, 2025)


Regulation NMS Amendments (Tick Size/Access Fees)
Variable tick sizes, lower access fee caps
Adopted (September 2024)


Rule 605 Amendments (Execution Quality Disclosure)
Modernized execution quality statistics; expanded to cover broker-dealers
Adopted (March 2024)



On June 12, 2025, the SEC (under Chair Paul Atkins, appointed by President Trump in 2025) formally withdrew 14 outstanding rule proposals, including Regulation Best Execution and the Order Competition Rule. Any future rulemaking on these topics must start anew with a fresh proposal and comment period.
[Source: SEC, “Regulation Best Execution — Withdrawal”, June 2025, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Proskauer, “SEC Formally Withdraws Fourteen Rule Proposals”, June 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]
PFOF Status: - Payment for order flow remains legal in the United States as of April 2026 - The EU agreed to phase out PFOF by mid-2026 under MiFID II reforms - The SEC’s December 2022 Order Competition Rule, which would have required auction exposure for retail orders (indirectly targeting PFOF), was withdrawn in June 2025 - FINRA continues to monitor broker-dealer best execution obligations and order routing disclosures under its existing framework


8.4 Rule 605 Amendments (Execution Quality Disclosure)
Adopted in March 2024, amendments to Rule 605 of Regulation NMS modernize execution quality reporting:

Expanded Coverage: Requires not only market centers but also broker-dealers (including wholesalers) to publish monthly execution quality statistics
Enhanced Metrics: Includes new statistical measures such as effective-over-quoted spread ratios, size improvement, and fill rates
Order Size Categories: Updated to reflect modern trading patterns (including fractional shares and odd lots)
Compliance: Market centers by early 2026; broker-dealers phased in through 2026 [estimated]

9. Comparison with Korean Framework

9.1 Regulatory Structure Comparison








Aspect
United States
South Korea




Primary Regulator

SEC (OCIE) + FINRA (for broker-dealers)

SRO for Broker-Dealers

No equivalent SRO; FSS directly supervises securities firms


Exchange Operator
Multiple competing exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, Cboe, IEX, MEMX, etc.) — each a separate SRO
KRX (Korea Exchange) — single, unified exchange operating KOSPI, KOSDAQ, KONEX markets


Exchange SRO Status
Each exchange is an SRO with regulatory obligations
KRX has market surveillance and listed company oversight functions, but is not a full SRO in the US sense


Enforcement
SEC Enforcement Division (civil/administrative); DOJ (criminal)
FSC/FSS investigation → prosecution referral to prosecutors; fragmented across FSC, FSS, KRX


Dispute Resolution

Financial Dispute Resolution Committee under FSS; courts



[Source: FSC, “Introduction”, fsc.go.kr, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Korea Herald, “Korea weighs SEC-style agency to tackle unfair trading”, 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]


9.2 Market Structure Comparison








Aspect

South Korea

1 (KRX — operating KOSPI, KOSDAQ, KONEX)

Highly fragmented: ~60% on-exchange, ~40% off-exchange (ATSs, wholesalers, OTC) [estimated]
Centralized: virtually all exchange trading on KRX; limited OTC market (K-OTC)

30-40+ active NMS stock ATSs [estimated]
No equivalent dark pool market

Single-venue routing to KRX

KRX provides single consolidated feed (no need for separate tape)

9:00 AM - 3:30 PM KST (pre-market 8:00-9:00, post-market 3:40-4:00)


Settlement Cycle
T+1 (since May 2024)
T+2

Competitive market making (DMMs on NYSE; multiple market makers on Nasdaq)
Limited market maker system on KOSDAQ; competitive auction model on KOSPI





9.3 Circuit Breaker / Volatility Mechanism Comparison








Mechanism
United States
South Korea (KRX)




Market-Wide Circuit Breaker
3 levels: 7% / 13% / 20% decline in S&P 500
3 phases: 8% / 15% / 20% decline in KOSPI or KOSDAQ index


MWCB Halt Duration
Level 1 & 2: 15 min (before 3:25 PM); Level 3: rest of day
Phase 1: 20 min (order entry suspended); Phase 2: 20 min; Phase 3: market closed for day


MWCB Reference
Prior day’s S&P 500 closing value
Prior day’s KOSPI/KOSDAQ closing value


Individual Stock Mechanism
LULD (5%/10%/20% bands depending on tier and time)

Program Trading Control
No specific US equivalent
Sidecar: suspends program trading orders for 5 minutes when KOSPI 200 futures move 5%+


Daily Price Limits

+/- 30% daily price limit from prior close (KOSPI and KOSDAQ)



[Source: Korea Times, “KRX issues circuit breaker on KOSPI trading”, March 2026, accessed 2026-04-06]


9.4 Regulatory Process Comparison








Aspect
United States
South Korea




Rulemaking
Notice-and-comment process (proposed rule → public comment → final rule); SRO rules require SEC approval
FSC/FSS regulatory directives; KRX rules subject to FSC approval


Enforcement Speed
SEC can bring civil actions relatively quickly; average investigation duration ~2-3 years [estimated]
Fragmented investigation across FSC/FSS/KRX leads to ~1 year to sanctions, up to 3 years for court rulings


Market Surveillance
FINRA cross-market surveillance + CAT
KRX Market Surveillance Division + FSS investigation


Audit Trail
CAT (Consolidated Audit Trail) — comprehensive, covers all venues
KRX maintains internal audit trail for all orders on its platform


Investor Protection
SIPC (Securities Investor Protection Corporation) — up to $500,000 per customer
Korea Investor Protection Fund





9.5 Korea’s Ongoing Reform Discussions
As of 2025-2026, South Korea is actively discussing restructuring its financial regulatory framework:

SEC-Style Consolidated Agency: Proposals to create a single agency with both investigative and prosecutorial powers for unfair financial trading (similar to SEC), replacing the current fragmented structure across FSC, FSS, and KRX
Rationale: The SEC model’s “one-stop system” enables swifter response to stock manipulation and insider trading; Korea’s current process involves handoffs between multiple agencies causing procedural delays
Corporate Value-Up Program: Launched in 2024 to address the “Korea Discount” — encouraging companies to improve corporate governance, shareholder returns, and disclosure (influenced by Japan’s similar initiative)

[Source: Korea Herald, “Korea weighs SEC-style agency to tackle unfair trading”, 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]

text:
1. Japan (FSA/JFSA + JPX)

1.1 Regulatory Authority Structure
Japan’s securities market regulation follows a multi-layered structure comprising a government regulator, a surveillance commission, and exchange-level self-regulation.








Authority
Full Name
Role




JFSA
Financial Services Agency of Japan (éèåº)
Primary regulator; rulemaking, licensing, supervision of financial institutions and markets


SESC
Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (è¨¼å¸åå¼ç­ç£è¦å§å¡ä¼)
Investigative and surveillance arm under JFSA; inspections, market monitoring, criminal referrals


JPX-R
Japan Exchange Regulation, Inc.
Self-regulatory organization (SRO) of JPX; conducts listing examinations, trading participant inspections, market surveillance on behalf of TSE and OSE


MOF
Ministry of Finance (è²¡åç)
Oversees Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act (FEFTA); foreign investment screening



[Source: JFSA, “About FSA”, accessed 2026-04-06; JPX, “Self-Regulation”, accessed 2026-04-06]
JFSA was established in 2000 (reorganized from the Financial Supervisory Agency, originally created in 1998) and exercises comprehensive regulatory authority over securities markets, banking, and insurance. The JFSA sets policy, drafts legislation, issues licenses, and supervises compliance. It reports directly to the Prime Minister and the Cabinet.
SESC was established in 1992 as an independent commission within the JFSA (structurally analogous to the relationship between the SEC’s Division of Enforcement and the full Commission in the US). The SESC conducts: - Market surveillance for insider trading, market manipulation, and other unfair trading practices - Inspections of financial instruments business operators (broker-dealers, asset managers) - Investigations of disclosure violations - Recommendations for administrative sanctions and criminal referrals to prosecutors
As of February 2026, the SESC continues to expand its enforcement capabilities, including proposed authority over crypto-asset insider trading under forthcoming FIEA amendments.
[Source: SESC, “Overview”, published February 2026, accessed 2026-04-06]
JPX-R (Japan Exchange Regulation, Inc.) was established as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Japan Exchange Group to serve as the dedicated self-regulatory organization for TSE and Osaka Exchange (OSE). JPX-R is described as the “quality control center” of the exchanges and performs: - Listing examinations: Reviews applications for new listings and continued listing compliance - Listed company compliance: Monitors corporate disclosure, governance compliance, and timely disclosure obligations - Trading participant examination and inspection: Examines and inspects broker-dealers (trading participants) for compliance with exchange rules - Market surveillance: Real-time monitoring of trading activity for manipulation, insider trading, and other anomalies; as of April 2025, JPX-R has introduced AI-powered market surveillance tools
[Source: JPX, “Outline of Self-Regulatory Operations”, accessed 2026-04-06; Mondovisione, “Japan Exchange Regulation Annual Report 2025”, August 2025]


1.2 Key Legislation

Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA / éèåååå¼æ³)
The FIEA (Act No. 25 of 1948, substantially revised in 2006) is the principal statute governing Japan’s securities markets. Originally enacted as the Securities and Exchange Act (modeled on the US Securities Act of 1933 and Securities Exchange Act of 1934), it was comprehensively reformed and renamed the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act in 2006 (effective September 2007) to broaden its scope to cover a wider range of financial instruments beyond traditional securities.
[Source: JFSA, “Financial Instruments and Exchange Act”, accessed 2026-04-06]
Key Provisions:







Area
FIEA Provisions




Registration
Type 1 (securities broker-dealer), Type 2 (fund sales), Investment Advisory, Investment Management â all require JFSA registration


Disclosure
Continuous disclosure (annual securities reports/æä¾¡è¨¼å¸å ±åæ¸, quarterly reports, timely disclosure via TDnet), large shareholding reports (5% rule)


Unfair trading
Prohibition of insider trading (Art. 166, 167), market manipulation (Art. 159), fraudulent acts (Art. 157)


Tender offers
Mandatory TOB rules for acquiring >30% of a listed company (effective May 1, 2026, lowered from one-third)


Market infrastructure
Regulation of financial instruments exchanges, clearing organizations, book-entry transfer institutions


Investor protection
Suitability obligations, segregation of customer assets, conflict-of-interest management





2024 FIEA Amendments (Effective May 1, 2026)
Major amendments enacted in 2024 include:

Tender Offer Bid (TOB) threshold: Lowered from one-third to 30% for mandatory tender offers
“30% Rule” exemption: Small-scale purchases increasing shareholding by less than 0.5% are exempt from TOB, provided no acquisitions occurred in the previous six months
Large shareholding reporting clarifications: Scope of “joint holders” and “acts of material proposal” clarified; format of reports modernized through EDINET updates
Crypto-asset reclassification: JFSA proposed bringing crypto-assets under FIEA oversight (as “Type 1 Financial Instruments”), with legislative drafting targeted for 2026

[Source: Funds-Axis, “Japan’s 2024 FIEA Amendments”, accessed 2026-04-06; DLA Piper, “Recent developments on TOB rules and shareholding transparency in Japan”, January 2026]


Other Key Legislation







Statute
Scope




Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act (FEFTA / å¤çºæ³)
Foreign investment screening; prior notification requirements for investments in designated sectors


Companies Act (ä¼ç¤¾æ³)
Corporate governance, directors’ duties, shareholder rights


Act on Book-Entry Transfer of Company Bonds, Shares, etc.
Dematerialization of securities


Financial Instruments Exchange Act Enforcement Order (æ¿ä»¤)
Detailed implementing rules for FIEA






1.3 Market Structure Rules
Trading Regulations: - Order types: Limit orders, market orders, and various conditional orders processed through the arrowhead trading engine - Price limits: Daily price limits (å¤å¹ å¶é) based on the previous day’s closing price; limits range from +/-30 yen (for stocks under 100 yen) to +/-7,000 yen (for stocks at 30,000-50,000 yen level), with wider limits for higher-priced stocks - Tick sizes: Multi-tiered based on price level and index membership (TOPIX 500 constituents have finer ticks) - Trading unit: Standardized at 100 shares for all listed stocks since October 2018 - Closing auction: Introduced November 2024 with a 5-minute pre-closing period (15:25-15:30) followed by Itayose matching
Listing Requirements: Governed by TSE listing rules and examined by JPX-R. Three main market segments (Prime, Standard, Growth) established in April 2022 market restructuring, plus TOKYO PRO Market for professional investors.


1.4 Market Surveillance
Japan employs a two-tier surveillance model:
JPX-R (First Line): - Real-time surveillance of all trading on TSE and OSE - AI-powered detection systems (introduced April 2025) for identifying suspicious trading patterns - Investigation of potential rule violations by trading participants and listed companies - Referral of suspected violations to SESC
SESC (Second Line): - Conducts formal investigations upon referral from JPX-R or on its own initiative - Authority to recommend administrative monetary penalties (èª²å¾´é) to JFSA - Criminal referrals to public prosecutors for serious violations - Inspection of financial instruments business operators - Cross-border coordination with overseas regulators - In Q4 2024, the SESC investigated inappropriate sharing of customer information between banks and securities affiliates
[Source: JPX, “JPX-R Inspection Plan for FY2025”, March 2025; SESC overview, February 2026]


1.5 Reporting and Disclosure Requirements







Requirement
Details




Annual securities report (æä¾¡è¨¼å¸å ±åæ¸)
Filed via EDINET within 3 months of fiscal year-end; comprehensive financial and operational disclosure


Quarterly reports
Filed within 45 days of each quarter-end


Timely disclosure (é©æéç¤º)
Material information disclosed immediately via TDnet (TSE Timely Disclosure Network); covering decisions, events, and financial results


Large shareholding reports
5% threshold; filing within 5 business days via EDINET; 1% change triggers amendment


Short position reporting
Positions >= 0.2% reported to TSE; positions >= 0.5% publicly disclosed with investor name


Insider trading reporting
Officers, major shareholders, and other insiders must report trading in issuer shares





1.6 Short Selling Regulations
Japan maintains a permanent regulatory framework for short selling under the FIEA and its Enforcement Order:







Rule
Details




Naked short selling ban
Permanent prohibition (originally a temporary crisis measure in 2008, made permanent); sellers must secure securities before selling short


Uptick rule (trigger-based)
Price restriction activated when a stock’s price drops 10% or more from the base price; once triggered, short sales may only be executed at a price above the last traded price; restriction lasts until the end of the next trading day


Marking requirement
All short sale orders must be flagged/marked as short sales


Position reporting
Positions >= 0.2% must be reported to TSE; >= 0.5% publicly disclosed


Aggregation
Short positions calculated on a per-investor, per-issue basis



[Source: JPX, “Short Selling Restrictions”, accessed 2026-04-06; Clifford Chance, “Significant changes to the Japanese short selling regulations”, 2013]


1.7 Foreign Investor Access
Japan’s securities market is generally open to foreign investors with no major restrictions on portfolio investment:

No pre-registration requirement for general portfolio investment in listed securities
No foreign ownership limits on most listed companies (sector-specific restrictions apply under FEFTA for national security sectors such as defense, nuclear energy, telecommunications)
Free repatriation of capital and profits

2025 FEFTA Amendments (effective May 19, 2025): - New “Specified Foreign Investors” classification for investors with obligations to disclose information to foreign governments (particularly targeting entities linked to foreign intelligence services) - Specified Foreign Investors must file prior notification when acquiring >= 1% of listed shares, with no eligibility for exemptions - Enhanced screening for investments in designated sensitive sectors
[Source: Lexology, “Japan’s 2025 FEFTA Amendments”, accessed 2026-04-06; Norton Rose Fulbright, “Global rules on foreign direct investment: Japan”, accessed 2026-04-06]


1.8 Corporate Governance Code and Stewardship Code

Corporate Governance Code (ã³ã¼ãã¬ã¼ãã¬ããã³ã¹ã»ã³ã¼ã)
First introduced in June 2015 and revised in June 2018 and June 2021, the Corporate Governance Code is a principles-based framework jointly published by the JFSA and TSE. It applies on a “comply or explain” basis.
Key Principles: - Board independence: At least one-third independent outside directors for Prime Market companies (majority encouraged) - Cross-shareholding: Companies should disclose rationale and reduce strategic cross-shareholdings; major insurance companies committed to full divestment - Cost of capital awareness: TSE’s January 2023 initiative requesting all Prime and Standard Market companies to disclose plans for improving cost of capital and stock price (PBR initiative); as of March 2025, over 90% of Prime Market companies have disclosed such plans
2025-2026 Revision Process: - JPX and JFSA convened the Expert Panel on the Revision of the Corporate Governance Code (third meeting held April 3, 2026) - Key topics under review include: further strengthening board effectiveness, sustainability disclosure, engagement with shareholders, and cross-shareholding unwinding
[Source: JPX, “Follow-up Council”, accessed 2026-04-06; Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, “Tokyo Stock Exchange Initiative on Cost of Capital”, October 2025]


Stewardship Code (Version 3.0, June 26, 2025)
Japan’s Stewardship Code was first introduced in February 2014 and revised in May 2017 and March 2020. Version 3.0 was published on June 26, 2025.
Key Changes in Version 3.0: - Emphasis on moving from “form to substance” â discouraging box-ticking approaches - Beneficial shareholder transparency: Institutional investors should be prepared to disclose shareholding details to investee companies upon request (Guidance 4-2) - Collaborative engagement: Principle 4.5 encourages joint investor engagement to address governance and sustainability challenges - Principles-based flexibility: Recognition that sustainable value creation cannot be reduced to formulaic approaches
[Source: JFSA, “Revision of the Stewardship Code”, June 26, 2025; ACGA, “Decoding Japan’s New Stewardship Code and 2025 FSA Action Programme”, accessed 2026-04-06]

2. Hong Kong (SFC + HKEX)

2.1 Regulatory Authority Structure
Hong Kong operates under a dual regulatory model combining a statutory regulator (SFC) and exchange-based regulation through HKEX’s Listing Division.








Authority
Full Name
Role




SFC
Securities and Futures Commission (è­å¸åæè²¨äºåç£å¯å§å¡æ)
Statutory regulator; licensing, supervision, enforcement, market conduct


HKEX Listing Division

Government policy bureau; legislative proposals


HKMA

Banking regulator; oversees banks’ securities activities



[Source: SFC, “About the SFC”, accessed 2026-04-06]
SFC was established in 1989 following the 1987 stock market crash. It is an independent statutory body funded by transaction levies and fees. The SFC’s functions include: - Licensing and supervising intermediaries (10 types of regulated activities, including Type 1 â dealing in securities, Type 4 â advising on securities, Type 9 â asset management) - Administering the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) - Market surveillance and enforcement - Regulating collective investment schemes - Approving listing rules and exercising oversight of HKEX’s listing function
HKEX Listing Division acts as the front-line regulator for listed companies under authority delegated by the SFC. The Listing Committee (comprising market practitioners and independent members) makes listing decisions. The SFC retains the power to: - Object to listing applications - Direct HKEX to amend listing rules - Exercise “dual filing” oversight of listing documents


2.2 Key Legislation

Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO / Cap. 571)
The SFO (enacted 2002, effective April 1, 2003) is the principal legislation governing Hong Kong’s securities and futures markets. It consolidated 10 former ordinances into a single comprehensive statute.
[Source: SFC, “Securities and Futures Ordinance”, accessed 2026-04-06; Hong Kong e-Legislation, Cap. 571]

Each RA requires a separate license from the SFC. Individuals carrying out regulated activities must be registered as licensed representatives.


Other Key Legislation

2.3 Market Structure and Licensing
Market Structure: - Main Board: Premier market for established companies (HK$500 million minimum market cap at IPO) - GEM (Growth Enterprise Market): Growth board for smaller companies - Chapter 18A (2018): Pre-revenue biotech companies - Chapter 18B (2022): SPAC listings (minimum HK$1 billion IPO proceeds; de-SPAC within 36 months) - Chapter 18C (2023): Specialist Technology Companies (commercial: HK$4 billion min cap after September 2024 temporary reduction from HK$6 billion; pre-commercial: HK$8 billion, reduced from HK$10 billion, valid until August 2027) - Chapter 19C: Secondary listings of qualifying overseas-listed companies
Licensing: All intermediaries conducting regulated activities must be licensed by the SFC. Firms are subject to ongoing capital requirements, conduct rules, and regular examinations.


2.4 Stock Connect with Mainland China
Stock Connect is a landmark cross-border market access scheme linking Hong Kong with the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges.

Key Rules: - Daily quota: Northbound daily quota of RMB 52 billion; Southbound daily quota of HK$42 billion (expanded multiple times since launch) - Settlement: T+0 for Northbound (pre-delivery of shares required); T+2 for Southbound - Pre-trade checking: Northbound investors must have sufficient shares before selling (no naked short selling) - Short selling via Stock Connect: Covered short selling of eligible A-shares is permitted for Northbound investors, subject to SSE/SZSE requirements including front-end monitoring and volume limits - Holiday arrangement: Trading only occurs on days when both markets are open and settlement is available in both markets
[Source: HKEX, “Stock Connect”, accessed 2026-04-06; IFEC, “Trading rules and arrangement”, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.5 Market Surveillance
SFC Market Surveillance: - Conducts real-time monitoring of trading activity across all SEHK-listed securities - Investigates suspected insider dealing, market manipulation, false trading, and other market misconduct - In Q3 2024, the SFC conducted 468 investigations spanning corporate disclosure, insider dealing, intermediary misconduct, and market manipulation - Dual enforcement routes: Market misconduct can be prosecuted through either (a) the Market Misconduct Tribunal (civil route) or (b) criminal prosecution before the courts
Recent Enforcement Highlights (2025): - In July 2025, joint SFC-ICAC operation targeted a market manipulation syndicate involving listed company executives; searches at 14 locations, multiple arrests - SFC probed alleged insider dealing involving staff at HKEX and SFC themselves, concerning leaks about dozens of listed companies [Source: Bloomberg, September 2025] - Market Sounding Guidelines took effect in May 2025, requiring licensed persons to implement information barrier protocols during market soundings (block trades, private placements)
[Source: SFC, “Regulatory update”, accessed 2026-04-06; A&O Shearman, “Hong Kong White-Collar/Financial Crime”, 2025]


2.6 Short Selling Rules
Hong Kong permits only covered short selling â naked short selling is a criminal offence under Part XIV of the SFO.







Rule
Details




Covered short selling only
Sellers must have a presently exercisable and unconditional right to vest the securities before executing a short sale


Designated securities
Short selling permitted only for securities on the HKEX “Designated Securities Eligible for Short Selling” list (updated regularly; covers high-liquidity stocks)


Tick rule
Short sales must be executed at or above the best current ask price


Reporting
Net short positions >= 0.02% of issued shares (or HK$30 million) in specified shares must be reported to the SFC weekly


Stock Connect
Covered short selling of eligible A-shares permitted for Northbound investors, subject to SSE/SZSE volume limits


Penalties
Illegal short selling (naked) can result in criminal prosecution, fines up to HK$100,000, and imprisonment up to 2 years



[Source: HKEX, “Regulated Short Selling”, accessed 2026-04-06; SFC, “Aggregated reportable short positions”, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.7 Foreign Investor Access
Hong Kong operates one of the most open securities markets in Asia:

No pre-registration requirement for foreign investors
No foreign ownership limits on Hong Kong-listed securities (mainland China A-shares via Stock Connect are subject to aggregate and daily quotas)
Free capital movement: No foreign exchange controls; HKD freely convertible
Tax advantages: No capital gains tax, no dividend withholding tax on Hong Kong-listed securities, stamp duty of 0.1% per side (reduced from 0.13% in November 2023)
Settlement: T+2 for CCASS (Central Clearing and Settlement System) securities

3. Singapore (MAS + SGX)

3.1 Regulatory Authority Structure
Singapore adopts an integrated regulatory model where the central bank (MAS) serves as the single financial regulator, with SGX RegCo providing exchange-level self-regulation.








Authority
Full Name
Role




MAS
Monetary Authority of Singapore
Integrated financial regulator (central bank + securities regulator + banking regulator + insurance regulator); licensing, supervision, enforcement, monetary policy


SGX RegCo
SGX Regulation (SGX RegCo Pte. Ltd.)
Independent regulatory subsidiary of SGX Group; listing regulation, market surveillance, member supervision


CAD

Criminal investigation of financial crimes (works jointly with MAS)



[Source: MAS, “About MAS”, accessed 2026-04-06]
MAS is unique among major financial regulators as it combines central banking functions with securities regulation, banking supervision, and insurance oversight in a single institution. Established in 1971, MAS administers the Securities and Futures Act (SFA) and has authority to: - License and supervise capital markets services (CMS) license holders - Investigate and enforce market misconduct - Approve exchange and clearing house rules - Issue prohibition orders against individuals - Impose civil penalties for market abuse
SGX RegCo was established in 2016 and began operations in 2018 as an independent regulatory subsidiary of SGX Group. It maintains operational independence from SGX’s commercial functions and is governed by a Regulatory Conflicts Committee. SGX RegCo’s functions include: - Reviewing listing applications and administering listing rules for Mainboard and Catalist - Monitoring ongoing compliance of listed companies - Conducting market surveillance - Supervising trading members (securities and derivatives)
[Source: SGX, “About SGX RegCo”, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.2 Key Legislation

Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA)
The SFA (Act 42 of 2001, as amended) is Singapore’s principal legislation governing capital markets. It was significantly amended in 2005 and 2012, with further amendments ongoing.

3.3 Market Structure and Licensing
Market Segments: - Mainboard: Primary market for established companies; quantitative entry criteria including profit track record and/or market capitalization; minimum 25% public float - Catalist: Sponsor-supervised growth board for SMEs; no quantitative entry criteria set by SGX (sponsor determines suitability) - GlobalQuote: For secondary listings of foreign companies - Global Listing Board (proposed): Announced November 19, 2025 â a new dual-listing bridge between SGX and Nasdaq for companies with market cap above SGD 2 billion
[Source: MAS, “MAS Proposes Legislative and Regulatory Changes to Facilitate Dual Listings on Global Listing Board”, January 2026]
Global Listing Board â Key Proposed SFA Amendments (consultation closed February 8, 2026): - Single prospectus for dual listings on SGX and Nasdaq - Aligned IPO timelines between US and Singapore - Safe harbours for forward-looking statements, share repurchases, and pre-determined trades - Retail investors permitted to engage earlier in the IPO process


3.4 Market Surveillance
MAS-SGX Joint Surveillance Framework:
MAS and SGX RegCo operate a coordinated surveillance framework: - SGX RegCo conducts first-line real-time market surveillance using automated systems to detect unusual trading patterns - MAS conducts second-line oversight and formal enforcement investigations - MAS-SGX Trade Surveillance Practice Guide: Published jointly by MAS and SGX, provides guidance on trade surveillance practices for intermediaries
Enforcement Actions (2025): - In Q4 2025, MAS opened 163 review and investigation cases, with 58 cases pertaining to market misconduct (insider trading and false trading) - Civil penalty of S$50,000 imposed on Tan Tee Beng for insider trading in Tee International and Tee Land shares - Civil penalty of S$137,000 imposed on Ang Yew Jin Eugene for insider trading in Alpha Energy Holdings shares - Criminal charges filed against Xie Jianfeng for insider trading and deception under the SFA (October 2025)
Enforcement Priorities (2025-2026): MAS outlined enforcement priorities including: market misconduct (insider trading, false trading), intermediary misconduct, and technology-related risks.
[Source: MAS, “Key Enforcement Actions Taken by MAS in Q4 2025”, January 2026; Sidley Austin, “Monetary Authority of Singapore Outlines Enforcement Priorities for 2025-26”, April 2025]

Requirement
Details




Annual report
Listed companies must issue annual reports within 4 months (Mainboard) or 5 months (Catalist) of fiscal year-end

Quarterly reporting required for companies with market cap < SGD 75 million on Mainboard; half-yearly for others; Catalist: half-yearly

Prospectus
Required for public offers of securities under Part XIII of the SFA





3.6 Foreign Investor Access
Singapore maintains one of the most open capital markets in Asia:

No pre-registration requirement for foreign investors
No foreign ownership limits on SGX-listed securities (sector-specific restrictions may apply under other legislation, e.g., banking, media)
Free capital movement: No foreign exchange controls; SGD freely convertible

text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Opening Auction (Market on Open / MOO): - Conducted at 9:30 AM ET as a single-price call auction - During the Pre-Open session (7:00 AM â 9:30 AM), the Calculated Opening Price (COP) is continuously broadcast and updated as orders are entered/modified - COP determination logic (in priority order): 1. Price at which the most shares may be executed 2. If tied, the price that leaves the least imbalance 3. If still tied, the price closest to the previous trading day’s closing price - When trades execute in the opening auction, the COP sets the last sale price - If no trades execute at the opening, the previous day’s closing price sets the opening price - Eligible order types: Market on Open (MOO), Limit on Open (LOO), and regular limit orders carried forward
Closing Auction (Market on Close / MOC): - Electronic call market that establishes the official closing price for eligible TSX-listed securities - MOC imbalance information disseminated beginning at 3:40 PM ET - At 4:00 PM ET, the Calculated Closing Price (CCP) is determined by combining the MOC Book orders with the Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) orders - CCP uses similar logic to the COP: maximum volume, minimum imbalance, closest to last sale - Price Movement Extension (PME): If the CCP would violate the PME range (greater of 5 trading increments or PME percentage from the VWAP of the last 20 minutes and the last board-lot sale price), a PME period is initiated between 4:00 PM and 4:10 PM to allow additional order entry and price discovery - MOC facility provides equal access in setting the closing price and reduces closing price volatility [Source: TSX MOC FAQ]
Volatility Auctions: - When a Single Stock Circuit Breaker (SSCB) is triggered, a 5-minute trading halt occurs across all Canadian marketplaces - Re-opening after a halt follows an auction-like process similar to the opening mechanism


3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven model: Fully electronic Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) with price-time priority
Priority rules:

Price priority: Best-priced orders execute first
Time priority: At the same price level, earlier orders execute first (FIFO)
Broker preferencing: TSX supports intentional crosses and broker preferencing under certain conditions as defined by UMIR

RT participation: Registered Traders may receive a participation entitlement allowing them to trade against a fraction of incoming orders with execution priority in their assigned securities
Dark interaction: Dark orders (Dark Limit, Dark Pegged) are fully integrated within the order book but not displayed; they interact with incoming orders after all displayed volume at the same or better price



3.3 Price Discovery

Pre-open: COP broadcast continuously from 7:00 AM â 9:30 AM ET, providing indicative opening price and imbalance data
MOC imbalance: Imbalance information published from 3:40 PM ET; PME mechanism ensures closing price reflects genuine supply/demand
RT role: Registered Traders maintain continuous two-sided markets in their assigned securities, supporting orderly price discovery
Bypass orders: Orders with a bypass flag can avoid interaction with non-displayed volume (including undisclosed iceberg volume, dark orders, and RT participation), enabling transparent price discovery for participants who prefer displayed liquidity only

Primary facility: TMX Data Centre, 3500 Steeles Avenue East, Markham, Ontario

Up to 1.8 MW of power capacity
Power density of 150 watts per square foot, supporting high-density computing
Co-location cabinets are pre-wired to receive low latency data feeds directly from TMX trading engines
Direct high-speed access to TSX, TSXV, and Montreal Exchange trading engines and market data feeds
Available to market participants as well as technology/network service providers to market participants

FIX 4.3 (order entry)

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Single Stock Circuit Breaker (SSCB)








Time Period
Trigger Threshold
Action




9:30 AM â 9:50 AM (first 20 minutes)
20% price move in a 5-minute period (and >= 40 trading increments)
5-minute trading halt across all Canadian marketplaces


9:50 AM â 3:30 PM (core session)
10% price move
5-minute trading halt across all Canadian marketplaces


All hours
20% price move in a 5-minute period (and >= 40 trading increments)
5-minute trading halt across all Canadian marketplaces




SSCB applies to both upward and downward price movements
Administered by CIRO (Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization)
When triggered, the halt applies across ALL Canadian equity marketplaces simultaneously, not just the venue where the trigger occurred
After the halt period, trading resumes via an auction-like re-opening process [Source: CIRO Guidance on Single-Stock Circuit Breakers]



8.2 Market-Wide Circuit Breaker (MWCB)








Level
Trigger
Halt Duration




Level 1
7% decline in S&P/TSX Composite Index (or S&P 500 if U.S. markets open)
15-minute halt


Level 2
13% decline
15-minute halt


Level 3
20% decline
Trading halted for remainder of the day




When U.S. markets are open, Canadian MWCBs are harmonized with U.S. triggers (based on S&P 500 declines)
When U.S. markets are not open, the S&P/TSX Composite Index is used to determine MWCB thresholds
Circuit breaker levels are recalculated daily based on the prior day’s closing price [Source: CIRO Market Volatility guidance, RBC]



8.3 Pre-Trade Risk Controls

Cancel on Disconnect (COD): Mandatory feature; automatically cancels all open orders if the trading session disconnects
Pre-Trade Risk Management Solution: TMX offers a comprehensive risk management system enabling participants to apply risk checks, trading limits, and controls to their order flow; provides real-time monitoring of committed capital, open order exposure, and intraday market risk across all major Canadian equity venues [Source: Markets Media]
Price reasonability controls: TMX systems validate incoming order prices against control parameters; orders significantly outside reasonable price ranges are rejected
Montreal Exchange controls (MX):

“X” limit: Price filter based on calculated control price; orders above/below the limit are automatically rejected
“Y” limit: Narrower price limit validating potential execution price of the next executable order
Maximum volume thresholds: Validate incoming order sizes [Source: MX Exchange Market Thresholds and Controls]

Short sale regulations: Subject to UMIR short sale rules; CIRO monitors short selling activity across Canadian marketplaces
Erroneous trade policy: TMX can cancel clearly erroneous trades under defined circumstances



8.4 Regulatory Halts

Material news halt: TSX can halt trading in individual securities pending dissemination of material information
CIRO-coordinated halts: CIRO can coordinate halts across all Canadian marketplaces
SSCB halt: Automatic 5-minute halt triggered by circuit breaker thresholds (see Section 8.1)
MWCB halt: Market-wide trading suspension (see Section 8.2)

title: TMX Group / Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Regulatory Structure
Canada’s securities regulation is unique in that it operates under a provincial/territorial model rather than a single national regulator:







Regulator
Role




Ontario Securities Commission (OSC)
Lead regulator for TMX Group and TSX; recognizes TSX, TSXV, TSX Alpha, and MX as exchanges


Canadian Securities Administrators (CSA)
Council of provincial/territorial securities regulators; coordinates and harmonizes regulation across Canada


Provincial/Territorial Securities Commissions
Each province/territory has its own securities regulator (e.g., BCSC, ASC, AMF in Quebec); all participate in the CSA framework


Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO)
National self-regulatory organization (SRO); oversees investment dealers, mutual fund dealers, and market integrity; formed January 1, 2023 from merger of IIROC and MFDA; renamed CIRO on June 1, 2023





9.2 CIRO Oversight (formerly IIROC)

Market integrity: CIRO administers and enforces the Universal Market Integrity Rules (UMIR), which apply to all Canadian equity marketplaces
Cross-marketplace surveillance: CIRO oversees ALL equity market activity across Canadian marketplaces, including exchanges and alternative trading systems (ATS)
Cross-asset surveillance: By integrating equity, debt, and MX-listed derivatives data, CIRO can detect potential cross-market manipulation
Enforcement: When evidence of rule violations is found, CIRO refers cases to its Enforcement team or to provincial/territorial securities regulators for further investigation and possible disciplinary action
Insider trading: Potential insider trading matters are referred to provincial/territorial securities regulators
Registration delegation: Effective April 1, 2025, the OSC delegates the registration function for investment dealers, mutual fund dealers, and futures commission merchants to CIRO, though the OSC retains concurrent authority under an enhanced risk-based oversight framework [Source: OSC, CIRO]



9.3 TMX Self-Regulatory Functions

TMX Group exchanges operate under recognition orders issued by provincial securities regulators
TSX and TSXV maintain their own rule books (TSX Rule Book effective January 13, 2026; TSXV Policy Manual) governing listing standards, trading rules, and issuer obligations
Market regulation (trade surveillance and enforcement) is outsourced to CIRO under agreements with the marketplaces
TMX provides market surveillance data feeds to CIRO for monitoring purposes



9.4 Key Regulatory Instruments

UMIR (Universal Market Integrity Rules): National rules governing trading conduct on all Canadian equity marketplaces; includes provisions on manipulative trading, short selling, best execution, and market making
National Instrument 21-101 (Marketplace Operation): Governs the operation of exchanges and ATS in Canada
National Instrument 23-101 (Trading Rules): Establishes best execution obligations and order protection rules
TSX Rule Book: Exchange-specific rules governing listing, trading, and participation on TSX

11.1 CIRO Formation (2023)

On January 1, 2023, the Investment Industry Regulatory Organization of Canada (IIROC) and the Mutual Fund Dealers Association of Canada (MFDA) amalgamated to form the New Self-Regulatory Organization of Canada

11.2 T+1 Settlement (2024)

Canada transitioned to T+1 (trade date plus one business day) settlement on May 27, 2024, in coordination with the United States and Mexico
Reduces counterparty and systemic risk by shortening the settlement cycle from T+2

title: Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Call Auction (9:15â9:25):

Orders entered during 9:15â9:20 may be submitted and cancelled.
During 9:20â9:25, orders may be submitted but not cancelled (prevents manipulation of the indicative opening price).
At 9:25, the system determines the opening price via a single-price auction algorithm that maximizes executable volume â the price at which the greatest number of shares can be traded.
Unexecuted orders automatically carry forward into the continuous trading session at 9:30.

Closing Call Auction (14:57â15:00):

Introduced in 2006, replacing the previous method (last-trade closing price).
During this 3-minute window, orders are accepted but cannot be cancelled.
At 15:00, a single-price auction determines the closing price using the same volume-maximization algorithm as the opening auction.
This mechanism reduces susceptibility to closing price manipulation compared to last-trade methods.

Intraday Auction: Not applicable â SZSE uses continuous matching during regular trading hours.
Volatility Auction: Not currently implemented. China relied on market-wide circuit breakers briefly in January 2016 (linked to CSI 300 Index, with 5% and 7% triggers), but these were suspended after only 4 trading days due to exacerbating volatility. Individual stock price limits (Section 8) serve as the primary volatility control mechanism.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market â all trades matched by the exchange’s electronic order book.
Price-time priority: Orders matched first by best price, then by earliest time of entry at the same price level.
No quote-driven or hybrid mechanism for equities (unlike HKEX or LSE).



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening price: Determined by call auction at 9:25; if no trades occur, the opening price is carried from the most recent transaction price.
Closing price: Determined by closing call auction at 15:00.
Intraday price: Continuous matching on price-time priority during regular sessions.
The T+1 settlement rule and daily price limits (Section 8) significantly constrain intraday price discovery compared to western markets, reducing speculative volatility but also limiting rapid price adjustment to new information.

Background: In January 2016, CSRC introduced market-wide circuit breakers linked to the CSI 300 Index with 5% (15-min halt) and 7% (full halt) triggers. They were activated on January 4 and January 7, 2016, exacerbating panic selling (the “magnet effect” â traders rushed to sell before the circuit breaker triggered). CSRC suspended the mechanism after just 4 operating days. Individual stock daily price limits remain the primary risk control mechanism.

title: SIX Swiss Exchange (SIX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Begins at 09:00 CET following a pre-opening period (from 06:00). Orders accumulate and the matching algorithm determines the price at which the maximum volume can execute. A random end period (typically up to 2 minutes) prevents manipulation of the uncrossing moment
Closing Auction: At 17:20 CET for equities (17:30 for ETFs/ETPs), continuous trading halts and a closing auction call period begins. The closing price is determined by maximum executable volume principle. Followed by a random end period
Volatility Auction (Stop Trading): Triggered when a potential execution would breach Stop Trading Range thresholds. Continuous trading is suspended and a call auction is initiated for orderly price discovery. Duration is typically 5 minutes, followed by random end period
Trading-At-Last: After the closing auction uncrossing, a Trading-At-Last session allows additional volume to execute at the established closing price



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-Driven Market: Primary mechanism is a Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) with price-time priority
SwissAtMid (MPOB): Non-displayed Mid-Point Order Book operating in parallel with the CLOB; executions at midpoint of CLOB best bid/offer; size-time priority (not price-time); Large-in-Scale (LIS) and Reference Price Waiver orders eligible
Dual Order Book: For SwissAtMid-eligible securities, SIX maintains both the lit CLOB and the dark MPOB within the same On Book Matcher (OBM)
Limit Plus and Iceberg Plus: Special order types that simultaneously access both the lit CLOB and SwissAtMid, with dynamic price alignment



3.3 Price Discovery

Price discovery occurs primarily through the opening and closing auctions and continuous order book interaction on the CLOB
The uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume, then minimizes surplus, then references the last traded price or prior auction price to determine the final auction price
All market orders must be executable at the opening auction price (if sufficient contra-side liquidity exists)
Reference prices for Stop Trading thresholds are derived from auction uncrossing prices and dynamically updated during continuous trading



3.4 Order Priority

CLOB: Strict price-time priority; best price first, then earliest timestamp at same price
SwissAtMid (MPOB): Size-time priority; larger orders have priority at the midpoint price, then earliest timestamp

4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Order to buy/sell at a specified price or better; rests on the book if not immediately matched


Market Order
Executes at the best available price; unmatched portion remains on the book as a market order (converted behavior depends on trading period)


Market-to-Limit Order
Executes at the best available price, then converts any remaining quantity to a limit order at the execution price [unverified]





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Iceberg Order
Only the visible peak quantity is displayed; hidden reserve replenishes automatically as the visible portion fills


Limit Plus Order
Simultaneously accesses the lit CLOB and SwissAtMid; arrives in the CLOB as a normal limit order pegged to the passive side of the book; dynamic price alignment


Iceberg Plus Order
Combines iceberg functionality with SwissAtMid access; hidden reserve and midpoint execution


Stop Loss Order
Triggered when market reaches a specified trigger price; enters the order book as a market order upon activation


Stop Limit Order
Triggered when market reaches a specified trigger price; enters the order book as a limit order upon activation


Market-on-Close Order
Eligible to participate in the closing auction only


Midpoint Order (SwissAtMid)
Executes at the midpoint of the CLOB best bid/offer in the non-displayed MPOB





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF
Description




Good for Day (GFD)
Order valid for the current trading day only; cancelled at end of trading; can be entered, amended, or deleted during all trading periods except post-trading


Good till Cancelled (GTC)
Order remains active until executed or explicitly cancelled (maximum duration set by exchange)


Good till Date (GTD)
Order valid until a specified expiry date


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Execute as much as possible immediately; any remaining quantity is cancelled


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be executed in full immediately or the entire order is cancelled


At the Open (ATO)
Valid only during the opening auction


At the Close (ATC)
Valid only during the closing auction





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled during all trading periods except post-trading
Price amendments that improve priority result in a new timestamp (loss of time priority)
Quantity reduction does not affect time priority
During auction call periods, orders can be entered, amended, and cancelled but no matching occurs
Mass cancellation functionality available through trading interface
Stop Loss and Stop Limit orders can be entered, modified, or cancelled at any time during the trading day

Licensed from Nasdaq; sub-11 microsecond latency; SIX was the first exchange globally to deploy X-stream INET


2027 (planned)
Equinox (Aquis Equinox)
Next-generation platform; equity migration planned H1 2027; fixed income/structured products 2028; derivatives to follow





Technology Stack

Matching Engine: X-stream INET (Nasdaq technology); C/C++ based
Network Protocol: TCP/IP for trading gateways; UDP/IP multicast for market data
Trading Interfaces: OUCH (binary, lowest latency), FIX 4.4 (STI – Standard Trading Interface), QTI (Quote Trading Interface for market makers)
Market Data: ITCH Market Data Interface (IMI) for ultra-low latency; SIX MDDX for broader distribution
Hardware: Hosted in Equinix data center in Zurich
Microwave Network: SIX operates its own international ultra-low latency microwave network – the first regulated exchange in Europe to do so; connects Zurich to key European financial centers



Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity

Primary data center in Zurich (Equinix)
Secondary/disaster recovery site with failover capability [specific location not publicly disclosed]
Dual redundant market data feeds
Business continuity plans tested regularly as required by FINMA regulations
Notable incident: July 31, 2024 – trading halted due to technical issues; services subsequently restored [source: Bloomberg]

6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols








Protocol
Description
Use Case




ITCH Market Data Interface (IMI)
Binary protocol providing order-by-order full depth market data; highest speed, lowest latency
Ultra-low latency market data for algorithmic and high-frequency trading; available for both equities OBM and non-equities OBM


SIX MDDX
SIX’s proprietary market data distribution service; consolidated real-time data
Broader market data distribution to data vendors, trading firms, and institutional clients


FIX Market Data
Market data via FIX protocol (within STI)
Firms preferring standardized FIX connectivity for trading and data


Exfeed
Real-time data feed service from SIX
Commercial data distribution to end users, data vendors, and financial institutions globally





6.2 Data Levels

Level 1: Best bid/offer (BBO), last trade price, volume; available real-time or delayed (typically 15-minute delay for non-subscribers)
Level 2 / Full Depth: Full order book depth via ITCH IMI; order-by-order granularity for all visible price levels
SwissAtMid Data: Non-displayed order book; trade prints published post-execution but no pre-trade transparency (dark pool by design)



6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

Market data disseminated via UDP multicast for ITCH IMI (lowest latency)
SIX MDDX distributed through co-location, proximity services, and access points
Co-location in Zurich Equinix data center provides lowest-latency access to both trading and market data
Microwave connectivity available for ultra-low latency data transmission to European financial centers (London, Frankfurt)
Third-party data vendors (Refinitiv/LSEG, Bloomberg, ICE) redistribute SIX market data globally



6.4 Historical Data

Historical tick data available through SIX Financial Information
End-of-day data, corporate actions, and reference data accessible via SIX data products
Business Intelligence & Statistics service offers tailor-made data analyses at CHF 250/hour
Volume and turnover statistics published monthly on SIX website
Academic and research data access available

text:
7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Trading Participants: Must be authorized financial institutions (banks, securities dealers) licensed by FINMA or a recognized equivalent foreign regulator
Onboarding: Institutions can start trading within approximately four weeks through SIX’s onboarding process
Trader Registration: All persons carrying out trading activities must be registered; must pass SIX Exchange Trader Exam to obtain a trader license
Sponsored Access: Permitted; sponsoring participant responsible for the sponsored user’s activity; monthly fee of CHF 1,000 per sponsored user
Remote Membership: Available to foreign-domiciled institutions subject to equivalent home-country regulation
Number of Participants: ~140 trading participants from ~20 countries [unverified]



7.2 Connection Methods







Method
Description




Co-Location
Direct fiber connection in Zurich Equinix data center; fastest access (~10.6 us latency); 10 Gbps bandwidth


Microwave
SIX-owned ultra-low latency microwave network connecting Zurich to London and Frankfurt; faster than fiber for long-distance


Proximity / Access Point
Hosted connectivity at designated proximity sites outside the primary data center


Leased Line / WAN
Dedicated network connections for participants not co-located


Deutsche Borse N7 Connectivity
SIX Swiss Exchange connectivity available through Deutsche Borse’s network infrastructure for participants already connected to Xetra [source: deutsche-boerse.com]





7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

Primary Data Center: Equinix data center, Zurich, Switzerland
Co-Location: Direct cross-connect to SWXess on-book matchers for both equities and non-equities
Bandwidth: 10 Gbps connections available
Latency: Average round-trip latency of 10.6 microseconds from co-location
Microwave: Proprietary microwave network – first regulated European exchange to own and operate such infrastructure; provides lower end-to-end latency than fiber between Zurich and London/Frankfurt because microwave signals travel at the speed of light through air on a more direct path



7.4 API Protocols







Protocol
Use Case




OUCH Trading Interface (OTI)
Binary protocol for price takers, proprietary traders, and sponsored users; lowest latency; industry-standard OUCH protocol


Standard Trading Interface (STI)
FIX 4.4 protocol; basic trading and reporting capability; not designed for high-speed/high-volume trading


Quote Trading Interface (QTI)
Dedicated interface for market makers and liquidity providers; quote entry, amendment, cancellation


ITCH Market Data Interface (IMI)
Binary market data protocol; highest speed; order-by-order depth


FIX Drop Copy
FIX-based real-time copy of executions and order updates; used by sponsoring participants for monitoring sponsored user order flow





7.5 Certification / Testing

Conformance Testing: Required before production access; validates correct message handling, order management, and error handling for each interface (OTI, STI, QTI)
Test Environment: SIX provides test/simulation environments replicating production functionality
Trader Exam: Mandatory SIX Exchange Trader Exam covering trading rules, order types, market structure; separate exams for traders and reporting agents
Release Testing: Participants notified in advance of SWXess maintenance releases (e.g., SMR15) with testing windows provided

title: SIX Swiss Exchange (SIX)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

SIX Swiss Exchange does not impose fixed daily price limits (no hard up/down limit)
Uses dynamic Stop Trading Ranges to detect abnormal price movements
Stop Trading parameters are defined per instrument and reviewed periodically by SIX Exchange Regulation



8.2 Circuit Breakers (Stop Trading)








Type
Trigger
Response




Stop Trading (Avalanche)
If the potential follow-up price deviates by more than the Stop Trading Range from the reference price within a predefined Avalanche Time period (typically 10 seconds)
Continuous trading automatically suspended; instrument enters a 5-minute volatility auction (call period), followed by random end period


Stop Trading “No Quote”
If no quotes exist in the order book for a predefined period even though executable orders exist on both sides
Stop Trading condition imposed for a predefined Stop Time Duration


Opening/Closing Auction Extension
If the indicative uncrossing price of an auction would breach Stop Trading thresholds
Auction call period is extended



Specific Stop Trading Range percentages vary by instrument and liquidity class. Typical ranges for SMI blue chips are narrower than for small caps [specific percentages set in Trading Parameters Guideline, updated periodically by SER].


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Value / Quantity: Configurable per firm/gateway; orders exceeding threshold are rejected
Price Reasonability Checks: Orders with prices significantly deviating from the current market may be rejected or flagged
Message Throttling: Rate limits on order submissions per second to prevent system overload
Sponsored Access Controls: Sponsoring participants must monitor and control sponsored user order flow in real time via FIX Drop Copy; pre-trade risk limits enforced
Self-Trade Prevention: Mechanisms to prevent a participant from trading against its own orders [unverified]



8.4 Kill Switch

Trading participants and SIX market operations can cancel all outstanding orders for a participant in emergency situations
Sponsoring participants have the ability to disable sponsored user access
SIX market operations can intervene in extraordinary circumstances to halt trading in individual instruments or the entire market

title: SIX Swiss Exchange (SIX)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

FINMA (Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority): Primary regulator; authorizes SIX Swiss Exchange as a stock exchange under the Financial Market Infrastructure Act (FMIA)
SIX Exchange Regulation AG (SER): Independent self-regulatory body established by SIX; responsible for listing rules, trading rules, real-time market surveillance, and enforcement; operates at arm’s length from SIX’s commercial operations
Swiss National Bank (SNB): Oversight of systemically important financial market infrastructure



9.2 Key Regulations

Financial Market Infrastructure Act (FMIA / FinfraG): Primary legislation governing financial market infrastructure in Switzerland; enacted 2016; covers exchanges, trading venues, CCPs, CSDs
Financial Institutions Act (FinIA): Governs licensing of financial intermediaries
Stock Exchange Act (BEHG): Historical legislation (largely superseded by FMIA) on stock exchange and securities trading
Swiss Code of Obligations: Corporate law requirements for listed companies
SIX Listing Rules: Detailed admission, maintenance, and disclosure requirements for listed issuers
SIX Trading Rules: Rules governing on-exchange trading, order management, trade reporting
Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA): Applicable to exchange participants
MiFID II Alignment: Although Switzerland is not an EU member, SIX voluntarily adopts many MiFID II provisions (e.g., tick size regime, pre/post-trade transparency standards) to maintain competitiveness and facilitate cross-border access



9.3 Market Surveillance

SIX Exchange Regulation (SER): Conducts real-time market surveillance of all trading activity on SIX Swiss Exchange for suspicious patterns, potential market abuse, insider trading, and rule violations
Surveillance Technology: Automated alert systems monitoring trading patterns, price anomalies, and unusual volume
Enforcement: SER can impose sanctions including fines, trading suspensions, and referrals to FINMA or criminal authorities
FINMA Oversight: FINMA conducts its own supervision and can investigate market abuse under FMIA



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Ad-hoc Disclosure: Listed issuers must immediately disclose price-sensitive information (similar to EU MAR requirements)
Major Shareholding Notifications: Disclosure required when crossing 3%, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 33 1/3%, 50%, and 66 2/3% thresholds of voting rights
Management Transactions: Board members and senior management must disclose transactions in the company’s securities
Financial Reporting: Annual report (audited) and semi-annual interim report required; must use IFRS, US GAAP, or Swiss GAAP FER (depending on listing standard)
Corporate Governance Reporting: Annual corporate governance report required per SIX Directive on Corporate Governance
Transaction Reporting: Trading participants report transactions to SIX; SIX forwards relevant data to FINMA



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

EU Equivalence – A Significant Issue

2017: EU Commission initially granted equivalence to Swiss stock exchanges (allowing EU firms to trade Swiss stocks on SIX)
2018: EU extended equivalence only for 1 year, linking it to broader EU-Swiss institutional framework negotiations
June 2019: EU equivalence recognition expired / was not renewed; EU firms prohibited from trading Swiss shares on EU venues
June 2019: Swiss Federal Council enacted protective countermeasure – prohibited trading of Swiss-ISIN equity securities on recognized foreign trading venues (effectively forcing all Swiss stock trading back to SIX)
May 2025: Swiss Federal Council lifted protective measures following a pragmatic resolution; the EU narrowed the scope of the share trading obligation to EEA-ISIN instruments, meaning Swiss-ISIN (CH-prefix) shares are no longer within scope of Article 23 MiFIR
January 2026: UK-Switzerland Berne Financial Services Agreement (BFSA) implemented mutual recognition of trading venue regulations, enabling cross-border market integration



Other Cross-border Arrangements

Bilateral regulatory cooperation agreements with multiple jurisdictions
IOSCO MMOU signatory
Foreign participants can access SIX through remote membership if home-country regulation is recognized as equivalent by FINMA

title: SIX Swiss Exchange (SIX)
text:
11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2021: SWXess platform stability and capacity enhancements; Sparks segment infrastructure deployed
2022-2023: Ongoing latency optimization and throughput upgrades on X-stream INET platform
2024: Continued system improvements; July 31, 2024 technical outage required trading halt and service restoration [source: Bloomberg]
2025: SIX acquires Aquis Exchange (July 1); announces selection of Aquis Equinox matching engine as the core of new harmonized trading platform across all SIX trading venues (Swiss Exchange, BME, Aquis)
2025: Partnership with viaNexus announced to enhance market data distribution alongside the Equinox platform migration
2026 (announced): Equinox platform migration – Phase 1a targets equity instruments migration to Equinox Production Environment in H1 2027; fixed income and structured products in 2028; derivatives to follow. “One Plug, Multiple Trading Venues” concept allows participants to access all SIX exchanges through one standardized connection
2025: Extended trading hours launched for structured products (08:00 - 21:45 CET, effective December 2025)



New Products / Segments

SwissAtMid Enhancement: Ongoing development of non-displayed midpoint pool; Limit Plus and Iceberg Plus order types providing simultaneous lit/dark access
Sparks (SME Segment): Launched October 2021; shortened trading hours (15:00-17:40) to concentrate liquidity; biotech and technology SMEs among early adopters (e.g., XLIFE Sciences)
Structured Products: Record 169,099 new products listed in 2025 (+52.6% YoY); world’s largest structured products market
Extended Trading Hours: New segment for structured products with trading until 21:45 CET (launched December 2025)
Separate Trading Line for Foreign-Listed Equities: Introduced March 2, 2026, with associated fee adjustments



SIX Digital Exchange (SDX) – Digital Assets

FINMA Licensed: SDX is the world’s first fully regulated financial market infrastructure for digital assets, licensed as both a stock exchange and central securities depository (CSD) on distributed ledger technology (DLT)
Tokenized Securities: SDX enables issuance, trading, settlement, and custody of digital bonds and other tokenized securities; from a legal standpoint, digital bonds are equivalent to traditional bonds – “digital” refers to the DLT-based main registry
Trading Consolidation: From June 1, 2025, digital bonds issued on SDX trade solely on SIX Swiss Exchange, leveraging the operational link between SIX SIS and SDX CSD; SDX continues to handle issuance, custody, settlement, and asset servicing
Institutional Partnerships: Citi and SDX partnership announced (2025) to unlock access to tokenized private market assets for global issuers and investors
Issuance Volume: SDX facilitated tokenized bond issuance exceeding CHF 400 million in notional value in 2024 [unverified]; average daily trading volumes ~CHF 2-5 million in 2025 [unverified]
Project Helvetia III: Swiss National Bank (SNB) successfully completed wholesale central bank digital currency (wCBDC) pilot for tokenized securities settlement on SDX; SNB announced continuation of the Helvetia Pilot for settlement in Swiss franc digital central bank money



Regulatory Changes

EU Equivalence Resolution (2025): Swiss Federal Council lifted protective measures on May 1, 2025; EU narrowed share trading obligation scope, excluding Swiss-ISIN securities from Article 23 MiFIR constraints
UK-Switzerland BFSA (2026): Berne Financial Services Agreement implemented January 1, 2026, establishing mutual recognition of trading venue regulations between UK and Switzerland
Sparks Listing Rule Changes (2021): Main market minimum equity capital raised from CHF 2.5 million to CHF 25 million; Sparks segment created with reduced requirements for SMEs
Separate Trading Line Directive (2026): New provisions for equity securities listed abroad, effective March 2, 2026
Trading Parameters Update (2026): Updated Trading Parameters Guideline effective April 1, 2026



Strategic Initiatives

Aquis Acquisition and Equinox Platform: SIX’s acquisition of Aquis Exchange (2025) and selection of Aquis Equinox technology positions SIX as a pan-European exchange operator with a unified, ultra-low latency, 24/7-capable matching engine
CCP Consolidation: SIX announced plans (December 2025) to integrate SIX x-clear and BME Clearing into one international, multi-asset CCP, creating a scaled, open, and competitive clearing alternative in Europe
Vertically Integrated Model: SIX Group continues to operate the full Swiss Value Chain – trading (SIX Swiss Exchange), clearing (SIX x-clear), settlement and custody (SIX SIS) – providing end-to-end integration unique among European exchanges
Digital Assets Leadership: SDX positions Switzerland as a global leader in regulated digital asset infrastructure; wCBDC integration via Project Helvetia represents cutting-edge central bank collaboration
BME Exchange Integration: Continued integration of Spanish exchange operations following 2020 acquisition; harmonized platform planned under Equinox
IPO Activity: 20 successful listings across Switzerland and Spain in 2025; SMI reached all-time highs (13,288.7 in December 2025), up 14.4% for the year
SIX Group Financial Strength: Net operating income CHF 1,496.5 million in 2025; EBITDA margin improvement driven by scale and operating leverage

1. Overview & Profile







Item
Details




Official Name
New York Stock Exchange LLC

Year Established
1792 (Buttonwood Agreement); formalized 1817 as New York Stock & Exchange Board


Country / City
United States / New York, NY (trading floor at 11 Wall Street)


Ownership Structure
Wholly-owned subsidiary of Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (ICE); ICE is publicly traded (NYSE: ICE) with widely held institutional ownership


Parent Company / Group
Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (ICE) — acquired NYSE Euronext in November 2013 for approximately $11 billion


Regulatory Authority
U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC); NYSE is itself a Self-Regulatory Organization (SRO) with regulatory services agreements with FINRA


Market Capitalization (listed companies)
~$28 trillion (NYSE-listed equities, 2025); total domestic market cap exceeding $44 trillion when combined with all U.S. exchanges as of January 2026 [Source: Statista, Siblis Research]


Total Listed Instruments
~2,400+ listed companies (including 530+ international companies); additionally hosts 2,000+ ETPs on NYSE Arca


Average Daily Trading Volume
~1.54 billion shares (November 2025) [Source: NYSE equity volumes data]


Average Daily Trading Value
~$80.6 billion (November 2025) [estimated]




Key Historical Milestones

1792: Buttonwood Agreement signed on May 17 by 24 stockbrokers under a buttonwood tree at 68 Wall Street, establishing organized securities trading in New York
1817: Formalized as the “New York Stock & Exchange Board” on March 8; adopted a constitution and rules
1863: Renamed to “New York Stock Exchange”
1867: Introduction of stock ticker by Edward Calahan
1903: NYSE moves to its current location at 18 Broad Street (11 Wall Street)
1929: Stock market crash (Black Tuesday, October 29) triggers the Great Depression
1934: SEC created under the Securities Exchange Act; NYSE registers as a national securities exchange
1971: NYSE incorporates as a not-for-profit corporation
1980: Market capitalization of NYSE-listed securities tops $1 trillion for the first time
1987: “Black Monday” (October 19) — Dow plunges 508 points (22%); market-wide circuit breakers subsequently introduced
1995: Wireless handheld computers introduced on the trading floor, beginning electronic automation
2005-2006: NYSE Hybrid Market launched, blending floor-based auction with electronic trading; NYSE merges with Archipelago Exchange (Arca)
2006: NYSE Group goes public via IPO; becomes NYSE Group, Inc.
2007: NYSE Group merges with Euronext to form NYSE Euronext
2010: Mahwah, NJ data center opens (396,000 sq ft facility)
2012: Superstorm Sandy forces NYSE to close for two consecutive days (first weather-related two-day closure since 1888)
2013: Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) completes acquisition of NYSE Euronext
2017: NYSE Pillar trading platform begins rollout
2024: NYSE announces plan to extend NYSE Arca trading to 22 hours/day
2025: NYSE Texas launches (March 2025), rebranding and relocating NYSE Chicago to Dallas
