SEC approval has been granted for 22-hour trading (1:30 AM – 11:30 PM ET Mon-Thu; 1:30 AM – 8:00 PM ET Fri), targeted for launch in late 2026 pending SIP and DTCC readiness.


2.3 Tick Sizes







Price Range
Tick Size




Stocks >= $1.00
$0.01 (1 cent) — per SEC Regulation NMS Rule 612 (Sub-Penny Rule)


Stocks < $1.00
$0.0001 (1/100th of a cent)



Note: The SEC adopted amendments in September 2024 to allow sub-penny quoting in certain circumstances and adjusting tick sizes based on time-weighted average spread. These changes are phasing in through 2025-2026. Tick sizes of $0.005, $0.01, and $0.025 may apply depending on security characteristics under the new framework.


2.4 Lot Sizes

Standard (round) lot: Historically 100 shares
New variable round lot definition (effective November 2025): Based on stock price:

Share price >= $250.00: round lot = 40 shares
Share price >= $1,000.00: round lot = 10 shares
Share price >= $10,000.00: round lot = 1 share
Share price < $250.00: round lot = 100 shares (unchanged)

Odd lot trading: Supported; odd lots (less than round lot) are executable but historically excluded from NBBO. SEC reforms effective 2025 require odd-lot information to be included in consolidated market data.



2.5 Market Maker / Liquidity Provider Programs
Designated Market Makers (DMMs): - Unique to NYSE; one DMM assigned per NYSE-listed security - Obligated to maintain fair and orderly markets; must meet stringent depth and continuity standards - Facilitate price discovery during openings, closings, and periods of significant trading imbalances - Operate both manually (on floor) and electronically - Current DMM firms: Citadel Securities LLC, GTS Securities LLC, Virtu Americas LLC
Supplemental Liquidity Providers (SLPs): - High-volume electronic liquidity providers trading for proprietary accounts only - Must maintain bid or offer at NBBO in assigned securities >= 10% of the trading day - Must add liquidity averaging > 10 million shares ADV monthly across assigned securities - Two categories: SLP-Prop (proprietary trading units) and SLMM (registered market makers at the Exchange) - Receive rebates when their posted liquidity executes
Retail Liquidity Program (RLP): - Offers price improvement for individual (retail) investor orders - Retail Price Improvement (RPI) orders provide non-displayed interest priced better than the public best bid/offer - Minimum price improvement of $0.001 per share

title: New York Stock Exchange (NYSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Conducted at 9:30 AM ET for NYSE primary-listed securities. DMMs facilitate price discovery by balancing accumulated buy/sell interest from pre-opening session. Imbalance information is disseminated starting at 8:30 AM ET. The auction establishes the official opening price. Orders eligible include Market-on-Open (MOO), Limit-on-Open (LOO), and other limit orders.
Closing Auction: Conducted at 4:00 PM ET. Closing imbalance period begins at 3:50 PM ET; MOC/LOC orders must be entered by 3:50 PM. DMMs set the official closing price — the most widely referenced price in financial publications, index calculations, and mutual fund NAV calculations. NYSE’s closing auction handles a significant percentage (~10-15%) of daily consolidated volume.
Intraday Auction: No scheduled intraday auctions on NYSE. However, trading halts followed by re-openings function similarly to auctions, with DMMs facilitating orderly re-openings.
Volatility Auction: When a Limit Up-Limit Down (LULD) trading pause occurs, the security enters a limit state and may trigger a 5-minute trading pause. Re-opening after the pause follows an auction-like process facilitated by the DMM.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Hybrid model: Order-driven electronic matching combined with floor-based trading and DMM participation — “high tech, high touch”
Priority rules: Parity/Priority model (unique to NYSE):

Price priority: Best-priced orders execute first
Parity allocation: At the same price level, incoming orders are allocated across multiple resting orders at parity, rather than strict time priority
This model rewards aggressive price improvement and encourages multiple participants to post competitive quotes, promoting deeper liquidity

For non-displayed orders, price-time priority applies



3.3 Price Discovery

Pre-open: Indicative opening prices and imbalance information published starting at 8:30 AM ET
DMM role: DMMs have unique visibility into order flow and are obligated to use this information to facilitate orderly price discovery, particularly during openings, closings, and volatile periods
Floor brokers: Physical presence on the trading floor allows for human judgment in price discovery, particularly for large block orders and complex situations
Closing price: NYSE’s closing auction is the industry standard reference price for index calculations, derivatives settlement, and portfolio valuations

4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Market Order
Executes immediately at the best available price; no price protection


Limit Order
Executes at the specified price or better; can be displayed or non-displayed


Market-on-Open (MOO)
Market order to be executed only in the opening auction


Limit-on-Open (LOO)
Limit order to be executed only in the opening auction at specified price or better


Market-on-Close (MOC)
Market order to be executed only in the closing auction


Limit-on-Close (LOC)
Limit order to be executed only in the closing auction at specified price or better





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Reserve Order
Limit order with a displayed portion and a non-displayed (reserve) quantity; reserve quantity replenishes displayed quantity as it executes


Non-Displayed Limit Order
Fully hidden limit order; eligible for execution but not visible on the order book


Add Liquidity Only (ALO)
Order that will only post to the book and add liquidity; will not execute against resting orders (prevents taking liquidity and incurring taker fees)


Intermarket Sweep Order (ISO)
Limit order asserting the sender has simultaneously routed to all protected quotes at better prices at other venues; bypasses Order Protection Rule routing


Primary Pegged Order
Pegs to the NBB (for buy orders) or NBO (for sell orders); reprices as the NBBO changes


Midpoint Liquidity (MPL) Order
Non-displayed order that executes at the midpoint of the NBBO; eligible for price improvement


Retail Price Improvement (RPI) Order
Non-displayed order offering price improvement to retail flow; must improve the NBBO by at least $0.001


D-Order (Floor Broker Discretion)
Order entered by floor brokers with discretionary price range


Closing D-Order
Discretionary order specifically for the closing auction


Stop Order
Triggered when the market reaches a specified price; becomes a market order upon trigger


Stop Limit Order
Triggered when the market reaches a specified price; becomes a limit order upon trigger





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF
Description




Day
Order valid only for the current trading day; expires at market close if unfilled


Good Till Cancelled (GTC)
No longer permitted on NYSE due to potential risks from temporary volatility spikes triggering automatic execution; brokers may simulate GTC orders internally


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Must execute immediately (in whole or in part); any unfilled portion is cancelled


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must execute in full immediately or the entire order is cancelled; no partial fills


At the Open (OPG)
Valid only for the opening auction


At the Close
Valid only for the closing auction


Good Till Date (GTD)
Valid until a specified date [unverified — broker-level implementation]





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be modified or cancelled electronically via Pillar Binary or FIX gateway at any time before execution
MOC/LOC orders cannot be cancelled or reduced after 3:50 PM ET except to correct a legitimate error (with exchange approval)
During LULD limit states, certain order modifications may be restricted
NYSE provides a Trade Ops Portal (TOP) for order management, risk control configuration, and clearing functions

Pillar Binary Gateway: Lowest-latency order entry protocol; fixed-length binary messages
Pillar FIX Gateway: FIX protocol-based order entry; wider compatibility but slightly higher latency (~48 μs vs ~34 μs median)

Primary facility: US Liquidity Center (USLC), 1700 MacArthur Blvd, Mahwah, New Jersey

396,000 sq ft, Tier 4-guided data center on 28-acre site

Pillar FIX Gateway Protocol (FIX 4.2-based with Pillar extensions)

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits (Limit Up-Limit Down / LULD)








Type
Threshold
Action




Tier 1 NMS Stocks (S&P 500, Russell 1000, select ETPs) — price > $3.00
5% above/below reference price
Limit state: orders cannot execute outside price bands


Tier 2 NMS Stocks (all other NMS stocks) — price > $3.00
10% above/below reference price
Limit state: orders cannot execute outside price bands


Stocks priced $0.75 – $3.00
20% above/below reference price
Limit state


Stocks priced < $0.75
Lesser of $0.15 or 75%
Limit state


Last 25 minutes of trading (3:35 PM – 4:00 PM ET)
Price bands double
Wider bands during close


15-second limit state
If LULD band is touched and no trades occur for 15 seconds
5-minute trading pause triggered




Reference price is the average price over the preceding 5-minute trading period
LULD applies during regular trading hours only (9:30 AM – 4:00 PM ET)
LULD Plan updated effective January 2, 2026



8.2 Market-Wide Circuit Breakers (MWCB)








Level
Trigger (S&P 500 decline from prior close)
Halt Duration




Level 1
7% decline
15-minute halt (triggered only before 3:25 PM ET; if triggered at or after 3:25 PM, no halt)


Level 2
13% decline
15-minute halt (triggered only before 3:25 PM ET; if triggered at or after 3:25 PM, no halt)


Level 3
20% decline
Trading halted for the remainder of the day (any time)




Circuit breaker levels are recalculated daily based on the prior day’s S&P 500 closing price
A Level 1 or Level 2 halt can only be triggered once per day
After a Level 1 or Level 2 halt, trading resumes with a re-opening auction



8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Price collars / Price reasonability checks: Orders that would execute significantly away from the current market price are rejected or held
Order size limits: Maximum order size restrictions configurable by member firms
Credit/position limits: Real-time monitoring of aggregate exposure
Erroneous trade policy: NYSE can break (bust) clearly erroneous trades based on defined price deviation thresholds
Short sale restrictions: SEC Rule 201 (Alternative Uptick Rule) — short sale circuit breaker triggers when a stock declines 10% from prior close; once triggered, short sales must be at a price above the national best bid for remainder of day and following day



8.4 Kill Switch

Member-level kill switch: Firms can request immediate cancellation of all open orders across all NYSE markets via the Trade Ops Portal (TOP) or by contacting NYSE Operations
Exchange-level controls: NYSE can halt trading in individual securities, groups of securities, or market-wide
Regulatory halt: NYSE can declare a regulatory halt to disseminate material news
MWCB activation: Acts as a market-wide kill switch for extreme declines (see Section 8.2)

title: New York Stock Exchange (NYSE)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Primary regulator: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
NYSE is registered as a national securities exchange under Section 6 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934
NYSE is itself a Self-Regulatory Organization (SRO) with authority to establish and enforce rules governing its members
All NYSE rules and amendments must be filed with and approved by the SEC pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Exchange Act and Rule 19b-4



9.2 Key Regulations

Securities Exchange Act of 1934: Foundation of U.S. securities regulation; establishes SEC authority over exchanges
Regulation NMS (2005): Modernized U.S. equity market structure:

Order Protection Rule (Rule 611): Trade-through protection requiring routing to best available prices
Access Rule (Rule 610): Fair access and fee caps for accessing protected quotations
Sub-Penny Rule (Rule 612): Minimum pricing increments
Market Data Rules (Rules 601, 603): Consolidated data distribution

Regulation SHO: Short selling rules, including locate requirements and close-out obligations
Rule 201 (Alternative Uptick Rule): Short sale circuit breaker
Regulation ATS: Framework for alternative trading systems
CAT (Consolidated Audit Trail): Comprehensive order tracking system; CAT Fee assessed at $0.000009 per executed equivalent share (2025-2)
SEC Rule 15c3-5 (Market Access Rule): Risk management controls and supervisory procedures for broker-dealers with market access
Dodd-Frank Act (2010): Enhanced oversight of financial markets and systemic risk
Reg NMS Amendments (2024-2026): Tick size reforms, access fee cap reductions, round lot redefinition, odd-lot transparency improvements — phasing in through 2026



9.3 Market Surveillance

NYSE Market Regulation: Internal team responsible for enforcing compliance with NYSE Exchange rules and federal securities laws
FINRA RSA (Regulatory Services Agreements): FINRA conducts significant market surveillance on behalf of NYSE Exchanges
Cross-market surveillance: NYSE Market Regulation and FINRA regularly bring cross-market enforcement actions on behalf of multiple SROs
CAT reporting: All orders and executions reported to the Consolidated Audit Trail for regulatory analysis
Real-time surveillance: Automated surveillance systems monitor for insider trading, market manipulation, spoofing, layering, and other abusive practices



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Trade reporting: All transactions reported in real-time via CTS/CQS consolidated tape
Large trader reporting: SEC Rule 13h-1 requires registration of large traders (>= 2 million shares or $20 million in a day, or >= 20 million shares or $200 million in a month)
Form 13F: Institutional investment managers with >= $100 million in qualifying securities must file quarterly
Short interest reporting: FINRA collects short interest data twice monthly
CAT reporting: All broker-dealers report order lifecycle events to the Consolidated Audit Trail
Listed company obligations: Continuous disclosure (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K); corporate governance standards; annual CEO certification



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Foreign Private Issuers (FPIs): NYSE lists 530+ international companies from ~45 countries; FPIs can use home-country governance standards with limited exceptions
ADR/GDR programs: NYSE is the leading venue for American Depositary Receipt listings
Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): SEC maintains MOUs with foreign securities regulators under IOSCO framework for cross-border enforcement and information sharing
Exempt foreign private issuer status: Allows simplified reporting and governance compliance for non-U.S. companies

11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2022: Completion of NYSE Pillar migration for all NYSE equities markets; latency reduced from ~592 μs to ~32 μs for Binary gateway (95% improvement), and from ~96 μs to ~26 μs for FIX [Source: NYSE Pillar migration insights]
2023-2024: Continued Pillar optimization; options markets migrated to Pillar Options platform
2024: NYSE Pillar Options Gateway Binary Protocol specification updated; enhanced deterministic matching
2025: NYSE Texas launched on Pillar platform with industry-leading latency (P50 ~21 μs Binary)
2025 (4Q): Published latency metrics showing NYSE Binary P50 at 34 μs, NYSE Arca Binary P50 at 31 μs



New Products / Segments

NYSE Texas (March 2025): Launched as NYSE’s sixth equities exchange, rebranded from NYSE Chicago and relocated to Dallas; plans for listing capability pending regulatory filings
22-Hour Trading (NYSE Arca): SEC approved NYSE Arca’s proposal to extend trading to 22 hours/day (1:30 AM – 11:30 PM ET Mon-Thu); targeted for launch late 2026 pending SIP readiness and DTCC Universal Trade Capture (UTC) 24x5 support (client testing from January 2026, production targeted June 2026)
Retail Liquidity Program expansion: Continued growth of retail-focused price improvement offerings
ETF/ETP listings growth: NYSE Arca continues to be the dominant listing venue for ETFs, with U.S. ETF AUM exceeding $10 trillion and 4,000+ products



Regulatory Changes

Reg NMS Amendments (SEC, September 2024): Tick size reforms (variable tick sizes of $0.005, $0.01, $0.025), access fee cap reduction, variable round lot definition, odd-lot transparency — phasing in November 2025 through 2026
LULD Plan update (January 2, 2026): Updated Limit Up-Limit Down parameters
Options Regulatory Fee reduction (January 2026): ORF decreased from $0.0038 to $0.0026 per contract
Listing fee restructuring (2025-2026): Proposals to simplify listing fee tiers, including a flat $75,000 original listing fee for NYSE American stock issues
First 5-year listing fee waiver: New issuers only subject to initial and annual listing fees for their primary class of equity during first five years



Strategic Initiatives

Extended trading hours: NYSE is actively leading the U.S. industry push toward near-24x5 equity trading; collaborating with SIPs (proposing 8:00 PM Sunday to 8:00 PM Friday operations) and DTCC for clearing infrastructure readiness
Competition with TXSE: Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) received SEC approval in September 2025, backed by BlackRock, Citadel Securities, and Charles Schwab; represents the first significant new competitor to the NYSE-Nasdaq duopoly in decades; operational launch expected Q1 2026
NYSE Texas: Proactive competitive positioning in Texas market; provides ICE/NYSE with a presence in the growing Texas financial ecosystem
Data and analytics: Expanding market data and research offerings; NYSE Research publishes market insights and statistics
ESG and sustainability: NYSE-listed companies increasingly adopting sustainability reporting frameworks [unverified]

title: Nasdaq Nordic (OMX Nordic Exchanges)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: During the pre-open phase, orders accumulate. At 09:00 CET, the opening uncross determines the opening price by maximizing executable volume. Each order book uncrosses randomly within a 5-second window (09:00:00 - 09:00:05) to prevent manipulation
Closing Auction: At the end of continuous trading (~17:25 CET), the market enters a closing call period. The closing uncross at ~17:30 CET determines the official closing price, which is used by index providers, fund managers, and for NAV calculations
Scheduled Intraday Auctions: For less liquid instruments in the “Auction Only” trading segment, scheduled intraday auctions occur at set intervals (e.g., 11:00, 13:00, 15:00 CET) without continuous trading between them
Volatility Auctions: Triggered when a potential execution price would breach Volatility Guard thresholds (see Section 8). Continuous trading is halted and an auction call period of 60-180 seconds is initiated to allow orderly price discovery



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with price/time priority
Continuous matching occurs between the opening and closing auctions (approximately 09:00 - 17:25 CET)
The INET matching engine processes incoming orders against the resting order book using strict price/time priority
Market makers (liquidity providers) can provide continuous quotes but the system is fundamentally order-driven, not quote-driven
Dark order functionality is available (hidden and midpoint orders)



3.3 Price Discovery

Primary price discovery occurs through the opening and closing auctions
The uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume, then minimizes surplus, then references the prior price
Reference prices for Volatility Guards are dynamically updated based on recent trades (Dynamic) and the day’s opening auction price (Static)
Trading@Closing session allows additional volume to trade at the established closing price, ensuring end-of-day liquidity

Order Type

Description

title: Nasdaq Nordic (OMX Nordic Exchanges)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

Nasdaq Nordic does not impose fixed daily price limits (no hard up/down percentage limit)
Instead, uses Volatility Guards (dynamic and static) to detect and manage abnormal price movements



8.2 Circuit Breakers (Volatility Guards)








Type
Trigger
Response




Dynamic Volatility Guard
Potential execution price deviates beyond a percentage threshold from the last traded price (continuously updated reference)
Continuous trading halted; instrument enters a volatility auction lasting 60-180 seconds


Static Volatility Guard
Potential execution price deviates beyond a percentage threshold from the reference price (typically the day’s opening auction price)
Continuous trading halted; instrument enters a volatility auction lasting 60-180 seconds


Auction Safeguards
Opening auction uncross price deviates beyond 2x the Dynamic Volatility Guard threshold; Scheduled intraday auction safeguard equals the Dynamic Volatility Guard value
Auction period is extended




Volatility Guard thresholds are configured per instrument and reviewed periodically by the exchange
Specific percentage thresholds are defined in Appendix M of the Nasdaq Nordic Market Model and are not publicly disclosed in summary form [unverified]
After the volatility auction completes, the instrument returns to continuous trading



8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls (PRM)
Nasdaq Nordic’s Pre-trade Risk Management (PRM) service validates orders entered via OUCH and FIX protocols:







Control
Description




Blow-Through Protection
Prevents orders from triggering Volatility Guards by checking price deviation before submission


Maximum Order Value
Configurable per firm; orders exceeding the threshold are rejected


Maximum Order Quantity
Limits on maximum shares per single order


Fat-Finger Protection
Price and size reasonability checks to prevent erroneous orders


Message Throttling
Rate limits on order submissions per second


FIX Drop On-Disconnect
Automatically cancels all open orders and prevents new order entry upon client disconnect



PRM is designed for highly automated trading flows and adds no latency to order execution. It is compliant with ESMA guidelines on systems and controls in automated trading (MiFID II Article 48).


8.4 Kill Switch

Kill Switch for Mass Cancellation: Administrator function that cancels all outstanding orders for a firm or user
Available through PRM interface
Can be activated by the member firm or by Nasdaq Market Operations upon request
Supports cancellation at the CompID, user, or firm-wide level [unverified]

text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authorities








Country
Regulator
Role




Sweden

Supervises Nasdaq Stockholm as a Regulated Market

Supervises Nasdaq Copenhagen

Supervises Nasdaq Iceland


Estonia

Supervises Nasdaq Tallinn


Latvia

Supervises Nasdaq Riga


Lithuania

Supervises Nasdaq Vilnius



Each exchange entity holds a Regulated Market license (Main Market) and/or MTF license (First North) in its respective jurisdiction. Although operated under common Nasdaq Nordic branding and harmonized rules, each entity is a separate legal entity supervised by its national regulator.


9.2 Key Regulations

MiFID II / MiFIR (Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II / Regulation): Core regulatory framework for all Nasdaq Nordic and Baltic markets as EU/EEA Regulated Markets; governs transparency, best execution, investor protection, algorithmic trading controls, and tick sizes
Market Abuse Regulation (MAR): EU-wide prohibition of insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure of inside information; directly applicable in all member states
Prospectus Regulation: EU regulation governing public offers of securities and admission to trading; prospectus must be approved by the home-country FSA
Transparency Directive: Disclosure requirements for issuers of listed securities (periodic financial reporting, major shareholding notifications)
EU Takeover Directive: Governs mandatory and voluntary takeover bids (transposed into local law)
CSDR (Central Securities Depositories Regulation): Governs settlement discipline and CSD authorization; Nasdaq CSD SE operates across Baltic and Icelandic markets
Nasdaq Nordic Main Market Rulebook for Issuers of Shares: Harmonized listing rules applied across Stockholm, Helsinki, Copenhagen, and Iceland with local supplements per jurisdiction



9.3 Market Surveillance

Nasdaq Nordic Market Surveillance: Centralized real-time surveillance monitoring trading activity across all Nordic and Baltic markets for potential market abuse, suspicious patterns, and rule violations
Nasdaq uses its own surveillance technology to monitor order flow, trading patterns, and price movements
Cooperation with national regulators: Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports (STORs) are filed with relevant FSAs
Nasdaq published its first European Financial Crime Report in 2025, and signed its first proof of concept with a Tier 1 European bank for anti-financial crime technology



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: Investment firms report to their national competent authority under MiFIR Article 26 (65 data fields per transaction, by T+1)
Post-trade Transparency: Real-time publication of trade details (MiFID II pre- and post-trade transparency regime)
Short Selling Disclosure: Per EU Short Selling Regulation; net short positions above 0.1% reported to NCA, above 0.5% disclosed publicly
Major Shareholding Notifications: Varies by country but generally aligned with the EU Transparency Directive thresholds



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements / Nordic Cooperation

Harmonized Rulebook: Nasdaq Nordic operates under a common Nordic Main Market Rulebook for Issuers of Shares, with local supplements (Supplement A for Stockholm, B for Copenhagen, C for Helsinki, D for Iceland) ensuring consistency while respecting local legal requirements
EU/EEA Passporting: Member firms authorized in one EU/EEA country can access other Nasdaq Nordic/Baltic markets under MiFID II passporting without additional local authorization
Nordic Cooperation: The Nordic and Baltic FSAs cooperate closely on cross-border supervision; joint memoranda of understanding facilitate information sharing
Nasdaq CSD SE: A single CSD entity authorized in Latvia, operating across Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Iceland under EU CSDR passporting, facilitating harmonized post-trade infrastructure
IOSCO MMOU: All relevant Nordic and Baltic regulators are signatories to the IOSCO Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding

text:
1. Overview & Profile







Item
Details




Official Name
London Stock Exchange


Abbreviation
LSE


Website
https://www.londonstockexchange.com


Year Established
1801 (origins trace to coffee house trading in the 1690s)


Country / City
United Kingdom / London (Paternoster Square, City of London)


Ownership Structure
Publicly listed subsidiary of LSEG (ticker: LSEG on LSE)


Parent Company / Group
London Stock Exchange Group plc (LSEG)


Regulatory Authority
Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)


Market Capitalization (listed companies)
~GBP 4.5 trillion / ~USD 5.9 trillion (as of mid-2025) [estimated]


Total Listed Instruments
~1,900+ companies from 60+ countries (~1,025 Main Market, ~680 AIM, plus IOB and other segments)


Average Daily Trading Volume
~500,000 to 2,000,000 trades per day across order books [estimated]


Average Daily Trading Value
~GBP 4.0-4.5 billion across all segments (FTSE 100 YTD 2025: GBP 3,365M/day; FTSE 250: GBP 459M/day)




Key Historical Milestones

1698: John Castaing begins publishing stock and commodity prices at Jonathan’s Coffee House in Change Alley
1801: London Stock Exchange formally established with regulated membership
1812: First codified rule book published
1973: Merger of regional UK exchanges into a unified Stock Exchange of Great Britain and Ireland; first female members admitted
1986: Big Bang deregulation – abolished fixed commissions, ended broker-jobber separation, shifted from open-outcry to electronic trading via SEAQ
1997: SETS (Stock Exchange Electronic Trading Service) launched as flagship electronic order book
2000: LSE demutualised, becoming London Stock Exchange plc
2004: LSE moved to new headquarters at Paternoster Square
2007: Merger with Borsa Italiana for EUR 1.6 billion, forming London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG); SETSqx launched as hybrid trading platform
2009: Acquisition of MillenniumIT (Sri Lanka) for GBP 18 million to develop next-generation trading technology
2011: Millennium Exchange trading platform launched (14 February 2011), replacing TradElect
2012: Acquisition of majority stake in LCH.Clearnet (now LCH), a major clearing house
2014: LSEG acquires Frank Russell Company (Russell Indexes)
2021: Completion of USD 27 billion acquisition of Refinitiv, pivoting LSEG into data and analytics (now ~70% of revenue)
2024: Material enhancements to Workspace platform; first products from Microsoft partnership generally available
2025: LSEG integrates financial data into ChatGPT; GBP 2.1 billion returned to shareholders via buybacks
2026: Launch of LSEG Sustainability Ratings and Data; on-chain settlement initiative (Digital Markets Infrastructure) announced pending regulatory approval

2.5 Market Maker / Liquidity Provider Programs

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Begins at 08:00 following a 10-minute order entry period (07:50-08:00). Orders accumulate and the matching algorithm determines the price at which the maximum volume can execute. Followed by a random end period (up to 30 seconds) to prevent manipulation
Closing Auction: At 16:30, continuous trading halts and a closing auction period begins. The closing auction uncrossing determines the official closing price (used by index providers, fund managers). Followed by a random end period
Intraday Auctions (SETSqx): Scheduled at 08:00, 09:00, 11:00, 14:00, and 16:35 for SETSqx securities. Orders collect between auctions and uncross at scheduled times
Volatility Auctions: Triggered when a potential execution would breach price monitoring thresholds (circuit breaker). Trading is suspended and a call auction is initiated to allow orderly price discovery



3.2 Continuous Trading

SETS (Stock Exchange Electronic Trading Service): Primary order book for FTSE 100, FTSE 250, FTSE SmallCap, and other liquid securities. Pure order-driven market with optional market maker participation. Price/time priority matching algorithm during 08:00-16:30 continuous session
SETSqx: Hybrid system combining periodic auctions with continuous market maker quotes. Between auctions, investors can trade against market maker quotes. Order book execution only occurs at auction uncrossings
SEAQ: Quote-driven system for less liquid securities. No electronic order matching; trades executed via market maker quotes displayed on screen



3.3 Price Discovery

Price discovery occurs primarily through the opening and closing auctions and continuous order book interaction on SETS
The uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume, then minimizes surplus, then references the prior price to determine the auction price
Closing Price Crossing session (16:35-16:40) allows additional volume to trade at the established closing price
Reference prices for circuit breakers are derived from auction uncrossing prices and dynamically updated during continuous trading

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Order to buy/sell at a specified price or better; rests on the book if not immediately matched


Market Order
Executes at the best available price; any unmatched portion is cancelled (not held on book)





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Iceberg Order
Only a portion (the visible peak) is displayed on the order book; as the visible quantity is filled, a new peak is automatically replenished from the hidden reserve


Hidden Order
Entire order quantity is hidden from the public order book; lower priority than visible orders at the same price


Mid-Price Pegged Order
Pegged to the midpoint of the best bid and offer (BBO); automatically adjusts as the BBO changes; available on SETS dark order book


Stop Order
Triggered when the market reaches a specified stop price, at which point it becomes an active order


Passive Only Order
Ensures the order does not immediately execute on entry; it is placed on the book as a passive order or rejected if it would aggress [unverified]


Named Order
Used in SETSqx – market maker quotes entered as named executable orders





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF
Description




Good for Day (GFD)
Order valid for the current trading day only; cancelled at end of day


Good till Cancelled (GTC)
Order remains active until executed or explicitly cancelled (up to maximum calendar days set by exchange)


Good till Date (GTD)
Order valid until a specified expiry date


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Execute as much as possible immediately; any remaining quantity is cancelled


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be executed in full immediately or the entire order is cancelled


At the Open (ATO)
Valid only during the opening auction


At the Close (ATC)
Valid only during the closing auction


Execute and Eliminate (EaE)
Similar to IOC – execute available quantity and cancel remainder





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled at any time during the trading session via FIX or Native gateway
Price amendments that improve priority result in a new timestamp (loss of time priority)
Quantity reduction does not affect time priority
During auction call periods, orders can be entered, amended, and cancelled but no matching occurs
Mass cancellation functionality available; Kill Switch can cancel all outstanding orders for a firm

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols








Protocol
Description
Use Case




MITCH (Level 2)
LSE’s native binary market data protocol, based on ITCH; full order-by-order depth
Ultra-low latency market data for algorithmic and high-frequency trading


MITCH (Level 1)
Aggregated best bid/offer and trade data in MITCH binary format
Real-time top-of-book for trading applications


FIX Market Data
Market data via FIX protocol
Firms preferring standardized FIX connectivity


RDF (Reference Data Feed)
Daily reference data files for instrument parameters, tick tables, trading calendars
Pre-trade setup, instrument static data





6.2 Data Levels

Level 1: Best bid/offer (BBO), last trade price, volume, VWAP; available as real-time or delayed (15-minute delay for free)
Level 2: Full order book depth (all visible orders at every price level); order-by-order granularity via MITCH
Level 3: Not applicable (Level 2 provides full depth on LSE)



6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

Market data disseminated via UDP multicast over IP version 4 (IPv4)
Dual redundant feeds: Feed A and Feed B (identically sequenced)
Each UDP packet contains one Unit Header
Load balanced across multiple IP multicast channels
TCP/IP replay service for gap recovery (up to 65,000 most recent messages)
Snapshot recovery service for initial state rebuild



6.4 Historical Data

Historical tick data available through LSEG (Refinitiv) Tick History
End-of-day data, corporate actions, reference data available
Data accessible via LSEG Data Platform, Workspace, and third-party vendors
Academic and research access available through partnerships

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Member Firms: Must be authorized by the FCA (or equivalent EU/EEA regulator with passporting arrangements); apply to LSE for membership
Types of Membership: Trading members (direct electronic access), market makers, sponsored access (via a sponsoring member firm)
Requirements: Adequate financial resources, competent personnel, robust systems and controls, compliance arrangements
General Clearing Members (GCMs): Must be members of the designated CCP (LCH or other) to clear trades



7.2 Connection Methods

LSE Extranet: Dedicated managed network service for reliable connectivity
Co-location / Proximity Hosting: Direct cross-connect from co-located racks in the primary data center
Third-party Networks: Via approved network providers (BT Radianz, IPC, etc.)
VPN: Secure VPN connectivity option for lower-volume participants [unverified]
Internet: Not typically used for production trading; may be available for testing/UAT



7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

Primary Data Center: Located at Interxion LON1 (City of London) for proximity to matching engine [unverified – some sources cite LD4 Slough for certain LSEG venues]
Cross-connect: Direct fibre cross-connects available for lowest latency
Proximity Hosting: Rack space, power, and cooling in the same data center as the matching engine
Additional Venues: Equinix LD4 (Slough) hosts related venues including Turquoise and BATS Chi-X Europe
Managed hosting services available through third-party providers (e.g., Beeks Group)



7.4 API Protocols

Native Trading Gateway: Proprietary binary protocol (SAIL); lowest latency (~126 microseconds); MIT203 specification
FIX 5.0 SP2 Trading Gateway: Industry-standard FIX protocol for order entry and execution; MIT202 specification
Drop Copy Gateway: FIX 5.0 based; real-time copy of executions and order updates; MIT205 specification
MITCH Market Data: Binary protocol for Level 1 and Level 2 market data (MIT303)
Reference Data Service: MIT401 specification for instrument reference data



7.5 Certification / Testing

Customer Development Service (CDS): Test environment replicating production functionality for member firms to test connectivity and order management
Conformance Testing: Required before production access; validates correct message handling, order management, and error handling
New Release Testing: Member firms given advance notice and testing windows for system upgrades
Technical Account Management Team: londontam@lseg.com – supports onboarding and certification

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

LSE does not impose fixed daily price limits (no hard up/down limit)
Instead, uses dynamic and static price monitoring bands to detect abnormal price movements
Price monitoring thresholds are set per instrument and reviewed periodically



8.2 Circuit Breakers








Type
Trigger
Response




Dynamic Circuit Breaker
Potential execution price deviates beyond a dynamic threshold from a continuously updating reference price (based on recent trades)
Trading automatically suspended; instrument enters a volatility auction (call period)


Static Circuit Breaker
Potential execution price deviates beyond a static threshold from the last auction uncrossing price (opening/closing)
Trading automatically suspended; instrument enters a volatility auction


FTSE 100 stocks
~8% deviation from opening auction price triggers static circuit breaker
Volatility auction initiated


Auction Extension
If the indicative uncrossing price of a volatility auction would breach monitoring thresholds again
Auction call period is extended


Market Order Extension
2-minute extension at end of final Price Monitoring Event (PME) if market orders would remain unexecuted
Followed by a random end period of up to 30 seconds





8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Value: Configurable per firm/gateway; orders exceeding threshold are rejected
Maximum Order Quantity: Limits on the maximum number of shares in a single order
Maximum Gross Consideration: Sum of the value of all trades today plus value of all open orders/quotes; controllable at global and instrument group level
Message Throttling: Rate limits on order submissions per second to prevent system overload
Price Collar Checks: Orders with prices significantly away from the current market may be rejected
Risk Controllers: Typically the General Clearing Member (GCM), CCP, or the member firm itself can set and monitor pre-trade limits in real time via GUI



8.4 Kill Switch

GUI Kill Switch: Available through the risk management interface; allows authorized personnel to cancel all outstanding orders for a specific CompID or user
Telephone Kill Switch: Can be activated by contacting LSE market operations; must be followed up with written (email) confirmation for audit purposes
Scope: Can cancel all orders for a trading gateway CompID, a Native UserID, or across the entire firm
Real-time Monitoring: Risk exposure monitored in real time; alerts sent when configured thresholds are breached

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Financial Conduct Authority (FCA): Primary regulator for LSE as a Recognised Investment Exchange (RIE) under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA)
Bank of England / Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA): Prudential oversight of systemically important financial infrastructure
HM Treasury: Sets the legislative framework (e.g., onshoring EU regulations post-Brexit)



9.2 Key Regulations

UK MiFID Framework: Onshored version of MiFID II/MiFIR post-Brexit, governing trading venues, transparency, and investor protection
Market Abuse Regulation (UK MAR): Prohibits insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure of inside information
Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA): Primary legislation governing UK financial services; provides RIE recognition framework
Listing Rules / Prospectus Regulation: FCA Listing Rules govern admission to the Official List; UK Prospectus Regulation governs public offers of securities
Transparency Directive (DTRs): Disclosure and Transparency Rules for issuers of listed securities
Settlement Discipline Regime: UK CSDR provisions for settlement efficiency



9.3 Market Surveillance

LSE Market Surveillance: Real-time monitoring of trading activity for suspicious patterns, potential market abuse, and rule violations using Millennium Surveillance technology
FCA Market Monitoring: FCA conducts its own surveillance using transaction reporting data submitted by firms under UK MiFIR Article 26
Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports (STORs): Member firms required to report suspicious activity to the FCA
Cross-market Surveillance: Coordination with other UK and international regulators



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: Investment firms must report 65 data fields per transaction to the FCA by T+1 (end of following working day) under UK MiFIR Article 26
Post-trade Transparency: Real-time publication of trade details (price, volume, timestamp) as close to real-time as possible; deferrals available for large-in-scale and illiquid instruments
Pre-trade Transparency: Display of bid/offer prices and depth for order book instruments
Short Selling Disclosure: Net short positions above 0.2% of issued share capital reported to FCA; above 0.5% disclosed publicly
Major Shareholding Notifications: Disclosure required when crossing 3% and subsequent 1% thresholds of voting rights (DTR 5)
Annual/Semi-Annual Financial Reporting: Required for issuers under DTRs



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Post-Brexit, the UK operates an independent regulatory framework; EU equivalence decisions remain limited
UK-domiciled firms can access EU venues under local EU member state rules (no blanket passporting)
Overseas firms can apply for recognition by the FCA to access LSE
Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with international regulators for information sharing and supervisory cooperation
IOSCO MMOU signatory

title: London Stock Exchange (LSE)
text:
11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2021-2022: Continued Millennium Exchange enhancements; LCH EquityClear migrated to new LSEG Technology post-trade platform
2023: Ongoing latency reduction and capacity upgrades to matching engine [unverified specific details]
2024: Material enhancements to LSEG Workspace platform; first products from Microsoft Cloud partnership made generally available; strong pipeline for 2025 cloud-based data delivery
2025: Trading system stability improvements; enhanced market data infrastructure [unverified]
2026: Digital Markets Infrastructure (DMI) on-chain settlement initiative announced, leveraging Microsoft Azure distributed ledger technology, pending regulatory approval



New Products / Segments

Africa’s Largest Exchange: The JSE is the largest stock exchange on the African continent by a significant margin, accounting for approximately 60% of Africa’s total equity market value. Its market capitalization exceeds that of the next nine largest African stock exchanges combined.

Key Historical Milestones

1887: Founded on 8 November by Benjamin Minors Woollan following the 1886 Witwatersrand gold rush; first share transactions took place in a canvas tent
1887 (end Nov): 68 companies listed within weeks of founding
1890 (end Jan): Over 300 companies listed, driven by mining speculation
1903: New exchange building constructed on Hollard Street, Johannesburg
1947: Joined the World Federation of Exchanges (then Federation Internationale des Bourses de Valeurs)
1961: Second exchange building opened
1963: Became a member of the Federation International Bourses de Valeurs (FIBV)
1993: Joined the African Stock Exchanges Association
1996: Transitioned from open outcry floor trading to electronic trading (JET system) after 108 years of floor-based trading
1997: SENS (Stock Exchange News Service) launched for real-time corporate announcements (August 1997)
2000: Relocated headquarters from Johannesburg CBD to Sandton, Gauteng
2001: Cross-dealing agreement signed with the London Stock Exchange
2003: AltX (Alternative Exchange) launched for small and medium-sized growth companies
2005: Demutualized on 1 July 2005, becoming JSE Limited (Reg No: 2005/022939/06), a public unlisted company
2006: Listed on its own Main Board (June 2006) – one of the first African exchanges to self-list
2009: Acquired the Bond Exchange of South Africa (BESA) for ZAR 240 million
2012: Migrated equities trading to Millennium Exchange platform (LSEG Technology), replacing TradElect; founding member of UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative
2013: Settlement cycle reduced from T+5 to T+3 (Phase 1, July 2013)
2016: ITaC (Integrated Trading and Clearing) programme delivered, migrating derivatives and bond markets to Millennium Exchange and Cinnober Real-Time Clearing
2022: Launched JSE Trade Explorer service for peer rankings
2025: FTSE/JSE All-Share Index (ALSI) hit 100,000 points for the first time (July 2025); record financial results with 16.7% increase in Net Profit After Tax to ZAR 1,071 million

title: Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Takes place between approximately 08:45 and 09:00 SAST. During the auction call phase, orders can be entered, amended, or cancelled but no matching occurs. At the end of the call period (with a random end to prevent manipulation), the system determines the price at which maximum volume can execute and uncrosses the order book at that price. The opening price of an instrument is the uncrossing trade price
Closing Auction: Takes place approximately between 16:50 and 17:00 SAST. Works identically to the opening auction – orders accumulate during a call period, and the system determines the closing price by maximizing executable volume at the uncrossing
Intraday Auction: Scheduled between approximately 12:00 and 12:15 SAST [unverified]. Provides an additional price discovery opportunity during the trading day. Same mechanism as opening/closing auctions
Volatility Auction: Triggered automatically when a potential trade would breach a static or dynamic circuit breaker threshold. Trading in the affected instrument is suspended and a volatility auction call period is initiated to allow orderly price discovery before continuous trading resumes



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven central limit order book (CLOB) with price/time priority
During continuous trading (09:00 - 16:50 SAST), incoming orders are matched against the order book in real time
The JSE operates a fully electronic, order-driven market – no specialist or designated market maker is required for continuous trading (though voluntary market maker programmes exist)



3.3 Price Discovery

Price discovery occurs through the interaction of buy and sell orders on the central order book
The auction uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume at a single price, providing transparent price discovery at market open, midday, and close
Volatility auctions serve as additional price discovery events when prices move beyond predefined thresholds
The closing auction is particularly important as the closing price is used by index providers, fund managers, and for portfolio valuations

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits
The JSE uses dynamic and static price monitoring bands rather than fixed daily price limits. These thresholds trigger volatility auctions rather than outright trading halts.








Type
Threshold
Action




Static Circuit Breaker
~5% deviation from the last auction uncrossing price
Instrument enters a Volatility Auction Call session


Dynamic Circuit Breaker
~2% deviation from a continuously updating reference price (based on recent trades)
Instrument enters a Volatility Auction Call session



Note: The 5% static and 2% dynamic thresholds are representative values; actual tolerances may vary by instrument and are set by JSE. These were reported in JSE documentation but specific current values should be confirmed [values based on JSE Service Hotline 6214].


8.2 Circuit Breakers








Type
Trigger
Response




Dynamic Circuit Breaker
Potential execution price deviates beyond the dynamic threshold from the continuously updating reference price
Automatic transition to Volatility Auction Call – no outright halt


Static Circuit Breaker
Potential execution price deviates beyond the static threshold from the last auction price
Automatic transition to Volatility Auction Call


Volatility Auction Extension
If the indicative uncrossing price of a volatility auction would breach thresholds again
Auction call period is extended




The JSE uses volatility interruptions (auction-based) rather than outright trading halts – trading is suspended in the affected instrument and a call auction period begins
Circuit breakers are applied at the individual instrument level, not market-wide
The mechanism allows participants to correct order prices or adjust to new information before continuous trading resumes



8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Value: Configurable per firm/gateway; orders exceeding threshold are rejected [unverified]
Maximum Order Quantity: Limits on the maximum number of shares in a single order [unverified]
Message Throttling: Rate limits on order submissions to prevent system overload
Price Collar Checks: Orders with prices significantly away from the current market may be rejected
Consistent with Millennium Exchange pre-trade risk control framework used across LSEG Technology deployments



8.4 Kill Switch

Kill switch functionality expected to be available consistent with Millennium Exchange platform capabilities [unverified – JSE-specific implementation not publicly confirmed]
Allows cancellation of all outstanding orders for a specific user or firm

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA): Primary market conduct regulator for the JSE as a licensed exchange under the Financial Markets Act, 19 of 2012 (FMA). The FSCA supervises the JSE in its regulatory duties, investigates potential market abuse, and institutes enforcement actions
South African Reserve Bank (SARB) – Prudential Authority (PA): Prudential oversight of financial market infrastructure under the Twin Peaks regulatory model. The PA was established on 1 April 2018 within the SARB under the Financial Sector Regulation (FSR) Act, 2017. SARB is involved in approval of JSE’s prudential rules and clearing/settlement functions
JSE as Frontline Regulator: The JSE itself acts as the frontline regulator – it is the Listings Authority, sets listings requirements, and enforces trading rules under the FMA. The JSE Market Regulation division monitors trading activity across all JSE markets



9.2 Key Regulations

Financial Markets Act, 19 of 2012 (FMA): Primary legislation governing exchanges, central securities depositories, clearing houses, and trade repositories in South Africa. The JSE is licensed as an exchange under the FMA
Financial Sector Regulation Act, 9 of 2017 (FSR Act): Established the Twin Peaks model – creating the FSCA (market conduct) and the Prudential Authority within SARB (prudential regulation)
Financial Intelligence Centre Act, 38 of 2001 (FICA): Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing obligations for JSE members
JSE Listings Requirements: Detailed rules governing admission, maintenance, and disclosure obligations for listed companies
JSE Equities Rules: Trading rules governing order entry, matching, clearing, and settlement for the equity market
Companies Act, 71 of 2008: General corporate governance requirements applicable to listed companies



9.3 Market Surveillance

JSE Market Regulation Division: Real-time monitoring of trading activity across all JSE markets using Millennium Surveillance technology to identify possible market abuse, insider trading, and rule violations
FSCA Investigation and Enforcement: The FSCA is responsible for investigating market abuse and taking enforcement action where appropriate
SENS Monitoring: Corporate announcements via SENS (Stock Exchange News Service) are monitored for compliance with continuous disclosure obligations



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: Member firms required to report trading activity to JSE and FSCA
Disclosure Obligations: Listed companies must comply with continuous disclosure requirements under JSE Listings Requirements and the FMA
Major Shareholding Notifications: Required disclosure when crossing specified ownership thresholds
Short Selling: Subject to JSE rules and FSCA oversight [unverified – specific thresholds not confirmed]



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

JSE is a member of the World Federation of Exchanges (WFE)
Cross-dealing agreement with the London Stock Exchange (since 2001)
Member of the African Stock Exchanges Association
Founding member of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative (2012)
IOSCO MMOU signatory for international regulatory cooperation [unverified]

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
1. Overview & Profile







Item
Details




Official Name
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited


Abbreviation
HKEX


Website
https://www.hkex.com.hk


Year Established
2000 (merger of SEHK, HKFE, and HKSCC); SEHK originally established 1891


Country / City
Hong Kong SAR, China / Central, Hong Kong (Head Office); Tseung Kwan O (Data Centre)


Ownership Structure
Publicly listed on its own exchange (SEHK: 0388); widely held by institutional investors; Hong Kong SAR Government holds a 5.87% stake via the Financial Secretary


Parent Company / Group
HKEX is the listed holding company; principal subsidiaries include The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited (SEHK), Hong Kong Futures Exchange Limited (HKFE), Hong Kong Securities Clearing Company Limited (HKSCC), and LME Holdings Limited (London Metal Exchange)


Regulatory Authority
Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) of Hong Kong


Market Capitalization (listed companies)
~HK$48.5 trillion (~US$6.2 trillion) as of February 2026; HK$44.9 trillion as of July 2025 (YoY +44%) [Source: HKEX Monthly Market Highlights]


Total Listed Instruments
2,673 listed companies (as of February 2026); Main Board: ~2,283, GEM: ~326 [data as of 2024]; plus ~2,600+ ETPs, warrants, and structured products


Average Daily Trading Volume
Cash market ADT: HK$230.7 billion (~US$29.6 billion) for Jan-Nov 2025, up 43% YoY; record monthly ADT of HK$316.7 billion in September 2025 [Source: HKEX 2025 Year in Review]


Average Daily Trading Value
HK$230.7 billion (Jan-Nov 2025); ETPs ADT: HK$37.6 billion (doubled YoY) [Source: HKEX 2025 Year in Review]




Key Historical Milestones

1891: Association of Stockbrokers in Hong Kong established, the earliest formal securities trading organization
1914: Renamed to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange
1947: Hong Kong Stock Exchange re-established after World War II
1969–1972: Three additional exchanges established (Far East Exchange, Kam Ngan Stock Exchange, Kowloon Stock Exchange), creating the “four exchanges” era
1986: Four exchanges unified into The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited (SEHK); trading floor opened at Exchange Square in Central
1993: Automatic Order Matching and Execution System (AMS) introduced in November, beginning electronic trading
1997: Asian Financial Crisis severely impacts Hong Kong markets; government intervenes with HK$118 billion stock-buying operation in 1998
1999: Hong Kong government announces reform plan to merge and demutualize the stock and futures exchanges
2000 (March 6): Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) established through merger of SEHK, HKFE, and HKSCC
2000 (June 27): HKEX lists on its own exchange (IPO raised ~HK$4.3 billion)
2000 (October): AMS/3 trading system launched, replacing AMS/2
2003: SARS outbreak disrupts markets; HKEX introduces Closing Auction Session (CAS) concept development
2007: Average daily turnover exceeds HK$100 billion for the first time amid China bull market
2012 (December): HKEX completes acquisition of London Metal Exchange (LME) for £1.39 billion (~US$2.2 billion)
2014 (November 17): Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect launches, enabling cross-border equity trading
2016 (August): Volatility Control Mechanism (VCM) introduced for the securities market
2016 (December 5): Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect launches
2017 (July 3): Northbound Bond Connect launches
2018 (February 5): Orion Trading Platform - Securities Market (OTP-C) goes live, replacing AMS/3.8
2018 (April): New listing regime takes effect (Chapter 18A for biotech, weighted voting rights structures)
2022 (July 4): ETF Connect launches (ETFs included in Stock Connect)
2023 (May 15): Swap Connect (Northbound) launches — world’s first derivatives mutual market access programme
2023 (November): Stamp duty on stock transactions reduced from 0.13% to 0.1%
2024 (April): HKEX announces in-house development of Orion Derivatives Platform (ODP), targeted for 2028 launch
2025: HKEX becomes global leader in IPO proceeds; ADT surges 43% YoY; new minimum spread reduction (Phase 1) takes effect August 5

2. Market Structure

2.1 Market Segments








Segment
Description
Listing Requirements (Summary)




Main Board
Premier market for established companies; accounts for vast majority of market capitalization and trading volume
Market cap >= HK$500 million at IPO; profit test: aggregate profit >= HK$50 million over 3 years (with >= HK$20 million in most recent year); or market cap/revenue test: market cap >= HK$4 billion with revenue >= HK$500 million; or market cap/revenue/cashflow test: market cap >= HK$2 billion with revenue >= HK$500 million and positive aggregate cashflow >= HK$100 million over 3 years; minimum public float 25% (or 15-25% for large-cap); >= 300 public shareholders


GEM (Growth Enterprise Market)
Market for smaller, high-growth companies and startups with less stringent requirements
Trading record >= 2 financial years; cashflow test: market cap >= HK$150 million with positive 2-year aggregate operating cashflow >= HK$30 million; or R&D company test: 2-year revenue >= HK$100 million (with YoY growth), R&D expenditure >= HK$30 million (>= 15% of total operating expenditure each year); minimum public float 25%; >= 100 public shareholders


Chapter 18A (Biotech)
Specialist listing pathway for pre-revenue biotech companies on the Main Board (introduced 2018)
Market cap >= HK$1.5 billion at IPO; must have at least one core product beyond concept stage; experienced management; adequate working capital for >= 125% of group costs for next 12 months


Chapter 18C (Specialist Technology)
Listing route for specialist technology companies in certain industries (introduced 2023)
Commercial Companies: market cap >= HK$6 billion; Pre-Commercial Companies: market cap >= HK$10 billion with revenue >= HK$250 million


Chapter 19C (Secondary Listings)
Allows qualifying overseas-listed companies to secondary list in Hong Kong
Primarily targets Greater China and international companies already listed on a qualifying exchange (NYSE, NASDAQ, LSE Main Market); market cap >= HK$3 billion (or HK$10 billion for non-Greater China issuers without WVR)





2.2 Trading Sessions









Session
Local Time (HKT)
UTC (HKT = UTC+8)
Description




Pre-Opening Session (POS)
9:00 AM – 9:30 AM
01:00 – 01:30
Order input period (9:00–9:15), pre-order matching period (9:15–9:20), order matching period (9:20–9:28), blocking period (9:28–9:30); At-auction Orders and At-auction Limit Orders accepted; single-price auction determines opening price


Morning Continuous Trading
9:30 AM – 12:00 PM
01:30 – 04:00
Continuous order matching on price-time priority; all continuous session order types accepted


Lunch Break
12:00 PM – 1:00 PM
04:00 – 05:00
No trading occurs; orders cannot be submitted, modified, or cancelled during this period. This is a distinctive feature of Asian exchanges including HKEX, unlike Western exchanges that trade continuously


Afternoon Continuous Trading
1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
05:00 – 08:00
Continuation of morning session; continuous order matching resumes


Closing Auction Session (CAS)
4:00 PM – ~4:10 PM
08:00 – ~08:10
Four phases: (1) Reference Price Fixing Period (4:00–4:01); (2) Order Input Period (4:01–4:06); (3) No-Cancellation Period (4:06–4:08); (4) Random Closing Period (4:08–4:10, closes randomly within 2 min to prevent manipulation); At-auction Orders and At-auction Limit Orders only



Notes: - Total trading hours: ~5.5 hours (excluding lunch break) plus ~10 minutes CAS - Lunch break is maintained per Hong Kong market tradition, though there has been periodic discussion about its elimination (the break was shortened from 1.5 hours to 1 hour in 2011) - Half-day trading sessions (e.g., before holidays) end at 12:00 PM with no afternoon session, and CAS runs from 12:00–12:10 PM - Hong Kong does not observe daylight saving time; HKT is fixed at UTC+8

These changes align Hong Kong with international peers. Separate spread tables (codes 03, 04, 05) apply to debt securities, ETPs, and structured products.


2.4 Lot Sizes

Board lot (trading unit): Varies by issuer; currently 44+ different board lot units are in use (e.g., 100, 200, 400, 500, 1,000, 2,000 shares per lot)
Most common: 100, 500, and 1,000 shares per lot
Board lot value guidance: Floor of HK$2,000 per lot (proposed reduction to HK$1,000)
Odd lot trading: Odd lots (less than one board lot) can be traded on the exchange via a separate odd-lot order book, typically at a discount to board lot prices
Reform proposal (December 2025): HKEX published a consultation paper proposing to reduce board lot options from 44+ to 8 standard choices (1, 50, 100, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 5,000, 10,000 shares) and introducing a board lot value ceiling of HK$50,000 for lots larger than 100 shares. Consultation closed March 12, 2026
Northbound Stock Connect: Board lot of 100 shares for A-shares



2.5 Market Maker / Liquidity Provider Programs

Securities Market Makers (SMMs): Registered market makers provide liquidity for specific securities, including structured products (derivative warrants, callable bull/bear contracts)
Designated Specialist Programme for ETPs: Allows global liquidity providers (not just HKEX SMMs) to act as market makers for exchange-traded products, with minimum quotation obligations
Dual Counter Designated Specialists (DCS-DS): Market makers for HKD-RMB dual counter securities; must maintain credit rating of A- (S&P) or A3 (Moody’s) or above, paid-up capital >= HK$50 million, shareholders’ funds >= HK$100 million
Stock Options Market Makers: Appointed for individual stock options series with continuous two-sided quotation obligations
Derivatives Market Maker/Liquidity Provider Programme: Commercial arrangements for futures and options products; Market Maker Programme governed by exchange rules, LP Programme offering more flexible terms for new products

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (Pre-Opening Session):

Single-price auction mechanism during 9:00–9:30 AM
At-auction Orders (AAO, no price specified) have higher matching priority than At-auction Limit Orders (AALO, price specified)
Indicative Equilibrium Price (IEP) is calculated and disseminated during the session
Orders matched at the final IEP at ~9:20–9:28 AM
Unmatched At-auction Limit Orders with prices at or better than IEP are converted to limit orders and carried into continuous trading
Opening quotation rule: orders limited to ±5% (or 24 spreads, whichever is greater) from the previous closing price

Closing Auction (Closing Auction Session):

Four-phase mechanism (4:00–~4:10 PM) designed to determine the official closing price
Reference Price Fixing Period: establishes the reference price (typically the nominal price from the last 5 minutes of continuous trading)
Order Input Period: at-auction orders accepted within ±5% of the reference price
No-Cancellation Period: new orders accepted but cancellations not permitted
Random Closing Period: session ends at a random time between 4:08 and 4:10 PM to prevent last-second manipulation
The final IEP becomes the official closing price for index calculation and settlement

Volatility Control Mechanism (VCM): See Section 8.2



3.2 Continuous Trading

Matching method: Order-driven, continuous matching on strict price-time priority (no specialist/DMM system)
Price priority: Best price matched first (highest buy / lowest sell)
Time priority: Among orders at the same price, earliest order matched first
Maximum order size: 3,000 board lots for automatch orders
Quotation rules: During continuous trading, incoming orders cannot deviate more than 24 spreads from the current nominal price (for securities with a previous closing price of HK$0.01–HK$0.50, this is relaxed to 9 spreads below the bid and above the ask)



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening price determined via pre-opening auction IEP
Continuous price discovery through order-driven matching during the trading day
Closing price determined via closing auction session IEP (replacing the previous median-of-five-snapshots method)
No formal price limits (daily limit up/down) — HKEX does not impose statutory daily price limits on securities, unlike mainland China exchanges (SSE/SZSE have ±10% daily limits); instead, HKEX uses the VCM as a targeted cooling-off mechanism for constituent stocks

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order (LO)
Executes only at the specified limit price; unexecuted portion remains in the order book at the limit price until end of day or cancelled


Enhanced Limit Order (ELO)
Matches at up to 10 price queues better than or equal to the specified limit price; unexecuted portion remains in the order book as a limit order at the original input price


Special Limit Order (SLO)
Matches at up to 10 best price queues not worse than the specified limit price; unexecuted portion is cancelled (not queued) — effectively a fill-or-kill up to 10 levels


At-auction Order (AAO)
No price specified; for use during Pre-Opening and Closing Auction Sessions only; matched at the final IEP; highest priority among auction orders


At-auction Limit Order (AALO)
Price specified; for use during Pre-Opening and Closing Auction Sessions; matched at the final IEP if order price is at or better than IEP; lower priority than AAO





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Good Till Date Order (GTD)
Order remains active in the order book until the specified date (up to a maximum number of calendar days) or until fully executed or cancelled


Stop Loss Limit Order (SLLO)
Triggered when the last traded price reaches or passes the specified trigger price; converts to a limit order at the specified limit price upon activation


Session Order
An order that applies to a specific trading session (morning or afternoon); automatically cancelled at the end of the designated session





4.3 Time-in-Force Options

Day order: Default; valid for the current trading day only
Good Till Date (GTD): Valid until a specified future date
Session: Valid for the current trading session only (morning or afternoon)
Fill-and-Kill (FAK): Immediate partial execution with remaining portion cancelled (via SLO behavior)
Note: HKEX does not support Fill-or-Kill (FOK) or Immediate-or-Cancel (IOC) as explicitly named TIF options in the securities market; SLO provides similar functionality



4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled during continuous trading sessions
During the No-Cancellation Period of CAS (4:06–4:08 PM), order cancellation is not permitted
During the lunch break (12:00–1:00 PM), no order amendments or cancellations are processed
Order amendments that change price result in loss of time priority
OTP-C supports Self-Match Prevention (SMP) functionality to prevent an Exchange Participant’s orders from matching against each other

text:
5. Trading System (Technology)







Item
Details




System Name
Orion Trading Platform – Securities Market (OTP-C)


Vendor / In-house
In-house development by HKEX


Architecture
Scalable, high-performance platform based on open systems technology; modular design allowing phased introduction of new functionalities


Matching Engine
Central matching engine with price-time priority; supports multiple instrument types


Round-trip Latency
Information not publicly available in exact microseconds; SDNet/3 network described as providing “lower latency” than predecessor SDNet/2 [estimated sub-millisecond for co-located participants]


Order Processing Capacity
60,000 order transactions per second at launch (100% increase over AMS/3.8), with scope for further increases [Source: HKEX, February 2018]


Messages Per Second
Information not publicly available (order capacity of 60,000/sec implies comparable message throughput)


Launch Year
February 5, 2018




System History








Year
System
Notes




1986
Manual floor trading
Unified exchange opens at Exchange Square


1993
AMS (Automatic Order Matching and Execution System)
First electronic trading system


1996
AMS/2
Upgraded version with enhanced capacity


2000
AMS/3
Deployed October 23, 2000; multi-workstation architecture


2008–2011
AMS/3.8
Progressive upgrades to AMS/3 with capacity enhancements


2013
HKEX Data Centre
State-of-the-art facility opens in Tseung Kwan O


2018
OTP-C (Orion Trading Platform – Securities Market)
Go-live February 5; replaced AMS/3.8; development began 2012


2018
SDNet/3
New backbone network; lower latency, higher bandwidth vs SDNet/2


2024
ODP announced
Orion Derivatives Platform (in-house) development commenced; target launch 2028





Technology Stack

Trading Platform: OTP-C — open systems technology (Linux-based), designed for flexibility and scalability
Derivatives Trading: HKATS (Hong Kong Automated Trading System) — based on NASDAQ’s Genium INET technology; to be replaced by Orion Derivatives Platform (ODP) in 2028
Order Gateway: Orion Central Gateway – Securities Market (OCG-C); FIX protocol-based connectivity for exchange participants
Market Data: Orion Market Data Platform (OMD-C for securities, OMD-D for derivatives) — binary multicast protocol over UDP/IP
Network: SDNet/2 (Securities and Derivatives Network) for derivatives and some services; SDNet/3 for OTP-C securities trading; Optical Ethernet, 1 Gbps physical speed
Clearing: CCASS (Central Clearing and Settlement System) for securities settlement; DCASS for derivatives
Stock Connect Trading: OTP-CSC (Orion Trading Platform – China Stock Connect) and CCCG (China Connect Central Gateway)



Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity

HKEX maintains disaster recovery facilities with full replication capability
Regular system rehearsals conducted for OTP-C and CSC system recovery (multiple rehearsals per year)
SDNet/2 and SDNet/3 networks designed for high resilience with redundant paths
Co-location and hosting services at Tseung Kwan O Data Centre provide direct access with redundancy
Regular market rehearsals (MR) conducted before major system changes; documented in publicly available information packages

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols

OMD-C (Orion Market Data Platform – Securities Market): Primary market data feed for securities

Binary message format designed for high throughput and low latency
IP multicast and UDP transport protocols for one-to-many distribution
Retransmission recovery service running on Unicast TCP

OMD-D (Orion Market Data Platform – Derivatives Market): Equivalent feed for derivatives
OMD-CC (Orion Market Data Platform – China Connect): Market data for Stock Connect securities
MMDH (Mainland Market Data Hub): Market data distribution for mainland securities via Stock Connect
IIS (Index Information Service): Hang Seng Index data feeds



6.2 Data Levels







Product
Description




Securities Standard (OMD-C)
Conflated/snapshot data; periodic updates


Securities Premium (OMD-C)
Streaming real-time data


Securities FullTick (OMD-C)
Streaming tick-by-tick data including every order book change


Index Feed
Real-time Hang Seng and other index data


Derivatives Market Data (OMD-D)
Real-time futures and options data





6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

Market data distributed via SDNet/2 network to Exchange Participants, Information Vendors, and direct subscribers
Co-located participants at Tseung Kwan O Data Centre receive lowest-latency feeds
HKEX licenses market data to approximately 100+ Information Vendors globally
Data available through major terminal providers (Bloomberg, Refinitiv, etc.)



6.4 Historical Data

HKEX Data Products offers historical tick data, end-of-day data, and reference data via the HKEX website
Historical data available for securities, derivatives, and index products
Data formats include CSV downloads and API-accessible datasets
Third-party vendors (TickData, Refinitiv, etc.) also provide HKEX historical data
