title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Stock Exchange (SEHK) Participant: Must be a corporation licensed or registered under the Securities and Futures Ordinance; minimum liquid capital requirements apply; application assessed by SEHK Listing Committee
Types: Exchange Participant (EP), China Connect Exchange Participant (CCEP) for Stock Connect trading
Requirements: SFC Type 1 licence (dealing in securities); adequate financial resources; fit and proper criteria; competency requirements for responsible officers
Non-Exchange Participant access: Through Direct Market Access (DMA) arrangements with Exchange Participants



7.2 Connection Methods

OCG-C (Orion Central Gateway – Securities Market): Primary order submission interface; TCP/IP point-to-point connection using FIX protocol
BSS (Broker Supplied Systems): Exchange Participants connect proprietary or vendor trading systems to OCG-C
HKEX Terminal: HKEX-provided trading terminals for smaller participants
CCCG (China Connect Central Gateway): Dedicated gateway for Northbound Stock Connect order routing
DMA (Direct Market Access): Exchange Participants may offer DMA to qualified clients subject to SFC requirements



7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

HKEX Hosting Services: Co-location at the HKEX Data Centre, 1 Chun Ying Street, Tseung Kwan O Industrial Estate, Hong Kong
Facility: Purpose-built state-of-the-art data centre opened January 2013; houses HKEX core trading, clearing, and market data systems
Ecosystem: Co-located Exchange Participants, technology service providers, Information Vendors, and network service providers
Benefits: Lowest-latency access to OTP-C matching engine, OMD-C market data, and clearing systems
Network: Multiple Accredited Vendors provide cross-connect services within the facility
Third-party proximity providers: IPC, Beeks, and others offer managed hosting and connectivity within the HKEX Data Centre



7.4 API Protocols

FIX Protocol: Primary API for order submission via OCG-C; FIX 4.4-based with HKEX-specific extensions; CompID “HKEXCO” for OCG-C sessions
Binary Protocol: Used for OMD market data feeds (OMD-C, OMD-D)
HKATS API: Derivatives trading API for the Hong Kong Automated Trading System
Session management: FIX sessions reset daily (sequence numbers initialize to 1 each trading day); each EP can register multiple sessions with IP address pre-registration



7.5 Certification / Testing

Readiness testing: Mandatory connectivity and system readiness testing before go-live for new Exchange Participants or system changes
Market rehearsals: Regular rehearsals conducted for OTP-C, OTP-CSC, and other systems; participation by EPs is expected
Test environment: HKEX provides dedicated test environments for OCG-C and OMD-C connectivity testing
Conformance testing: Exchange Participants must pass conformance testing for FIX protocol implementation before production access
crumbs: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

No statutory daily price limits: Unlike mainland China exchanges (SSE/SZSE: ±10%, ±20% for ChiNext/STAR), HKEX does not impose daily price limit bands on securities trading
Quotation rules: Orders during continuous trading are subject to a ±24 spread deviation limit from the nominal price (reduced to ±9 spreads for low-priced securities HK$0.01–0.50)
Opening auction price limit: ±5% from previous closing price (or 24 spreads, whichever is greater)
Closing auction price limit: ±5% from reference price established during CAS



8.2 Circuit Breakers (Volatility Control Mechanism)

Introduction: August 22, 2016
Mechanism: Individual stock-level cooling-off mechanism (not a market-wide trading halt)
Applicable securities: Constituent stocks of the Hang Seng Index (~50 stocks) and Hang Seng China Enterprises Index (~80 securities); ~80 securities total (with overlap)
Trigger: If potential trade price deviates by more than ±10% from the reference price (last traded price 5 minutes ago), VCM is triggered
Cooling-off period: 5 minutes during which trading in the security continues but only within ±10% of the reference price
Frequency: Only one VCM trigger per trading session (morning and afternoon) per security
Exclusion periods: VCM does not apply during the first 15 minutes of each session, the first 15 minutes after market reopening, or the last 20 minutes of the afternoon session
Key distinction: VCM is NOT a trading halt — the security continues to trade within the price band during the cooling-off period
Derivatives VCM: Separate VCM for futures with ±5% trigger threshold



8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Securities market:

Maximum order size: 3,000 board lots per order
Order price deviation limits (±24 spreads from nominal price)
Position limit monitoring through OTP-C
Self-Match Prevention (SMP): prevents an EP’s buy and sell orders from matching against each other

Derivatives market (PTRM - Pre-Trade Risk Management):

PTRM 2.0 system within HKATS monitors exposure across multiple Prescribed Risk Controls
Execution Throttle: at-trade risk check for exposure limits over configurable periods (300–600 seconds)
Four exposure limit types; order breaching any limit triggers PTLG (Post-Trade Limit Group) blocking
Clearing Participants (CPs) and Exchange Participants (EPs) can set risk limits for their trading units




8.4 Kill Switch

Derivatives market: Kill Switch function available for Risk Limit Managers and Trading Units; blocks the PTLG and performs mass order cancellation on all outstanding orders in a single action; prevents further order submission while activated
Securities market: Exchange Participants can perform mass cancellation via OCG-C sessions; HKEX can intervene to suspend an EP’s trading access if necessary
Note: After Kill Switch activation in derivatives, order cancellations can still be processed but new orders and block trades are rejected
crumbs: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)

title: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Securities and Futures Commission (SFC): Independent statutory body established under the Securities and Futures Commission Ordinance; primary regulator of Hong Kong’s securities and futures markets
Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB): Government policy bureau overseeing financial services regulation
Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA): Regulates banking aspects; jointly supervises OTC derivatives clearing with SFC
Three-tiered regulatory structure:

Government (FSTB) — policy and legislation
SFC — market regulation, licensing, enforcement
HKEX — front-line regulation of listed companies and exchange participants (as a recognized exchange controller)




9.2 Key Regulations

Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO, Cap. 571): Primary legislation governing securities and futures markets; covers licensing, market conduct, disclosure, and enforcement
Rules of the Exchange (Main Board Listing Rules): Comprehensive listing and continuing obligations rules for Main Board issuers
GEM Listing Rules: Equivalent rules for GEM-listed companies
Code on Corporate Governance: Comply-or-explain code incorporated into Listing Rules; enhanced climate-related disclosure requirements effective 2025
Securities and Futures (Stock Market Listing) Rules: Subsidiary legislation under SFO
Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance: AML/CFT requirements for licensed corporations



9.3 Market Surveillance

HKEX operates a dedicated Market Surveillance team using advanced technology for real-time monitoring of trading activities
Surveillance covers detection of potential market misconduct including insider dealing, market manipulation, false trading, and price rigging
Close cooperation with SFC Enforcement Division for investigation and prosecution
SFC has powers to impose disciplinary measures, seek court orders, and prosecute offenders under the SFO
HKEX monitors listed company compliance with disclosure obligations (price-sensitive information, connected transactions, etc.)



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Listed company disclosures: Inside information disclosure (continuous disclosure obligation under SFO Part XIVA); annual reports, interim reports, quarterly reports (GEM); connected transaction announcements; results announcements
Short selling reporting: Daily short selling turnover reports published by HKEX; short position reporting (bimonthly) for positions exceeding specified thresholds
Substantial shareholder disclosure: Notification required when crossing 5% threshold (and each subsequent 1% change)
Trade reporting: All on-exchange trades automatically reported; off-exchange reportable trades must be reported to HKEX



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements (Stock Connect, Bond Connect, etc.)

Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect (November 2014):

Northbound: Hong Kong and international investors trade eligible SSE-listed A-shares
Southbound: Mainland investors trade eligible SEHK-listed stocks
Daily Northbound quota: RMB 52 billion; Daily Southbound quota: RMB 52 billion
No aggregate quota (abolished August 2016 for Shanghai Connect)
Eligible stocks: SSE 180 Index / SSE 380 Index constituents and dual-listed A+H shares (Northbound); Hang Seng Composite LargeCap/MidCap Index constituents and dual-listed A+H shares (Southbound)

Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (December 2016):

Similar structure to Shanghai Connect
Daily Northbound quota: RMB 52 billion; Daily Southbound quota: RMB 52 billion
Eligible stocks: SZSE Component Index / SZSE Small/Mid Cap Innovation Index constituents with market cap >= RMB 6 billion (Northbound)

ETF Connect (July 2022):

Eligible ETFs included in Stock Connect for cross-border trading
Northbound: 225 eligible mainland-listed ETFs; Southbound: 8 eligible Hong Kong-listed ETFs [data as of 2024]

Bond Connect (July 2017 Northbound; September 2021 Southbound):

Access to China Interbank Bond Market (CIBM) for international investors
Operated through Bond Connect Company Limited (joint venture of HKEX subsidiary and CFETS)
Service fees reduced by 60% effective January 1, 2025

Swap Connect (May 2023):

World’s first derivatives mutual market access programme
Northbound: international investors access mainland interbank financial derivatives (interest rate swaps)
Cleared through Shanghai Clearing House with HKEX subsidiary OTC Clear as correspondent clearing house

Technical infrastructure:

OTP-CSC (Orion Trading Platform – China Stock Connect) for Stock Connect order routing
CCCG (China Connect Central Gateway) for Northbound trading connectivity
SEHK subsidiary acts as Special Participant of SSE/SZSE for order routing
ChinaClear and HKSCC maintain cross-participantship for settlement

Deutsche Borse Group – a vertically integrated exchange group encompassing trading (Xetra, Eurex, EEX), clearing (Eurex Clearing), settlement & custody (Clearstream), index (STOXX/DAX indices), data & analytics (Qontigo), and fund services (IFS)

Key Historical Milestones

2.5 Market Maker / Liquidity Provider Programs – Designated Sponsors
The Designated Sponsor model is a defining feature of Xetra:

Designated Sponsors: Registered market-making firms contracted by issuers (or by Deutsche Borse for index constituents) to provide continuous two-sided quotes during trading hours, ensuring minimum liquidity and maximum spread requirements
Obligations: Designated Sponsors must quote minimum volumes and maximum spreads defined by Deutsche Borse; requirements vary by instrument liquidity category (A, B, C, D); must respond to Quote Requests within a defined time
Incentives: Reduced trading fees; priority for XLM (Xetra Liquidity Measure) reporting; marketing visibility
XLM (Xetra Liquidity Measure): Deutsche Borse’s proprietary measure of implicit trading costs (market impact) used to evaluate Designated Sponsor performance; published monthly
Requirement for certain segments: Instruments in the Scale segment and less liquid equities typically require at least one Designated Sponsor for admission

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Starts at 08:50 CET with a call phase during which orders are collected but not matched. An indicative auction price and volume are displayed in real time. At 09:00 CET, the auction enters a random end period of up to 30 seconds, after which the uncrossing match occurs at the price that maximizes executable volume. If no price can be determined, the best bid/ask is displayed and continuous trading begins without a trade
Closing Auction: Begins at 17:30 CET. A call phase of approximately 2 minutes collects orders. Random end period (up to 30 seconds) follows to prevent manipulation. The uncrossing determines the official closing price, which is critical for index calculations, fund NAVs, and derivatives settlement
Intraday Auctions: Scheduled for specific instrument groups (e.g., DAX constituents may have an intraday auction at 13:00 CET). The purpose is to provide additional price discovery points for instruments that may benefit from periodic re-assessment
Volatility Interruptions (Volatility Auctions): Triggered automatically when a potential execution price breaches dynamic or static price corridors. The instrument enters an extended call auction to allow orderly price discovery. The volatility auction runs for a defined period (typically 2 minutes) followed by a random end period



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market: Xetra is a pure electronic order-driven market during continuous trading (09:00-17:30 CET)
Price/time priority: Orders are matched first by price (best price has priority), then by time (earlier orders have priority at the same price). Visible orders have priority over hidden portions of iceberg orders at the same price
Designated Sponsors provide supplementary liquidity by quoting two-sided markets, but continuous trading is fundamentally an order book model, not a quote-driven market
Borse Frankfurt floor operates as a specialist-supported system where a Specialist (Skontrofuhrer) sets indicative prices and facilitates trading with order book support; this is a hybrid model



3.3 Price Discovery

Primary price discovery occurs through the opening and closing auctions and the continuous order book on Xetra
The auction uncrossing algorithm follows the principle of: (1) maximum executable volume, (2) minimum surplus (unmatched volume at the auction price), (3) reference price (previous price) used to resolve ties
The Xetra closing price is the most widely referenced price for German equities and is used for DAX/MDAX/SDAX index calculations
Xetra accounts for approximately 90% of all on-exchange equity trading volume in Germany, making it the dominant price discovery venue
Reference prices for volatility interruptions are set from the last auction price (static) and the last trade price (dynamic), updated continuously



3.4 Order Priority

Price priority: Best-priced orders always match first
Visible over hidden: At the same price, visible order quantities have priority over hidden (iceberg reserve) quantities
Time priority: Among orders at the same price and same visibility, the earliest entry time has priority
Market orders have priority over limit orders (they are treated as having the best possible price)

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Market Order
Executes at the best available price(s); unlimited price validity; in auctions, guaranteed execution if counterpart exists; in continuous trading, executes immediately against resting orders


Limit Order
Specifies a maximum buy price or minimum sell price; rests on the order book if not immediately matched





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Market-to-Limit Order
Enters as a market order; first execution sets a limit price; unexecuted remainder rests as a limit order at that price


Iceberg Order
Displays only a specified peak quantity on the order book; hidden reserve automatically refreshes the visible peak when it is fully executed; the re-displayed peak gets a new time stamp


Hidden Order
Entire order quantity is hidden from the public order book; executed only against incoming aggressive orders; minimum order value typically EUR 10,000 [unverified]


Stop Order (Stop Market)
Dormant until a specified trigger price is reached; becomes a market order upon activation


Stop Limit Order
Dormant until a trigger price is reached; becomes a limit order at a specified limit price upon activation


One-Cancels-Other (OCO)
Pair of orders where execution of one automatically cancels the other [unverified – may be supported via broker-side rather than natively on T7]


Trailing Stop Order
Stop price automatically adjusts with favorable price movements by a specified trailing amount [unverified]


Midpoint Order
Pegged to the midpoint of the best bid and offer; available for certain dark order book segments [unverified]





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF
Description




Good for Day (GFD)
Valid for the current trading day; cancelled at end of trading session


Good till Cancelled (GTC)
Remains active until executed, cancelled by the participant, or until a maximum validity period (typically 360 calendar days)


Good till Date (GTD)
Valid until a specified date


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Execute immediately for any available quantity; cancel any unfilled remainder


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be fully executed immediately or the entire order is cancelled


Opening Auction Only (OA)
Valid only during the opening auction call and uncrossing


Closing Auction Only (CA)
Valid only during the closing auction call and uncrossing


Auction Only
Valid during any auction (opening, intraday, closing)





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be modified (price, quantity, and other attributes) or cancelled at any time during valid trading phases via the T7 ETI (Enhanced Trading Interface) or FIX gateway
Price modification: Changing the price results in a new time priority timestamp (loss of queue position)
Quantity decrease: Reducing quantity preserves time priority
Quantity increase: Increasing quantity results in a new timestamp (loss of priority)
Self-match prevention: T7 supports self-match prevention (SMP) functionality, allowing firms to prevent unintended crosses between their own orders
Mass cancellation: Supported via T7 ETI; firms can cancel all orders for a specific session, instrument, or instrument group
Persistent and non-persistent orders: T7 distinguishes between persistent orders (survive a system failover) and non-persistent orders (cancelled on failover); non-persistent offers lower latency

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
5. Trading System (Technology)







Item
Details




System Name
T7 (officially “T7 trading architecture”)


Vendor / In-house
In-house, co-developed by Deutsche Borse for both Xetra (cash markets) and Eurex (derivatives)


Architecture
High-performance, low-latency, event-driven architecture; partition-based design where each instrument group is assigned to a dedicated matching engine partition for parallel processing


Matching Engine
Central limit order book (CLOB) with price/time/visibility priority; each partition handles a subset of instruments independently


Round-trip Latency
Median round-trip latency in the low single-digit microsecond range (~5 microseconds for co-located participants); 99th percentile typically under 10 microseconds [estimated based on Deutsche Borse publications]


Order Processing Capacity
Designed to handle millions of order transactions per day; peak capacity significantly exceeds typical daily load


Messages Per Second
T7 supports throughput of several hundred thousand messages per second per partition; system-wide capacity in the millions of messages per second [unverified specific numbers]


Launch Year
2012 (T7 for Eurex derivatives); 2017 (T7 for Xetra cash market, replacing legacy Xetra system)




System History








Period
System
Notes




Pre-1991
Floor-only trading
Manual trading floor at the Frankfurt Stock Exchange


1991-1997
IBIS (Integriertes Borsenhandels- und Informationssystem)
First electronic trading system for German equities; screen-based but not fully automated matching


1997-2017
Xetra (original platform)
Fully electronic order-driven trading; launched November 28, 1997; became dominant German equity trading venue; multiple releases (Xetra 7.0 through 17.0)


2012-present
T7 (Eurex)
Launched for Eurex derivatives in December 2012; unified architecture


2017-present
T7 (Xetra)
Migrated Xetra cash market to T7 in June 2017 (T7 Release 5.0); unified cash and derivatives on a single platform





Technology Stack

Architecture: Partition-based, with each matching engine partition running on dedicated hardware for isolation and deterministic performance
Programming Language: C++ (core matching engine) [unverified]
Operating System: Linux-based
Network: High-speed, low-latency network fabric within co-location facility; 10GbE and 40GbE connections [unverified]
Trading Gateways:

T7 ETI (Enhanced Trading Interface): Native binary protocol for lowest-latency order entry; session-based, asynchronous
T7 FIX Gateway: FIX 4.2/4.4 protocol for order entry and execution reporting

Market Data:

T7 EMDI (Enhanced Market Data Interface): Full depth, unnetted market data via UDP multicast
T7 MDI (Market Data Interface): Netted/aggregated top-of-book market data via UDP multicast
T7 EOBI (Enhanced Order Book Interface): Ultra-low latency, order-by-order market data feed directly from the matching engine partition; available to co-located participants

Simulation Environment: T7 provides a comprehensive simulation environment for member testing



Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity

Dual data center architecture: Primary and secondary data centers with real-time replication
Failover: T7 supports transparent failover; persistent orders survive a gateway or matching engine failover
Non-persistent orders: Cancelled on failover (trade-off for lower latency)
Regular DR testing: Deutsche Borse conducts mandatory disaster recovery exercises with participants
Market data redundancy: Dual feed (A/B) architecture for all market data interfaces
RPO/RTO: Aligned with BaFin and ESMA regulatory requirements for critical market infrastructure [specific values not publicly disclosed]

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols








Protocol
Description
Use Case




T7 EOBI (Enhanced Order Book Interface)
Order-by-order, unnetted, ultra-low latency market data directly from matching engine partitions; binary protocol via UDP multicast
HFT and algorithmic trading requiring lowest latency; co-location only


T7 EMDI (Enhanced Market Data Interface)
Full depth-of-book, unnetted market data; binary protocol via UDP multicast
Full order book reconstruction for non-co-located participants


T7 MDI (Market Data Interface)
Aggregated/netted top-of-book data (best bid/offer, last trade); UDP multicast
Surveillance, display systems, lower-bandwidth applications


T7 RDI (Reference Data Interface)
Instrument reference data, trading parameters, product definitions
Pre-trade setup, static data management


CEF (Common Exchange Format)
Historical and end-of-day data files
Back-office, reconciliation, historical analysis





6.2 Data Levels

Level 1 (Top of Book): Best bid/offer (BBO), last trade price and size, cumulative volume, VWAP; available via T7 MDI; delayed data (15-minute) available free on xetra.com
Level 2 (Full Depth): Complete order book depth at every price level; available via T7 EMDI (all participants) and T7 EOBI (co-located)
Order-by-Order: Individual order additions, modifications, and deletions visible via EOBI; highest granularity for market microstructure analysis



6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

UDP multicast delivery for all real-time market data feeds (EOBI, EMDI, MDI, RDI)
Dual-feed redundancy: Feed A and Feed B carry identical sequenced data for client-side arbitration and gap detection
TCP recovery service: For requesting retransmission of missed multicast packets
Snapshot service: Full order book snapshots available for initial state recovery or reconnection
Co-location distribution: EOBI feed available only within the co-location facility (lowest latency path from matching engine)
Third-party vendors: Market data available through major data vendors (Bloomberg, Refinitiv/LSEG, ICE)



6.4 Historical Data

Deutsche Borse Market Data + Services: Provides historical tick data, end-of-day data, reference data, and corporate actions
A7 Analytics Platform: Deutsche Borse’s analytics offering for transaction cost analysis (TCA) and market quality metrics
CEF files: End-of-day common exchange format files for full trading day reconstruction
Academic access: Available through partnerships and data licensing programs
XLM data: Monthly Xetra Liquidity Measure data published for all Xetra-traded instruments

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Admitted Trading Participants: Firms must apply to Deutsche Borse for admission as a trading participant on Xetra; must be authorized by their national regulator (BaFin for German firms, or equivalent EU/EEA authority under MiFID II passporting)
Types: Direct trading participants, Designated Sponsors (market makers), and participants accessing via Sponsored Access (DEA – Direct Electronic Access) through a sponsoring member
Requirements: Adequate financial resources, qualified trading personnel (trader examinations required), robust IT systems and controls, compliance and risk management infrastructure
Number of participants: Over 200 trading participants from 20+ countries active on Xetra [unverified]



7.2 Connection Methods







Method
Description




Deutsche Borse Network (N7)
Managed network service (previously called “Member Section Network”); dedicated leased lines connecting participant premises to the T7 trading infrastructure


Co-location Cross-connect
Direct fibre cross-connect from co-located racks to T7 matching engine infrastructure within the co-location facility


Third-party Network Providers
Access via approved network service providers (e.g., BT, Colt, IPC/Connexus) connecting to Deutsche Borse’s access points


Internet (GUI)
Web-based trader GUI (T7 Trader GUI) accessible via internet for manual trading and monitoring [unverified]





7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

Primary Location: equinix FR2 data center, Frankfurt area (the T7 matching engines for both Xetra and Eurex are hosted here) [unverified – Deutsche Borse has used multiple Frankfurt-area facilities]
Co-location Offerings: Rack space, power, cooling, and direct cross-connects to T7 infrastructure; multiple rack configurations available
Proximity Services: For firms not requiring full co-location, proximity hosting is available in nearby data centers with managed connectivity to T7
Latency advantage: Co-located participants achieve the lowest possible latency (single-digit microsecond round-trip)
Network equipment: Participants can place their own servers and networking equipment in co-location racks
Multiple cross-connect options: Dedicated fibre links to T7 ETI gateways, market data (EOBI) switches, and other services



7.4 API Protocols







Protocol
Use Case




T7 ETI (Enhanced Trading Interface)
Native binary, session-oriented; lowest-latency order entry, modification, cancellation, and execution reporting; supports high-frequency strategies


T7 FIX Gateway
FIX 4.2/4.4 compliant; standard protocol for order routing; higher latency than ETI but industry-standard


T7 GUI (Trader GUI)
Java-based graphical interface for manual order entry, market monitoring, and trade management


T7 Admin GUI
Administrative interface for session management, risk parameter configuration, and user administration


Common Report Engine
XML/CSV-based post-trade reporting; trade confirmations, settlement instructions, regulatory reports


T7 RDI
Reference data interface for instrument master data





7.5 Certification / Testing

T7 Simulation Environment: Full functional replica of the production environment; available for member testing of order entry, market data reception, and fail-over scenarios
Conformance/Certification Testing: Mandatory before production go-live; Deutsche Borse verifies correct implementation of T7 protocols (ETI, FIX, market data)
Release Testing: Advance notice provided for T7 software releases; dedicated testing windows in simulation
Member Readiness Program: Deutsche Borse coordinates member readiness for major system upgrades
Technical contact: Member Services and Technical Account Management teams available for onboarding support

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits








Type
Threshold
Action




Static Price Range
Defined per instrument based on a percentage deviation from the last auction price (e.g., ~10% for DAX stocks) [unverified specific percentages]
Potential execution prices outside the static range trigger a volatility interruption


Dynamic Price Range
Defined per instrument based on a percentage deviation from the last trade price or best bid/offer; narrower than static range (e.g., ~2-5% for liquid stocks) [unverified]
Potential execution prices outside the dynamic range trigger a volatility interruption


Extended Price Range
Maximum allowable price range for an instrument during a volatility interruption; if the auction uncrossing would breach this, the auction is extended
Auction extension



Note: Xetra does not impose fixed daily price limits (no hard up/down percentage cap for the day). Instead, it uses the volatility interruption mechanism described below.


8.2 Circuit Breakers – Volatility Interruptions








Type
Trigger
Halt Duration




Volatility Interruption (Dynamic)
Potential continuous trade or auction uncrossing price breaches the dynamic price corridor (based on last trade)
Automatic switch to a call auction; typically 2 minutes followed by a random end period of up to 30 seconds


Volatility Interruption (Static)
Potential price breaches the static price corridor (based on last auction price)
Automatic switch to a call auction; typically 2 minutes + random end


Extended Volatility Interruption
The indicative uncrossing price of a volatility interruption auction itself breaches the extended price range
Auction extended for another period; may repeat


Market-wide Circuit Breaker
No explicit market-wide halt mechanism at the exchange level [unverified]; individual instrument-level volatility interruptions serve the same purpose
Per-instrument; does not halt entire market




Volatility interruptions are transparent: the T7 system publishes a dedicated message notifying all participants when a volatility interruption is triggered and when it ends
During a volatility interruption, orders can be entered, modified, and cancelled, but no matching occurs until the auction uncrossing



8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Value: Configurable per session/instrument; orders exceeding the threshold are rejected by T7
Maximum Order Quantity: Limits on maximum number of shares/contracts per order
Price Reasonability Checks: T7 validates incoming order prices against the current market and rejects orders with unreasonable prices (extreme limit prices)
Throttling / Message Rate Limits: T7 enforces message rate limits per session (e.g., a maximum number of transactions per second); excessive message rates result in throttling or session disconnection
Advanced Risk Protection (ARP): Cumulative execution monitoring per time interval; if a firm’s executed volume/value exceeds configured thresholds within a rolling time window, further orders are automatically rejected or the session is suspended
Pre-trade Risk Limits by Clearing Member: Clearing members (via Eurex Clearing) can set and monitor pre-trade limits for their clients in real time
Self-match prevention: Prevents a firm’s own buy and sell orders from matching against each other



8.4 Kill Switch

T7 Kill Switch (Stop Button): Available via the T7 Admin GUI; authorized risk managers can delete all orders and quotes for a specific session, user, or business unit
Clearing Member Stop: Clearing members can trigger emergency stop for their non-clearing member clients via Eurex Clearing interfaces
Scope: Can cancel all open orders for a specific trader, session, business unit, or the entire firm
Urgency Stop via Market Operations: Participants can contact Deutsche Borse Market Operations (telephone) to request an emergency halt of a participant’s trading activity
Automated triggers: ARP can automatically function as a kill switch when cumulative thresholds are breached

title: Deutsche Borse / Xetra (XETR)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

BaFin (Bundesanstalt fur Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht): Germany’s federal financial supervisory authority; regulates Deutsche Borse AG as a market operator and supervises trading participants
Exchange Supervisory Authority (Borsennaufsichtsbehorde): The Hessisches Ministerium fur Wirtschaft, Energie, Verkehr und Wohnen (Hesse Ministry of Economic Affairs) directly supervises the Frankfurt Stock Exchange as the state-level exchange supervisory authority under the German Exchange Act (Borsengesetz)
ECB / Bundesbank: Oversight of Clearstream and Eurex Clearing as systemically important financial market infrastructures
ESMA: EU-level coordination; Deutsche Borse venues operate under the MiFID II/MiFIR framework as transposed into German law



9.2 Key Regulations

Borsengesetz (German Exchange Act): Primary legislation governing the organization and operation of exchanges in Germany
Wertpapierhandelsgesetz (WpHG – Securities Trading Act): Implements EU MiFID II/MiFIR into German law; governs securities trading, market abuse, and transparency
MiFID II / MiFIR: EU-wide framework for trading venues, transparency, investor protection, and market structure; directly applicable (MiFIR) and transposed (MiFID II)
Market Abuse Regulation (MAR): EU Regulation 596/2014; prohibits insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure of inside information
EU Prospectus Regulation: Governs public offerings and admissions to regulated markets
EMIR (European Market Infrastructure Regulation): Governs clearing obligations and CCP regulation (relevant to Eurex Clearing)
CSDR (Central Securities Depositories Regulation): Governs settlement and CSD operations (relevant to Clearstream)
Transparenzrichtlinie-Umsetzungsgesetz: Implementation of the EU Transparency Directive for ongoing issuer disclosure



9.3 Market Surveillance

Trading Surveillance Office (HuSt – HandelsÃ¼berwachungsstelle): Independent department within the exchange (legally required under the Borsengesetz) that monitors real-time trading activity for potential market manipulation, insider trading, and rule violations
Market Surveillance by BaFin: BaFin operates its own transaction monitoring using data reported by investment firms under MiFIR Article 26
Automated surveillance: Real-time pattern detection using proprietary surveillance systems analyzing order flow, trade execution, and participant behavior
Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports (STORs): Member firms must report suspicious trading activity to BaFin
Cross-market coordination: Deutsche Borse participates in inter-exchange surveillance programs and cooperates with ESMA and other EU national competent authorities



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: Investment firms must report to their national competent authority (BaFin for German firms) within T+1 under MiFIR Article 26; 65 data fields per transaction
Post-trade Transparency: Real-time publication of trade details (price, volume, timestamp) as close to real-time as technically possible; deferrals available for LIS trades and illiquid instruments
Pre-trade Transparency: Display of bid/offer prices and order book depth for instruments on regulated markets
Short Selling Disclosure: Net short positions above 0.2% reported to BaFin; above 0.5% publicly disclosed (EU Short Selling Regulation)
Major Holdings Notifications: Disclosure required when crossing 3%, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, 50%, 75% voting rights thresholds (under German WpHG implementing EU Transparency Directive)
Directors’ Dealings (PDMR transactions): Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities must report transactions in the issuer’s instruments to BaFin and the issuer



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

EU MiFID II Passporting: Investment firms authorized in any EU/EEA member state can access Xetra as a remote member without establishing a German branch
Third-country access: Non-EU firms may access Xetra subject to equivalence assessments and bilateral MoUs between BaFin and the firm’s home regulator
ESMA cooperation: Deutsche Borse cooperates with ESMA on pan-European supervisory convergence
IOSCO MMOU: BaFin is a signatory, facilitating cross-border information sharing
Post-Brexit: UK firms access Xetra under third-country arrangements; a Memorandum of Understanding exists between BaFin and the FCA

10.2 Other Fees

Listing Fees (Annual): Annual fee for maintaining listing/inclusion; depends on segment (Prime Standard, General Standard, Scale, Basic Board)
Connectivity Fees: Monthly charges for T7 ETI sessions, FIX sessions, market data connections, and co-location cross-connects
Market Data Fees: Per-user and enterprise license fees for real-time data (Level 1, Level 2, EOBI); separate pricing for display vs. non-display use; delayed data freely available on xetra.com
Co-location Fees: Monthly rack rental, power, and cross-connect charges within the co-location facility
Clearing Fees: Eurex Clearing charges per transaction for CCP clearing of Xetra trades; included in the overall cost chain



10.3 Revenue Breakdown (Deutsche Borse Group)
Deutsche Borse Group’s consolidated net revenue for FY 2024 was approximately EUR 5.6 billion [Source: Deutsche Borse AG Annual Report 2024], with the following segment breakdown: - Trading & Clearing (Eurex, Xetra, EEX, 360T): ~40% of net revenue [estimated] - Securities Services (Clearstream): ~25% of net revenue [estimated] - Fund Services (IFS): ~10% of net revenue [estimated] - Data & Analytics (Qontigo, ISS): ~15% of net revenue [estimated] - SimCorp: ~10% of net revenue [estimated]
Note: Xetra cash equities trading represents a portion of the Trading & Clearing segment, which also includes Eurex derivatives, EEX commodities/energy, and 360T FX.

11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2021: T7 Release 9.1 – enhanced matching engine performance; new order types and risk controls; migration of Borse Frankfurt Zertifikate (structured products) to T7
2022: T7 Release 10.0 – latency improvements; expanded self-match prevention; enhanced EOBI feed capabilities
2023: T7 Release 11.0 – further performance optimization; cloud-readiness enhancements to infrastructure; support for new instrument types
2024: T7 Release 12.0 – improved pre-trade risk controls; expanded Advanced Risk Protection (ARP); enhanced GUI trader functionality
2025: Continued incremental T7 performance upgrades; focus on cloud-native infrastructure and hybrid deployment models [unverified specific release number]
D7 Post-Trade Platform: Launched in 2024 for digital/tokenized securities settlement on DLT (Distributed Ledger Technology); first issuances settled on D7 in 2024



New Products / Segments

D7 Digital Post-Trade: DLT-based issuance and settlement platform for digital securities under Germany’s eWpG (Electronic Securities Act); first crypto securities and digital bonds processed [Source: Deutsche Borse press releases]
Crypto Finance AG: Deutsche Borse acquired a majority stake in the Swiss-regulated crypto asset service provider, enabling trading, custody, and settlement of digital assets
ESG Data & Analytics: Expansion of ISS ESG (acquired 2021) data coverage; ESG ratings and screening tools integrated into the Qontigo analytics suite
DAX 40 Expansion: DAX index expanded from 30 to 40 constituents in September 2021, improving index diversification
Xetra ETF Segments: Continued growth; Xetra is Europe’s largest ETF trading venue with over 1,800 ETFs/ETPs listed [unverified exact current count]



Regulatory Changes

MiFID II/MiFIR Review: EU co-legislators adopted revisions to MiFIR in 2024-2025, including creation of a consolidated tape provider (CTP) for equities in the EU; Deutsche Borse positioned as a potential CTP operator or contributor [unverified]
DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act): EU regulation effective January 2025 requiring financial entities (including exchanges) to strengthen ICT risk management, resilience testing, and third-party risk oversight
EU Listing Act: Reforms to EU listing rules adopted in 2024 to make public markets more accessible for SMEs; reducing prospectus requirements and adapting transparency rules
eWpG (Electronic Securities Act): German law enabling issuance of securities on DLT without physical certificates; foundation for D7 platform
Settlement Cycle (T+1): EU industry discussion ongoing regarding migration from T+2 to T+1 settlement; target date expected 2027-2028 [unverified]



Strategic Initiatives

“Horizon 2026” Strategy: Deutsche Borse’s medium-term strategy targeting secular growth through expansion in data/analytics, fund services, and digital assets alongside organic trading growth
SimCorp Acquisition: EUR 3.9 billion acquisition completed in 2023; adds investment management software to the Group’s offerings, creating a front-to-back solution for the buy-side
ISS Acquisition: Completed in 2022; Institutional Shareholder Services adds governance and ESG data capabilities
Cloud Strategy: Progressive migration of non-latency-sensitive infrastructure to cloud; partnership with major cloud providers [unverified specific partners]
Digital Assets Ecosystem: Building a regulated end-to-end digital asset infrastructure: trading (Crypto Finance), issuance and settlement (D7), and custody; positioning for tokenized securities market
Sustainability / ESG: Deutsche Borse expanding ESG product offerings across indices (STOXX ESG indices), data (ISS ESG), and trading (carbon-related products on EEX)
Consolidated Tape: Deutsche Borse actively engaged in EU consolidated tape discussions; potential operator or data contributor for the EU equity CTP
Revenue Growth: Group net revenue grew from ~EUR 3.5 billion (2021) to ~EUR 5.6 billion (2024), driven by acquisitions (SimCorp, ISS) and organic growth; targeting continued mid-to-high single digit growth

Key Historical Milestones

1875: “The Native Share & Stock Brokers’ Association” established under a banyan tree by Premchand Roychand and other brokers â Asia’s first stock exchange
1928: Association moves to its current location on Dalal Street, Mumbai
1957: BSE recognized as a stock exchange under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCRA) â the first exchange in India to receive permanent recognition from the Government of India
1986: BSE introduces the S&P BSE SENSEX (Sensitive Index), tracking 30 prominent stocks, becoming India’s benchmark equity index (base year: 1978-79 = 100)
1995: BSE launches BOLT (BSE On-Line Trading System), transitioning from open-outcry floor trading to screen-based electronic trading
2000: BSE shifts to a T+5 rolling settlement cycle; subsequently shortened over the years
2005: BSE (Corporatisation and Demutualisation) Scheme notified by SEBI
2007 (May 19): BSE officially demutualized and corporatized, transforming from a broker-owned association to a shareholder-owned company
2013 (November): BOLT Plus platform launched for equity derivatives, based on Deutsche Borse’s T7 architecture
2014 (April 7): BOLT Plus extended to equity cash segment, replacing the legacy BOLT system
2017 (February 3): BSE lists on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) via IPO at INR 806 per share; debut at INR 1,085 (+33%)
2018 (October): BSE becomes first Indian exchange to launch commodity derivatives (gold and silver)
2022 (October): BSE launches Electronic Gold Receipts (EGR) platform
2023: India transitions to T+1 settlement cycle (completed January 2023), among the first major markets globally
2025: BSE celebrated 150th anniversary; Sensex crossed 80,000 milestone; Securities Markets Code 2025 introduced in Parliament to consolidate SCRA, SEBI Act, and Depositories Act

title: BSE Ltd (formerly Bombay Stock Exchange)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Pre-Open Call Auction (Opening): During the pre-open session (9:00â9:15 AM), orders are accumulated and matched at a single equilibrium price via multilateral matching. Buy orders are aggregated into a downward-sloping demand curve and sell orders into an upward-sloping supply curve; the intersection determines the opening price. Limit orders receive priority over market orders. Orders at or better than the equilibrium price are executed; remaining orders carry forward to continuous trading.
Closing Price Determination: The closing price is determined as the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of the last 30 minutes of continuous trading. This is not an auction mechanism but a calculation-based approach. After 3:30 PM, a post-close session allows order entry at the determined closing price.
Periodic Call Auction (PCA): Applied to illiquid securities (identified by BSE/SEBI based on trading frequency). PCA sessions run every hour during market hours (9:30 AM â 3:30 PM). Orders accumulate over a set period and are matched at a single price, improving price discovery for thinly traded stocks.
Special Call Auction: Used for re-listing events, corporate actions, or when SEBI/exchange determines that a call auction is needed for fair price discovery.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with continuous matching during 9:15 AM â 3:30 PM
Price-time priority: Orders are matched first by best price, then by earliest time of entry at the same price level
Anonymous trading: Counterparty identity is not revealed during order matching
The matching engine processes orders on a strict FIFO (first-in, first-out) basis within each price level



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening price discovered through pre-open call auction (multilateral matching)
Intraday prices discovered through continuous order matching (price-time priority)
Closing price derived from VWAP of last 30 minutes of continuous trading
For illiquid securities, periodic call auctions enhance price discovery by concentrating order flow into discrete intervals
Block deals (>= INR 10 crore) negotiate prices within permitted bands (+/- 1% of reference price)

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits (Individual Securities)
Daily price bands are applied to individual securities to curb abnormal volatility. The applicable band depends on the security’s classification and surveillance status:



Band
Applicable Securities




No price band
Securities in derivatives segment (F&O stocks)


2%

5%
Securities under ESM or periodic call auction regime


10%
Standard price band for select securities


20%
Standard price band for most other securities



Note: Price bands are reviewed periodically by BSE in consultation with SEBI. Securities may be shifted to narrower bands based on surveillance triggers.


8.2 Circuit Breakers (Index-Based, Market-Wide)
SEBI mandates index-based market-wide circuit breakers at three levels, triggered by movement in either the BSE SENSEX or NSE NIFTY 50 (whichever breaches first). When triggered, trading halts in all equity and equity derivative markets nationwide (both BSE and NSE halt simultaneously).










Level
Trigger
Halt if Before 1:00 PM
Halt if 1:00â2:30 PM
Halt if After 2:30 PM




Level 1
10% movement (either direction)
45-minute halt + 15-min pre-open
15-minute halt + 15-min pre-open
No halt


Level 2
15% movement (either direction)
1 hour 45 minutes halt + 15-min pre-open
45-minute halt + 15-min pre-open
Remainder of day


Level 3
20% movement (either direction)
Trading halted for remainder of the day
Trading halted for remainder of the day
Trading halted for remainder of the day



Notes: - Circuit breaker limits are calculated daily based on the previous day’s closing level of SENSEX/NIFTY 50 - After a halt, markets reopen with a pre-open call auction session (15 minutes) before resuming continuous trading - This system was introduced by SEBI in 2001 and revised in 2013 (thresholds changed from absolute point limits to percentage-based)


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Fat-finger checks: Maximum order value and quantity limits set at member/exchange level to prevent erroneous large orders
Order size limits: Maximum order size controls prescribed by SEBI; brokers must implement pre-trade risk checks under SEBI’s December 2012 circular on pre-trade risk controls
Throttling: Order rate limits per connection to prevent system overload
Real-time margin monitoring: ICCL monitors margin adequacy in real-time; positions can be squared off if margins fall below required levels
DMA risk controls: SEBI requires brokers offering DMA to implement pre-trade risk management including order-level and client-level checks



8.4 Kill Switch

Brokers are required to have the ability to immediately disable or disconnect client trading in case of malfunctioning algorithms or systems
BSE can disable a member’s trading access in extreme situations [unverified â specific kill switch implementation details not confirmed]



8.5 Graded Surveillance Measures (GSM) and Additional Surveillance Measures (ASM)

GSM: Applied to securities whose price movement is not commensurate with financial health. Actions include: transfer to Trade-to-Trade segment, additional surveillance deposit requirements, weekly-only trading, and price freeze on upper side
ASM: Applied to securities showing abnormal price/volume movements. Actions include: reduced price bands (5% or 2%), transfer to T2T settlement, 100% margin requirement

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) â primary regulator of securities markets in India
SEBI established in 1988 (statutory authority since 1992 under the SEBI Act)
SEBI has jurisdiction over stock exchanges, listed companies, intermediaries (brokers, depositories, clearing corporations), and investor protection
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) jointly regulates currency derivatives with SEBI



9.2 Key Regulations







Regulation
Description




Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCRA)
Primary legislation governing stock exchanges, listing, and trading of securities in India; provides for recognition and regulation of stock exchanges


Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
Establishes SEBI and confers powers for regulation of the securities market; investor protection mandate


Depositories Act, 1996
Governs depositories (NSDL, CDSL) and dematerialization of securities


SEBI (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018
Governs governance, operations, and risk management of stock exchanges and clearing corporations


SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR)
Mandates continuous disclosure obligations for listed entities


SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
Prohibits insider trading and mandates disclosure of trades by designated persons


SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2003
Prohibits market manipulation, front-running, and other unfair trade practices


Securities Markets Code, 2025 (Bill)
Introduced in Lok Sabha on December 18, 2025; proposes consolidation of SCRA, SEBI Act, and Depositories Act into a single unified statute; expands SEBI board from 9 to 15 members; decriminalizes minor lapses; introduces 8-year limitation on investigations; pending parliamentary approval as of April 2026





9.3 Market Surveillance

BSE Surveillance Department: Established July 1999; conducts on-line surveillance (real-time price/volume monitoring) and off-line surveillance (post-trade investigations and analysis)
SEBI Integrated Market Surveillance System (IMSS): Went live in 2007; collects transaction and master data from exchanges and depositories daily; generates alerts for predefined market manipulation scenarios
Joint Surveillance Meetings: BSE, NSE, and SEBI hold regular joint surveillance meetings to coordinate surveillance actions (e.g., GSM, ASM, price band changes)
Automated Alerts: Systems flag unusual price movements, volume spikes, concentrated positions, and potential front-running



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Listed companies must comply with SEBI LODR 2015 â quarterly financial results, corporate governance reports, material event disclosures, shareholding pattern disclosures
Brokers must report daily client-level trading data to exchange and SEBI
Large traders and foreign institutional investors (FIIs) subject to additional position reporting
Suspicious transaction reporting (STR) obligations under PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act)



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) can access BSE through SEBI-registered custodians under SEBI FPI Regulations
India-Singapore connectivity via NSE IX-SGX GIFT Connect (became operational July 2023) â primarily NSE products but represents India’s approach to cross-border market access

text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (08:30-09:00 CET): 30-minute order accumulation period. The order book is partially visible, showing the equilibrium auction price, bid and ask volumes tradable at that price, and the number of corresponding orders. Ends with a random period of up to 30 seconds to prevent manipulation. The uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume
Closing Auction (17:30-17:35 CET): At 17:30, continuous trading halts and a closing auction period begins. The closing auction determines the official closing price used by index providers and fund managers. Followed by a random end period of up to 30 seconds
Volatility Auctions: Triggered when a potential execution would breach static or dynamic price ranges (see Section 8). A 5-minute call auction is initiated with a 30-second random end period to allow orderly price discovery



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with price/time priority on SIBE
All orders submitted to SIBE go to a single central matching engine and are prioritized by price, then by time of entry
SIBE handles more than 90% of all Spanish equity transactions
Optional market maker participation provides additional liquidity for less liquid securities
SpainAtMid: Dark pool/midpoint matching functionality available during the open market phase [unverified]



3.3 Price Discovery

Price discovery occurs primarily through the opening and closing auctions and continuous order book interaction on SIBE
The auction uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume, then minimizes surplus, then references the prior price to determine the auction price
Reference prices for circuit breakers are derived from auction uncrossing prices (static reference) and dynamically updated during continuous trading (dynamic reference)
The closing auction price is the official closing price for the session and is used for index calculation and NAV purposes

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled during trading sessions
Price amendments that improve priority typically result in a new timestamp (loss of time priority)
During auction call periods, orders can be entered, amended, and cancelled but no matching occurs

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits








Type
Threshold
Action




Static Range
Set per security based on historical volatility; calculated relative to the last auction price (static reference price)
Breach triggers a 5-minute volatility auction with 30-second random end


Dynamic Range
Set per security based on historical volatility; calculated relative to the last traded price (dynamic reference price); always <= static range
Breach triggers a 5-minute volatility auction with 30-second random end




Static reference price: established at the most recent auction uncrossing (opening or volatility auction)
Dynamic reference price: updated continuously based on the last trade price (whether from an auction or continuous session)
Both static and dynamic ranges are expressed as percentages and are calibrated per security based on recent historical volatility
Specific percentage values vary by instrument and are set by BME via Operating Instructions [exact thresholds not publicly listed in general documentation]



8.2 Circuit Breakers








Level
Trigger
Action




Individual Security – Static
Price breaches the static range relative to the static reference price
Volatility auction: 5 minutes + 30-second random end


Individual Security – Dynamic
Price breaches the dynamic range relative to the dynamic reference price
Volatility auction: 5 minutes + 30-second random end


Market-wide
Extraordinary circumstances determined by BME/CNMV
Trading may be suspended for all or specific securities; no fixed automatic market-wide percentage threshold publicly documented [unverified]





8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Fat-finger checks: Maximum order size and value limits configurable by members and enforced by SIBE [unverified]
Order size limits: Maximum quantity and notional value per order
Throttling: Rate controls on order submission to prevent excessive message traffic, as required by MiFID II algorithmic trading provisions



8.4 Kill Switch

Market members have the ability to cancel all outstanding orders rapidly, in compliance with MiFID II requirements for kill switch functionality [unverified]

title: Bolsas y Mercados Espanoles (BME)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

CNMV (Comision Nacional del Mercado de Valores): Primary supervisory authority for securities markets in Spain, responsible for oversight of BME, market participants, listed companies, and market conduct
Banco de Espana: Oversees payment systems and settlement infrastructure (Iberclear)
European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA): EU-level coordination and harmonization



9.2 Key Regulations

Ley de los Mercados de Valores y de los Servicios de Inversion (LMVSI) – Law 6/2023: Principal Spanish securities market legislation; replaced the prior Ley del Mercado de Valores (Law 24/1988); transposes MiFID II into Spanish law
MiFID II / MiFIR (Directive 2014/65/EU and Regulation 600/2014): EU-wide framework governing markets in financial instruments; directly applicable in Spain; covers transparency, algorithmic trading, tick sizes (RTS 11), market structure, best execution, and investor protection
Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) (Regulation 596/2014): EU-wide rules on insider dealing, market manipulation, and disclosure of inside information
Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR): Governs Iberclear as Spain’s CSD
EMIR (European Market Infrastructure Regulation): Governs BME Clearing as a CCP



9.3 Market Surveillance

CNMV conducts ongoing market surveillance using automated systems to detect insider trading, market manipulation, and other abuses
BME operates its own first-line surveillance function, monitoring trading activity on SIBE and reporting suspicious activity to CNMV
Post-trade transparency requirements under MiFID II/MiFIR; all trades must be reported to Approved Publication Arrangements (APAs) and trade repositories



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction reporting to CNMV under MiFIR Article 26 (all investment firms must report transactions within T+1)
Listed company disclosure obligations: periodic financial reporting (annual, semi-annual), ad hoc disclosure of inside information (MAR), major shareholding notifications
Short selling disclosure under EU Short Selling Regulation
Penalties: CNMV can impose fines ranging from EUR 60,000-5,000,000 for “serious” infractions to EUR 300,000-10,000,000 (or 10% of turnover) for “very serious” infractions; fines can be tripled for aggravating factors



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

EU passporting under MiFID II allows EEA-authorized firms to access BME without separate Spanish authorization
CNMV maintains Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with securities regulators worldwide
BME/Iberclear connected to Eurosystem’s T2S for cross-border settlement
Latibex provides a specific cross-border listing framework for Latin American companies
Tender offer rules now extended to companies listed on MTFs (including BME Growth) domiciled in Spain

11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2023: SIX abandoned plans to migrate BME’s SIBE platform to SIX’s trading infrastructure, citing unexpected legal and technological complexity; SIBE continues as an independent platform
2025: Ongoing technology enhancements to SIBE-Smart for capacity and resilience [unverified]



New Products / Segments

2025: Launch of BME Easy Access – a simplified IPO mechanism allowing shares to be admitted without requiring minimum share distribution; approved by CNMV
2025: Launch of European-style stock options in Spain
2020: MAB rebranded as BME Growth to align with European SME growth market branding



Regulatory Changes

2023: Law 6/2023 (LMVSI) enacted, replacing the prior securities market law and completing MiFID II transposition
2025: Tender offer rules extended to MTF-listed companies (BME Growth) domiciled in Spain
MiFID II/MiFIR ongoing: Continued regulatory evolution affecting transparency, algorithmic trading, and market structure



Strategic Initiatives

CCP Integration: SIX announced (December 2025) the merger of SIX x-clear and BME Clearing into a single international multi-asset CCP, headquartered in Madrid with offices in Zurich and Oslo
SIX Group Synergies: Despite the trading platform integration being abandoned, SIX and BME continue to pursue synergies in clearing, settlement, data services, and index products
Retail Participation: Extended trading hours and simplified access mechanisms (BME Easy Access) to encourage retail investor participation
Latin American Bridge: Continued operation of Latibex as a unique EUR-denominated market for Latin American securities; BME holds participations in clearing houses in Colombia and the Mexican Stock Exchange

title: Comparative Analysis of Global Equities Exchanges
text:
9. Key Observations and Trends

9.1 Technology Convergence and Divergence
The global exchange landscape exhibits a clear technology stratification. At the top tier, Deutsche Borse T7 (~5 us), Nasdaq INET (~14 us), and Euronext Optiq (~15 us) deliver single-digit to low double-digit microsecond latencies. A second tier includes NYSE Pillar (~34 us), SGX REACH (sub-90 us), and Nasdaq-powered exchanges like Tadawul (<40 us) and SIX (~10.6 us). Notably, Chinese exchanges (SSE, SZSE) have diverged from the global technology ecosystem entirely, building proprietary systems aligned with national technology self-sufficiency mandates. This creates a bifurcated landscape: Western/global exchanges converging on a handful of platform families (Nasdaq INET, Millennium, Optiq, T7), while China’s exchanges operate in a largely opaque, domestically developed environment.


9.2 Platform Consolidation
Nasdaq technology (across INET, Genium INET, and X-Stream INET variants) powers the most exchanges globally – at least 8 of the 22 exchanges reviewed, plus 130+ other marketplaces. LSEG’s Millennium Exchange powers at least 3 exchanges (LSE, JSE, and until recently Borsa Italiana). This concentration of exchange technology in a few vendors creates both efficiency (shared development costs, proven platforms) and systemic risk (a vulnerability in one platform could affect multiple markets simultaneously).


9.3 Market Structure Modernization
Several exchanges are undergoing significant market structure reforms: - TWSE transitioned from call auction to continuous trading only in 2020, among the last major exchanges to do so - HKEX is reducing tick sizes in phases (2025-2026), narrowing the gap with Western peers - JPX extended trading hours and introduced a closing auction in 2024 (arrowhead 4.0) - ASX unified its opening auction and introduced post-close trading in 2025 (SR15 reforms) - NSE India is implementing the most aggressive tick size reform, moving from a uniform INR 0.05 to a 6-tier price-dependent structure


9.4 Settlement Cycle Acceleration
The global move toward shorter settlement is accelerating: - T+1 achieved: US (May 2024), Canada (May 2024), India (Jan 2023), China (T+1 with unique same-day sale restriction) - T+1 planned: EU (targeting 2027), UK (targeting 2027), Australia (post-CHESS replacement, likely 2029+) - T+2 standard: Most of Europe, Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, Saudi Arabia currently on T+2


9.5 Foreign Investor Liberalization
The trend toward barrier-free foreign investor access continues: - Tadawul abolished the QFI regime entirely in February 2026, granting barrier-free access - China expanded Stock Connect scope and abolished QFI quotas, though structural barriers (T+1, capital controls) remain - India simplified FPI registration and expanded GIFT City international access - TWSE has eliminated most foreign ownership limits (45% foreign ownership at end of 2024)


9.6 ESG and Sustainability Integration
ESG reporting and sustainability are becoming universal exchange requirements: - TWSE: All 1,029 listed companies submitted sustainability reports by August 2025; ESG Evaluation system launched 2026 - Tadawul: Launched ESG Disclosure Guidelines (2021); 29 Unified ESG Metrics across GCC exchanges - HKEX: Enhanced ESG reporting aligned with ISSB standards - Euronext: Bergamo data center powered by green energy - LSEG: Launched Sustainability Ratings and Data (March 2026)


9.7 24-Hour Trading Ambitions
Multiple exchanges are exploring extended or round-the-clock trading: - NASDAQ: Plans for 24/5 trading (pending SEC approval, H2 2026 target) - NYSE Arca: SEC approved 22-hour trading; implementation targeted late 2026 - JSE: Reported to be considering 24-hour trading (July 2025) - This trend reflects the globalization of capital flows and competition from crypto markets that trade 24/7

text:
10. KRX Positioning
Korea Exchange (KRX) serves as the reference benchmark for this research project. Based on the comparative analysis above, KRX’s positioning relative to global peers can be characterized as follows:

10.1 Market Size

Market capitalization: KRX KOSPI is approximately USD 1.6 trillion, placing it in the middle tier globally – comparable to JSE (~$1.5T) and larger than BME, Borsa Italiana, or SGX, but smaller than TWSE (~$2.9T), Tadawul (~$2.7T), or ASX (~$2.2T)
Listed companies: KOSPI + KOSDAQ combined total approximately 2,500+ companies, comparable to NYSE or HKEX



10.2 Trading System

KRX operates the Exture+ trading system. Compared to global peers, its latency and capacity specifications should be benchmarked against:

Top tier: Deutsche Borse T7 (~5 us), Nasdaq INET (~14 us), Euronext Optiq (~15 us)
Peer tier: HKEX OTP-C (60K orders/sec), SGX REACH (sub-90 us), ASX Trade (100K+ orders/sec)




10.3 Market Structure

Trading hours: KOSPI trades 09:00-15:30 KST (6.5 hours continuous, no lunch break since 2000), longer than TWSE (4.5 hrs), JPX (5.5 hrs), and SSE/SZSE (4 hrs), but shorter than SGX (7 hrs)
Daily price limits: KRX uses +/-30% limits (since 2015), among the widest in Asia (vs. TWSE +/-10%, SSE/SZSE +/-10-20%, HKEX no daily limit)
Lot size: KRX uses 1 share as the standard lot, aligned with global best practice
Circuit breakers: KRX employs both stock-level Volatility Interruption (VI) and market-wide SAPI mechanisms, consistent with the dual-layer approach used by most sophisticated exchanges



10.4 Settlement and Access

Settlement: T+2 (Korea is not yet on T+1, unlike the US, Canada, and India)
Foreign access: Relatively open with foreign investor registration; foreign ownership limits apply per company. No Stock Connect-style mechanism exists, though MSCI EM inclusion has long been a goal (Korea remains in MSCI EM, with discussions about potential DM reclassification contingent on FX market reforms)



10.5 Regulatory Framework

KRX operates under the Financial Services Commission (FSC) and Financial Supervisory Service (FSS), with KRX performing SRO functions – a structure similar to JPX-R (Japan), SGX RegCo (Singapore), and JSE (South Africa)
The regulatory framework is well-developed and IOSCO-aligned, comparable to other advanced Asian markets



10.6 Areas of Relative Strength

Continuous trading without lunch break (eliminated in 2000, ahead of many Asian peers)
Wide daily price limits (+/-30%) allowing efficient price discovery
Strong derivatives market (world-class options volume)
Well-developed electronic infrastructure



10.7 Areas for Potential Enhancement

T+1 settlement adoption (behind US, Canada, India)
MSCI DM reclassification (requires FX market liberalization)
Extended trading hours consideration (23-hour trading trend)
Enhanced international connectivity mechanisms (no Stock Connect equivalent)

title: Global Equities Markets — Overview
text:
1. Introduction
This document provides a high-level overview of global equities (securities) markets, their structure, key players, and trends. It serves as the entry point for the detailed exchange-by-exchange research in this project.

title: Global Equities Markets — Overview

2. Global Equities Market Landscape

2.1 Market Size & Scale

Total global market capitalization: ~USD 115 trillion (as of early 2026; WFE member exchanges aggregate). The U.S. alone accounts for over USD 50 trillion, representing roughly 44% of global equity market value.
Number of listed companies worldwide: ~58,000+ across WFE member exchanges (2025). This figure includes main boards and growth/SME boards. The largest exchanges by listing count include BSE (~5,936), NASDAQ (~4,075), JPX/TSE (~3,945), TMX Group (~3,400+ across TSX and TSXV), SZSE (~2,879), and HKEX (~2,673).

The U.S. markets (NYSE + NASDAQ + other U.S. venues) alone account for approximately USD 500+ billion/day. title: Global Equities Markets — Overview
text:
3. Market Structure Models

3.1 Order-Driven Markets
An order-driven market matches buy and sell orders directly through a central limit order book (CLOB) based on price-time priority, without designated intermediaries providing obligatory quotes.
Pure Order-Driven Examples: - NASDAQ — Fully electronic order-driven market with competing market makers providing liquidity voluntarily (not obligatory for all securities). Price-time priority matching. - JPX/TSE — Pure order-driven market using Itayose (call auction) for opening/closing and Zaraba (continuous matching) during the session. No designated market makers for most securities (though ETF market making incentive schemes exist). - SSE and SZSE — Order-driven markets with call auction opening/closing and continuous matching. No formal market maker system for A-shares on the main boards (STAR Market and ChiNext have introduced voluntary market making in 2023-2024). - Euronext — Order-driven across all markets (Amsterdam, Brussels, Paris, Dublin, Lisbon, Milan, Oslo, Athens) with optional Liquidity Provider and Supplemental Liquidity Provider programmes. - ASX — Pure order-driven CLOB with no obligatory market makers for equities (though designated price makers exist for ETFs and some less liquid securities). - TMX / TSX — Order-driven CLOB with no designated market makers; however, assigned Market Makers and Odd Lot Dealers exist for certain securities.


3.2 Quote-Driven Markets
A quote-driven market relies on market makers (dealers) who continuously post bid and ask quotes, with investors trading against these quotes rather than directly with each other.
Examples: - LSE SEAQ — The Stock Exchange Automated Quotations system is a pure quote-driven platform for the least liquid UK securities. Market makers are obligated to provide continuous two-sided quotes. - LSE SETSqx — A hybrid system where market makers provide continuous quotes throughout the day, supplemented by periodic intraday auctions (at 08:00, 09:00, 11:00, 14:00, and 16:35).
Note: Pure quote-driven markets have become rare in modern equities trading. Most exchanges have adopted order-driven or hybrid models due to the transparency and efficiency advantages of central limit order books.


3.3 Hybrid Markets
Hybrid markets combine elements of both order-driven and quote-driven structures, typically featuring an electronic order book supplemented by designated intermediaries with obligations to provide liquidity.
Examples: - NYSE — The archetypal hybrid market. Features a central limit order book combined with Designated Market Makers (DMMs) who are assigned to specific securities and obligated to maintain fair and orderly markets. DMMs operate both on the physical trading floor and electronically. The NYSE is the last major exchange to maintain a physical trading floor with human intermediaries. - LSE SETS — Primarily order-driven with registered market makers who can provide continuous quotes but are not strictly obligated to do so. Market makers receive certain benefits (reduced fees, short-selling exemptions). - Deutsche Borse / Xetra — Order-driven CLOB supplemented by Designated Sponsors (liquidity providers) who are contractually obligated to provide continuous quotes for less liquid securities. On the Frankfurt floor, Specialists provide indicative and binding quotes. - HKEX — Primarily order-driven but allows designated securities market makers for structured products, ETFs, and derivatives. - SGX — Order-driven market with Designated Market Makers (DMMs) for less liquid securities and ETFs, obligated to maintain continuous two-sided quotes. - SIX Swiss Exchange — Order-driven CLOB with Market Maker and Liquidity Provider programmes for ETFs, structured products, and less liquid equities. - Tadawul — Order-driven with Liquidity Provider programmes to enhance market quality.
