title: Global Equities Markets — Overview
text:
5. Regulatory Landscape

5.1 North America

United States:

Regulation NMS (2005, amended 2024-2025): Core framework for U.S. equity market structure. Mandates order protection (trade-through rule), access fees, sub-penny rule, and market data. SEC adopted amendments in 2024 to reduce minimum tick sizes for liquid stocks and adjust access fee caps.
Reg SHO: Short selling regulation (locate requirement, close-out obligations).
Reg ATS: Governs alternative trading systems (dark pools, ECNs).
LULD (Limit Up-Limit Down): Dynamic price bands preventing trades outside specified percentage thresholds.
MWCB (Market-Wide Circuit Breakers): S&P 500-based halts at 7%, 13%, 20% declines.
CAT (Consolidated Audit Trail): Comprehensive regulatory database tracking all equity/options order events.
SRO model: NYSE, NASDAQ, and FINRA function as self-regulatory organizations under SEC oversight.
T+1 settlement: Implemented May 2024 in the U.S. and Canada.

Canada:

Provincial securities regulation coordinated via CSA (Canadian Securities Administrators) with the OSC as lead regulator.
CIRO (Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization): Formed 2023 from merger of IIROC and MFDA; administers UMIR (Universal Market Integrity Rules).
T+1 settlement implemented May 27, 2024.




5.2 Europe

MiFID II / MiFIR (2018, ongoing reform): Comprehensive EU framework for financial markets. Key provisions: pre-/post-trade transparency, tick size regime (RTS 11), systematic internalisers, dark pool volume caps (reformed to single 7% cap under MiFIR Refit), best execution obligations.
MiFIR Refit (2024-2025): Reforms include consolidated tape for equities, bond transparency, and designation of a single CT provider.
CSDR (Central Securities Depositories Regulation): Settlement discipline regime, mandatory buy-ins (delayed implementation), CSD authorization.
EMIR: OTC derivatives clearing obligations, CCP requirements.
MAR (Market Abuse Regulation): Insider dealing, market manipulation, unlawful disclosure prohibitions.
DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act): Applied January 2025; ICT risk management requirements for financial entities.
ESMA: EU-level supervisory coordination; administers waivers, registers, and MiFID II delegated acts.
Switzerland: FINMA supervision under the Financial Market Infrastructure Act (FMIA). EU equivalence recognition was revoked in 2019 (protective measures enacted by Swiss Federal Council) and lifted in May 2025.
UK (post-Brexit): Retained EU acquis (UK MAR, UK MiFIR) administered by the FCA under FSMA. Diverging from EU on topics such as the consolidated tape and Listings Rules reform.



5.3 Asia-Pacific

Japan:

FIEA (Financial Instruments and Exchange Act): Primary securities law governing trading, disclosure, and market conduct.
JFSA / SESC: Financial Services Agency regulates; SESC investigates market violations.
JPX-R: Self-regulatory organization within JPX handling listing examination, surveillance, and compliance.
Corporate Governance Code: Principles-based governance framework administered by TSE (PBR initiative since 2023).

Hong Kong:

SFC (Securities and Futures Commission): Statutory regulator under the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO).
HKEX operates as a recognized exchange company with SFC oversight. Government holds a 5.87% stake.

China (Mainland):

CSRC (China Securities Regulatory Commission): Central regulatory authority managing SSE, SZSE, and BSE.
Registration-based IPO system: Introduced on STAR Market (2019), ChiNext (2020), fully rolled out across all boards (2023), replacing the approval-based system.
QFI (Qualified Foreign Investor) scheme: Unified from QFII/RQFII in 2020; quota limits abolished. QFI regime fully abolished February 2026 for Tadawul (Saudi); in China, remains the framework for foreign institutional access though barriers have been significantly reduced.
Daily price limits: +/-10% (main boards), +/-20% (STAR Market, ChiNext), no limit first 5 days for new STAR/ChiNext listings.

India:

SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India): Primary regulator for NSE, BSE, and other exchanges.
T+1 settlement: India completed transition in January 2023, among the first major markets globally.
Securities Markets Code 2025: Proposed consolidation of SCRA, SEBI Act, and Depositories Act.

Singapore:

MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore): Central bank and integrated financial regulator under the Securities and Futures Act (SFA).
SGX RegCo: Independent regulatory subsidiary of SGX.

Taiwan:

FSC (Financial Supervisory Commission): Primary regulator for TWSE.
Transitioned from periodic call auction to continuous trading (March 2020).

Australia:

ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission): Primary market conduct regulator. Launched formal Inquiry into ASX Group in June 2025.
RBA: Oversees clearing and settlement stability.
Competition: Cboe Australia operates as a competing lit venue (since 2012).




5.4 Middle East & Africa

Saudi Arabia:

CMA (Capital Market Authority): Established 2003 under the Capital Market Law. Oversaw progressive foreign investor liberalization culminating in full barrier-free access (February 2026).
MSCI and FTSE Russell Emerging Market inclusion (2019) catalyzed institutional development.

South Africa:

FSCA (Financial Sector Conduct Authority): Primary market conduct regulator for JSE.
Twin Peaks model: FSCA (conduct) + SARB Prudential Authority (stability).




5.5 Cross-Border and Global Trends

T+1 settlement adoption: U.S. and Canada (May 2024), India (January 2023). EU targeting T+1 by October 2027. UK consulting on T+1 timeline.
Stock Connect programs: Shanghai-Hong Kong (2014), Shenzhen-Hong Kong (2016), Bond Connect (2017), ETF Connect (2022), Swap Connect (2023). GIFT Connect (SGX-NSE IX, 2023) for India derivatives.
Consolidated tape mandates: EU pursuing a single CT provider for equities under MiFIR Refit. U.S. operates existing SIP infrastructure (CTS/CQS, UTP).
ESG disclosure harmonization: GCC Exchanges Committee (chaired by Tadawul) introduced 29 Unified ESG Metrics (2023). TWSE mandated sustainability reports for all listed companies (2025). LSEG launched Sustainability Ratings (2026).

title: Global Equities Markets — Overview
text:
6. Key Trends

6.1 T+1 / T+0 Settlement Transition

U.S. and Canada implemented T+1 on May 27-28, 2024. The SEC is considering T+0 as a longer-term goal.
India completed T+1 in January 2023 and is piloting optional T+0 settlement for select securities.
EU has set a target of October 2027 for T+1 adoption.
UK is consulting on a T+1 timeline, likely to follow the EU.
Impact: Reduces counterparty risk and margin requirements but increases operational demands for same-day trade confirmation, allocation, and funding.



6.2 Cloud Adoption

JPX conducted a proof of concept with AWS Outposts and Fujitsu in 2025 for potential cloud migration of the arrowhead trading system.
ASX exploring cloud for post-trade infrastructure after abandoning DLT-based CHESS replacement.
Nasdaq offers cloud-based market technology to client exchanges globally.
LSEG partnering with Microsoft Azure for data and analytics platform enhancements.
Challenge: Regulatory concerns about operational resilience, data sovereignty, and latency remain barriers to cloud adoption for core matching engines.



6.3 Digital Assets / Tokenization

SIX Digital Exchange (SDX): Operational since 2021 with FINMA license; world’s first fully regulated digital asset exchange and CSD.
Deutsche Borse D7: Digital post-trade platform launched 2024; Crypto Finance AG acquisition for digital asset trading.
NASDAQ: SEC approved tokenized stock settlement for certain securities (March 2026).
LSE/LSEG: On-chain settlement initiative (Digital Markets Infrastructure) announced 2026.
ASX: Abandoned DLT/blockchain for CHESS replacement (2022, ~AUD 250M write-off); pivoted to conventional technology with TCS.



6.4 ESG Integration

TWSE: All 1,029 listed companies submitted sustainability reports by August 2025 deadline; ESG Evaluation system launched in 2026.
GCC Exchanges (Tadawul-chaired): 29 Unified ESG Metrics introduced in 2023.
LSEG: Launched Sustainability Ratings and Data in 2026.
Bursa Malaysia: MSPO certification mandated for commodity derivatives delivery (2021), first exchange globally to require sustainability certification.
JPX/TSE: PBR (price-to-book ratio) initiative since 2023 requesting companies to disclose plans for improving capital efficiency and stock price.
Trend: ESG reporting moving from voluntary to mandatory across major markets, with increasing focus on climate-related financial disclosures (TCFD/ISSB standards).



6.5 Retail Trading Growth

China (SSE/SZSE): Retail investors account for ~60-80% of trading volume, among the highest globally.
India (NSE/BSE): Demat account openings surged; retail participation growing rapidly in both cash and derivatives markets.
U.S.: Post-2020 retail surge (commission-free trading, fractional shares, social media-driven). NYSE introduced Retail Price Improvement (RPI) orders.
Saudi Arabia: QFI restrictions abolished (February 2026); previously retail-dominated market opening to foreign flows.
Korea: High retail participation (~60-70% of turnover); KOSPI surged from 2,500 to 6,000 (Oct 2025 - Feb 2026); Nextrade (NXT) launched March 2025 as first alternative exchange, reaching a 10–15% market share by October 2026; broker Smart Order Routing (SOR) fully operational; KRX introduced maker-taker fees (Dec 2025), Midpoint & Stop-Limit orders, and full operation of the National Short-sale Detecting System (NSDS) alongside T+1 roadmap planning as of October 2026.
Taiwan: High retail participation (~60-70% of turnover) with active options/derivatives retail trading.



6.6 AI/ML in Surveillance and Trading

LSEG: Integrated financial data into ChatGPT (2025); Microsoft partnership for AI-powered analytics.
Nasdaq: AI-driven market surveillance across 130+ market operator clients globally.
Exchanges generally: Deploying ML for anomaly detection in order flow, insider trading pattern recognition, market manipulation surveillance.
NSE India: Planning nanosecond-level trading system upgrade with capacity of ~100 million transactions/second (April 2026).
Regulatory implication: Regulators (SEC, ESMA, MAS) increasingly focused on AI governance in trading, algorithmic accountability, and model risk management.



6.7 Extended Trading Hours

NYSE Arca: SEC approved 22-hour trading (1:30 AM - 11:30 PM ET Mon-Thu), targeted late 2026.
NASDAQ: Planning 23-hour sessions (pending SEC approval, H2 2026).
JPX/TSE: Extended trading hours by 30 minutes (to 15:30) and introduced closing auction session in November 2024.
HKEX: Shortened lunch break from 1.5 hours to 1 hour (2011); periodic discussions about further reduction or elimination.
Trend: Driven by globalization, institutional demand for risk management during non-home-market hours, and competition from crypto markets operating 24/7.

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
1. Overview & Profile







Item
Details




Official Name
ASX Limited (operating the Australian Securities Exchange)


Abbreviation
ASX


Website
https://www.asx.com.au


Year Established
1987 (merger of six state-based stock exchanges); ASX Limited formed in 2006 via merger of ASX and SFE (Sydney Futures Exchange)


Country / City
Australia / Sydney (Exchange Centre, 20 Bridge Street, Sydney NSW 2000)


Ownership Structure
Publicly listed on its own exchange (ticker: ASX); ~50% retail investors, ~49% institutional (top holders: UniSuper ~14%, BlackRock ~6.1%, AustralianSuper ~6.1%), insiders <1%


Parent Company / Group
ASX Limited (self-listed holding company)


Regulatory Authority
Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC); Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) for clearing and settlement stability


CEO
Helen Lofthouse (appointed August 2022)


Market Capitalization (listed companies)
~AUD 3.4 trillion / ~USD 2.2 trillion (February 2026)


ASX Limited Market Cap (exchange operator)
~AUD 9.6 billion (2026)


Total Listed Instruments
~2,241 listed companies (as of 2025)


Average Daily Trading Volume
~AUD 4.7 billion average daily turnover


FY2025 Operating Revenue
AUD 1,107.2 million (+7.0% YoY)


FY2025 Underlying Net Profit
AUD 510.0 million (+7.5% YoY)




Vertical Integration
ASX is one of the world’s few vertically integrated exchange groups, operating across the full value chain: - Listings: ASX Listing Rules govern admission and ongoing obligations - Trading: ASX Trade (cash equities), ASX 24 (derivatives) - Clearing: ASX Clear (cash equities and equity options), ASX Clear (Futures) - Settlement: ASX Settlement (via CHESS – Clearing House Electronic Subregister System) - Registry: Austraclear (debt securities)


Key Historical Milestones

1861: First stock exchange established in Melbourne
1871: Sydney Stock Exchange established
1987: Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) formed on 1 April through the merger of six independent state-based stock exchanges (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Hobart, Perth) under the Australian Securities Exchange and National Guarantee Fund Act 1987
1987: Fully electronic trading introduced (SEATS – Stock Exchange Automated Trading System), replacing floor trading
1990: ASX became a national market; Australian Securities Commission (predecessor to ASIC) established
1996: CHESS (Clearing House Electronic Subregister System) launched for electronic settlement and subregistry
1998: ASX demutualised and listed on its own exchange (13 October), becoming one of the first exchanges globally to do so
2006: ASX merged with the Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) to form ASX Limited, creating a multi-asset exchange group
2010: ASX Trade launched (powered by NASDAQ OMX Genium INET), replacing SEATS/ITS
2010-2011: Proposed merger with Singapore Exchange (SGX) for AUD 8.4 billion; blocked by the Australian government on national interest grounds (April 2011)
2012: Chi-X Australia (now Cboe Australia) launched as a competing lit market, ending ASX’s trading monopoly; ASIC assumed market supervision from ASX
2015: ASX selected Digital Asset Holdings (DA) to explore distributed ledger technology (DLT) for CHESS replacement
2017: ASX formally announced the CHESS replacement using DLT/blockchain technology
2022: ASX abandoned the DLT-based CHESS replacement project in November, writing off ~AUD 250 million
2023: ASX selected Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as the new implementation partner for CHESS replacement using conventional technology
2024: CHESS batch settlement failure on 20 December triggered major regulatory scrutiny
2025: ASIC launched formal Inquiry into ASX Group (June 2025) following “repeated and serious failures”
2025: Market structure changes (SR15) implemented on 23 June – single opening auction, new closing auction format, and post-close trading session

Warrant Market Making: Issuers of structured warrants are required to make markets in their products

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Orders accumulate during the pre-open phase (from 07:00). At a randomised time between 09:59:00 and 09:59:15, the system executes a single-price auction that maximises tradable volume. The equilibrium price algorithm considers: (1) maximum executable volume, (2) minimum order imbalance at that volume, (3) reference price proximity. All securities open simultaneously (single open, effective June 2025).
Closing Single Price Auction (CSPA): The pre-CSPA phase begins at 16:00, allowing orders to accumulate. At a randomised time around 16:10-16:11, the closing auction executes using the same equilibrium price algorithm. The CSPA closing price is the official closing price used for index calculations, margin calculations, and NAV determinations.
Post-Close Session: Introduced June 2025, this 10-minute continuous trading session allows orders to match at the official closing price only. Provides additional liquidity for participants needing to execute at the close (e.g., index funds, benchmark-driven strategies).
Volatility Auction: Not a formal separate auction; instead, ASX uses Extreme Trade Range (ETR) and Anomalous Order Threshold (AOT) mechanisms to pause or restrict trading when price volatility is excessive (see Section 8).



3.2 Continuous Trading

Model: Pure order-driven Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) for ASX TradeMatch (lit market)
Priority: Strict price-time priority – orders matched first by best price, then by time of entry at the same price level
Dark Liquidity: ASX Centre Point operates as an integrated dark pool alongside the lit order book (see Section 4.2)
Session Duration: 6 hours continuous (10:00-16:00), no lunch break



3.3 Price Discovery
Equilibrium Price Algorithm (for auctions): 1. Calculate the price that maximises executable volume 2. If multiple prices yield the same maximum volume, select the price with the smallest imbalance 3. If still tied, select the price closest to the reference price (last traded price or previous close) 4. Market orders participate with highest priority
Continuous Session: - Price discovery through continuous matching of incoming aggressive orders against resting passive orders - ASX TradeMatch (lit) and ASX Centre Point (dark) operate as two integrated venues within the same matching engine - Centre Point orders execute at or within the NBBO (National Best Bid and Offer), with midpoint being the default execution price

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types (ASX TradeMatch – Lit Market)







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Buy or sell at a specified price or better; rests on the order book if not immediately matched


Market Order
Execute immediately at the best available price; any unfilled quantity converts to a limit order at the last execution price (market-to-limit behaviour)


Market-to-Limit Order
Execute at the best available price; unfilled portion rests as a limit order at the price of the last partial fill





4.2 Advanced Order Types (ASX Centre Point – Dark)







Order Type
Description




Centre Point
Non-displayed order matched at the midpoint of the NBBO; provides price improvement over the lit market


Centre Point Block
Centre Point order with a user-defined Minimum Acceptable Quantity (MAQ); only executes when the MAQ can be satisfied


Single Fill MAQ
Executes only when the full MAQ can be satisfied by a single opposing order; designed for block discovery with minimal information leakage


Dark Limit
Non-displayed order executed at any permitted dark price up to the specified limit price (not restricted to midpoint)


ASX Sweep
Single transaction that sweeps dark liquidity in Centre Point first, then lit liquidity in TradeMatch; remaining volume rests in TradeMatch


ASX Sweep Dual Post
Simultaneously posts orders in both Centre Point and TradeMatch at limit +1/2 tick; no risk of overfill


Pegged Order
Order that automatically adjusts its price to track the best bid or offer [unverified – specific pegged order availability may vary]





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF Option
Description




Day
Valid for the current trading day only; cancelled at end of day


IOC (Immediate or Cancel)
Execute immediately (fully or partially); cancel any unfilled portion


FOK (Fill or Kill)
Execute immediately in full or cancel the entire order


GTC (Good-till-Cancel)
Remains active until executed or explicitly cancelled (subject to maximum order lifetime)


GTD (Good-till-Date)
Remains active until specified date or until filled/cancelled


GTE (Good-till-Expiry)
Remains active until the expiry date of the instrument





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled during the pre-open and continuous trading sessions
Price amendments result in loss of time priority (new timestamp assigned)
Quantity reductions (downward amendments) preserve time priority
During the Non-Cancel period of auctions, no cancellations or amendments are permitted
ASX Operating Rules require participants to have adequate systems to manage and control orders

text:
6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols








Protocol
Description
Use Case




ASX ITCH
Ultra-low latency binary multicast protocol; delivers full order book detail with nanosecond timestamps
Primary feed for algorithmic/HFT firms; full depth of book


GLIMPSE
Point-to-point TCP snapshot feed complementing ITCH
Order book recovery/synchronisation; provides current state snapshot with sequence number for ITCH resync


FIX Market Data
Industry-standard FIX protocol for market data delivery
Broader participant community; lower-latency requirements


ASX MDF (Market Data Feed)
[Legacy/alternative market data distribution]
General market data consumption





6.2 Data Levels

Level 1 (Top of Book): Best bid/offer prices and sizes; last traded price, volume; daily high/low/open/close
Level 2 (Market Depth): Multiple price levels of the order book (typically 5-10 levels of aggregated depth)
Full Depth (ITCH): Complete order-by-order view of the order book; every order addition, modification, cancellation, and execution event; all price levels



6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

Direct Feeds: Available via co-location at the ALC or via ASX Net connectivity
Redistributors: ASX real-time data distributed through major vendors including Refinitiv (LSEG), Bloomberg, FactSet, and others
ASX Information Services: Manages licensing and distribution of all ASX market data products
Delivery: ITCH via UDP multicast; GLIMPSE via TCP (SoupBinTCP); FIX via TCP



6.4 Historical Data

ASX provides end-of-day data, tick-by-tick historical data, and reference data through ASX Information Services
Third-party providers (e.g., Refinitiv, TickData) offer processed historical ASX data products
Corporate actions and announcement data available through ASX’s company announcements platform

7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Market Participants: Must hold an Australian Market Licence (AML) or be authorised by ASIC as a market participant under the Corporations Act 2001
Trading Participants: Must meet ASX Operating Rules requirements including capital adequacy, organisational capacity, and system certification
Clearing Participants: Separate membership required for ASX Clear (cash) and ASX Clear (Futures); subject to capital requirements and risk management obligations
Settlement Participants: Must be approved by ASX Settlement to participate in CHESS



7.2 Connection Methods







Method
Description




Co-location (ALC)
Direct rack space in the Australian Liquidity Centre; equal-length cross-connects to matching engine


ASX Net
ASX’s high-performance dark fibre network connecting ALC to participant offices and other data centres in Sydney and Melbourne


Third-party Networks
Carrier-neutral ALC allows connection via preferred network providers (e.g., BT Radianz, IPC, TNS)


Internet/VPN
Available for non-latency-sensitive connectivity (e.g., surveillance, reporting)





7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

Location: Australian Liquidity Centre (ALC), Gore Hill, Sydney, NSW
Facility: Purpose-built Tier III data centre, opened 2012; designed specifically for financial markets
Equal Access: All co-located participants receive identical-length cross-connects to the matching engine
Tenants: 100+ financial organisations including buy-side firms, sell-side firms, alternative liquidity venues, ISVs, and network providers
Peer-to-Peer: Cross-connect fabric enables direct participant-to-participant connectivity within the ALC



7.4 API Protocols







Protocol
Use Case




FIX (Financial Information eXchange)
Standard order entry and execution; widely supported; suitable for most participants


OUCH
Ultra-low latency binary order entry protocol; optimised for algorithmic and high-frequency trading


ITCH
Ultra-low latency binary market data protocol; full depth of book via multicast


GLIMPSE
TCP-based order book snapshot recovery; complements ITCH for session recovery


OMNet / OMEX
Legacy API interfaces [unverified – may have been retired with platform upgrades]





7.5 Certification / Testing

All market participants must complete ASX certification testing before connecting to the production environment
ASX provides a Customer Development Environment (CDE) for testing
Participants must re-certify following significant system changes (either ASX or participant-side)
Technical documentation available via ASX Online (asxonline.com)

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits








Type
Threshold
Action




Anomalous Order Threshold (AOT)
+/- 10% from a rolling 2-minute VWAP reference price (updated every minute)
Orders priced beyond the AOT are rejected; prevents fat-finger and erroneous orders


Extreme Trade Range (ETR)
Stock-specific price bands (calculated for each security based on its characteristics)
If a potential trade would breach the ETR, trading in that security is paused for 2 minutes





8.2 Circuit Breakers








Mechanism
Trigger
Action




Extreme Trade Range (ETR) Pause
Trade would execute outside the ETR band for a specific security
2-minute trading pause in the affected security; other securities continue trading normally


Market-wide Circuit Breaker
ASX does not operate a formal market-wide circuit breaker based on index decline thresholds (unlike NYSE/NASDAQ)
ASX relies on individual security-level controls (ETR/AOT) and has the discretion to halt the market under extraordinary circumstances


Trading Halt
Requested by the listed entity or imposed by ASX for pending price-sensitive announcements
Trading suspended until the announcement is released and the market has time to absorb the information


Suspension
Imposed by ASX for non-compliance with listing rules, at ASIC direction, or for other regulatory reasons
Trading suspended indefinitely until the issue is resolved



ASX’s Philosophy: ASX has publicly articulated a preference for individual security-level controls (AOT/ETR) over broad market-wide circuit breakers, arguing that targeted mechanisms are more effective at maintaining orderly markets without unnecessarily disrupting trading in unaffected securities.


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Anomalous Order Threshold (AOT): Prevents aggressive orders beyond +/- 10% of the reference price
Order Size Limits: ASX Operating Rules require participants to implement their own order size controls; ASX can also set system-level limits
Participant-level Controls: Trading participants are required to maintain pre-trade risk management systems including maximum order value checks and position limits
Kill Switch: ASX provides functionality for participants to cancel all resting orders (mass cancel) in emergency situations



8.4 Kill Switch

Participants can issue mass cancel requests via FIX or OUCH protocols to cancel all outstanding orders
ASX can also exercise its own authority to cancel or remove orders from the market in exceptional circumstances under the ASX Operating Rules

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission): Primary regulator; responsible for market supervision, licensing of market operators and participants, enforcement of market integrity rules, and consumer protection
RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia): Oversees clearing and settlement facility licensees under the Financial Stability Standards; assesses ASX Clear and ASX Settlement annually for compliance
ASX Compliance: ASX’s internal compliance function monitors listing rule compliance by listed entities (separate from ASIC’s market supervision role)



9.2 Key Regulations

Corporations Act 2001 (Cth): Primary legislation governing financial markets, including Part 7.2 (market licences), Part 7.3 (clearing and settlement facility licences), and Part 7.10 (market integrity)
ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017: Detailed rules governing trading conduct, best execution, order handling, and market manipulation
ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Competition in Exchange Markets) 2011: Rules governing competition between trading venues (ASX vs. Cboe Australia)
ASX Operating Rules: Exchange-specific rules governing trading participants, order entry, and market conduct
ASX Listing Rules: Govern the admission and ongoing obligations of listed entities, including continuous disclosure, related party transactions, and shareholder approval requirements
ASX Clear Operating Rules / ASX Settlement Operating Rules: Govern clearing and settlement participants
Financial Stability Standards (RBA): Standards that ASX Clear and ASX Settlement must meet to maintain their clearing and settlement facility licences



9.3 Market Surveillance

ASIC Market Supervision: ASIC assumed direct market supervision responsibility from ASX in August 2010 (formalised 2012), using the SMARTS surveillance system
Real-time Monitoring: ASIC monitors all trading activity across ASX and Cboe Australia in real time for market manipulation, insider trading, and other misconduct
ASX Listing Compliance: ASX retains responsibility for monitoring compliance with Listing Rules (continuous disclosure, corporate governance)
ASIC Inquiry into ASX (2025-2026): ASIC launched a formal inquiry into the ASX Group in June 2025, following the December 2024 CHESS settlement failure and other incidents; the inquiry examined governance, capability, and risk management across all ASX licensed entities



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Continuous Disclosure: Listed entities must immediately disclose price-sensitive information under ASX Listing Rule 3.1 and Section 674 of the Corporations Act
Transaction Reporting: Market participants must report all transactions to ASIC
Substantial Holder Notices: Required when ownership crosses 5% threshold (and for each 1% change thereafter)
Short Selling Reporting: Daily reporting of covered short sales; naked short selling is prohibited



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

ASX has mutual recognition arrangements with several overseas exchanges and regulators
Foreign companies can list on ASX under the Foreign Exempt listing category
ASIC participates in IOSCO and has MoUs with numerous international regulators
The proposed ASX-SGX merger (2010-2011) was blocked by the Australian government under the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act on national interest grounds

title: Australian Securities Exchange (ASX)
text:
11. Recent Developments

CHESS Replacement Saga (Major Story)
The failed CHESS replacement project is one of the most significant technology failures in global exchange history:
Phase 1 – DLT/Blockchain Approach (2015-2022): - 2015: ASX selected Digital Asset Holdings (DA) to explore DLT for CHESS replacement - 2017: ASX formally announced CHESS replacement using DA’s distributed ledger technology - 2018-2022: Repeated delays; go-live date pushed back multiple times (originally 2020, then 2021, 2022, 2023) - November 2022: ASX abandoned the DLT-based project after an independent review by Accenture found the software was only 63% complete with an uncertain timeline and overly complex integrated design - Financial impact: ~AUD 250 million write-off - Key lesson: Attempting to replace critical market infrastructure with unproven technology (enterprise blockchain) was identified as a fundamental strategic error
Phase 2 – Conventional Technology Approach (2023-present): - 2023: ASX selected Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as the new implementation partner - Two-phased approach: Phase 1 (clearing) targeted for late April 2026; Phase 2 (settlement and subregistry) targeted for 2028-2029 - Complete pivot away from DLT to conventional technology stack - CHESS replacement Release One go-live targeted for late April 2026 [subject to change]


December 2024 CHESS Settlement Failure

20 December 2024: CHESS batch settlement failed to complete, pushing all settlements to the following Monday
Root cause: A memory allocation coding error introduced in 2014 that went undetected for a decade until specific conditions triggered it
Impact: Disrupted settlement of all cash equity transactions for the Australian market
Triggered unprecedented joint RBA-ASIC intervention in March 2025



ASIC Inquiry into ASX Group (2025-2026)

March 2025: RBA and ASIC issued joint letter expressing “deep concerns” about ASX’s operational risk management
June 2025: ASIC launched formal Inquiry into the ASX Group covering governance, capability, and risk management across all ASX licensed entities (market licences and clearing/settlement facility licences)
The inquiry examined “repeated and serious failures” across the ASX Group
December 2025: ASIC announced a “transformational package” to safeguard financial markets based on the inquiry’s interim report
March 2026: ASIC published the ASX Inquiry Panel Final Report with observations and recommendations for change



Market Structure Changes – SR15 (June 2025)

Single Opening Auction: All securities now open simultaneously (replaced the previous 5-group staggered open)
Enhanced Closing Auction: Extended pre-CSPA window from 16:00 (was 16:07); improved handling of late price-sensitive announcements
Post-Close Trading Session: New 10-minute continuous lit session after the CSPA at the official closing price (16:11-16:21:30)
These changes align ASX more closely with global best practice (similar to NASDAQ, HKEX, LSE)



T+1 Settlement Plans

Australia currently settles on T+2
ASX published an industry whitepaper in April 2024; T+1 Working Group established December 2023
Industry consensus: T+1 is desirable but should not proceed until the CHESS replacement is complete
No confirmed T+1 implementation date; earliest feasible timeline likely 2029+ (after CHESS Phase 2)
International context: US moved to T+1 in May 2024; EU targeting 2027; UK targeting 2027



Other Developments

Tokenised Government Bond Settlement: ASX launched a pilot for tokenised government bond settlement in March 2026

Key Historical Milestones

1808: Borsa di commercio di Milano established by Napoleonic decree (16 January and 6 February 1808)
1808-1996: Operated as a government-regulated public institution; trading conducted on the physical floor at Palazzo Mezzanotte
1991: Electronic trading introduced alongside floor trading
1994: Floor trading ceased; full migration to electronic systems
1997: Privatisation of the Italian stock exchange; Borsa Italiana S.p.A. formally created
1998: Borsa Italiana S.p.A. becomes effective as a private entity (2 January 1998), consolidating all Italian regulated markets
2007: London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) acquires Borsa Italiana for EUR 1.6 billion (23 June 2007), forming LSEG
2010: MTA renamed and modernized under LSEG ownership; Millennium Exchange technology deployed
2020: LSEG agrees to divest Borsa Italiana Group to Euronext for EUR 4.325 billion (9 October 2020), a condition of LSEG’s acquisition of Refinitiv to satisfy EU antitrust requirements
2021: Euronext completes acquisition of Borsa Italiana Group (29 April 2021); Euronext’s Core Data Centre migration from Basildon (UK) to Aruba IT3, Bergamo (Italy) announced
2022: Core Data Centre migration to Bergamo completed
2023: Phase 1 Optiq migration – equities and ETFs migrated to Euronext Optiq platform (27 March 2023); Phase 2 – fixed income, warrants, and certificates migrated (11 September 2023); market segments rebranded (MTA to Euronext Milan, AIM Italia to Euronext Growth Milan)
2024: Phase 3 Optiq migration – Italian derivatives migrated to Optiq (April 2024); full integration onto Euronext single trading platform completed
2025: Market capitalisation surpasses EUR 1 trillion; 71st listing on Euronext in 2025


Note on LSEG-to-Euronext Transition: The sale of Borsa Italiana was driven by EU antitrust conditions imposed on LSEG’s USD 27 billion Refinitiv acquisition. Euronext’s acquisition included not only Borsa Italiana’s markets but also CC&G (central counterparty, now Euronext Clearing) and Monte Titoli (central securities depository). The full technology migration from LSEG’s Millennium platform to Euronext’s Optiq platform was completed in three phases across 2023-2024, less than three years after acquisition.

title: Borsa Italiana (Euronext Milan)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Begins after the pre-open order accumulation phase. Orders accumulate and the uncrossing algorithm determines the price that maximizes executable volume. Includes a random end period (typically up to 30 seconds) to prevent last-second manipulation
Closing Auction: At 17:25, continuous trading halts and a closing auction period begins. The uncrossing determines the official closing price (used by index providers, fund managers, and for NAV calculations). Includes a random end period
Volatility Auction: Triggered when a potential execution would breach dynamic or static price monitoring thresholds (circuit breakers). Trading is suspended and a call auction is initiated to allow orderly price discovery. Minimum duration 5 minutes; can be extended if the indicative price would breach thresholds again (average duration in Borsa Italiana historically ~10 minutes, with extensions up to 50 minutes observed)
Trading at Closing Price: After the closing auction, a brief session allows execution at the established closing price only



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with price/time priority matching during the continuous session (~09:00-17:25 CET)
Each new order is immediately matched against opposite orders in the order book; any unmatched portion rests on the book
Optional market maker participation provides additional liquidity
Runs on the Euronext Optiq matching engine (since March 2023 for equities)



3.3 Price Discovery

Price discovery occurs primarily through the opening and closing auctions and continuous order book interaction
The uncrossing algorithm maximizes executable volume, then minimizes surplus, then references the prior price
Reference prices for circuit breakers are derived from auction uncrossing prices and dynamically updated during continuous trading
The closing price (from closing auction) is the primary reference for indices, settlements, and fund valuations

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits








Type
Threshold
Action




Dynamic Collar
+/-5% from dynamic reference price (last traded price); +/-3% for flagship index constituents (e.g., FTSE MIB)
Trading halted; instrument enters volatility auction


Static Collar
+/-10% from static reference price (last auction uncrossing price); +/-8% for flagship index constituents
Trading halted; instrument enters volatility auction




The dynamic reference price updates after each trade (the last traded price becomes the new reference)
The static reference price remains fixed throughout the session unless manually changed by Euronext Market Operations
Borsa Italiana-specific parameters are published in the “Guide to the Parameters” document



8.2 Circuit Breakers








Level
Trigger
Halt Duration




Dynamic collar breach
Potential execution price exceeds dynamic threshold
Volatility auction; minimum ~5 minutes


Static collar breach
Potential execution price exceeds static threshold
Volatility auction; minimum ~5 minutes


Auction extension
Indicative uncrossing price would breach thresholds again
Auction call period extended




Borsa Italiana historically has the highest average circuit breaker duration among Euronext venues (~10 minutes average), with extensions ranging from 5 to 50 minutes

title: Borsa Italiana (Euronext Milan)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Societa e la Borsa): Primary regulator for Italian securities markets; established in 1974. Responsible for regulating and supervising securities markets and issuers, approving listing and offering prospectuses, and enforcing market abuse rules
Bank of Italy (Banca d’Italia): Prudential oversight of financial intermediaries; supervises market infrastructure stability
ESMA (European Securities and Markets Authority): EU-level coordination and oversight under MiFID II/MiFIR framework



9.2 Key Regulations

Consolidated Law on Finance (Testo Unico della Finanza, TUF – Legislative Decree No. 58/1998): Primary Italian legislation governing financial markets, intermediaries, issuers, and market abuse. The foundational law for Italian securities regulation
MiFID II / MiFIR (EU Directive 2014/65/EU and Regulation 600/2014): EU-wide framework governing trading venues, transparency, investor protection, and market structure; directly applicable in Italy
Market Abuse Regulation (EU MAR – Regulation 596/2014): Prohibits insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure of inside information
Borsa Italiana Markets Rulebook: Exchange-level rules approved by CONSOB; governs listing, trading, and membership
EU Prospectus Regulation (Regulation 2017/1129): Governs prospectus requirements for public offerings and admissions to trading
CSDR (Central Securities Depositories Regulation): Governs settlement discipline and CSD operations (applicable to Monte Titoli / Euronext Securities Milan)



9.3 Market Surveillance

Borsa Italiana Market Surveillance: Real-time monitoring of trading activity for suspicious patterns, potential market abuse, and rule violations
CONSOB Surveillance: Independent market monitoring using transaction reporting data; enforcement of MAR
Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports (STORs): Member firms required to report suspicious activity to CONSOB
Cross-market coordination: Through ESMA and bilateral MoUs with other EU and international regulators



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: Investment firms must report trades to CONSOB under MiFIR Article 26 (65 data fields, T+1 deadline)
Post-trade Transparency: Real-time publication of trade details as required by MiFID II; deferrals for large-in-scale and illiquid instruments
Pre-trade Transparency: Display of bid/offer prices and depth for order book instruments
Short Selling Disclosure: Per EU Short Selling Regulation; net short positions above 0.2% reported to CONSOB, above 0.5% publicly disclosed
Major Shareholding Notifications: Disclosure required when crossing specified thresholds of voting rights (per TUF and Transparency Directive)
Italian Financial Transaction Tax (FTT): Applies to trades in Italian equities; 0.10% on regulated market transactions, 0.20% on OTC transactions [unverified exact current rates]



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

EU MiFID II passporting allows investment firms authorised in any EU/EEA member state to access Borsa Italiana as remote members
Euronext operates as a single cross-border exchange group with harmonised rules across its markets (Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin, Lisbon, Milan, Oslo, Paris)
CONSOB is a signatory to IOSCO MMOU for international regulatory cooperation
ESMA coordinates cross-border supervision within the EU

Key Historical Milestones

1930: Earliest formal securities trading in Malaya via the Singapore Stockbrokers’ Association
1964: Stock Exchange of Malaysia established (joint exchange with Singapore)
1973: Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) formally established as a separate entity following the de-linking of currencies between Malaysia and Singapore

1994: KLSE moved to its current location at Exchange Square, Bukit Kewangan, Kuala Lumpur

2009 (3 Aug): Tick sizes reduced to improve liquidity and narrow bid-ask spreads

2019 (29 Apr): Settlement cycle shortened from T+3 to T+2
2021 (1 Apr): MSPO (Malaysian Sustainable Palm Oil) certification mandated for FCPO physical delivery â first exchange globally to require sustainability certification for commodity derivatives delivery

title: Bursa Malaysia Berhad (Bursa Malaysia)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: During the Pre-Opening phase (08:30-09:00 morning; 14:00-14:30 afternoon), orders accumulate without matching. The Automated Trading System (ATS) computes and disseminates the Theoretical Opening Price (TOP) and Theoretical Opening Volume (TOV). At the end of the pre-opening phase, a single-price auction determines the opening price, maximizing tradable volume.
Closing Auction: During the Pre-Closing phase (16:45-16:50), orders accumulate. At 16:50, a single-price matching determines the closing price. This is followed by the “Trading at Last” phase (16:50-17:00), where orders are matched continuously at the fixed closing price only.
Intraday Auction: No formal intraday volatility auctions are implemented [unverified].



3.2 Continuous Trading

Market Type: Order-driven
Matching Algorithm: Price-time priority â orders are matched first by best price, then by earliest entry time at the same price level
Morning Session: 09:00 - 12:30 MYT (3.5 hours)
Afternoon Session: 14:30 - 16:45 MYT (2.25 hours)
Total Continuous Trading: ~5.75 hours per normal trading day
All unmatched orders from the morning session are automatically carried forward to the afternoon session



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening and closing prices are determined by single-price auction algorithms that maximize tradable volume and minimize order imbalance
During continuous trading, prices are discovered through real-time order matching at the best available prices
The Theoretical Opening Price (TOP) is continuously updated and disseminated during pre-opening phases to provide transparency to market participants

8.2 Circuit Breakers
The market-wide circuit breaker is triggered automatically when the FBM KLCI declines by specified thresholds from the previous day’s closing level:








Level
Trigger
Halt Duration




Level 1
FBM KLCI drops 10%
If triggered 09:00-11:15 or 14:30-15:30: 1-hour halt. If triggered 11:15-12:30 or 15:30-17:00: halt for rest of session

Circuit breakers halt trading on both Bursa Malaysia Securities Berhad and equity-linked derivative products on Bursa Malaysia Derivatives Berhad
Purpose: Provides a cooling-off period for information dissemination, enabling market participants to make well-considered investment decisions

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Securities Commission Malaysia (SC): Established 1 March 1993 under the Securities Commission Act 1993; self-funded statutory body with regulatory and developmental responsibilities for the Malaysian capital market
Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM): Central bank; oversees monetary policy and banking sector; coordinates with SC on financial stability matters
Bursa Malaysia itself operates as a front-line regulator (Self-Regulatory Organisation / SRO), conducting market surveillance, enforcement of listing rules, and regulation of Participating Organisations



9.2 Key Regulations







Legislation / Rule
Description

Primary legislation governing securities markets; regulates stockbroking, fund management, derivatives, and securities offerings


Securities Commission Act 1993
Establishes the SC and defines its regulatory powers

Enabled the conversion of KLSE from member-owned to a demutualized company

Technical and operational rules for POs

Governs the central depository system (Bursa Depository)





9.3 Market Surveillance

Bursa Malaysia operates a market surveillance department that monitors trading activity for potential market manipulation, insider trading, and other irregularities
Real-time surveillance using automated systems to detect abnormal trading patterns
Cross-market surveillance coordination with SC Malaysia



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Listed companies must comply with continuous disclosure obligations (timely disclosure of material information)
Quarterly financial reporting for listed companies
Annual reports and audited financial statements required
Substantial shareholding notifications (threshold: 5% and above)



9.5 Shariah-Compliant Securities Framework
This is a distinguishing feature of Bursa Malaysia’s regulatory environment:

Shariah Advisory Council (SAC): Established under the SC, the SAC is the sole authoritative body for Shariah-compliant classification of securities on Bursa Malaysia
Screening Methodology: Two-tier quantitative approach:

Business Activity Benchmark: Non-permissible activities (e.g., conventional banking, gambling, alcohol, tobacco) must be below threshold levels (5% for clearly prohibited activities, 20% for mixed activities, 25% for activities generally permissible but with some Shariah concerns) [unverified â exact thresholds may have been updated]
Financial Ratio Benchmark: Conventional debt and interest-related metrics must remain below specified thresholds relative to total assets

Biannual Updates: The Shariah-compliant securities list is updated every May and November
Scale: ~80% of Bursa-listed securities are Shariah-compliant (~850 of 1,056 as of May 2025), making Malaysia one of the world’s largest Islamic capital markets
Effective April 2024: Companies seeking listing no longer need to submit separate SAC applications; the SAC reviews all new listings automatically

Shariah Screening Simplification (2024): Removed requirement for separate SAC applications for new listings
Circuit Breaker Restoration (2021): Reverted to original parameters after temporary COVID-19 widening



Strategic Initiatives

Islamic Capital Market Leadership: Positioning as the global hub for Islamic finance and Shariah-compliant capital markets; Shariah-compliant assets exceeding RM 2.6 trillion
ASEAN IPO Leadership: Maintained leading position in Southeast Asian IPO activities in 2025
Palm Oil Derivatives: Global benchmark status for crude palm oil pricing through FCPO (traded since 1980, with daily settlement accessible globally via CME Globex)
Retail Participation: Active retail investor base with significant participation in daily trading value



Palm Oil Futures â Derivatives Highlight
While this file focuses on the equities domain, Bursa Malaysia’s derivatives arm (Bursa Malaysia Derivatives Berhad) is globally significant:

FCPO (Crude Palm Oil Futures): Launched October 1980; the global benchmark for crude palm oil pricing. Ringgit-denominated, physically delivered. Actively used by plantation companies, refineries, millers, exporters, global fund managers, and CTAs.
Global Access: FCPO and other Bursa derivatives products are accessible via CME Globex electronic trading platform, enabling worldwide participation.
MSPO Certification: From 1 April 2021, all FCPO physical deliveries require MSPO (Malaysian Sustainable Palm Oil) certification â a world first for exchange-traded commodity derivatives.
Contract Size: 25 metric tonnes per contract; minimum price fluctuation of RM 1.00 per metric tonne.

Multi-national: AMF (France), AFM (Netherlands), FSMA (Belgium), CMVM (Portugal), CBI (Ireland), Finanstilsynet (Norway), CONSOB (Italy), HCMC (Greece) – coordinated via the College of Euronext Regulators

~EUR 6.8 trillion aggregate across all Euronext markets (as of end 2025)

~1,900+ issuers across all markets (equities); plus ETFs, bonds, warrants, and structured products

~EUR 11.0-13.8 billion ADV in cash equities (2025 quarterly range; full-year 2024 average ~EUR 10.5 billion)

~EUR 12.0 billion ADV (Q4 2025), up +14.0% YoY




Key Historical Milestones

1602: Amsterdam Stock Exchange (Amsterdamse Beurs) founded – widely regarded as the world’s first formal securities exchange
1724: Paris Bourse formally organized under royal decree
1801: Brussels Stock Exchange established
1891: Lisbon Stock Exchange (Bolsa de Valores de Lisboa) established
2000: Euronext N.V. formed through merger of Amsterdam Exchanges, Brussels Exchanges, and Paris Bourse SBF
2002: Euronext acquires LIFFE (London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange) and merges with Bolsa de Valores de Lisboa e Porto (BVLP), adding Lisbon
2007: Euronext merges with NYSE Group to form NYSE Euronext, creating the first transatlantic exchange group
2013: IntercontinentalExchange (ICE) acquires NYSE Euronext for ~USD 11 billion
2014: Euronext re-IPOs as an independent company on Euronext Amsterdam and Paris (June 2014); ICE retains NYSE
2018: Euronext acquires the Irish Stock Exchange (renamed Euronext Dublin); Optiq trading platform goes live for cash markets
2019: Euronext completes acquisition of Oslo Bors VPS (Oslo Stock Exchange and central securities depository)
2020: Acquires Nord Pool (European power exchange) and VP Securities (Danish CSD)
2021: Euronext completes acquisition of Borsa Italiana Group (including MTS and CC&G, now Euronext Clearing) from LSEG for EUR 4,444 million – transformative deal making Italy its largest revenue contributor
2022: Core Data Centre migrated from Basildon (UK) to Bergamo, Italy (Aruba IT3); completed 6 June 2022
2023: Borsa Italiana cash markets migrated to Optiq platform (Phase 1 and Phase 2)
2024: Borsa Italiana derivatives migrated to Optiq (Phase 3, final); Euronext Clearing expanded to all Euronext financial derivatives markets, completing separation from LCH SA
2025: Acquisition of ATHEX Group (Athens Stock Exchange, ~75.6% stake by year-end); acquisition of Admincontrol (Nordic SaaS); launched Mini Bond Futures on European government bonds; Nasdaq Nordic power futures acquisition announced; full-year adjusted EBITDA of EUR 1,143.1 million (+13.6%)
2026: Power futures launch (March 2026); European CSD harmonization and Repo market expansion in progress

title: Euronext N.V. (Euronext)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: Pre-opening phase begins at 07:15 CET allowing order accumulation. At 09:00, the uncrossing algorithm determines the opening price by maximizing executable volume. A random end period (up to 30 seconds) is applied to prevent last-second manipulation. Surplus orders remain on the book for continuous trading
Closing Auction: At 17:30, continuous trading halts and a pre-closing order accumulation phase begins (typically 5 minutes). The closing auction uncrossing determines the official closing price used by index providers and fund NAV calculations. Random end period applies
Intraday (Volatility) Auction: Triggered automatically when a potential trade would breach dynamic or static price collars. The instrument enters a “reservation” period (typically 5 minutes) during which orders accumulate, followed by an uncrossing to resume trading at a new equilibrium price
Auction Price Discovery Algorithm: Maximizes executable volume; if multiple prices yield the same volume, minimizes surplus (unmatched) volume; if still tied, selects price closest to the last reference price



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with price/time priority (first priority: best price; second priority: earliest timestamp at the same price)
Pure central limit order book (CLOB) model for liquid equities
Market makers provide supplemental liquidity but do not operate as obligatory dealers
Euronext Block: Dark midpoint matching service operating as an MTF for block-sized institutional orders
All Euronext cash markets share a single harmonized matching engine via the Optiq platform



3.3 Price Discovery

Primary price discovery through opening and closing auctions and continuous order book interaction
The uncrossing algorithm is designed to maximize volume at a single equilibrium price
Reference prices for circuit breaker collars are derived from auction prices and dynamically updated during continuous trading (last traded price becomes new dynamic reference)
Closing price established via closing auction is the official reference for settlement, index calculation, and derivative valuation
Trading at Last (TAL) session allows additional volume to trade at the closing price, further concentrating closing liquidity

text:
4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit Order
Order to buy/sell at a specified price or better; rests on the book if not immediately matched


Market Order
Executes at the best available prices until fully filled; any unmatched portion converts to a limit order at the last execution price (Euronext-specific behavior)


Market-to-Limit Order
Executes at the best available price; any unfilled quantity is converted to a limit order at the price of the initial execution


Stop Loss Order
Triggered when the market price reaches a specified stop price; becomes a market order upon activation


Stop Limit Order
Triggered when the market price reaches a specified stop price; becomes a limit order at a specified limit price upon activation





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Iceberg Order
Displays only a portion (peak quantity) of the total order; as the visible portion is filled, a new peak is automatically refreshed from the hidden reserve; each refresh gets a new timestamp


Pegged Order
Price automatically tracks a reference price (best bid, best offer, or midpoint); adjusts in real time as the BBO changes


Pegged-to-Midpoint Order
Pegged to the midpoint of the best bid and offer; commonly used in Euronext Block for dark trading


Mid-Point Order (Euronext Block)
Executes at the midpoint of the primary market BBO; designed for large institutional block trades with reduced market impact


Trailing Stop Order
Stop price adjusts with favorable market movements by a defined offset; triggered on adverse moves [unverified]





4.3 Time-in-Force Options







TIF
Description




Day (DAY)
Valid for the current trading day only; cancelled at end of day


Good till Cancelled (GTC)
Remains active until executed or cancelled (subject to maximum duration set by the exchange, typically 365 days)


Good till Date (GTD)
Valid until a specified expiry date


Immediate or Cancel (IOC)
Execute as much as possible immediately; cancel any remaining quantity


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be executed in full immediately or the entire order is cancelled


Valid for Closing Auction
Order participates only in the closing auction


Valid for Opening Auction
Order participates only in the opening auction [unverified]





4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be amended (price, quantity) or cancelled during any phase via OEG (Order Entry Gateway) using FIX 5.0 or native SBE protocol
Price amendments that improve the order (more aggressive price) result in a new timestamp (loss of time priority)
Quantity reduction preserves time priority; quantity increase may or may not depending on the order type
During auction call periods, orders can be entered, amended, and cancelled but no matching occurs
Mass cancellation functionality available for risk management; Kill Switch allows cancellation of all outstanding orders for a member firm

text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits
Euronext employs a multi-layered safeguard system combining dynamic and static collars:









Type
Reference Price
Threshold
Action




Dynamic Collar
Last traded price (updated after each trade)
Percentage varies by instrument liquidity/index membership (e.g., +/-2% to +/-5% typical) [unverified]
Instrument enters reservation (volatility auction) if a potential trade would breach the collar


Static Collar
Opening price of the day or last reference price from previous session
+/-8% for flagship index constituents; +/-10% for other instruments (typical)
Instrument enters reservation if potential trade breaches static threshold from the daily reference price





8.2 Circuit Breakers








Level
Trigger
Halt Duration




Dynamic Collar Breach
Potential trade would breach dynamic price band around last traded price
Reservation period (~5 minutes) followed by volatility auction uncrossing with random end


Static Collar Breach
Potential trade would breach static price band around the daily reference price
Reservation period (~5 minutes) followed by volatility auction uncrossing


Multiple Successive Triggers
Repeated reservation triggers on same instrument
Duration may be extended; Market Operations may intervene manually


Market-wide Halt
Extraordinary circumstances (coordinated with regulators)
Duration determined by regulators; Euronext Market Operations coordinates with the College of Regulators





8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Aberrant order rejection: Orders that are unusually large in size, quantity, or price are automatically rejected before entering the order book
Maximum order size limits: Configurable per instrument to prevent fat-finger errors
Throttling: Rate-limiting controls on message submission per connection to prevent system overload
Price collar validation: Orders priced outside the current collar range are rejected or trigger a reservation
Member-level controls: Members must implement their own pre-trade risk management in accordance with MiFID II/RTS 6 requirements (algorithmic trading controls)



8.4 Kill Switch

Euronext provides a Kill Switch functionality that allows members (or Euronext Market Operations) to cancel all outstanding orders for a specific member/connection in a single action
Compliant with MiFID II Article 48 requirements for circuit breaker and kill switch mechanisms
Members can also implement their own kill switch through OEG mass cancellation messages

title: Euronext N.V. (Euronext)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

College of Euronext Regulators: Multi-national coordination body comprising:

AMF (Autorite des Marches Financiers) – France (lead regulator)
AFM (Autoriteit Financiele Markten) – Netherlands
FSMA (Financial Services and Markets Authority) – Belgium
CMVM (Comissao do Mercado de Valores Mobiliarios) – Portugal
CBI (Central Bank of Ireland) – Ireland
Finanstilsynet (Financial Supervisory Authority) – Norway
CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Societa e la Borsa) – Italy
HCMC (Hellenic Capital Market Commission) – Greece (from 2025)

The College operates under a Memorandum of Understanding coordinating supervision across all Euronext jurisdictions



9.2 Key Regulations

MiFID II / MiFIR (Markets in Financial Instruments Directive/Regulation): Core framework governing Euronext as a Regulated Market operator and MTF
Market Abuse Regulation (MAR): EU Regulation 596/2014 governing insider dealing, market manipulation, and disclosure
EU Prospectus Regulation: Governs prospectus requirements for securities admitted to Euronext Regulated Markets
CSDR (Central Securities Depositories Regulation): Governs Euronext Securities (CSDs in Denmark, Italy, Norway)
EMIR (European Market Infrastructure Regulation): Governs Euronext Clearing (formerly CC&G)
Euronext Rule Book: Harmonised Rules (Book I, applicable across all markets) and local supplementary rules (Book II, market-specific)
RTS 6 (Algorithmic Trading): Requirements for algorithmic trading controls, testing, and record-keeping
RTS 11 (Tick Size Regime): Standardized tick sizes based on price and liquidity



9.3 Market Surveillance

Euronext operates a centralized Market Surveillance department monitoring all markets in real time
Surveillance covers potential market abuse (insider trading, price manipulation, spoofing, layering)
Cross-market surveillance across all Euronext venues (regulated markets, Growth, Access, Block)
Automated alert systems detect anomalous trading patterns, unusual price movements, and order book irregularities
Findings reported to relevant national regulators (AMF, CONSOB, etc.) for enforcement action
Euronext also operates as an ARM (Approved Reporting Mechanism) and APA (Approved Publication Arrangement) under MiFID II for trade reporting



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Members must report transactions to national competent authorities under MiFIR Article 26
Post-trade transparency: Trades published in real time (or deferred for large-in-scale transactions per MiFID II waivers)
Pre-trade transparency: Full order book visible for lit markets; waivers available for dark trading (reference price waiver, negotiated trade waiver, LIS waiver)
Listed companies subject to ongoing disclosure obligations (regulated information, inside information under MAR)



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Single Rule Book (Harmonised Rules) creates a unified regulatory framework across all Euronext markets
Passporting under MiFID II enables EEA-regulated firms to access all Euronext markets via remote membership
Third-country equivalence determinations may apply for non-EEA firms
Euronext’s multi-jurisdictional structure is unique among major exchanges, requiring coordination between 8 national regulators
Post-Brexit: Euronext relocated its primary data centre from Basildon (UK) to Bergamo (Italy) in 2022, reducing dependency on UK infrastructure

11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2022: Core Data Centre relocated from Basildon (UK) to Bergamo, Italy (Aruba IT3); completed June 2022
2023: Borsa Italiana cash markets (equities, ETFs, bonds) migrated to Optiq in two phases
2024: Borsa Italiana derivatives migrated to Optiq (Phase 3, April 2024) – completing full Borsa Italiana technology integration; Euronext Clearing expanded to cover all Euronext financial derivatives
2025: Continued Optiq platform enhancements; ATHEX Group integration planning underway; MDG and OEG version upgrades (v5.38.0 specification documents published)
Ongoing: Optiq platform offered as a technology solution to third-party exchanges and venue operators



New Products / Segments

2024: Launch of integrated European ETF market platform (support from issuers representing >90% of European ETF AUM)
2025: Launch of cash-settled Mini Bond Futures on Italian, French, German, and Spanish government bonds (September 2025)
2026: Power futures launch (March 2026), diversifying commodities franchise following Nasdaq Nordic power futures acquisition
2026: European Repo market expansion (target completion June 2026)
Euronext Block: Continues to grow as dark midpoint venue for institutional block trading



Regulatory Changes

MiFID II/MiFIR Review: EU Commission published market integration legislative package (December 2025) aiming to simplify regulatory framework and move toward EU-level supervision; potential impact on Euronext’s multi-jurisdiction structure
CSDR Refit: Ongoing implementation affecting Euronext Securities (CSDs)
Consolidated Tape Provider (CTP): EU regulatory push for a consolidated tape for equities; Euronext has positioned itself as a potential contributor/operator
T+1 Settlement: Industry discussions on migrating European markets from T+2 to T+1 settlement; Euronext preparing infrastructure



Strategic Initiatives

“Innovate for Growth 2027”: Strategic plan focused on growing non-volume-based businesses, scaling technology, and expanding the European footprint
European CSD Model: Announced December 2025; plan to harmonize CSD operations across Denmark, Italy, Norway, and Portugal, reducing costs and improving cross-border settlement. Euronext Securities to begin settling Amsterdam, Brussels, and Paris cash equities by September 2026
ATHEX Integration: Athens Stock Exchange acquired (75.6% stake by end 2025); targeting EUR 12 million annual run-rate synergies by 2028
Admincontrol Acquisition: Nordic SaaS platform for board portals; expanded Corporate Solutions business to 8,500+ companies
Power Futures / Commodity Expansion: Building on Nord Pool acquisition; power futures launching March 2026; expanding energy trading franchise
Euronext Clearing Expansion: After separating from LCH SA, Euronext Clearing now handles all Euronext financial derivatives; further expansion into cash equities clearing planned

1. Overview & Profile







Item
Details




Official Name
Tokyo Stock Exchange, Inc. (TSE), a subsidiary of Japan Exchange Group, Inc. (JPX)


Abbreviation
JPX / TSE


Website
https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/


Year Established
TSE: 1878 (originally); re-established 1949. JPX: January 1, 2013 (merger of TSE Group and Osaka Securities Exchange)


Country / City
Japan / Tokyo (Head office: 2-1 Nihombashi Kabutocho, Chuo-ku, Tokyo)


Ownership Structure
Publicly traded holding company; JPX is listed on TSE Prime Market (Ticker: 8697). Widely held by institutional and retail investors


Parent Company / Group
Japan Exchange Group, Inc. (JPX) — encompasses TSE (cash equities), Osaka Exchange (derivatives), Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM), and Japan Securities Clearing Corporation (JSCC)


Regulatory Authority
Financial Services Agency of Japan (JFSA); Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC); Japan Exchange Regulation (JPX-R) as self-regulatory organization


Market Capitalization (listed companies)
~JPY 1,213 trillion (~USD 8.1 trillion) total market cap of all TSE-listed shares (March 2026); reached all-time high of ~USD 8.8 trillion in February 2026


Total Listed Instruments
~3,945 companies (as of 2025): Prime Market ~1,599, Standard Market ~1,569, Growth Market ~614, TOKYO PRO Market ~163; plus ~300+ ETFs/ETNs


Average Daily Trading Volume
~1.8 billion shares (Prime Market domestic common stocks, FY2025) [estimated]


Average Daily Trading Value
JPY 6.70 trillion (~USD 44.7 billion) for Prime Market domestic common stocks (FY2025); JPY 367.5 billion daily average for ETFs




Key Historical Milestones

1878: Tokyo Stock Exchange established on May 15 under the Stock Exchange Ordinance, one of the first modern exchanges in Asia
1943: Merged with 10 other Japanese exchanges to form the Japan Securities Exchange during World War II
1947: Japan Securities Exchange dissolved under post-war reforms
1949: Tokyo Stock Exchange re-established on May 16 as a membership organization; trading resumed on April 1
1969: TSE introduces the Tokyo Stock Price Index (TOPIX) as a market-wide capitalization-weighted index
1982: MOTHERS (Market of the High-growth and Emerging Stocks) concept introduced (later launched in 1999)
1999: TSE fully transitions to electronic trading; establishes ToSTNeT off-auction trading system
2000: TSE demutualizes, converting from a membership organization to a stock corporation
2001: TSE Group, Inc. established as holding company
2010: First-generation arrowhead trading system launched on January 4, achieving sub-millisecond order processing
2013: Japan Exchange Group (JPX) formed on January 1 through merger of Tokyo Stock Exchange Group and Osaka Securities Exchange; JPX listed on TSE First Section (8697) on January 4; OSE cash equities market integrated into TSE on July 16
2015: Second-generation arrowhead system launched (September 24)
2018: Trading unit standardized to 100 shares for all listed stocks (October 1); ETF Market Making Incentive Scheme launched (July)
2019: Third-generation arrowhead system launched (November 5)
2020: Full-day trading halt on October 1 due to hardware failure in arrowhead — worst outage since electronic trading began; TSE President Miyahara resigned
2022: Market restructuring on April 4 — TSE reorganized from four sections (1st Section, 2nd Section, Mothers, JASDAQ) into three new segments: Prime Market, Standard Market, and Growth Market
2023: TSE requests all Prime and Standard Market companies to disclose plans for improving cost of capital and stock price (PBR initiative)
2024: arrowhead 4.0 (fourth generation) launched on November 5; trading hours extended by 30 minutes to 3:30 PM; closing auction session introduced
2025: Cloud technology proof of concept conducted with AWS and Fujitsu for future arrowhead migration; Growth Market continued listing criteria tightened (market cap threshold raised to JPY 10 billion after 5 years); Corporate Governance Code revision process initiated

text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (Itayose): Call auction method used at 9:00 AM and 12:30 PM to determine opening prices. All accumulated orders are matched at a single equilibrium price that maximizes executed volume. Three conditions must be met: (1) all market orders are executed, (2) higher buy limit orders and lower sell limit orders are fully executed, (3) either all buy or all sell orders at the determined price are executed.
Closing Auction (Itayose): Introduced November 5, 2024 as part of arrowhead 4.0 upgrade. A 5-minute pre-closing period (15:25-15:30) freezes order execution while displaying order book information, followed by Itayose matching at 15:30 to determine official closing prices. This mechanism improves closing price transparency and reduces manipulation risk.
Intraday Auction: Not a scheduled event, but Itayose is triggered upon trading resumption after Special Quote halts (see below).
Volatility Auction (Special Quote / Tokubetsu Kehai): When a potential trade price would deviate beyond the “renewal price range” (a predefined price interval), the exchange displays a Special Quote instead of executing the trade. This Special Quote is displayed for a cooling period to attract offsetting orders. If sufficient offsetting orders arrive, an Itayose auction occurs. If not, the Special Quote is updated stepwise in the direction of the imbalance at set intervals (typically every 3-5 minutes, depending on the price level) until balance is achieved or the daily price limit is reached.



3.2 Continuous Trading (Zaraba)

Pure order-driven market — no designated market makers for equities
Price-time priority: Orders are matched first by price priority (best price first), then by time priority (earliest order first among same-price orders). Market orders always take priority over limit orders.
Zaraba method is used during continuous trading sessions (morning and afternoon sessions, excluding opening/closing auctions)



3.3 Price Discovery

Itayose provides primary price discovery at market open, post-lunch reopen, and market close
Special Quote mechanism provides orderly price discovery during periods of order imbalance by signaling the indicative price direction to the market
Sequential Trade Quotes: When an execution might exceed twice the renewal price interval, a Sequential Trade Quote is displayed for one minute to attract offsetting orders before execution
ToSTNeT (Tokyo Stock Exchange Trading NeTwork System): Off-auction trading system for large-lot, basket, and negotiated transactions. Launched 1998. Types include:

Single Issue Trading (ToSTNeT-1): Negotiated trades within +/- 7% of last auction price
Basket Trading: Portfolio transactions
Closing Price Trading (ToSTNeT-2): Trades at closing price
Off-auction Repurchase: Companies repurchasing own shares

4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Market Order (Nariyuki)
Execute at best available price; takes priority over all limit orders. No price specified.


Limit Order (Sashine)
Execute at specified price or better. Buy limit = maximum price; sell limit = minimum price.





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




On Open (Yoritsuki)
Order valid only for the opening Itayose auction of the designated session (morning or afternoon). If not executed at open, automatically cancelled.


On Close (Hikake)
Order valid only for the closing Itayose auction. If not executed at close, automatically cancelled.


Funari
Limit order that automatically converts to a market order at the closing auction if not already executed during continuous trading. Provides limit price protection during the session with guaranteed participation in the close.


IOC (Immediate or Cancel)
Attempts to execute immediately at the specified price or better; any unfilled portion is immediately cancelled. No partial orders remain on the book.


FOK (Fill or Kill)
Must be executed immediately in its entirety or the entire order is cancelled. No partial fills permitted.

Item

arrowhead (current version: arrowhead 4.0)

Co-developed by TSE and Fujitsu Limited

Synchronized 3-node data server architecture for high availability; system processes orders, executions, and order book data across redundant nodes

Scalable architecture; capacity flexibly adjustable to accommodate increases in order volume

Period
System
Notes

Technology Stack

Hardware: Fujitsu servers with synchronized 3-node redundancy
Network: arrownet — JPX’s proprietary high-speed network backbone, offering bandwidth from 512 kbps to 10 Gbps via dedicated lines
Layer 1 Switch: Launched January 2024, providing “L1 Multicast Line” for ultra-low-latency, fair market data distribution (latency as low as 5 nanoseconds for data delivery)
Cloud Exploration: PoC conducted in 2025 with AWS (using AWS Outposts) and Fujitsu to test long-term applicability of cloud technology to the arrowhead trading system. This represents a potential future migration path.
AI/GenAI: JPX uses Amazon Bedrock for enhancing searchability of timely disclosure documents and generating metadata tags



Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity

Primary Site: JPX data center in the Tokyo metropolitan area (co-location facility)
Secondary (Backup) Site: Kansai region (western Japan), geographically distant from Tokyo to mitigate wide-area disaster risk (e.g., Tokyo metropolitan earthquake)

AT TOKYO Kansai Chuo Center (KC1) designated as Kansai Proximity Area
Osaka site capable of taking over entire JPX operations in the event of a catastrophic Tokyo-area disaster
arrowhead deployment at Kansai backup site completed after FY2022

Kansai Proximity Service: Network infrastructure in the Kansai region near the AP4 data center, providing participants with access to JPX systems for business continuity
Contingency Plan: Formal BCP established; significantly strengthened after the October 2020 full-day outage. Includes procedures for automatic failover, manual switchover, and market reopening protocols
3-Node Architecture: The synchronized 3-node data server design ensures no single point of failure during normal operations
