Limit Expansion Rule: If a stock hits the upper or lower daily price limit with zero trading volume for two consecutive business days, the limit range is expanded by 4x from the following business day.
Asia-Specific Note: Daily price limits are a common feature in Asian markets (also used by KRX, TWSE, SSE, SZSE). Unlike Western markets that primarily rely on circuit breakers, Asian exchanges layer daily price limits as a first line of defense against excessive volatility.


8.2 Circuit Breakers
Individual Stock Level — Special Quote (Tokubetsu Kehai): | Type | Trigger | Action | |——|———|——–| | Special Quote | Potential trade would exceed the renewal price range (a predefined price interval based on price level) | Trading halted; Special Quote displayed at the limit of the renewal range; quote updated stepwise at intervals (typically 3-5 minutes) until balance achieved or daily limit reached; Itayose auction triggered when offsetting orders arrive | | Sequential Trade Quote | Execution might exceed twice the renewal price interval | Quote displayed for 1 minute to attract offsetting orders before execution |
Index Level — Derivatives Circuit Breaker (affects cash market indirectly): | Level | Trigger | Halt Duration | |——-|———|—————| | Static Circuit Breaker (SCB) | Index futures (Nikkei 225, TOPIX) hit ~8% decline limit | 10-minute halt on all related futures/derivatives contracts |
Note: Cash equity trading on TSE continues even when index futures circuit breakers are triggered. Spot stock trading is not halted by derivative circuit breakers — this is an important distinction from markets where equity trading halts alongside futures.


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

User-designated hard limits: Trading participants can set maximum order value limits per user
Price limit validation: Orders outside daily price limits are automatically rejected
Order value limits: Maximum order quantity and value thresholds enforced by the exchange
Cancel on Disconnect: If a participant’s connection is lost, all outstanding orders can be automatically suspended
Mass Cancellation: Functionality to cancel all outstanding orders in a single operation (introduced with arrowhead 4.0)



8.4 Kill Switch

Forcible Entry Suspension (Kill Switch): Introduced with arrowhead 4.0, allows trading participants or the exchange to immediately suspend all order entry from a specific participant terminal or session. Prevents erroneous orders from cascading into the market.

title: Japan Exchange Group / Tokyo Stock Exchange (JPX / TSE)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Financial Services Agency of Japan (JFSA / Kinyu-cho): Central regulatory authority overseeing all financial markets in Japan. Responsible for rule-making, licensing, inspections, and enforcement under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA).
Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC): Independent oversight body under JFSA. Monitors, investigates, and sanctions violations of the FIEA, including insider trading, market manipulation, and disclosure fraud.
Japan Exchange Regulation (JPX-R): Self-regulatory organization (SRO) within the JPX Group. Operates independently to conduct:

Listing examination and approval
Listed company compliance monitoring
Real-time market surveillance
Inspections and examinations of trading participants




9.2 Key Regulations

Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA): Primary legislation governing securities markets, exchanges, trading participants, and investor protection in Japan
Companies Act (Kaisha-ho): Corporate governance framework for listed companies
Corporate Governance Code: Principles-based code (first issued 2015, revised 2018, 2021; under revision 2025-2026) outlining governance expectations for listed companies. Prime Market companies must comply with all principles or explain deviations.
Stewardship Code: Code of conduct for institutional investors engaging with investee companies
TSE Listing Rules: Detailed regulations covering initial listing criteria, continued listing criteria, timely disclosure requirements, and corporate governance standards specific to each market segment



9.3 Market Surveillance

Dual surveillance: Both JPX-R and SESC conduct market surveillance, with JPX-R focusing on real-time monitoring and SESC handling investigations and enforcement
AI-Enhanced Surveillance: JPX-R introduced artificial intelligence to market surveillance operations in 2018 to improve detection of market manipulation and insider trading patterns
Unfair Trading Detection: Continuous monitoring for market manipulation, insider trading, and other violations using pattern recognition and anomaly detection systems
Quarterly Reports: JPX publishes quarterly reports on the status of market surveillance activities



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Timely Disclosure (Tekiji Kaiji): Listed companies must promptly disclose material information including financial results, corporate actions, and significant events via TDnet (Timely Disclosure Network)
Annual Securities Report (Yuho): Comprehensive annual financial report filed with JFSA
Quarterly Reports: Financial statements filed quarterly
Large Shareholding Reports: Disclosure required within 5 business days when holding exceeds 5% of outstanding shares
Short Selling Reports: Short position disclosure required when net short position exceeds 0.5% of outstanding shares
English Disclosure: TSE has been actively promoting English-language disclosure by listed companies to attract foreign investment



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Remote Trading Participant System: Enables foreign brokers to trade directly on TSE without a Japanese office (since 2009)
International Connectivity: JPX-SGX Co-Location Direct (Singapore), JPX-Chicago Co-Location Direct (CME), and arrownet-Global services
Mutual Recognition Agreements: JFSA has regulatory cooperation arrangements with multiple overseas regulators
Foreign investor participation: Foreign investors account for over 60% of TSE turnover in peak periods, making cross-border access a critical priority

text:
11. Recent Developments

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2024 (November 5): arrowhead 4.0 launched — fourth-generation system with trading hours extension (close moved from 15:00 to 15:30), 5-minute closing auction session, Market by Order (MBO) data, mass cancellation functionality, and enhanced kill switch
2024 (January): Layer 1 Switch technology deployed providing L1 Multicast Line for fairer, ultra-low-latency market data distribution
2025 (November): Cloud technology proof of concept conducted with AWS Outposts and Fujitsu, testing arrowhead performance on cloud infrastructure for potential future migration
2025: AWS arrownet connectivity service launched, enabling participants to access JPX’s arrownet through AWS cloud infrastructure
2020 (October 1): Full-day trading halt due to arrowhead hardware failure (memory device malfunction with failed automatic failover). Worst outage since electronic trading began. Led to TSE CEO resignation and comprehensive BCP overhaul.



New Products / Segments

Closing Auction Session (2024): New 5-minute pre-closing period (15:25-15:30) followed by Itayose, improving closing price formation quality
CONNEQTOR RFQ Platform: Request-for-quote platform for institutional ETF trading, enhancing ETF liquidity ecosystem
ETF Market Making Scheme v2.0: Enhanced incentive program for developing ETFs across diverse asset classes
arrowhead Alternative Data Service: New data products providing system-level order flow statistics for quantitative research
JPX Startup100 ETF (2026): New index product targeting startup ecosystem



Regulatory Changes

PBR/Corporate Value Initiative (2023-ongoing): TSE requested all Prime and Standard Market companies to disclose action plans for improving cost of capital and stock price consciousness. Over 90% of Prime Market companies have disclosed plans as of March 2025. This has been a major catalyst for corporate governance reform and increased shareholder returns.
Growth Market Criteria Tightening (December 2025): Continued listing criteria revised — market cap threshold raised to JPY 10 billion after 5 years of listing (previously JPY 4 billion after 10 years). Designed to ensure Growth Market companies are genuinely pursuing high growth.
Transitional Measures Expiration (March 2025): Transitional measures for continued listing criteria from the 2022 market restructuring ended, requiring all companies to fully meet new segment criteria.
Corporate Governance Code Revision (2025-2026): Expert panel convened for third revision of the Corporate Governance Code, focusing on enhanced sustainability and board effectiveness requirements.
English Disclosure Promotion: Ongoing initiative to expand English-language corporate disclosures to improve foreign investor access.



Strategic Initiatives

Cloud Migration Exploration: JPX is actively evaluating cloud technology (AWS) for potential future migration of core trading systems, representing a strategic shift in exchange technology architecture
Data Business Expansion: JPX Market Innovation & Research (JPXI) expanding data distribution partnerships, alternative data products, and index co-branding
Derivatives Growth: Focus on expanding derivative product range including commodity electrification contracts (2024-2026)
Digital Assets: Medium-term roadmap (2026-2028) includes digital assets infrastructure development, subject to regulatory framework
ESG Instruments: New ESG-focused indices and investment products in development
International Partnerships: Expanding cross-border connectivity (Singapore, Chicago), exploring CCP interoperability and cross-margining efficiencies
GenAI Applications: Using Amazon Bedrock for enhanced disclosure document searchability and automated tagging

title: Korea Exchange (KRX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Opening Auction (개시 동시호가) [업무규정 Art. 23]: - Call auction (단일가격에 의한 개별경쟁매매) at market open (~09:00) - Orders collected 08:30-09:00; executed at single equilibrium price - Price determination: the price where aggregate sell volume equals aggregate buy volume (합치가격) - If multiple match prices exist, select the price closest to previous close [Art. 23④⑤]
Closing Auction (장종료 동시호가) [업무규정 Art. 23]: - Orders collected 15:20-15:30; executed at single closing price - 조건부지정가호가 (conditional limit orders) convert to market orders for closing auction
Volatility Interruption Auction [업무규정 Art. 26의2]: - Triggered when VI conditions are met (see Section 8) - 2-minute call auction with random end within 30 seconds [시행세칙 Art. 35(1)(4)]
Off-Hours Single-Price Trading (시간외단일가매매) [업무규정 Art. 34의2]: - Call auctions at 10-minute intervals from 16:00 to 18:00 - Price range: +/-10% of the day’s closing price, within daily price limits


3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with price-time priority (가격-시간 우선원칙)
Continuous matching (접속매매 / 복수가격에 의한 개별경쟁매매) [업무규정 Art. 24]
Execution price = the earlier (선행) order’s price when lowest ask meets highest bid



3.3 Price Discovery
Priority rules [업무규정 Art. 22②]:








Priority
Rule
Detail




1. Price priority (가격우선)
Art. 22②1
Lower sell price > higher sell price; Higher buy price > lower buy price; Market orders have priority over limit orders


2. Time priority (시간우선)
Art. 22②2
Same price: earlier submission takes priority


3. Simultaneous order rules
Art. 22③
For call auctions: orders at limit-up (buys) or limit-down (sells) during price determination treated as simultaneous

8.1 Price Limits

8.2 Circuit Breakers
Market-Wide Circuit Breaker (SAPI, 시장전체 매매거래중단) [업무규정 Art. 25; 시행세칙 Art. 39]:









Level
Trigger
Halt Duration
Conditions




Level 1
KOSPI drops 8%+ from previous close, sustained 1 minute
20-minute halt (then 10-min call auction to resume)
Once per day; not triggered after 14:50


Level 2
KOSPI drops 15%+ from previous close AND 1%+ further from Level 1 halt, sustained 1 min
20-minute halt
Once per day; not triggered after 14:50


Level 3
KOSPI drops 20%+ from previous close AND 1%+ further from Level 2 halt, sustained 1 min
Trading halted for remainder of day
Applies even after 14:50



Program Trading Sidecar (프로그램매매호가 효력정지) [업무규정 Art. 16; 시행세칙 Art. 20]: - Trigger: KOSPI 200 front-month futures price rises/falls 5%+ from base price, sustained 1 minute - Effect: Program trading orders suspended for 5 minutes - Applied once per day; not triggered after 14:50
Volatility Interruption (VI, 종목별 매매계약체결방법 변경) [업무규정 Art. 26의2; 시행세칙 Art. 41-2]:








Type
Trigger
Duration




Static VI — KOSPI 200 constituents
3% from last call auction price (reference price)
2-minute call auction + random 30-sec close


Static VI — Other stocks/ETF/ETN
6% from reference price
2-minute call auction + random 30-sec close

Thresholds halved: 2% (KOSPI 200) / 4% (others); 1% on derivatives last trading day
2-minute call auction

10% from last trade price
2-minute call auction + random 30-sec close



VI Exceptions: Delisting trading, short-term overheated stocks, abnormal surge stocks, cautionary stocks, IPO day stocks, prices within 3 tick sizes of prior price for stocks below KRW 1,000.


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls
Order validation checks (회원의 호가 사전통제의무) [업무규정 Art. 11의2; 시행세칙 Art. 12-2]: - Members must validate orders before submission to KRX system - Required checks: 1. Account validation (account number, type) 2. Instrument validation (security code, trading suspension status) 3. Quantity limits by market cap tier: - Market cap >= KRW 10T: max KRW 100B / base price per order - Market cap KRW 100B ~ 10T: max 1% of listed shares - Market cap KRW 20B ~ 100B: max KRW 1B / base price - Market cap < KRW 20B: max 5% of listed shares 4. Price validation (tick size, price limit compliance) 5. Order type validation per session 6. Margin requirements 7. HFT account validation
Algorithm trading controls [업무규정 Art. 104의2]: - Algo trading accounts must be registered with KRX - Members must identify and manage algo trading risks - Account-level kill switch available for emergencies
High-frequency trading (HFT) controls [업무규정 Art. 104의3-4]: - HFT participants must be registered with KRX before trading - Require: system adequacy, sufficient knowledge/experience - HFT accounts separately registered - KRX may revoke registration with 6-month re-registration ban - Members must refuse orders from unregistered HFT participants - Record retention: 10 years for all HFT-related records


8.4 Kill Switch

Disconnect kill switch (접속해제 호가취소): Automatic mass cancellation when member-exchange connection is severed [업무규정 Art. 13의2]
Bulk order cancellation (일괄호가취소): HFT traders cancel all orders by HFT ID [시행세칙 Art. 17-2]
Account-level kill switch (계좌단위호가처리): Cancel all orders or block new orders for specific algo accounts; 10-minute cooldown [시행세칙 Art. 130-2]

Erroneous trade relief [업무규정 Art. 28, 28의2]: - KRX may correct erroneous trade executions - Large erroneous trade relief (대규모착오매매 구제) available for trades risking settlement failure and market disruption
Short selling controls [업무규정 Art. 17, 18]: - Naked short selling prohibited - Covered short selling permitted with uptick rule: cannot sell below last trade price unless last price was an uptick - KRX may restrict short selling on specific stocks per 시행세칙 criteria - Overheated stock rules [시행세칙 Art. 24-3]: When price drops 5-10% AND short ratio is 3x market average AND short volume is 6x 40-day average, 1-day short selling ban applies
Short-term overheated stock (단기과열종목) designation [시행세칙 Art. 133-134]: - Triggers: Price up 130%+ vs 40-day avg, turnover 600%+ vs 40-day avg, volatility 150%+ vs 40-day avg - Effect: 3 trading days of 30-minute interval single-price auction (extendable)

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

FSC (Financial Services Commission, 금융위원회): Highest financial authority; policy formulation, licensing, and approval
FSS (Financial Supervisory Service, 금융감독원): FSC’s enforcement arm; examinations, investigations, sanctions across all financial sectors



9.2 Key Regulations

Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (자본시장법, FSCMA): Primary securities law; function-based regulation (same activities = same rules regardless of entity type); covers stocks, bonds, collective investment schemes, derivatives
유가증권시장 업무규정: KRX KOSPI Market Business Regulations (trading rules, order types, circuit breakers)
유가증권시장 상장규정: KRX KOSPI Market Listing Regulations (listing requirements, delisting criteria)
유가증권시장 공시규정: KRX KOSPI Market Disclosure Regulations (timely, periodic, fair, query disclosure)
회원관리규정: KRX Member Management Regulations



9.3 Market Surveillance

KRX as SRO: Self-regulatory functions including market surveillance, listed company supervision, market manipulation prevention, delisting authority
Market Surveillance Committee: Prevents market manipulation; investigates abnormal transactions
May impose sanctions including delisting or trading suspensions
Refers cases to FSS for further enforcement



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Disclosure types: Timely (수시공시), Periodic (정기공시), Fair (공정공시), Query (조회공시), Voluntary (자율공시), Clarification (해명공시) [공시규정 Art. 7-28]
Material event triggers: Same-day disclosure required for events exceeding 5% of revenue, 5% of equity capital, 10% of equity capital, etc. (thresholds halved for large-cap companies with KRW 2T+ total assets) [공시규정 Art. 7]
Settlement results: 30% YoY change in revenue/operating income/net income triggers disclosure (15% for large-cap)
English-language disclosure: Mandatory for companies with total assets >= KRW 10T (unless foreign ownership < 5%) or >= KRW 2T with >= 30% foreign ownership; deadline 3 trading days [공시규정 Art. 48]
Penalty system: Demerit points (벌점) for violations; max KRW 1 billion monetary penalty; unfaithful disclosure designation with ticker marking
Trading halts on disclosure: 30-minute halt for material disclosures; full-day halt for serious infractions [공시규정 Art. 40]



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

QFI (Qualified Foreign Investor) scheme for foreign institutional access (quota limits abolished)
Foreign companies may list on KOSPI under modified requirements [상장규정 Art. 53]

Fast-track for large foreign companies: 5+ years listed overseas, market cap KRW 2T+, revenue KRW 2T+
Must appoint Korean listing agent and disclosure agent
Accepted accounting standards: K-IFRS, IFRS, or US GAAP

Settlement cycle: T+2 (standard) [업무규정 Art. 7]

Key Historical Milestones

1971: NASDAQ launched on February 8 as the world’s first electronic stock market, providing automated quotations for over 2,500 OTC securities. Trades still executed by telephone.
1980: Apple Computer IPO listed on NASDAQ.
1984: Electronic execution introduced, replacing telephone-based trading.
1985: NASDAQ-100 Index launched, tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies.
1986: Microsoft IPO listed on NASDAQ.
1991: NASDAQ accounted for approximately 46% of U.S. securities trading volume.
1992: NASDAQ and London Stock Exchange formed the first intercontinental linkage.
1998: NASDAQ merged with the American Stock Exchange (AMEX).
2000: NASDAQ Composite reached peak of 5,048 during the dot-com bubble (March 10, 2000).
2002-2003: SuperMontage launched, integrating a public limit order book with market maker quotations.
2005: NASDAQ converted from an industry-owned organization to a publicly traded company; acquired Instinet for $1.9 billion, retaining the Inet ECN.
2006: Began operating as a national securities exchange (registered with SEC).
2007: Acquired OMX Group, forming NASDAQ OMX Group.
2013: Acquired Thomson Reuters’ IR, PR, and multimedia businesses.
2016: Company rebranded as Nasdaq, Inc.
2023: Acquired Adenza (risk management and regulatory technology) for $10.5 billion.
2024: Launched Nasdaq Eqlipse, the fourth generation of its marketplace technology platform.

title: NASDAQ Stock Market (NASDAQ)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Cross (9:30 AM ET): Aggregates all pre-market orders and continuous book orders to determine a single opening price per security. The Net Order Imbalance Indicator (NOII) is disseminated prior to the cross, providing supply/demand transparency via Nasdaq TotalView. Fully electronic with no human intervention. Processes millions of orders in microseconds.
Closing Cross (~4:00 PM ET): Determines the official closing price for Nasdaq-listed securities. NOII disseminated beginning at 3:50 PM ET. Handles approximately 16% of daily Nasdaq volume. This price is used for mutual fund NAV calculations, index calculations, and settlement.
IPO/Halt Cross: Used for IPO price discovery and resumption of trading after halts. Separate NOII disseminated for imbalance information.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market with competing market makers providing liquidity.
Price-time priority: Orders are matched first by price, then by time of entry at the same price level.
Supports both displayed and non-displayed (hidden) orders.
Midpoint pegging orders available for execution at the midpoint of the NBBO.



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening and closing crosses are the primary price discovery mechanisms, representing approximately 20% of total daily exchange volume.
NOII provides real-time reference prices, paired shares, and imbalance data for informed participation.
Continuous trading provides ongoing price discovery throughout the regular session.

5. Trading System (Technology)







Item
Details




System Name
Nasdaq INET (matching engine); Nasdaq Eqlipse (4th-generation platform, launched 2024)


Vendor / In-house
In-house developed by Nasdaq, Inc.


Architecture
Microservice-based, cloud-ready platform supporting both cloud and on-premise deployment


Matching Engine
Ultra-low latency INET matching engine; price-time priority; multi-asset capable


Round-trip Latency
Market data latency: ~3 microseconds; Order acknowledgment: ~20 microseconds; Door-to-door: ~14 microseconds (fastest production); 99th percentile: ~78 microseconds; 99.9th percentile: ~150 microseconds [Source: OUCH measurements, SIX X-Stream INET benchmarks]


Order Processing Capacity
Supports millions of orders per day; designed to handle peak volumes exceeding 10x average


Messages Per Second
Not officially disclosed; industry estimates suggest capacity in the millions of messages per second [unverified]


Launch Year
INET: 2006 (based on Instinet/Inet ECN acquired 2005); Eqlipse platform: 2024




System History








Period
System
Notes




1971-1982
Original NASDAQ Automated Quotation System
Quote-only system; no execution capability; CRT terminals


1982-1990s
SOES (Small Order Execution System)
First electronic execution; mandatory for market makers


2002-2006
SuperMontage
Integrated limit order book with market maker quotes; replaced legacy systems


2006-2024
INET
Acquired from Instinet; sub-millisecond latency; became the core matching engine across all Nasdaq markets globally


2024-Present
Nasdaq Eqlipse (with INET engine)
Fourth-generation platform; microservice architecture; cloud-ready; “evergreen” quarterly upgrade model; AWS Outposts integration





Technology Stack

Matching Engine: Custom-built INET engine optimized for ultra-low latency; FPGA-accelerated feed processing.
Network: 10 Gbps and 40 Gbps network connections; 40G Express Connect with <35 nanoseconds switching latency.
Protocol Support: OUCH (native low-level order entry), FIX (4.0/4.1/4.2), SoupBinTCP (transport layer), ITCH (market data).
Cloud Integration: AWS partnership; Nasdaq Eqlipse Trading cloud-based platform (launched May 2025 with AWS).
AI Integration: AI built into Verafin, eVestment, AxiomSL, Calypso, and Surveillance solutions.



Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity

Primary Data Center: Equinix NY11, Carteret, NJ (91,413 sq ft; expansion NY11-4 under construction to double capacity).
Disaster Recovery Site: Equinix CH4, 350 E. Cermak, Chicago, IL (migrated from Ashburn, VA in 2015 for greater regional diversity).
Rationale: Chicago DR site provides geographic separation from East Coast primary facility to mitigate regional disaster risk (hurricanes, coastal flooding).
Redundancy: POP (Point of Presence) nodes in multiple financial data centers; redundant high-speed fiber paths.

6. Market Data

6.1 Data Feed Protocols








Protocol
Description
Use Case




ITCH (TotalView-ITCH 5.0)
Native binary protocol; full order-by-order depth of book data; variable-length messages
Full book reconstruction; algorithmic trading; market microstructure analysis

Hardware-accelerated FPGA version of TotalView-ITCH; broadcast via MoldUDP64 only
Ultra-low latency applications; HFT; requires 10G or 40G connection

Transport layer protocol providing framing, authentication, heartbeats, sequencing, and recovery
Underlying transport for ITCH and OUCH protocols


MoldUDP64
UDP multicast protocol for market data dissemination
Primary multicast delivery mechanism for ITCH feeds





6.2 Data Levels

Level 1 (Nasdaq Basic): Best bid/offer (BBO), last sale price, volume. Suitable for retail investors.
Level 2 (Nasdaq TotalView): Full depth of book; every order at every price level with attribution; includes NOII data for opening/closing crosses. The most comprehensive Nasdaq data product.
Level 3: Market maker-only view with ability to enter and update quotes (not a separate product; refers to market maker functionality).



6.3 Distribution Infrastructure

Direct feeds: Available via co-location in Carteret, NJ or through Nasdaq POP sites.
SIP (Securities Information Processor): CTA/CQS for Tape A & B (NYSE-listed); UTP SIP for Tape C (Nasdaq-listed). Provides consolidated national best bid/offer.
Third-party distributors: Bloomberg, Refinitiv, ICE, and other major data vendors.
Nasdaq Data Link (formerly Quandl): Platform for accessing financial, economic, and alternative datasets.



6.4 Historical Data

Nasdaq Daily Share Volume (NDSV): Historical daily volume data by symbol.
TotalView-ITCH historical replay: Available through Nasdaq and third-party providers (e.g., Databento, LOBSTER).
Nasdaq Global Data Services: Offers historical tick data, end-of-day data, and reference data products.

7. Connectivity & Access

7.1 Membership / Participation

Open to SEC-registered broker-dealers who have obtained SRO membership.
Members must have an established connection to a clearing firm (self-clearing or correspondent clearing arrangement).
Categories include: Market Makers, Order Entry Firms, ECN participants.
Membership applications reviewed by Nasdaq; subject to ongoing examination and compliance oversight (outsourced to FINRA).



7.2 Connection Methods

Direct Connect (10G): <40 nanoseconds switching latency at Carteret data center.
Express Connect (40G): <35 nanoseconds switching latency; higher bandwidth for demanding applications.
Extranet providers: Approved third-party network providers offering managed connectivity.
Service Bureau: Indirect connection through approved FIX service bureaus.
Nasdaq POP (Point of Presence): Redundant high-speed fiber handoffs at Equinix NY11 (Carteret) and other strategic financial data centers. Available in 10G and 1G.



7.3 Co-location / Proximity Services

Location: Equinix NY11, Carteret, NJ.
Services: High-density cabinet hosting within the same facility as Nasdaq matching engines.
Benefits: Minimized latency; single hand-off for all Nasdaq U.S. markets (Nasdaq, BX, PSX).
Expansion: NY11-4 facility under construction on the north side of the Carteret campus, doubling available co-location space.
Cloud Integration: AWS Outposts being incorporated directly into the Carteret core network for hybrid cloud/co-location deployments.



7.4 API Protocols

Direction

7.5 Certification / Testing

Certification Environment: Nasdaq provides a dedicated test/certification environment for all connectivity protocols (OUCH, FIX, ITCH).
Conformance Testing: Required before production access; validates message formatting, order handling, and market data consumption.
Industry Testing: Participants must complete SEC Rule 15c3-5 (Market Access Rule) compliance testing for risk controls.
Ongoing Testing: Periodic industry-wide tests (e.g., disaster recovery failover tests, LULD testing).

title: NASDAQ Stock Market (NASDAQ)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

Limit Up-Limit Down (LULD): Price bands set at a percentage above and below the average reference price over the preceding 5-minute period.
Tier 1 NMS Stocks (S&P 500, Russell 1000, select ETPs):

Price > $3.00: 5% band
Price $0.75 - $3.00: 20% band
Price < $0.75: Lesser of $0.15 or 75%

Tier 2 NMS Stocks (all other NMS securities):

Price > $3.00: 10% band
Price $0.75 - $3.00: 20% band
Price < $0.75: Lesser of $0.15 or 75%

If price reaches the band and does not return within 15 seconds, a 5-minute trading pause is triggered.



8.2 Circuit Breakers








Level
Trigger (S&P 500 decline from prior close)
Halt Duration




Level 1
7% decline
15-minute halt (once per day; no halt if triggered after 3:25 PM ET)


Level 2
13% decline
15-minute halt (once per day; no halt if triggered after 3:25 PM ET)


Level 3
20% decline
Trading halted for remainder of the trading day





8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Maximum Order Value Checks: Configurable per-order maximum value limits; orders exceeding the limit are rejected.
Maximum Accumulated Value Checks: Cumulative order value tracking throughout the trading day; new orders rejected when the accumulated limit is reached.
Fat Finger Checks: Price reasonability checks comparing order price against current last sale / reference price to catch entry errors.
Credit Risk Controls: Real-time monitoring of execution exposure against pre-set limits.
FIX Drop-on-Disconnect: Automatic cancellation of all open orders and prevention of new order entry upon connection loss.



8.4 Kill Switch

Nasdaq Equity Kill Switch: Allows participants to establish Risk Exposure levels and receive notifications as execution value and open order value approach those levels.
Computes total value of all executions and open orders throughout the trading day.
When activated: immediately cancels all current orders and rejects all subsequent orders.
Available for manual activation by participant administrators or automated trigger based on pre-configured thresholds.

title: NASDAQ Stock Market (NASDAQ)
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Primary Regulator: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Self-Regulatory Organization: Nasdaq operates as an SRO; market regulation functions outsourced to FINRA under a Regulatory Services Agreement (RSA).
Oversight: SEC oversight of exchange rules, listing standards, and market structure.



9.2 Key Regulations

Securities Exchange Act of 1934: Foundation statute governing national securities exchanges.
Regulation NMS (2005): Modernized equity market structure; 14 rules covering trade reporting (601-603), investor protection (604-607), SRO governance (608-609), trading rules including protected quotes, decimal ticks, access fee caps (610-612), and Consolidated Audit Trail (613).
Regulation SHO: Short selling rules including locate requirements and close-out obligations.
SEC Rule 15c3-5 (Market Access Rule): Requires broker-dealers with market access to implement risk controls and supervisory procedures.
SEC Rule 606: Order routing disclosure requirements.
Regulation ATS: Rules for alternative trading systems operating alongside exchanges.



9.3 Market Surveillance

NASDAQ MarketWatch: Dedicated surveillance unit monitoring trading across Nasdaq, BX, PSX (equities) and NOM, BX Options, PHLX (options).
Real-time surveillance: Automated detection systems generating alerts on unusual trading activity, potential manipulation, and rule violations.
Post-trade surveillance: Pattern analysis and investigation of trading anomalies.
Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT): Industry-wide order tracking system capturing lifecycle of every order across all U.S. exchanges and broker-dealers.
Outsourced examination/investigation: FINRA conducts member examinations and investigations under the RSA.



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Transaction Reporting: All trades reported to the consolidated tape via CTA (Tape A/B) or UTP (Tape C) within seconds of execution.
OATS (Order Audit Trail System): Being replaced by CAT; requires recording of all order events.
Short Interest Reporting: Bi-monthly reporting of short positions by member firms.
Large Trader Reporting (SEC Rule 13h-1): Firms exceeding thresholds (2 million shares or $20 million in a day, or 20 million shares or $200 million in a month) must register and report.
Form 13F: Institutional investment managers with >$100 million AUM must report quarterly holdings.



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

NASDAQ lists securities of over 500 foreign companies (largest sources: China, Israel, UK, Canada).
ADR (American Depositary Receipt) listings enable foreign company access.
Nasdaq, Inc. operates exchanges globally (Nordic/Baltic exchanges, Nasdaq First North, others) providing cross-listing opportunities.
Information-sharing agreements with foreign regulators through SEC’s international cooperation framework (IOSCO MMoU).

System Upgrades (Last 5 Years)

2022: Continued INET matching engine optimizations; enhanced FPGA-based market data distribution.
2023: Acquired Adenza for $10.5 billion, adding Calypso (trading/risk) and AxiomSL (regulatory reporting) to the technology portfolio.

title: National Stock Exchange of India (NSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (Pre-open Session): Call auction during 9:00â9:08 AM determines the opening price. Orders are accumulated and matched at a single equilibrium price that maximizes tradeable volume. Unmatched orders carry forward to continuous trading.
Closing Price: Determined as the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of trades in the last 30 minutes of continuous trading (14:30â15:00 was previously used; current closing mechanism may involve a dedicated closing session) [unverified â exact current methodology should be confirmed with NSE]
Special Pre-open Sessions (SPOS): Used for stock re-listing, corporate action adjustments, or circuit-breaker recovery â the exchange initiates a call auction to re-establish equilibrium price
Periodic Call Auction (PCA): Applied to illiquid securities (those in the “Trade-to-Trade” segment or identified by surveillance); matches orders at fixed intervals rather than continuously

[Source: NSE Official Website, “Trading System”; Tandfonline, “Pre-open call auction and price discovery: Evidence from India”]


3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-Driven Market: NSE operates a fully order-driven, anonymous electronic market (no market makers required for main equities)
Price-Time Priority: The matching engine follows strict price-time priority â best-priced orders are matched first; among orders at the same price, the earliest order has priority
Passive orders rest in the order book; incoming aggressive orders are matched immediately against resting orders

[Source: NSE Official Website, “Trading System”]


3.3 Price Discovery

Pre-open session establishes the opening price via call auction (equilibrium price algorithm)
During continuous trading, price discovery is fully electronic and based on supply-demand interaction in the order book
NSE’s fully electronic system replaced the open outcry method previously used by BSE, vastly improving price transparency across India

8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Bands (Individual Securities)

Band

[Source: NSE Official Website, “Price Bands”; Kotak Neo, “NSE Price Band Changes”]
Notes: - Price bands are reviewed and revised periodically by NSE based on SEBI criteria. - Stocks in the Trade-to-Trade (T2T) segment or under additional surveillance measures (ASM/GSM) may have tighter bands. - F&O eligible stocks have no daily circuit limits but are subject to operating range (OR) checks by the exchange.


8.2 Circuit Breakers (Index-Based Market-Wide)
The index-based market-wide circuit breaker system halts trading across all equity and equity derivative markets nationwide. Triggered by movement of either BSE Sensex or Nifty 50, whichever is breached first:









Trigger Level
Before 1:00 PM
1:00 PM â 2:30 PM
After 2:30 PM




10% movement
Trading halt for 45 minutes
Trading halt for 15 minutes
No halt; trading continues


15% movement

Remainder of day halt


20% movement

Trading halted for remainder of day
Trading halted for remainder of day



[Source: NSE Official Website, “Circuit Breakers”; SEBI circular on market-wide circuit breakers]
Notes: - After a circuit breaker halt, the market reopens with a pre-open call auction session (special pre-open session). - The reference value for computing circuit breaker triggers is the previous day’s closing index value. - Circuit breakers apply uniformly to NSE, BSE, and all derivative segments across India.


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Quantity Freeze Limits: Maximum permissible order quantity per single trade in F&O contracts; orders exceeding this limit are automatically rejected by the exchange system [Source: ICICI Direct, “Revised Quantity Freeze Limits”]
Order Value Limits: Maximum order value checks to prevent fat-finger errors
Price Range Checks: Orders outside the allowed operating range are rejected
Broker-Level Controls: Brokers required to implement pre-trade risk checks auditable by NSE and SEBI (per SEBI circular, July 2021 and subsequent updates)
Algorithmic Trading Controls: All algo orders must be tagged; algo strategies require exchange approval; SEBI regulations effective August 1, 2025 mandate comprehensive risk checks for retail algo trading



8.4 Kill Switch

Brokers and trading members have kill switch capabilities to instantly halt all algo orders
Exchanges reserve the right to deactivate rogue algorithms affecting market integrity
SEBI mandates kill switch as part of algo trading risk management framework

[Source: Groww, “SEBI Regulations on Algorithmic Trading in India”; KillSwitch.in]

text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

Primary Regulator: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), established under the SEBI Act, 1992
Governing Legislation:

Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCRA)
Depositories Act, 1996
Securities Markets Code, 2025 â new unified code consolidating SCRA, SEBI Act, and Depositories Act into a single legislative framework [Source: Mondaq, “How India’s Securities Markets Code, 2025, Will Reshape Compliance”]

NSE operates as a recognized stock exchange under SCRA and is subject to SEBI’s regulatory oversight



9.2 Key Regulations

SEBI (Stock Brokers and Sub-Brokers) Regulations, 1992
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR)
SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices) Regulations, 2003
SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008
SEBI circulars on algorithmic trading, colocation, and market microstructure



9.3 Market Surveillance

Primary surveillance responsibility lies with NSE’s own surveillance department
SEBI maintains proactive oversight on market movements and trends
NSE conducts real-time surveillance using automated systems to detect abnormal trading patterns, price manipulation, and insider trading
Additional Surveillance Measures (ASM) and Graded Surveillance Measures (GSM) applied to securities exhibiting unusual price/volume patterns
Periodic surveillance reports circulated to SEBI and the Ministry of Finance

[Source: NSE Official Website, “Exchange Market Surveillance & Regulatory Actions”]


9.4 Reporting Requirements

Listed companies must comply with SEBI LODR for periodic and event-based disclosures
Trading members submit daily margin and risk reports
Large trader reporting and position limits for derivatives
Short-selling disclosure requirements



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

SEBI is a signatory to the IOSCO Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU) for cross-border cooperation
SEBI’s Office of International Affairs liaises with foreign securities regulators, central banks, and judicial authorities
Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) access NSE through SEBI’s FPI registration framework
NSE IFSC (International Financial Services Centre) subsidiary operates in GIFT City, Gujarat, for offshore trading



9.6 Colocation Controversy & Investigation
The NSE colocation case is one of the most significant regulatory controversies in Indian capital market history:

2010â2014: Certain high-frequency trading (HFT) firms allegedly received preferential access to NSE’s colocation servers, gaining unfair speed advantages in receiving market data. A non-empanelled internet service provider was reportedly allowed to lay dark fiber cables on NSE premises for select brokers.
January 2015: Whistleblower complaint filed with SEBI exposing the alleged manipulation.
May 2017: SEBI issued show cause notices to NSE and 14 individuals, including former Managing Directors Chitra Ramakrishna and Ravi Narain.
2019: SEBI directed NSE to disgorge INR 625 crore plus interest and imposed an additional penalty of INR 1,000 crore (~USD 131 million combined).
January 2023: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) largely quashed the 2019 SEBI order, citing contradictory findings and insufficient evidence, and remanded parts back to SEBI.
September 2024: SEBI dropped proceedings against NSE and several other officials in the colocation case, citing insufficient evidence of involvement and collusion.
Ongoing: CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) filed a final chargesheet naming 43 accused including Chitra Ramakrishna. The case also involved broader governance concerns at NSE, including revelations about an unknown “Himalayan Yogi” who allegedly influenced NSE decisions through Ramakrishna.
IPO Impact: The controversy significantly delayed NSE’s planned IPO, which remains pending as of early 2026.

[Source: Wikipedia, “NSE co-location scam”; Business Standard; Moneylife; Business Today, September 2024; The Print]

title: Singapore Exchange (SGX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: During the Pre-Open phase (08:30-08:58/59), orders accumulate without matching. At the Non-Cancel phase (random start between 08:58-08:59), the system computes an equilibrium price using a single-price auction algorithm. The equilibrium price maximises tradable volume and minimises order imbalance. Orders are matched at this single price to determine the opening price.
Closing Auction: Similar to the opening auction. During the Pre-Close phase (17:00-17:04/05), orders accumulate. The Non-Cancel phase (random start 17:04-17:05) determines the closing equilibrium price via single-price matching. This closing price is used for index calculations, NAV computations, and settlement purposes.
Mid-Day Auction: The lunch break includes its own Pre-Open (12:00-12:58/59) and Non-Cancel (12:58/59-13:00) phases, effectively creating a mid-session auction to re-establish prices before afternoon trading.
Volatility Auction: When the circuit breaker is triggered, a 5-minute cooling-off period begins during which trading continues within the price band but orders outside the band are rejected. There is no formal volatility interruption auction; rather, the mechanism moderates price movements.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Matching Algorithm: Price-time priority (orders matched first by best price, then by earliest entry time at the same price level)
Morning Session: 09:00 - 12:00 SGT (3 hours)
Afternoon Session: 13:00 - 17:00 SGT (4 hours)
Total Continuous Trading: 7 hours per normal trading day



3.3 Price Discovery
Equilibrium Price Algorithm: 1. The equilibrium price is the price with the largest tradable volume 2. If multiple prices yield the largest volume, the price with the lowest imbalance (net difference between cumulative bid and ask volume) is selected 3. If a Market Order Surplus exists (market order volume on one side exceeds cumulative order volume on the opposite side), one tick is added on the surplus side to determine the equilibrium price 4. If highest tradable volume and lowest imbalance occur at multiple prices (price overlap), market pressure determines the result: - With only buy pressure: highest price within the overlap - With only sell pressure: lowest price within the overlap - With both or neutral pressure: price closest to the last traded price
Forced Order Range: A pre-execution safeguard that prevents orders beyond +/- 30 bids from the reference price (widened from +/- 20 bids since 13 November 2017), helping investors avoid error trades.

Order Type / TIF Compatibility: - Limit orders: support all TIF options (Day, IOC, FOK, GTC, GTDate, On Open, On Close) - Market orders: support IOC, FOK, On Open, On Close - Market-to-Limit orders: support IOC, FOK, Day, GTC, GTDate


4.4 Order Modification / Cancellation

Orders can be modified (price, quantity) or cancelled during Pre-Open and Continuous Trading phases
During Non-Cancel phases (opening, mid-day, closing), no modifications or cancellations are permitted
During Trade-at-Close phase, only orders at the equilibrium price are accepted
Order modifications that change price result in loss of time priority

title: Singapore Exchange (SGX)
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Price Limits

Forced Order Range (FOR): Pre-execution mechanism that rejects orders beyond +/- 30 bids from the reference price (widened from +/- 20 bids since 13 November 2017)
Applies to all securities traded on SGX (excluding preference shares, structured warrants, ETFs, ETNs, debentures, bonds, and loan stocks)
Designed to prevent error trades by limiting the maximum deviation from the current market price



8.2 Circuit Breakers
SGX employs dynamic circuit breakers (Volatility Control Mechanism):







Parameter
Details




Price Band
+/- 10% from the dynamic reference price


Dynamic Reference Price
Last traded price as of 5 minutes prior to each potential trade


Trigger
Incoming order that would result in a trade outside the price band


Action
Incoming order is rejected; 5-minute cooling-off period begins


During Cooling-Off
Trading continues within the existing price bands; orders outside bands are rejected


Scope
Component stocks of the Straits Times Index (STI) and MSCI Singapore Free Index (SiMSCI), ETFs based on these indices, and Extended Settlement Contracts on these counters


Duration
5-minute cooling-off period



Asia-Specific Context: SGX’s dynamic circuit breakers differ from the static daily price limits used by some other Asian exchanges (e.g., KRX’s +/- 30%, JPX/TSE’s daily price limits). SGX’s approach is intraday and dynamic, triggering only when rapid price movement occurs, allowing the market to remain open throughout.


8.3 Pre-trade Risk Controls

Exchange-Level PTRC: SGX provides Pre-Trade Risk Controls that prevent orders exceeding preset thresholds
Member-Level Controls: Trading members and clearing members are required to adopt adequate policies and controls to manage risks from order acceptance, execution, and settlement
Iris-ST Enhancement (2027): The new trading engine will include a built-in pre-trade risk control system that members can use to fulfil their regulatory obligations
Fat-finger Controls: Forced Order Range mechanism prevents grossly mispriced orders
Position Limits: Clearing members must monitor and manage position limits



8.4 Kill Switch

SGX provides mechanisms for trading members to cancel all outstanding orders in emergency situations
Drop Copy API enables real-time monitoring across multiple books, supporting risk management decisions
Specific kill switch implementation details are not publicly available

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority







Authority
Role




Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)
Statutory regulator; integrated supervisor of Singapore’s financial industry; oversees SGX as an Approved Exchange under the Securities and Futures Act (SFA)


SGX RegCo
Independent regulatory subsidiary of SGX; carries out frontline regulatory functions including listing review, trade surveillance, member supervision, and enforcement; reports to its own Board and to MAS





9.2 Key Regulations







Regulation
Description




Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA)
Primary legislation governing capital markets in Singapore; covers licensing, market conduct, prospectus requirements, market misconduct, and cross-border provisions


Exchanges (Demutualisation and Merger) Act 1999
Enabled the merger of SES and SIMEX into SGX and the demutualization of the exchange


SGX-ST Mainboard Rules
Listing and trading rules for the Mainboard segment


SGX-ST Catalist Rules
Listing and trading rules for the Catalist growth board


Securities and Futures (Licensing and Conduct of Business) Regulations
Detailed requirements for capital markets services licence holders


Financial Advisers Act 2001
Regulates financial advisers and their representatives





9.3 Market Surveillance

Three-tier surveillance model: Brokers (first line), SGX RegCo (frontline exchange surveillance), and MAS (statutory oversight)
MAS-SGX Trade Surveillance Practice Guide: Jointly published guide to assist brokers in developing trade surveillance operations
SGX RegCo monitors trading activities in real-time for potential market misconduct (insider trading, market manipulation, front-running)
SGX RegCo conducts regular inspections, reviews, and company visits
Enforcement actions include trading halts, suspensions, public censures, fines, and referral to MAS for statutory enforcement



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Continuous Disclosure: Listed companies must promptly disclose material information that would affect the price of their securities
Periodic Reporting: Quarterly (if applicable) and annual financial reporting requirements
Substantial Shareholding: Disclosure required when crossing 5% ownership threshold
Short Selling Reporting: Designated short selling regime with reporting obligations
Trade Reporting: Off-market trades must be reported within prescribed timeframes



9.5 Cross-border Arrangements

Extra-territorial Reach (SFA Section 339): Acts outside Singapore with substantial and foreseeable effect in Singapore are subject to SFA regulation
Cross-Border Exemption Regulations (2021): Exemptions for foreign related corporations and foreign offices conducting qualifying businesses under cross-border arrangements
GIFT Connect: Cross-border connectivity between SGX and NSE IFSC (India) for Nifty derivatives trading
Global Listing Board (2025-2026): SGX-Nasdaq dual-listing framework for companies with market cap above SGD 2 billion; MAS proposing legislative amendments to SFA to facilitate
Mutual Recognition Arrangements: SGX maintains regulatory cooperation with multiple international exchanges and regulators

title: Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Opening Call Auction (9:15-9:30): - Orders collected during 9:15-9:25 pre-open period - System calculates a single price that maximizes executable volume at 9:25 - Price determination principle: the price at which the maximum volume of shares can be traded; if multiple prices satisfy this condition, the price closest to the previous close is selected - Unmatched orders carry forward to continuous trading session - Orders submitted between 9:20-9:25 cannot be cancelled (to prevent manipulation)
Closing Call Auction (14:57-15:00): - Replaces continuous trading for the final 3 minutes of the session - Same single-price auction principle as opening auction - Orders accepted but cannot be cancelled during this period - Determines the official closing price of each security - Applicable to both Main Board and STAR Market
STAR Market After-hours Fixed-price Trading (15:05-15:30): - All trades executed at the day’s closing price - Time priority for order matching - Provides additional liquidity window for STAR Market stocks


3.2 Continuous Trading

Order-driven market: Pure order-driven (no designated market makers for Main Board equities)
Price-time priority: Orders are matched first by best price, then by time of entry at the same price level
Buy orders at the highest price and sell orders at the lowest price are matched first
Trade execution price is determined by existing resting orders (passive side)



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening price: Determined by opening call auction; if no trades occur during auction, the first trade during continuous trading becomes the opening price
Closing price: Determined by closing call auction (14:57-15:00)
T+1 trading rule significantly affects intraday price discovery – shares purchased on day T cannot be sold until day T+1, reducing intraday liquidity and creating asymmetric trading patterns (investors can buy shares they sold earlier the same day, but cannot sell shares purchased the same day)

8.2 Circuit Breakers







Status
Details




Currently: No market-wide circuit breaker
China attempted an index-based circuit breaker mechanism in January 2016 but suspended it after only 4 trading days



2016 Circuit Breaker Episode: - Implemented: January 1, 2016, based on the CSI 300 Index - 5% decline threshold: Trading halted for 15 minutes; if triggered after 14:45, trading halted for remainder of day - 7% decline threshold: Trading halted for remainder of the day - Triggered: January 4, 2016 (both 5% and 7% thresholds hit) and January 7, 2016 (both thresholds hit within minutes) - Suspended: January 8, 2016 – CSRC suspended the mechanism permanently - Reason for failure: The circuit breaker created a “magnet effect” – investors rushed to sell before being locked in by the halt, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy that accelerated the decline. The proximity of the 5% and 7% thresholds (~2% gap) gave insufficient buffer time - Current status: Individual stock price limits (+/-10% / +/-20%) remain the primary volatility control mechanism; no plans to reintroduce market-wide circuit breakers as of 2026

9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Supervising Authority

China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC): Primary regulator of China’s securities and futures markets; equivalent to the U.S. SEC
SSE is directly supervised by CSRC since 1997 (by State Council directive)
SSE also functions as a front-line self-regulatory organization (SRO), conducting listing review, trading surveillance, and member supervision under CSRC delegation

SSE operates real-time market surveillance systems monitoring for insider trading, market manipulation, and abnormal trading

Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect): - Launched: November 17, 2014 - Northbound: International investors trade SSE-listed A-shares via HKEX brokers - Southbound: Mainland investors trade HKEX-listed stocks via SSE member brokers - Eligible stocks: Large/mid-cap A-shares (SSE 180, SSE 380 constituents, and dual-listed A+H stocks); scope has been gradually expanded - Daily quota: Northbound daily quota of RMB 52 billion (expanded from original RMB 13 billion); aggregate quota abolished in 2018 - Settlement: T+0 for Northbound (trades settle same day at HKSCC); underlying A-shares follow T+1 trading rule - ETF Connect: Expanded to include eligible ETFs since July 2022

China-Specific Features Summary







Feature
Description




T+1 Trading Rule
Shares purchased on day T cannot be sold until day T+1; this is asymmetric – shares sold on day T can be repurchased the same day. This fundamentally limits day-trading and affects market microstructure


Daily Price Limits
+/-10% Main Board / +/-20% STAR Market replace Western-style circuit breakers as the primary volatility mechanism


State Ownership
SSE is a state-owned, non-profit institution directly supervised by CSRC – unlike most major global exchanges which are publicly listed, for-profit corporations


A/B Share Dual Structure
Legacy system of dual share classes by currency/investor type; B-shares largely obsolete but still traded


Foreign Access Restrictions
Foreign investors cannot trade A-shares directly; access only through QFI scheme or Stock Connect; strategic/sensitive sectors may have additional restrictions


Registration vs. Approval IPO
STAR Market uses registration-based system (similar to Western markets); Main Board historically used approval-based system but is transitioning to registration


CSRC Dominant Role
CSRC exercises much more direct control over exchange operations, IPO approvals, and market interventions than Western regulators typically do


Stock Connect Mechanism
Unique cross-border trading link with HKEX that enables foreign access while maintaining China’s capital controls

title: Saudi Exchange (Tadawul)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction: During the Pre-Open phase (09:30-10:00 AST), orders accumulate without matching. The system displays indicative opening prices. At 10:00, a randomized uncross occurs within a 30-second window (10:00:00-10:00:30), determining the opening price via a single-price auction that maximizes executable volume.
Closing Auction: The Pre-Close phase begins at 15:00 AST. Orders accumulate for 10 minutes. At 15:10, a randomized uncross within 30 seconds determines the closing price. This closing price is the official price used for index calculations, NAV computations, and settlement.
Trade-at-Last: After the closing auction uncross (15:10-15:20 AST), participants may execute orders only at the closing auction price. This session provides additional liquidity at the established closing price.
Volatility Auction (Interruption): When a security price reaches the +/-10% static price limit, continuous trading halts and a 5-minute call auction is initiated. The auction price becomes the new reference price, after which continuous trading resumes.



3.2 Continuous Trading

Type: Order-driven market
Priority: Price-time priority (best price first, then earliest entry time at the same price)
Session: 10:00 - 15:00 AST (5 hours)
Matching: Continuous automatic matching via the X-Stream INET engine



3.3 Price Discovery

Opening price: Determined by single-price auction algorithm maximizing tradable volume at the uncross
Closing price: Determined by closing auction uncross; if no closing auction trade occurs, the last traded price during continuous trading is used [unverified]
Reference price: Previous session’s closing auction price; serves as the baseline for daily price limits
Randomized uncross: Both open and close uncross times are randomized within 30 seconds to prevent manipulation and enhance price integrity

3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms

Opening Auction (Call Auction): At 09:00, all orders accumulated during the pre-open period (08:30â09:00) are matched via a single-price call auction to determine the opening price
Closing Auction (Call Auction): During 13:25â13:30, orders are matched via call auction to determine official closing prices
Intraday Odd-Lot Auction: Odd-lot orders matched every 5 seconds by call auction during regular trading hours (first match at 09:10)



3.2 Continuous Trading
Historical Evolution: 1. Pre-2013: Pure call auction system with 20-second matching intervals 2. 2013â2014: Call auction interval progressively shortened â from 20 seconds to 15 seconds (July 1, 2013), then 10 seconds (February 24, 2014), then 5 seconds (December 29, 2014) 3. March 23, 2020: Full transition to continuous trading for stocks, ETFs, ETNs, and TDRs
Current Mechanism (post-March 2020): - Order-driven market with price-time priority - Orders are matched continuously on a real-time basis during the regular session (09:00â13:25) - Trading price, volume, and best 5 bid/ask prices and volumes are disclosed in real time - A “5-second snapshot” of market information is also provided for data dissemination purposes


3.3 Price Discovery

Opening and closing prices are determined via call auction, providing a transparent aggregation of supply and demand
Intraday prices are discovered through continuous matching under price-time priority
The intraday price stabilization mechanism (dynamic circuit breaker) pauses matching for 2 minutes if a potential execution price deviates more than Â±3.5% from the reference price, preventing excessive short-term volatility while allowing orders to accumulate

No restrictions on repatriation of capital or profits


Foreign ownership share
Foreign investors held 45.41% of total TWSE market capitalization by end of 2024, with market value exceeding NT$33 trillion

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
1. Regulatory Authority Structure

1.1 EU-Level: European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA)







Item
Details




Established
2011 (replacing CESR)


Legal Basis
Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010


Headquarters
Paris, France


Role
EU-level supervisory convergence, rulemaking (technical standards), direct supervision of specific entities (credit rating agencies, trade repositories, and now consolidated tape providers)


Governance
Board of Supervisors comprising heads of all 27 national competent authorities (NCAs), a Chair, and representatives from the European Commission, ECB, ESRB, EBA, and EIOPA



ESMA’s core functions in equities markets include:

Rulemaking: Drafting Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) and Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) under MiFID II/MiFIR, MAR, CSDR, and other Level 1 legislation. These are adopted as binding EU regulations by the European Commission.
Supervisory convergence: Issuing guidelines, Q&As, opinions, and supervisory briefings to harmonise NCA conduct across Member States.
Direct supervision: CTP operators, trade repositories, and credit rating agencies fall under ESMA’s direct authority. Under the MiFIR Review, ESMA now also directly authorises and supervises consolidated tape providers.
Data collection and publication: Operating FITRS (Financial Instruments Transparency System), FIRDS (Financial Instruments Reference Data System), and publishing volume cap, liquidity, and transparency calculations.
Market integrity coordination: Coordinating cross-border MAR enforcement, maintaining STORs (Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports) framework.

[Source: ESMA, “About ESMA”, accessed 2026-04-06]


1.2 National Competent Authorities (NCAs)
Day-to-day supervision and enforcement of EU securities regulation is carried out by NCAs in each Member State. Key NCAs for equities markets include:








Country
NCA
Key Responsibilities




United Kingdom
Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)
Post-Brexit independent regulator; prudential and conduct supervision of ~50,000 firms; operates UK’s own regulatory framework diverging from EU


Germany
BaFin (Bundesanstalt fur Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht)
Supervises Deutsche Borse/Xetra, banks, insurers; enforces MAR, MiFID II nationally


France
AMF (Autorite des marches financiers)
Supervises Euronext Paris; highest MAR fine amounts in Europe in 2024; market conduct and investor protection


Netherlands
AFM (Autoriteit Financiele Markten)
Supervises Euronext Amsterdam; robust algo/HFT oversight given Amsterdam’s role as post-Brexit trading hub


Italy
CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Societa e la Borsa)
Supervises Borsa Italiana (now part of Euronext); market abuse enforcement


Spain
CNMV (Comision Nacional del Mercado de Valores)
Supervises BME (Bolsas y Mercados Espanoles); short selling monitoring


Ireland
Central Bank of Ireland
Growing role due to post-Brexit relocations of asset managers and trading firms



NCAs retain authority for: - Authorising and supervising investment firms, trading venues (RMs, MTFs, OTFs), and systematic internalisers - Granting pre-trade transparency waivers (under ESMA opinion mechanism) - Enforcing MAR, including investigating insider dealing and market manipulation - Administering transaction reporting under MiFIR Article 26 - Imposing administrative sanctions (fines, suspensions, bans)
[Source: ESMA, “National Competent Authorities — MiFID”, accessed 2026-04-06]


1.3 Post-Brexit Divergence: UK vs EU
Since the UK’s departure from the EU single market on 31 December 2020, two parallel regulatory regimes have emerged:








Dimension
EU (ESMA + NCAs)
UK (FCA + PRA)




Legislative process
Commission proposes, Parliament and Council co-decide; ESMA drafts Level 2 measures
HM Treasury sets framework; FCA makes rules under FSMA 2023 (previously FSMA 2000)


Regulatory philosophy
Harmonised single rulebook; ESMA convergence
Outcomes-based regulation; secondary competitiveness objective added to FCA mandate (2023)


Speed of reform
Slower (27 Member States to align)
Faster (single jurisdiction); Edinburgh/Leeds Reforms agenda


Equivalence status
EU has not granted UK broad equivalence for investment services
UK has granted broad equivalence to EU (Temporary Transitional Power expired 2023; most retained)


Key divergence areas
MiFIR Review (new volume cap, CTP regime, transparency)
Wholesale Markets Review, new UKLR listing rules, own prospectus regime, lighter SI regime



The UK’s Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (FSMA 2023) gave the FCA and PRA power to replace retained EU law with UK-made rules — the so-called “Smarter Regulatory Framework.” This is resulting in a gradual unwinding of the direct transposition of EU directives into UK law, with the FCA writing bespoke rules in its Handbook.
[Source: FCA, “Statement on market reforms and what’s to come”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Davis Polk, “Capital markets reform in the UK”, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
2. Key Regulations

2.1 MiFID II / MiFIR (Markets in Financial Instruments)







Item
Details




Full name
Directive 2014/65/EU (MiFID II) and Regulation (EU) No 600/2014 (MiFIR)


In force since
3 January 2018


Scope
Investment firms, trading venues (RMs, MTFs, OTFs), systematic internalisers, data reporting services providers


Key content
Market structure (venue categories, transparency), investor protection, transaction reporting, algo/HFT rules, third-country regime


Level 2 measures
~30+ Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) and Implementing Technical Standards (ITS), plus numerous ESMA guidelines


Major review
MiFIR Review (Regulation (EU) 2024/791) entered into force 28 March 2024; MiFID II amendments transposition deadline 29 September 2025



UK equivalent: On-shored as UK MiFID and UK MiFIR under the EU Withdrawal Act. The FCA’s Wholesale Markets Review (2021-ongoing) is progressively replacing these with UK-specific rules.
[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II and MiFIR review”, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.2 Market Abuse Regulation (MAR)







Item
Details




Full name
Regulation (EU) No 596/2014


In force since
3 July 2016


Scope
All financial instruments admitted to trading on EU trading venues (including MTFs and OTFs, not just RMs as under the predecessor MAD)


Key prohibitions
Insider dealing (Art. 14), unlawful disclosure of inside information (Art. 14), market manipulation (Art. 15)


Key obligations
Disclosure of inside information by issuers (Art. 17), managers’ transaction notifications (Art. 19), insider lists (Art. 18), STORs (Art. 16)


Enforcement (2024)
377 enforcement actions across 24 Member States; >EUR 100 million in administrative fines; 77 criminal sanctions in 6 Member States totalling >EUR 72 million


Recent amendment
EU Listing Act amends MAR Art. 17 regarding protracted processes and delay conditions; effective 5 June 2026



UK equivalent: UK MAR (on-shored). The FCA maintains independent enforcement with its own case law.
[Source: ESMA, “Consolidated Report on Sanctions and Measures 2024”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: ESMA, “Final Report on changes to MAR inside information disclosure rules”, May 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.3 Central Securities Depositories Regulation (CSDR)







Item
Details




Full name
Regulation (EU) No 909/2014


In force since
17 September 2014 (phased implementation)


Scope
CSDs (e.g., Euroclear, Clearstream), settlement discipline, dematerialisation


Key provisions
CSD authorisation and supervision, settlement discipline regime (mandatory buy-ins deferred, cash penalties applied from 1 February 2022), T+2 standard settlement cycle


CSDR Refit
Published in EU Official Journal 14 October 2025; provides legal basis for T+1 migration on 11 October 2027


Settlement discipline
Cash penalty regime operational; mandatory buy-ins remain suspended pending review



UK equivalent: UK CSDR (on-shored). The UK has signalled it will move to T+1 by 11 October 2027, aligned with the EU timeline.
[Source: European Commission, “T+1 settlement”, February 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.4 Prospectus Regulation







Item
Details




Full name
Regulation (EU) 2017/1129


In force since
21 July 2019 (replacing Prospectus Directive)


Key provision
Requires a prospectus approved by the NCA for public offers of securities or admission to trading on a regulated market exceeding certain thresholds


EU Listing Act amendments (2024)
Small offering exemption raised from EUR 8M to EUR 12M (Member State option for EUR 5M floor); secondary issuance dilution threshold raised from 20% to 30%; minimum EUR 1M threshold removed; standard prospectus limited to 300 pages with 2-year (instead of 3-year) financials; most content reforms effective 5 March and 5 June 2026



UK equivalent: The FCA’s new Prospectus Rules: Admission to Trading on a Regulated Market (PRM) sourcebook came into force 19 January 2026, replacing the on-shored EU Prospectus Regulation with a UK-tailored regime. The FCA’s approach gives it greater flexibility to set disclosure standards.
[Source: Osborne Clarke, “The EU Listing Act: what are the key changes to the Prospectus Regulation?”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: FCA, “PS24/6: Primary Markets Effectiveness Review”, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.5 Short Selling Regulation (SSR)







Item
Details




Full name
Regulation (EU) No 236/2012


In force since
1 November 2012


Key provisions
Prohibition of naked short selling of shares and sovereign debt; net short position reporting to NCAs at 0.1% of issued share capital (and each 0.1% above); public disclosure at 0.5% (and each 0.1% above); locate requirement; emergency intervention powers for NCAs and ESMA


ESMA review proposals
Permanent 0.1% reporting threshold (previously temporary under COVID measures); ESMA centralised publication system for net short positions; enhanced ESMA intervention powers; clarified ban procedures



UK equivalent: The Short Selling Regulations 2025 (UK SI 2025/29) replaced the on-shored EU SSR with a lighter-touch UK regime. Key changes include removing the public disclosure requirement (positions reported to the FCA only, not publicly), raising the reporting threshold, and giving the FCA more flexible intervention powers.
[Source: ESMA, “Short Selling”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: UK Legislation, “The Short Selling Regulations 2025”, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
3. Market Structure Rules

3.1 Venue Categories
MiFID II establishes a comprehensive taxonomy of execution venues, closing the gap that existed under MiFID I where significant trading occurred outside regulated venues (in “dark pools” and via broker crossing networks).

3.1.1 Regulated Market (RM)







Attribute
Details




Definition
A multilateral system operated by a market operator, bringing together multiple third-party buying and selling interests in financial instruments under non-discretionary rules resulting in a contract (MiFID II Art. 4(1)(21))


Key feature
Non-discretionary matching; operator cannot exercise discretion over order execution


Asset classes
All financial instruments


Examples
Euronext Paris, Deutsche Borse (Xetra), Borsa Italiana, BME, LSE Main Market


Authorisation
Requires authorisation from the NCA of the home Member State


Operator restrictions
Must be operated by a market operator (not an investment firm in its own capacity)





3.1.2 Multilateral Trading Facility (MTF)







Attribute
Details




Definition
A multilateral system operated by an investment firm or market operator, which brings together multiple third-party buying and selling interests under non-discretionary rules resulting in a contract (Art. 4(1)(22))


Key feature
Non-discretionary like RMs; can be operated by investment firms (unlike RMs)


Asset classes
All financial instruments


Examples
Cboe Europe (formerly BATS Chi-X), Turquoise (LSEG), Aquis Exchange, LSE AIM


Distinction from RM
Lighter organisational requirements; admission to trading on an MTF does not constitute “listing”





3.1.3 Organised Trading Facility (OTF)







Attribute
Details




Definition
A multilateral system that is not an RM or MTF, in which multiple third-party buying and selling interests in bonds, structured finance products, emission allowances or derivatives are able to interact in a way that results in a contract (Art. 4(1)(23))


Key feature
Discretionary execution — the operator can exercise discretion over how orders interact; introduced by MiFID II to capture broker crossing networks


Asset classes
Non-equity only — bonds, structured finance, emission allowances, derivatives


Restrictions
Cannot trade equities; operator cannot use own capital (except for illiquid sovereign debt); cannot combine with SI activities





3.1.4 Systematic Internaliser (SI)







Attribute
Details




Definition
An investment firm which, on an organised, frequent, systematic and substantial basis, deals on own account when executing client orders outside a trading venue (Art. 4(1)(20))


Key feature
Bilateral (not multilateral); firm acts as counterparty to the client; not a “trading venue” under MiFID II


Asset classes
All financial instruments


Pre-trade transparency
Must publish firm quotes for liquid equity instruments when dealing in sizes up to Standard Market Size (SMS); quotes must be made available to other clients on a non-discriminatory basis


Examples
Major investment banks (Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Citadel Securities) operating SI desks


Quantitative thresholds
Under original MiFID II: a firm is an SI if dealing above thresholds of frequency (at least once a week or more than half of the total number of days in a quarter), and substantiality (at least 15% of total turnover or 25% of total EU turnover in the instrument). Under the MiFIR Review, these opt-in quantitative thresholds are replaced by a qualitative self-assessment approach



[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II Article 4 — Definitions”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Norton Rose Fulbright, “MiFID II: Trading venues and market infrastructure”, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.1.5 Venue Category Comparison
