3.2 Pre-Trade Transparency (Equities)
MiFIR Articles 3-4 and RTS 1 govern pre-trade transparency for equity instruments. Trading venues must publish current bid/offer prices and depth of trading interests on a continuous basis during trading hours.
Information to be published: - For order-book systems: the 5 best bid and offer price levels and volume at each level - For quote-driven systems: the best bid and offer of each market maker, with corresponding volumes - For periodic auction systems: the price at which the trading system would best satisfy its matching algorithm and the volume potentially executable at that price
Pre-trade transparency waivers (Art. 4 MiFIR):








Waiver
Description
Volume Cap Applicability




Reference Price Waiver (RPW)
Systems that match orders at the midpoint of the current bid/offer on the primary market or most relevant market in terms of liquidity
Subject to the single volume cap (SVC)


Large-in-Scale (LIS) Waiver
Orders large relative to normal market size; thresholds set per liquidity band in RTS 1 Annex II
Not subject to volume cap


Negotiated Trade Waiver (NTW)
Negotiated transactions subject to conditions other than the current market price (e.g., benchmark, VWAP)
Not subject to volume cap under MiFIR Review (previously subject to DVC)


Order Management Facility Waiver
Orders held in an order management facility of the trading venue pending disclosure
Not subject to volume cap



[Source: ESMA, “MiFIR Article 4 — Waivers for equity instruments”, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.3 Post-Trade Transparency (Equities)
MiFIR Article 6 and RTS 1 require trading venues and investment firms (including SIs) to publish the price, volume, and time of all equity transactions as close to real-time as technically possible. The standard maximum delay is 1 minute after execution.
Deferred publication (Art. 7 MiFIR): NCAs may authorise deferred publication for: - Transactions that are large in scale compared with the normal market size (LIS thresholds in RTS 1 Annex II) - Transactions in instruments for which there is not a liquid market
Deferral options under RTS 1: - Publication of all details no later than end of trading day (T) or 9:00 local time on T+1 for transactions executed after 15:30 local time - Publication of all details with limited volume information (aggregated daily) - Supplementary deferral of up to 4 weeks for very large transactions
UK approach: The FCA is reviewing the post-trade transparency regime under the Wholesale Markets Review. CP25/20 (July 2025) requests further input on the structure and transparency regime for UK equity markets.
[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II/MiFIR transparency”, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.4 Dark Pool Volume Cap

Original Double Volume Cap (DVC) — Now Discontinued
Under original MiFID II (2018-2025), the DVC mechanism limited dark trading under the reference price waiver and negotiated trade waiver: - 4% cap per venue: No more than 4% of total EU trading in a given equity instrument could occur under these waivers on a single trading venue over a 12-month rolling period - 8% cap EU-wide: No more than 8% of total EU trading in a given instrument could occur under these waivers across all EU venues over a 12-month rolling period - Breach consequence: If either cap was breached, ESMA required the relevant NCA(s) to suspend use of the waiver for that instrument for 6 months


New Single Volume Cap (SVC) — From October 2025
The MiFIR Review replaced the DVC with a single volume cap (SVC): - 7% single cap: Only the reference price waiver is subject to the cap; the negotiated trade waiver is excluded - Measurement basis: 7% of total trading in the instrument across all EU trading venues over a 12-month rolling period - Transition: The DVC was discontinued on 28 September 2025; the first SVC suspension data was published on 9 October 2025, with quarterly publication and suspension going forward - Rationale: The EU legislators considered the DVC overly complex and not effective at its stated goal of protecting price formation. The SVC is a simplified mechanism focusing on pure dark trading (midpoint matching)
[Source: ESMA, “Double Volume Cap Mechanism — Discontinued”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: PwC Legal, “MiFIR/MiFID II Review: making sense of the key amendments”, accessed 2026-04-06]



3.5 Tick Size Regime (RTS 11)
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/588 (RTS 11) establishes minimum tick sizes for equity instruments traded on EU trading venues.
How it works: - Tick sizes depend on two variables: (1) the price of the instrument, and (2) its liquidity band - Liquidity is measured by the average daily number of transactions (ADNT) in the most relevant market - ESMA publishes ADNT calculations annually (and updates mid-year for newly admitted instruments) - 13 liquidity bands exist, from Band 0 (0 ADNT) to Band 12 (>=9,000 ADNT [unverified])
Example tick sizes (EUR):









Price Range

Scope: Applies to shares, depositary receipts, ETFs, certificates, and other similar financial instruments. Also applies to SIs (they must quote in tick size increments for liquid instruments up to twice SMS).
UK approach: The FCA retained the RTS 11 tick size regime but has indicated it may review tick sizes as part of its broader market structure work. Under CP25/20, the FCA is exploring whether the current tick size regime remains appropriate.
[Source: ESMA, “RTS 11 — Minimum tick sizes”, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.6 Circuit Breakers and Volatility Mechanisms
MiFID II Article 48(5) requires regulated markets (and by extension MTFs via Article 18(5)) to implement mechanisms to temporarily halt or constrain trading in the event of significant price movements.
Legal framework: - Article 48(5) MiFID II: Trading venues must have appropriate mechanisms to automatically halt or constrain trading during significant price movements in a financial instrument on that market or a related market during a short period - RTS 7 (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/584): Specifies requirements for mechanisms to manage volatility, including testing, monitoring, and record-keeping - ESMA Supervisory Briefing (October 2023): Provides detailed guidance on calibrating circuit breakers
Key requirements: - Trading venues must have mechanisms operational at all times during trading hours - Must consider: liquidity profile, volatility profile, trading model, instrument type - Both dynamic references (last traded price or moving average) and static references (most recent auction price) should be used as trigger prices - Venues must maintain records of rules, parameters, changes, and activation instances - Circuit breaker activations must be communicated to NCAs and, under ESMA guidelines, to other EU venues trading the same instrument
Common European circuit breaker design:







Parameter
Typical Approach




Trigger type
Static (from last auction price) + Dynamic (from last continuous trade)


Mechanism
Transition to volatility auction (call phase)


Duration
Typically 2-5 minutes; may extend if price remains volatile


Scope
Individual instrument level


Cross-market coordination
ESMA encourages but does not mandate harmonised thresholds; venues typically use different parameters



Note: Unlike the US market-wide circuit breakers (LULD/MWCB), EU venues operate instrument-level circuit breakers without a harmonised EU-wide halt mechanism. There is no equivalent to the NYSE Rule 80B or S&P 500-based market-wide triggers.
[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II Article 48 — Systems resilience, circuit breakers and electronic trading”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: ESMA, “Supervisory Briefing on Circuit Breakers”, October 2023, accessed 2026-04-06]


3.7 Algorithmic and High-Frequency Trading Rules
MiFID II Articles 17 (investment firms) and 48 (trading venues) establish the most comprehensive algo/HFT regulatory framework globally.

3.7.1 Article 17 — Investment Firm Obligations
All algorithmic traders must: - Notify their home NCA and the NCAs of venues where they trade algorithmically - Implement effective systems and risk controls (pre-trade controls, real-time monitoring, post-trade surveillance) - Maintain systems that are fully tested, properly monitored, and subject to effective business continuity arrangements - Store time-sequenced records of all orders (placed, modified, cancelled, executed) for at least 5 years, available to the NCA on request - Have in place a “kill functionality” — the ability to cancel all outstanding orders immediately as an emergency measure
Market-making strategy obligations (Art. 17(3-4)): - An algorithmic trader is deemed to pursue a market-making strategy when it posts firm, simultaneous two-way quotes of comparable size at competitive prices on a regular and frequent basis - Such firms must enter into a binding written agreement with the trading venue - Must provide liquidity on a regular and predictable basis during a specified proportion of the trading venue’s hours (except under exceptional circumstances)
High-frequency trading (HFT) specific requirements (Art. 17(2)): - HFT is defined as an algorithmic trading technique characterised by: (a) infrastructure intended to minimise network and other types of latencies, including co-location, proximity hosting, or high-speed direct electronic access; (b) system determination of order initiation, generation, routing, or execution without human intervention for individual trades or orders; (c) high message intraday rates of orders, quotes, or cancellations - HFT firms must maintain accurate and time-sequenced records of all orders (including cancellations), with timestamps to microsecond granularity as specified in RTS 25 - Must provide these records to the NCA on request


3.7.2 Article 48 — Trading Venue Obligations
Trading venues permitting algorithmic trading must have: - Effective systems, procedures, and arrangements to ensure algorithms cannot create or contribute to disorderly trading conditions - Systems to limit the ratio of unexecuted orders to transactions (order-to-trade ratio controls) - Ability to slow down the flow of orders where there is a risk of system capacity being reached - Ability to limit and enforce the minimum tick size - Mechanisms to manage volatility (circuit breakers, as described in Section 3.6)
Direct Electronic Access (DEA) rules: - Investment firms providing DEA must have systems and controls to review the suitability of clients using DEA - Must set pre-trade controls on credit exposure for DEA users - Must be able to identify individually the orders submitted by each DEA client - DEA clients must be authorised investment firms (or otherwise authorised by the NCA)
[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II Article 17 — Algorithmic trading”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Norton Rose Fulbright, “MiFID II: High frequency and algorithmic trading obligations”, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
4. Market Data Rules

4.1 The Consolidated Tape Debate and CTP Regime
The lack of a pan-European consolidated tape for equities has been one of the most debated structural deficiencies of EU capital markets since MiFID I fragmented trading across multiple venues in 2007. Unlike the US, which has operated a consolidated tape (SIP) since the 1970s, the EU has relied on commercial data vendors (Bloomberg, Refinitiv, ICE) to aggregate data, resulting in high costs and incomplete coverage.

4.1.1 MiFID II Original Framework (2018-2024): Failed Attempts
MiFID II (Art. 65) established a voluntary framework for consolidated tape providers (CTPs), but no entity applied for authorisation because: - The business model was not commercially viable given the low latency requirements and high data licensing costs charged by exchanges - Exchanges resisted providing data at cost, viewing market data revenue as a key income stream - No mandatory contribution framework existed - The “reasonable commercial basis” (RCB) obligation on data providers lacked enforcement teeth


4.1.2 MiFIR Review (2024): Mandatory CTP Regime
The MiFIR Review (Regulation (EU) 2024/791) fundamentally changed the framework:







Feature
New Regime




Selection
ESMA selects a single CTP per asset class via a competitive tender process


Duration
5-year exclusive licence


Supervision
Direct ESMA supervision


Data contribution
Mandatory — all execution venues, SIs, and APAs must contribute data to the CTP


Data quality
Real-time post-trade data for equities; pre-trade data if technically feasible


Revenue sharing
CTP must share revenue with contributing venues according to a formula in the regulation


Asset classes
Three separate CTPs: (1) bonds; (2) shares and ETFs; (3) OTC derivatives





4.1.3 Current Status (as of April 2026)







Asset Class
Status




Bonds
Selection procedure launched 3 February 2025; CTP selected [unverified — expected by mid-2025]


Shares and ETFs
Selection procedure launched 20 June 2025; EuroCTP selected by ESMA on 19 December 2025; authorisation pending; expected to operate for 5 years under ESMA direct supervision


OTC Derivatives
Selection procedure launched 5 January 2026; ESMA intends to adopt a decision on the selected applicant by early July 2026



[Source: ESMA, “Consolidated Tape Providers”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: ESMA, “ESMA selects EuroCTP to become the first Consolidated Tape Provider for shares and ETFs”, December 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]



4.2 Real-Time Data Requirements
Under MiFIR, trading venues and SIs must make pre-trade and post-trade data available:
Pre-trade data (equities): - Must be available on a continuous basis during normal trading hours - Must be disaggregated (venue-by-venue) — or via a CTP once operational - Publication standard: as close to real-time as technically possible
Post-trade data (equities): - Must be published as close to real-time as technically possible, and no later than 1 minute after execution (under revised MiFIR; previously 15 minutes delayed) - The “15-minute delay” free data regime: trading venues must make post-trade data available free of charge 15 minutes after publication. Under the MiFIR Review, the European Parliament originally sought to remove this delay entirely, but the final text retains 15 minutes as the free data window


4.3 Reasonable Commercial Basis (RCB)
MiFIR requires that market data is made available on a “reasonable commercial basis.” This principle has been a source of significant controversy.
Original framework (2018-2024): - ESMA issued non-binding guidelines (2021) specifying that data fees should be based on cost of production plus a reasonable margin - Exchanges resisted, arguing their data has value beyond production cost - The WFE (World Federation of Exchanges) challenged the cost-based approach
MiFIR Review (2024) — New binding RTS: - Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1156 (12 June 2025) replaces the guidelines with binding technical standards - Data must be provided on a non-discriminatory basis - Fees must be based on the cost of producing and disseminating market data, plus a reasonable margin - Venues must publish their pricing policies and fee schedules - ESMA’s previous RCB guidelines were formally withdrawn (February 2026)
[Source: ESMA, “Final Report on bond transparency and reasonable commercial basis under MiFIR Review”, accessed 2026-04-06]


4.4 UK Approach to Market Data and Consolidated Tape
The UK is pursuing its own consolidated tape path:







Component
Status




Bond CT
FCA signed a contract with ETS (European Trading Solutions [unverified]) in January 2026 to provide the UK bond CT; ETS aims to launch 22 June 2026; FCA authorisation decision expected Q1 2026


Equity CT
FCA published CP25/31 in November 2025 proposing the framework; expressions of interest from suppliers due by 30 January 2026; Policy Statement expected H1 2026; operational launch targeted for 2027


Approach
The FCA is prioritising bonds first (where the UK has a leading global market), followed by equities



The UK approach differs from the EU in that the FCA is procuring and contracting with CT providers directly, rather than running a competitive selection process as ESMA does. The FCA has also indicated a more commercially pragmatic approach to data contribution obligations.
[Source: FCA, “Equities consolidated tape”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: FCA, “CP25/31: The framework for a UK equity consolidated tape”, November 2025, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
5. Market Surveillance

5.1 Transaction Reporting (MiFIR Article 26)
Transaction reporting is the core supervisory data feed enabling NCAs and ESMA to monitor for market abuse, enforce conduct rules, and assess systemic risk.
Legal basis: MiFIR Article 26 requires investment firms to report complete and accurate details of transactions in financial instruments to their NCA as quickly as possible, and no later than the close of the following working day (T+1).
Scope: - All financial instruments admitted to trading or traded on a trading venue (even if the specific transaction occurs OTC) - Includes equities, bonds, derivatives, ETFs, emission allowances - Both on-venue and off-venue (OTC, SI) transactions

5.1.1 Data Fields (RTS 22)
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/590 (RTS 22) specifies the reporting format. Each transaction report comprises 65 data fields organised into the following categories:








Category
Key Fields
Count




Report identification
Transaction reference number, executing entity LEI, reporting timestamp
~4 fields


Buyer/Seller identification
LEI (legal entities) or national client identifier (natural persons), decision maker, first name/surname/date of birth for natural persons
~12 fields


Transaction details
Trading date/time, quantity, price, currency, venue (MIC code), trading capacity (principal/agent/matched principal)
~10 fields


Instrument identification
ISIN, instrument full name, classification (CFI), underlying ISIN, notional, maturity, strike price, option type
~15 fields


Trader/Algo identification
Trader ID (short code for natural person responsible for the investment decision), algo ID, waiver indicator
~8 fields


Transmission/reporting chain
Transmitting firm LEI, executing firm LEI, reporting entity LEI
~6 fields


Other
Short selling indicator, commodity derivative indicator, aggregated transaction indicator, linked transaction reference
~10 fields





5.1.2 MiFIR Review — Revised Transaction Reporting
ESMA consulted on comprehensive revisions to RTS 22 in October 2024. Key proposed changes:

Additional fields for improved instrument identification
Alignment with EMIR and SFTR reporting (to reduce duplication and improve data quality)
New fields reflecting MiFIR Review amendments to Article 26 (including expanded scope)
Revised validation rules
ESMA final RTS submitted to the European Commission in Q1 2025 [unverified]; application aligned with the MiFIR Review transparency timeline (expected 2026)

[Source: ESMA, “MiFIR Article 26 — Obligation to report transactions”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: BaFin, “Transaction reporting (Article 26 of the MiFIR)”, accessed 2026-04-06]



5.2 Clock Synchronisation (RTS 25)
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/574 (RTS 25) requires:








Participant Type
Maximum Divergence from UTC
Timestamp Granularity




Trading venues (voice/request for quote)
1 second
1 second


Trading venues (continuous trading)
100 microseconds
1 microsecond


High-frequency algorithmic trading
100 microseconds
1 microsecond


Members/participants (non-HFT)
1 second
1 second



All business clocks used to timestamp reportable events must be synchronised to the UTC timescale disseminated by national metrology institutes or UTC from the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM).
[Source: ESMA, “RTS 25 — Clock synchronisation”, accessed 2026-04-06]


5.3 Order Record Keeping (RTS 24/25)
MiFID II Article 25(1) requires investment firms to keep records of all services, activities, and transactions sufficient to enable the NCA to fulfil its supervisory tasks. For orders, this includes:

All orders received from clients or generated internally (including algorithmic orders)
Time of receipt, modification, cancellation, and execution
Client identification
The algorithmic trading strategy that generated the order (where applicable)
Order-to-trade linkages

RTS 24 specifies the data fields for order record keeping at trading venues (the “order data” that venues must maintain). This includes: - Order priority timestamp (to the granularity specified in RTS 25) - Order type, validity period, and any specific instructions - Events (submission, modification, cancellation, execution, expiry) - Member/participant identifier and client identifier
Records must be retained for at least 5 years and be provided to the NCA within a reasonable timeframe on request.


5.4 ESMA Market Integrity Activities
ESMA coordinates market integrity across the EU through several mechanisms:
Suspicious Transaction and Order Reports (STORs): - Market operators, investment firms, and persons professionally arranging transactions must report to their NCA any order or transaction that could constitute insider dealing, market manipulation, or attempted insider dealing/manipulation (MAR Art. 16) - NCAs share STORs cross-border via ESMA’s coordination framework - In 2024, ESMA reported that NCAs received thousands of STORs annually, with the majority relating to suspected insider dealing and market manipulation [estimated]
ESMA peer reviews: - ESMA conducts periodic peer reviews of NCA enforcement practices under MAR - The 2024 consolidated sanctions report revealed “clear discrepancies” in national enforcement action, with some NCAs imposing significantly higher sanctions than others for comparable violations
Market surveillance coordination: - ESMA facilitates NCA cooperation on cross-border market abuse cases - The ESMA Board of Supervisors can issue warnings, recommendations, and emergency measures under Article 9 of the ESMA Regulation
[Source: ESMA, “Consolidated Report on Sanctions and Measures 2024”, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
6. Reporting Requirements

6.1 MiFIR Article 26 Transaction Reporting (Summary)
As detailed in Section 5.1, investment firms must report 65-field transaction reports to their NCA by close of business on T+1. This section summarises the reporting chain:
Who reports: - The executing investment firm (firm that executed the transaction) - Alternatively, via an Approved Reporting Mechanism (ARM) on behalf of the firm - Trading venues may report on behalf of their members (venue reporting)
Reporting chain:
Investment Firm → ARM → NCA → ESMA (for cross-border data sharing)
        or
Trading Venue → NCA → ESMA (for on-venue trades, if venue reports on behalf of member)
Key identifiers: - Legal Entity Identifier (LEI): mandatory for all legal entities in the reporting chain - National client identifier: for natural person clients (passport number, national ID, tax ID — varies by Member State, concatenated with country code) - ISIN: mandatory instrument identifier - MIC code: identifies the trading venue


6.2 Position Reporting

6.2.1 Commodity Derivatives Position Reporting (MiFID II Art. 57-58)
Trading venues trading commodity derivatives must apply position limits and report position data to NCAs and ESMA: - Weekly reports: Aggregated positions by category of position holder - Daily reports: Individual positions of members/participants and their clients when positions breach certain thresholds - ESMA publishes aggregate position data
This is less directly relevant to equities but can affect equity-linked derivatives and structured products.


6.2.2 Net Short Position Reporting (SSR)
As detailed in Section 2.5: - NCA reporting threshold: 0.1% of issued share capital (and each 0.1% increment above) - Public disclosure threshold: 0.5% of issued share capital (and each 0.1% above) - Reports must be made to the NCA of the Member State where the share was first admitted to trading on a regulated market - ESMA publishes aggregated net short position data



6.3 Short Selling Disclosure
The Short Selling Regulation requires:









Obligation
Threshold
Recipient
Timing




Private notification to NCA
0.1% (and each 0.1% above)
Relevant NCA
By 15:30 on the next trading day


Public disclosure
0.5% (and each 0.1% above)
Public (via NCA publication)
By 15:30 on the next trading day


Sovereign CDS disclosure
Thresholds published by ESMA per issuer
Relevant NCA
By 15:30 on the next trading day



ESMA reform proposals: ESMA has proposed an EU-wide centralised publication system and the obligation for NCAs to periodically publish aggregated net short positions per issuer.
UK approach: The UK Short Selling Regulations 2025 removed the public disclosure requirement. Positions are reported to the FCA only. The FCA may publish aggregate anonymised data.
[Source: ESMA, “SSR Reporting”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: FCA, “Notification and disclosure of net short positions”, accessed 2026-04-06]


6.4 Trade Repository Reporting
While primarily governed by EMIR (for derivatives), trade repository reporting interacts with equities markets through: - Securities Financing Transactions Regulation (SFTR): Requires reporting of securities lending, repos, buy-sell back transactions, and margin lending transactions to registered trade repositories (since 2020). This captures the securities lending and borrowing market that underpins short selling, market making, and collateral management for equities. - EMIR: Any OTC derivatives with equity underlyings must be reported to trade repositories.

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
7. Cross-border Arrangements

7.1 EU Passporting (Intra-EU)
Within the EU, the “passport” system allows investment firms authorised in one Member State to provide services across all 27 Member States without needing separate local authorisation.
How it works: - An investment firm authorised in its home Member State notifies its NCA of its intention to provide cross-border services or establish a branch in another Member State - The home NCA transmits the notification to the host NCA - The firm can begin providing services (notification-based, not approval-based) - Home NCA retains primary supervisory responsibility; host NCA has jurisdiction over conduct-of-business rules in some areas
Passporting under MiFID II applies to: - Investment services and activities (dealing, brokerage, portfolio management, investment advice) - Operation of MTFs and OTFs - Ancillary services
Does NOT apply to: - Operation of a Regulated Market (RMs require separate authorisation in each Member State where they wish to operate) - Activities outside MiFID II scope


7.2 Third-Country Equivalence (EU Framework)
For firms from non-EU countries (including the UK post-Brexit), access to EU markets is governed by the MiFIR third-country regime:
Equivalence-based access (MiFIR Art. 46-49): - The European Commission may adopt an equivalence decision if a third country’s regulatory and supervisory framework is considered equivalent to the EU’s - Once equivalence is granted, third-country firms can register with ESMA and provide investment services to professional clients and eligible counterparties in the EU without establishing a branch - Equivalence decisions are unilateral, can be withdrawn at any time, and are politically charged
Current UK status: - The EU has granted very limited equivalence to the UK: - Temporary equivalence for CCPs (LCH, ICE Clear Europe) — extended multiple times - Temporary equivalence for CSDs (limited scope) - No equivalence for investment services — UK firms cannot passport into the EU for MiFID services - UK firms serving EU clients must either: (a) establish an EU-authorised subsidiary, (b) rely on Member State national regimes (where available), or (c) serve only reverse-solicited clients
MiFIR Review changes to third-country regime: - Strengthened conditions for equivalence decisions - ESMA given enhanced powers to monitor third-country firm activities - New requirements for third-country firms to report their EU activities to ESMA - Provisions for withdrawal of equivalence where conditions are no longer met
[Source: UK Finance, “What the MiFIR third-country regime means for UK-EU cross-border services”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: ESMA, “Assessment of third-country venues under MiFID II and MiFIR”, accessed 2026-04-06]


7.3 UK-EU Cooperation Post-Brexit
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU): - A non-binding MoU on regulatory cooperation was agreed between the UK and EU in June 2023 - Covers information sharing, supervisory cooperation, and early notification of regulatory changes - Does not confer any market access rights
UK approach to EU equivalence: - The UK has been more generous in granting equivalence to the EU - Most EU equivalence determinations made under the Temporary Transitional Power (TTP) have been retained or made permanent - EU-authorised firms can access UK markets more easily than UK firms can access EU markets
Practical impact on equity markets: - Post-Brexit, significant equity trading volume shifted from London to EU venues (particularly Amsterdam) due to the “share trading obligation” (STO), which requires EU investment firms to trade EU shares on EU venues - The UK applies its own STO, requiring UK firms to trade UK shares on UK venues or equivalent venues - This has created a fragmented landscape where the same share (e.g., a dual-listed company) may be traded under different regulatory regimes depending on the client’s location
[Source: European Commission, “EU-UK relations — Financial Services”, accessed 2026-04-06] [unverified — based on general knowledge of the MoU framework]

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
8. Recent Changes (2021-2026)

8.1 MiFID II/MiFIR Review (MiFIR Refit)
Timeline: | Date | Event | |——|——-| | November 2021 | European Commission publishes legislative proposal for MiFIR Review | | February 2024 | Political agreement reached between European Parliament and Council | | 28 March 2024 | MiFIR Review (Regulation (EU) 2024/791) enters into force | | 29 September 2025 | Transposition deadline for MiFID II amendments | | October 2025 | Single Volume Cap (SVC) replaces Double Volume Cap (DVC) | | 2 March 2026 | New transparency obligations under amended RTS 1 and RTS 2 take general effect | | 2025-2026 | ESMA delivers Level 2 technical standards (RTS/ITS) in multiple packages |
Key changes summary: 1. Consolidated tape: Mandatory CTP regime with ESMA selection process (see Section 4.1) 2. Volume cap: DVC replaced with SVC (7% single cap on reference price waiver only) 3. Transparency: Revised pre- and post-trade transparency calibrations; new liquidity definitions 4. SI regime: Quantitative thresholds for SI designation replaced with qualitative self-assessment; revised quoting obligations 5. Market data: Binding RCB technical standards; mandatory data contribution to CTP 6. Transaction reporting: Enhanced Article 26 scope and revised RTS 22 7. Third-country regime: Strengthened conditions and ESMA oversight 8. Designated publishing entities (DPE): New concept replacing APAs for certain publishing functions
[Source: ESMA, “MiFID II and MiFIR review”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Ashurst, “ESMA final reports on MiFIR reform: Another piece of the jigsaw”, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.2 Edinburgh Reforms and UK Wholesale Markets Review
The UK government’s “Edinburgh Reforms” (December 2022) and subsequent “Leeds Reforms” set the strategic direction for UK financial services post-Brexit, with the overarching goal of enhancing UK competitiveness.
Key developments:








Reform
Status

In force (29 June 2023)

UK Listing Rules (UKLR)
In force (29 July 2024)
See Section 8.3 below

In force (19 January 2026)

Equity CT

Framework for UK equity CT; targeted launch 2027


Bond CT
Contract signed (Jan 2026)
ETS selected; launch targeted 22 June 2026



[Source: FCA, “FCA statement on market reforms and what’s to come”, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.3 UK Listing Rules Reform 2024 (UKLR)
The FCA published the most significant overhaul of UK listing rules in over three decades, effective 29 July 2024.
Core changes:







Old Regime
New Regime (UKLR)




Premium listing category
Equity Shares (Commercial Companies) — ESCC


Standard listing category
Transition category (closed to new entrants; existing standard-listed companies mapped automatically)


Dual-class share structures heavily restricted
Dual-class shares permitted with enhanced voting rights for up to 10 years (previously 5 years for premium)


Sponsor required at IPO and for significant transactions
Sponsor required at IPO; reduced ongoing role


Mandatory shareholder vote on significant transactions, related party transactions
No mandatory shareholder vote for significant transactions; related party transactions subject to board approval (with independent oversight)


3-year track record required (premium)
No minimum track record required


25% minimum free float (premium)
10% minimum free float



Additional categories: - Shell companies (SPACs): Dedicated category with tailored rules - Secondary listings: For companies primarily listed overseas - Non-equity shares and non-voting equity shares - Closed-ended investment funds
Rationale: The reforms aim to attract more IPOs to London by reducing the regulatory burden of listing while maintaining investor protections through disclosure and governance requirements. The FCA will conduct a post-implementation review in 5 years.
[Source: FCA, “PS24/6: Primary Markets Effectiveness Review”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: FCA, “FCA overhauls listing rules to boost growth and innovation on UK stock markets”, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.4 T+1 Settlement Transition
The move from T+2 to T+1 settlement is the most significant post-trade structural change in European markets.
Background: Following the US and Canada’s successful move to T+1 on 28 May 2024, pressure grew on European markets to follow suit to reduce settlement risk and maintain competitiveness.
EU timeline:








Phase
Period
Activities




Planning
2025
Finalisation of technical solutions by industry


Development
2026
Industry implementation; new requirements for allocations, confirmations, data standards take effect 7 December 2026; enhanced reporting and disclosure rules from 1 July 2027


Testing
2027 (until October)
Industry testing ahead of go-live


Go-live
11 October 2027
EU securities markets move to T+1 settlement



Legal basis: CSDR Refit published in EU Official Journal on 14 October 2025, providing the binding legal requirement.
UK timeline: The UK has committed to aligning with the EU’s 11 October 2027 date, recognising the operational benefits of moving simultaneously with the EU. The UK’s Accelerated Settlement Taskforce recommended this approach.
Switzerland: Also aligning to the October 2027 date.
Key challenges: - Cross-time-zone settlement for non-European investors (particularly Asian investors) - FX settlement for multi-currency transactions - Securities lending recall timing - Corporate actions processing - CSD interoperability
[Source: European Commission, “T+1 settlement”, February 2025, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: BNP Paribas Securities Services, “T+1 in Europe: what’s next for the EU, the UK and Switzerland?”, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.5 DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act)







Item
Details




Full name
Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 — Digital Operational Resilience Act


Application date
17 January 2025


Scope
20+ types of financial entities including banks, investment firms, trading venues, CCPs, CSDs, payment institutions, crypto-asset service providers, and critical ICT third-party service providers


Purpose
Harmonise ICT risk management, incident reporting, and operational resilience testing requirements across the EU financial sector



Five pillars of DORA:







Pillar
Description




1. ICT risk management
Comprehensive ICT risk management framework including governance, identification, protection, detection, response, recovery


2. ICT incident reporting
Mandatory reporting of major ICT-related incidents to competent authorities within specified timeframes


3. Digital operational resilience testing
Regular testing of ICT systems; advanced threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) for significant entities (at least every 3 years)


4. ICT third-party risk management
Management of risks from ICT third-party service providers; registers of information on all ICT third-party arrangements


5. Information sharing
Voluntary arrangements for sharing cyber threat intelligence among financial entities



Enforcement: - Penalties up to 2% of annual worldwide turnover for financial entities - Up to 1% of average daily worldwide turnover for critical ICT third-party providers - ESAs (EBA, ESMA, EIOPA) designated as “lead overseers” for critical ICT third-party providers
UK equivalent: The UK has its own operational resilience framework (PRA SS1/21 and FCA PS21/3, effective March 2022, full compliance by March 2025), which predates DORA but is narrower in scope. The UK framework focuses on “important business services” and impact tolerances rather than DORA’s prescriptive ICT risk management requirements.
[Source: EIOPA, “Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)”, accessed 2026-04-06]


8.6 EU Listing Act
The EU Listing Act (adopted 2024, phased implementation 2024-2026) is a package of amendments to the Prospectus Regulation, MAR, and MiFID II aimed at making EU public markets more attractive for companies, particularly SMEs.

title: EU/UK Equities Market Regulation
text:
9. Comparison with Korean Framework

9.1 Regulatory Authority Comparison








Dimension
EU/UK
Korea




Policy-maker
European Commission / HM Treasury
Financial Services Commission (FSC, 금융위원회)


Supervisor
ESMA + 27 NCAs (EU) / FCA (UK)
Financial Supervisory Service (FSS, 금융감독원)


Exchange oversight
NCAs authorise and supervise individual venues
FSC/FSS supervise KRX; KRX itself has self-regulatory functions (market surveillance, listed company oversight)


Structure
Multi-layered: supranational (ESMA) → national (NCAs) → SRO (limited)
Centralised: FSC (policy) → FSS (supervision) → KRX (self-regulation under FSC oversight)


Independence
ESMA is an EU agency; NCAs are generally independent from government
FSC is a government commission (under the Prime Minister’s Office); FSS is a special legal entity funded by industry



Key structural differences: - The EU has a fragmented supervisory architecture with 27 NCAs, creating coordination challenges that ESMA seeks to address. Korea has a unified supervisory structure under FSC/FSS. - In the EU, exchanges are private commercial entities (Euronext, Deutsche Borse, LSEG) regulated by NCAs. In Korea, KRX is a single, integrated exchange that is a special legal entity (not a listed company), combining functions that in Europe are split across multiple venues. - The EU’s regulatory framework is built on harmonised legislation (directives/regulations) applied across 27 jurisdictions. Korea’s framework is built on the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (FSCMA, 자본시장법), a single consolidated statute.
[Source: FSC, “Introduction”, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Chambers and Partners, “Financial Services Regulation 2025 — South Korea”, accessed 2026-04-06]


9.2 Market Structure Comparison








Dimension
EU/UK
Korea (KRX)




Number of equity venues
Dozens: ~20+ RMs, ~30+ MTFs, ~15+ SIs (for equities) [estimated]
1 exchange (KRX) with 3 markets (KOSPI, KOSDAQ, KONEX)


Fragmentation
High — same stock traded on multiple venues; best execution obligation drives venue competition
Low — centralised order book; no competing venues


Dark trading
Permitted under waivers (RPW, LIS, NTW); subject to volume cap (7% SVC)
Limited; block trading available but no dark pool ecosystem comparable to EU


Tick sizes
RTS 11 regime (price + liquidity band matrix)
KRX tick size table based on price level only (not liquidity-adjusted); different tables for KOSPI and KOSDAQ


Circuit breakers
Venue-level (instrument-specific); no harmonised EU-wide mechanism
Market-wide SIDECAR (program trading halt) + individual stock price limits (±30% daily) + Volatility Interruption (VI) mechanisms


Trading hours
Varies by venue; typically 08:00-16:30 or 09:00-17:30 local time
09:00-15:30 KST (single session)


Settlement cycle
T+2 (moving to T+1 on 11 October 2027)
T+2


CCP
Multiple (LCH, Eurex Clearing, CC&G, etc.)
KRX CCP (Korea Securities Depository, KSD, handles settlement)





9.3 Regulatory Approach Comparison








Area
EU/UK
Korea




Market abuse
MAR: civil/administrative + criminal sanctions; NCA enforcement
FSCMA Chapter 6: criminal-focused enforcement; FSS investigation → prosecution referral


Insider dealing
Broad definition under MAR Art. 7-8; covers all persons with inside information
Similar breadth under FSCMA; historically stronger criminal penalties


Short selling
Allowed with restrictions (SSR); locate requirement; disclosure obligations
Allowed with restrictions; periodic bans implemented (notably 2020 COVID ban through May 2021, and November 2023 ban through March 2025) [unverified — dates approximate]


Algorithmic/HFT trading
Comprehensive regulation under MiFID II Art. 17, 48; notification, risk controls, record-keeping
Less prescriptive; KRX rules on program trading; SIDECAR mechanism; co-location services available but HFT-specific regulation less developed


Prospectus/disclosure
Prospectus Regulation (EU) / PRM sourcebook (UK)
FSS review of registration statements; FSCMA disclosure requirements


Consolidated tape
Now being established (EuroCTP for equities, CTP for bonds)
Not applicable — single exchange provides all data; KRX Information Services division


Market data costs
Contentious — RCB regulation, high exchange data fees, CTP debate
Single source (KRX); data fees regulated; KOSCOM as data vendor





9.4 Key Takeaways for KRX Perspective

Fragmentation vs. consolidation: The EU’s most persistent challenge — fragmentation of trading, data, and supervision — is a problem Korea does not face. The EU’s CTP regime is essentially trying to recreate through regulation what Korea achieves naturally through a single centralised exchange.
Regulatory complexity: The EU’s multi-layered system (Level 1 legislation → Level 2 RTS/ITS → Level 3 guidelines → NCA implementation) creates a regulatory burden that is orders of magnitude higher than Korea’s single-statute approach. However, the EU approach may be more adaptable to diverse market structures.
Post-trade efficiency: The EU’s T+1 transition is complicated by the multi-CSD, multi-CCP, multi-currency landscape. Korea’s centralised post-trade infrastructure (KSD) makes settlement cycle changes more straightforward.
Dark trading and transparency: The EU’s complex waiver and volume cap system reflects the tension between institutional investor demand for execution quality and the regulatory desire to protect lit market price formation. Korea’s simpler approach avoids this complexity but also offers less execution flexibility for large institutional orders.
Technology regulation: The EU’s MiFID II algo/HFT rules (Articles 17, 48) are the global benchmark for regulating electronic trading. Korea may consider whether similar levels of prescriptive regulation (kill switches, order-to-trade ratios, microsecond record-keeping) would benefit KRX.
Competitiveness focus: Both the EU (Listing Act, CTP) and UK (Edinburgh Reforms, UKLR) are currently focused on attracting listings and improving market competitiveness — a global theme that KRX also faces given competition from regional exchanges (HKEX, SGX, JPX).

2. Architecture

2.1 High-Level Design

Deployment model: On-premise, dedicated data center infrastructure (primary site in Tokyo metropolitan area)
Topology: Centralized matching with synchronized 3-node data server clusters for each processing unit
Design pattern: In-memory, event-driven transaction processing
Redundancy model: Triple-modular redundancy (3-node synchronized data servers) for core matching; active-standby for overall system failover

The architecture is built around the concept of processing all trading information – orders, executions, and order books – on synchronized 3-node data servers. This triple-node design provides both high availability (any single node failure does not disrupt service) and data consistency. System capacity is designed to be flexibly and swiftly scalable to accommodate increases in order volumes.
[Source: JPX, “Services (arrowhead)”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/systems/equities-trading/01.html, accessed 2026-04-06]

text:
5. Resilience & Business Continuity

5.1 Redundancy

Architecture: Active-standby with triple-modular redundancy (3-node synchronized data servers) at the component level
Geographic distribution: Primary data center in the Tokyo metropolitan area; secondary (backup) data center in the Kansai region
Failover design: Within the primary site, the 3-node synchronized architecture allows continued operation upon single-node failure. If the primary data center is affected by a disaster and cannot continue operations, operations are switched to the backup center.
Failover time: Not publicly disclosed; designed to resume trading “as quickly as possible”



5.2 Disaster Recovery

DR site location: Kansai region (western Japan), specifically at AT TOKYO Kansai Chuo Center (KC1), designated as the Kansai Proximity Area for JPX
Rationale: Located in a geographically remote area from Tokyo to avoid simultaneous impact from a major large-scale earthquake in the Tokyo Metropolitan area; selected to ensure “little or no fear of damage to societal infrastructure causing a shortage of essential services such as electricity”
RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Not publicly disclosed
RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Not publicly disclosed; goal is to resume trading as quickly as possible
DR testing frequency: Not publicly disclosed; JPX’s BCP is reviewed and updated regularly
Access Point: AP4 was established in Kansai to connect trading participants with the JPX network for backup operations
Timeline: arrowhead backup at Kansai site established after FY2022 (derivatives system J-GATE was set up first in Q3 FY2021)



5.3 Capacity Management

Scalability approach: System capacity is “flexibly and swiftly scalable to accommodate an increase in the number of orders”
Infrastructure scaling: Hardware upgrades between generations (e.g., ~400 servers in 3rd gen to 462 in 4th gen [unverified]) provide capacity headroom
Load testing practices: Not publicly disclosed; Fujitsu conducts extensive testing prior to each generation launch
Monitoring: arrowhead System Stats service (launched July 2020) provides participants with real-time system performance statistics including FLEX throttling data, enabling market-wide capacity awareness

[Source: JPX, “BCP (Business Continuity Plan)”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/corporate/governance/risk/bcp/index.html, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: FinanceFeeds, “Japan Exchange Group Updates On Setting Up New Data Back-up Center”, https://financefeeds.com/japan-exchange-group-updates-setting-new-data-back-center/] [Source: AT TOKYO, “AT TOKYO Kansai Chuo Center Designated as Kansai Proximity Area for JPX”, November 2020, https://www.attokyo.com/news/20201104.html]

text:
6. Notable Technical Features

6.1 Itayose (Call Auction) Mechanism
The Itayose method is a call auction used to determine opening prices, closing prices, and prices after volatility interruptions. Orders are accumulated during a designated period, then matched simultaneously at a single equilibrium price where supply meets demand. Key rules: - All orders at or better than the equilibrium price are matched - Market orders have priority over limit orders - Used at the open of morning and afternoon sessions - With arrowhead4.0, a dedicated Closing Auction Session was introduced at the end of the afternoon session (15:25–15:30 JST) specifically for transparent closing price formation
[Source: JPX, “Transaction Methods”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/equities/trading/domestic/04.html, accessed 2026-04-06]


6.2 Zaraba (Continuous Trading) Method
Zaraba is the continuous auction method used during regular trading hours between the opening and closing auctions. Orders are matched on a price-time priority basis: - Best price has priority (price priority) - Among orders at the same price, earlier orders are matched first (time priority) - Market orders are executed ahead of limit orders at any price


6.3 Special Quote (Tokubetsu Kehai) – Volatility Interruption
Special Quotes serve as TSE’s primary circuit breaker / volatility control mechanism: - Indicated whenever prices are likely to jump beyond a certain price range from the last execution price - Once a Special Quote is indicated, execution switches from Zaraba (continuous) to Itayose (call auction) to prevent inappropriate price fluctuations - Can be triggered at any time during the trading session - Enhanced in arrowhead4.0: Excessive price fluctuations beyond double the update price range of Special Quotes are prevented until 60 seconds have passed from the reference execution - Daily price limits (å¤å¹ å¶é) also apply as a broader circuit breaker
[Source: JPX, “2024 Edition – Trading Rules Guide”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/equities/trading/domestic/tvdivq000000tpfi-att/eg.pdf]


6.4 ToSTNeT (Tokyo Stock Exchange Trading NeTwork System)
ToSTNeT is the off-auction trading platform operated alongside arrowhead: - Handles block trades, basket trades, and closing price transactions - Accepts orders from domestic and foreign investors (through securities companies) - Trades executed off the central order book at negotiated or reference prices - Processes include order acceptance, execution, and result reporting - Separate system from arrowhead’s auction matching but integrated into the TSE ecosystem
[Source: JPX, “Services (ToSTNeT)”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/systems/equities-trading/03.html, accessed 2026-04-06]


6.5 CONNEQTOR – RFQ Platform for ETFs
CONNEQTOR is JPX’s Request-for-Quote platform specifically designed for institutional ETF trading: - Launch: February 2021 - Purpose: Connects institutional investors, securities companies, and market makers for efficient ETF trading - Process: (1) Investor submits RFQ on CONNEQTOR, (2) market makers provide competitive quotes, (3) accepted trade is cleared and settled via ToSTNeT as an on-exchange trade - Adoption: Used by more than 250 institutional investors; monthly trading value surpassed JPY 200 billion (September 2023) - Benefits: Real-time best price quoting, reduced transaction costs, improved operational efficiency, no counterparty risk (exchange-cleared)
[Source: JPX, “Overview – RFQ Platform”, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/equities/products/etfs/rfq-platform/index.html, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: JPX, “Monthly Trading Value via the RFQ Platform CONNEQTOR Surpasses 200 Billion Yen”, September 2023, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/corporate/news/news-releases/0060/20230904-02.html]


6.6 arrowhead System Stats Service
Launched in July 2020, this alternative data service provides: - Real-time and historical statistics on arrowhead system performance - FLEX throttling data per multicast group - Order/trade activity metrics - Available to participants and data vendors for capacity planning and market microstructure research
[Source: JPX, “TSE to launch arrowhead System Stats Service”, July 2020, https://www.jpx.co.jp/english/corporate/news/news-releases/0060/20200703-01.html]


6.7 Cloud PoC for Future Architecture
TSE has conducted a Proof of Concept (PoC) to explore the long-term applicability of cloud technology to its cash equity trading system, signaling potential future architectural evolution beyond traditional on-premise infrastructure.
[Source: FX News Group, “Tokyo Stock Exchange conducts PoC to explore long-term applicability of cloud tech to its cash equity trading system”, https://fxnewsgroup.com/forex-news/exchanges/tokyo-stock-exchange-conducts-poc-to-explore-long-term-applicability-of-cloud-tech-to-its-cash-equity-trading-system/]

7. Comparison Notes

vs. KRX Exture+








Aspect
arrowhead (JPX/TSE)
Exture+ (KRX)




Launch

2014 (replaced original EXTURE)


Developer

Architecture

~0.2 ms (200 us) for 4th gen [unverified]; sub-ms for 3rd gen
~0.07 ms (70 us) – global top-tier level


Asset Coverage
Cash equities only (stocks, ETFs, REITs, CBs); derivatives on separate J-GATE system
All instruments in a single platform (stocks, bonds, futures, options, ETFs, warrants, commodities)


Market Data Protocol

Solace PubSub+ based distribution


Data Center

Primary: Seoul (KOSPI, KOSDAQ); Busan (derivatives); mutual backup between cities


Volatility Control
Special Quote (Tokubetsu Kehai) – switches to Itayose auction
SVAR (Static Volatility Interruption) and DVAR (Dynamic Volatility Interruption)


Off-Auction Trading

RFQ Platform

Not separately branded [unverified]


Closing Auction
Introduced November 2024 (arrowhead4.0)
Established feature





Key Differentiators

Latency: KRX Exture+ holds a latency advantage at ~70 us vs. arrowhead’s ~200 us [unverified], approximately 3x faster. This positions KRX among the fastest exchanges globally, while arrowhead remains competitive with major peers.
Platform Scope: Exture+ is a unified multi-asset platform (equities + derivatives + bonds on one system), whereas JPX separates cash equities (arrowhead) from derivatives (J-GATE). This gives KRX operational simplicity but JPX more specialized optimization per asset class.
Vendor Strategy: JPX relies heavily on Fujitsu as a technology partner, whereas KRX/Koscom develops Exture+ largely in-house. This gives KRX more direct control over system evolution but requires maintaining deep internal engineering capability.
Messaging Infrastructure: KRX selected Solace PubSub+ as its core data delivery infrastructure, an industry-standard messaging platform. JPX uses its proprietary FLEX protocol, which offers tight integration but less portability.
DR Geography: Both exchanges maintain geographically separated DR sites (JPX: Tokyo-Kansai ~400 km; KRX: Seoul-Busan ~325 km), following best practices for seismically active regions.
Market Structure Evolution: JPX’s late adoption of a closing auction (2024) compared to KRX indicates that arrowhead’s market microstructure has been evolving more conservatively, prioritizing stability and consensus-building with market participants.

text:
2. Architecture

2.1 High-Level Design
NASDAQ INET follows a single-threaded, event-driven architecture for its matching engine core, ensuring deterministic order processing with strict sequencing. The broader Eqlipse platform wraps this core in a modern microservices framework.
Design Principles: - Pure electronic matching — no human intervention (no specialists/DMMs, unlike NYSE) - Strict price-time priority — orders matched first by price, then by time of entry at the same price level - Single-threaded matching — one thread processes all orders for a given symbol, eliminating lock contention and ensuring deterministic behavior - Kernel bypass networking — user-space networking stack bypasses the Linux kernel to eliminate context-switching overhead - Hardware acceleration — FPGA cards handle critical feed processing and parsing operations - Immutable sequencing — every event receives a monotonically increasing sequence number, enabling reliable replay and recovery
Data Flow (simplified): 1. Order arrives via gateway (OUCH/FIX/RASH/FLITE) over SoupBinTCP 2. Risk/validation checks applied (price reasonability, credit limits, fat-finger guards) 3. Order dispatched to symbol-specific matching thread 4. Matching engine executes price-time priority algorithm 5. Execution reports returned to participant via same protocol 6. Market data update published via ITCH over MoldUDP64 (multicast) and SoupBinTCP (unicast)


2.2 Core Components

Function

Core order matching using price-time priority algorithm; processes new orders, cancels, modifications; handles auctions (Opening/Closing/Halt Cross)
Custom C/C++ engine; single-threaded per symbol; kernel-bypass networking; runs on commodity Linux servers

Accepts and validates inbound orders from participants; protocol translation (FIX → internal format); session management and authentication
Supports OUCH 4.2 (native binary), FIX 4.0/4.1/4.2 (industry standard), RASH (proprietary with routing strategies), FLITE (FIX Lite — FIX subset with OUCH-like speed)

Generates and disseminates real-time market data from matching engine events; full depth-of-book (TotalView) and BBO (Nasdaq Basic)

title: NASDAQ INET — NASDAQ Stock Market
text:
6. Notable Technical Features

6.1 Pure Electronic Market — No Human Intervention
Unlike NYSE (which retains Designated Market Makers with manual intervention capabilities), NASDAQ INET is a fully automated matching engine with zero human involvement in the matching process. All order matching, auction processing, and trade execution are handled algorithmically. This eliminates the latency variability associated with human decision-making and ensures consistent, deterministic processing times.


6.2 Opening and Closing Cross Auctions
INET’s auction mechanism aggregates all eligible orders and determines a single clearing price that maximizes executed volume. The Net Order Imbalance Indicator (NOII) is disseminated in the minutes leading up to each cross, providing unprecedented transparency into supply/demand dynamics. The Closing Cross handles approximately 16% of daily Nasdaq volume and sets the official closing price used for mutual fund NAVs, index calculations, and settlement. The June 2025 Russell Reconstitution Cross executed $102.455 billion in just 0.871 seconds — a record.


6.3 Eqlipse “Evergreen” Upgrade Model
The 4th-generation Eqlipse platform introduced a quarterly upgrade cycle, replacing the traditional approach of major system upgrades every few years. This allows continuous deployment of enhancements, security patches, and new features without disruptive migration projects. Client exchanges receive incremental improvements on a predictable cadence.


6.4 Multi-Asset, Multi-Venue Architecture
The INET matching engine is asset-class agnostic — a single core technology supports equities, fixed income, FX, commodities, derivatives, digital assets, and carbon credits. This same engine powers Nasdaq’s own 18 exchanges globally and is licensed to 130+ external marketplaces. The Eqlipse suite extends this across the full trade lifecycle: trading → clearing → CSD → data intelligence.


6.5 Cloud-Hybrid Deployment
Nasdaq’s partnership with AWS enables a unique deployment model where latency-critical components (matching engine, order gateways) remain on-premise at Carteret while analytics, surveillance, reporting, and non-latency-sensitive services run in the cloud. AWS Outposts physically located within the Carteret data center bridge the two environments seamlessly.


6.6 FPGA-Accelerated Market Data
FPGA cards at the colocation facility provide hardware-accelerated ITCH feed generation, achieving market data latencies that software alone cannot match. This gives collocated participants the fastest possible view of order book changes.


6.7 Protocol Hierarchy for Performance Tuning
NASDAQ offers a deliberate spectrum of protocols, allowing participants to choose their latency/complexity tradeoff: - OUCH — Maximum performance, minimal flexibility (HFT firms) - FLITE — Near-OUCH speed with FIX semantics (sophisticated firms wanting FIX workflow) - RASH — OUCH-like with routing strategy support - FIX — Industry standard, easiest integration, highest latency (institutional brokers)
All non-OUCH protocols are internally translated to OUCH by the gateway, meaning the matching engine itself only processes one native format.


6.8 24-Hour Trading Readiness (Planned)
NASDAQ has announced plans for 23-hour/day, 5-day/week trading (pending SEC approval, target H2 2026). The Eqlipse platform’s 24/7 operational capability — already proven in cryptocurrency exchange deployments — positions INET to support this extended session model with a 1-hour daily maintenance window.

Key Differentiators
NASDAQ INET Advantages: - Latency leadership: ~14 μs door-to-door is approximately 5x faster than Exture+’s ≤ 70 μs, reflecting NASDAQ’s intense HFT-driven optimization and FPGA acceleration - Protocol diversity: Four order entry protocols (OUCH, FIX, RASH, FLITE) offering explicit performance/flexibility tradeoffs vs. KRX’s more standardized access model - Global technology platform: INET/Eqlipse technology powers 130+ marketplaces worldwide, creating massive economies of scale and continuous improvement pressure - Cloud-hybrid innovation: AWS partnership and Outposts integration represent a leading-edge approach to exchange infrastructure modernization - Colocation ecosystem: Carteret facility with sub-35 ns switching and massive HFT participant base creates a deep, liquid ecosystem
KRX Exture+ Advantages: - Unified multi-asset platform: Single system handles all asset classes (equities, derivatives, bonds, commodities) vs. NASDAQ’s separate equity and options matching engines - Integrated value chain: KRX operates the entire Korean capital market infrastructure (exchange, clearing, settlement, depository) on a coordinated technology stack - Closing auction design: Random end time mechanism for closing auction provides better manipulation resistance compared to NASDAQ’s fixed-time Closing Cross - Simpler access model: Standardized connectivity through KOSCOM reduces complexity for domestic participants - Solace hardware messaging: Purpose-built messaging appliances provide guaranteed, deterministic data delivery without the complexity of kernel-bypass software stacks
Architectural Philosophy Differences: - NASDAQ INET is optimized for maximum speed in a fragmented market where multiple competing venues exist (14 U.S. stock exchanges + 30+ dark pools), demanding the lowest possible latency to attract order flow - KRX Exture+ is optimized for comprehensive coverage in a consolidated market where KRX operates as the sole exchange, prioritizing breadth of asset class support and system stability over raw speed competition

1. System Overview







Item
Details




System Name
Optiq


Operated By
Euronext N.V.


Purpose
Unified multi-market, multi-asset trading platform serving all Euronext regulated markets across seven European countries


Launch Year
2016–2019 phased rollout (MDG July 2017, Cash OEG/ME March 2018, Derivatives December 2019); subsequent expansion to Oslo (2020) and Borsa Italiana (2023–2024)


Current Version
Continuously updated; latest public OEG SBE specification v5.38.0, MDG specification v6.36.320


Vendor / In-house
In-house (developed by Euronext’s internal technology teams)



Optiq is Euronext’s proprietary, next-generation trading platform that provides a Single Order Book across all seven Euronext regulated markets. It replaced the legacy Universal Trading Platform (UTP) for cash markets and LIFFE CONNECT / SOLA for derivatives, as well as Millennium Exchange for Borsa Italiana following Euronext’s 2021 acquisition. The platform is described officially as delivering “ultra-low latency, predictability, high availability, and high scalability,” with a harmonized cash and derivatives messaging model.
Euronext has also positioned Optiq as a licensable technology product for other exchange and venue operators.

title: Optiq – Euronext
text:
2. Architecture

2.1 High-Level Design

Deployment model: On-premise, dedicated data center infrastructure (Aruba campus, Bergamo, Italy)
Topology: Single centralized platform serving all Euronext markets; modular component design
Design pattern: Event-driven; Apache Kafka (Confluent Platform) used as persistence layer; deterministic matching pipeline
Multi-venue: Single platform, Single Order Book architecture across 7 countries and 7 regulated markets (Amsterdam, Brussels, Dublin, Lisbon, Milan, Oslo, Paris)
Multi-asset: Cash equities, ETFs, bonds, derivatives (futures and options), warrants, securitised derivatives, commodities, FX products
Multi-currency: EUR, GBP, NOK, USD, CHF, and others traded across venues

The Optiq architecture uses a segmented design where each Optiq Segment defines a universe of instruments sharing common trading properties (e.g., “Euronext Cash Amsterdam,” “Euronext Derivatives Paris”). Each segment is subdivided into Partitions – technically independent processing units connected within the segment context. This partition-based architecture enables horizontal scalability and isolation.
The platform’s unique architecture minimizes jitter to enable clients to fine-tune their algorithms against stable and predictable latencies.
[Source: Euronext, “Optiq: technology solutions for exchanges and venue operators”, https://www.euronext.com/en/technology/optiq-tech-solutions-for-exchanges-and-venue-operators, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Confluent, “Euronext builds high-speed trading platform”, https://www.confluent.io/customers/euronext/, accessed 2026-04-06]


2.2 Core Components








Component
Function
Technology




Matching Engine (ME)
Deterministic order matching for all asset classes across all Euronext markets; supports continuous trading, auctions (opening, closing, intraday, volatility interruption), and call phases
Custom-built in-house engine; partitioned per segment; binary message processing


Order Entry Gateway (OEG)
Private interface between clients and the matching engine; manages authentication, session lifecycle, throttling, and order routing to partitions
TCP/IP connectivity; supports both SBE (binary) and FIX 5.0 protocols; per-partition physical connections


Market Data Gateway (MDG)
Real-time and snapshot market data dissemination; publishes full order book, BBO, and trade data
UDP/IP multicast with SBE encoding; dual redundant feeds (Feed A / Feed B); LZ4 compression for low-bandwidth connections


Drop Copy Gateway
Post-trade message dissemination; provides execution reports and trade confirmations to back-office systems
Dedicated logical accesses separate from trading OEG; SBE and FIX protocols


Risk Engine
Pre-trade risk controls; order throttling mechanism; kill switch functionality
Integrated into OEG layer; per-session throttle rates; configurable rejection/queuing behavior


Surveillance
Market surveillance for regulatory compliance (MAR, MiFID II); real-time and post-trade monitoring
Separate surveillance infrastructure [details not publicly disclosed]


Persistence Layer
Event sourcing and message persistence for the trading platform
Apache Kafka (Confluent Platform); designed for up to 1 million messages/second ingestion





2.3 Technology Stack







Layer
Technology




Programming Language
C++ (confirmed via Confluent case study referencing C++ API integration with Kafka); additional languages likely used for ancillary systems [unverified]


Operating System
Linux (confirmed; RedHat/CentOS-based environments referenced in SDK documentation)


Hardware
Commodity server hardware; no confirmed use of FPGA acceleration [unverified]


Network
Dedicated Euronext network infrastructure; 10 Gbps and 100 Mbps (shaped) connectivity options for market data; TCP/IP for order entry; UDP/IP multicast for market data


Database
Not publicly disclosed; Apache Kafka serves as the persistence/event sourcing layer


Messaging/Middleware
Apache Kafka (Confluent Platform) for persistence layer; SBE (Simple Binary Encoding) for wire protocol; UDP multicast for market data distribution; LZ4 compression available


Encoding
SBE (Simple Binary Encoding) – FIX Protocol Limited open standard; fixed-position, fixed-length fields for direct data access without sequential processing

text:
4. Interfaces & Protocols

4.1 Order Entry








Protocol
Version
Description




OEG SBE (Simple Binary Encoding)
v5.38.0 (latest published)
Lowest-latency order entry; fixed-position, fixed-length binary messages based on FIX Protocol Limited’s SBE standard; optimized for low-bandwidth utilization and minimal encoding/decoding overhead; supports all Euronext cash and derivatives markets


OEG FIX 5.0
v4.12.0 (latest published)
Standard FIX 5.0 protocol with Euronext-specific extensions; broader compatibility with existing client systems; slightly higher latency than SBE



Session Architecture: - Clients connect via TCP/IP to the Order Entry Gateway (OEG) - A Logical Access is an OEG entry point configured for a single Optiq Segment, containing the client’s connectivity configuration - Each Logical Access may have as many OE Sessions (physical connections) as there are Partitions in the Optiq Segment - Logon message must be sent individually to each partition - Separate Logical Accesses required for trading OEG and Drop Copy gateway - Session lifecycle: Logon -> Active Trading -> Logout; heartbeat mechanism for connection monitoring
Throttling Mechanism: - Per-session message rate limits enforced at the OEG level - Configurable burst size (maximum messages that can be sent consecutively before throttling activates) - When throttle limit breached: messages either rejected or queued (configurable) - Rejection returns TechnicalReject (SBE message 108) or Reject (FIX message 3) - Exchange also monitors for excessive breaching and may take additional action
[Source: Euronext, “Optiq OEG SBE Messages – Interface Specification v5.38.0”, https://connect.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/Optiq%20OEG%20SBE%20Messages%20-%20Interface%20Specification%20-%20Euronext%20Cash%20and%20Derivatives%20Markets%20-%20External%20-%20v5.38.0.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Euronext, “Optiq OEG Client Specifications – FIX 5.0 Interface v4.12.0”, https://connect2.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/Euronext%20Markets%20-%20Optiq%20OEG%20Client%20Specifications%20-%20FIX%205.0%20Interface%20-%20v4.12.0.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Euronext, “Optiq OEG Throttling Mechanism v2.2”, https://connect2.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/euronext_cash_markets_-oeg_throttling_mechanism-_v2.2.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06]


4.2 Market Data Dissemination









Feed
Protocol
Description
Data Content




MDG Real-time (Full)
UDP/IP multicast, SBE encoding
Full order book depth, real-time
All price levels, order counts, trade reports, auction data; unshaped 10 Gbps or shaped 1 Gbps


MDG Real-time (Compressed)
UDP/IP multicast, SBE + LZ4 compression
Compressed real-time feed for lower-bandwidth connections
Same content as full feed; shaped to 100 Mbps; body compressed with LZ4 (block mode, no headers)


MDG Snapshot
UDP/IP multicast, SBE + LZ4 compression
Periodic snapshots for recovery and initialization
Full instrument state at point-in-time; always LZ4 compressed


MDG Lite
UDP/IP multicast, SBE encoding
Simplified market data feed
Reduced data set for clients not requiring full depth [unverified – details limited]



Market Data Architecture: - Dual redundant multicast feeds: Feed A and Feed B published independently; clients should subscribe to both and arbitrate - Channels disaggregated by: asset class, currency, and country - Separate dedicated channels for pre-trade and post-trade data - Channel identification scheme: first digit = feed type (1 = real-time, 2 = snapshot); last three digits = multicast group IP suffix - SBE format: fixed-position, fixed-length fields supporting direct access to data; avoids sequential processing of variable-length elements - 10 Gbps line clients can subscribe to all available channels including Full Order Book
[Source: Euronext, “Optiq MDG Client Specifications v4.1.0”, https://connect2.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/Euronext%20Markets%20-%20Optiq%20MDG%20Client%20Specifications%20v4.1.0.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Euronext, “Optiq MDG Messages – Interface Specification v6.36.320”, https://connect.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/optiq-mdg-messages-interface-specification-euronext-cash-and-derivatives-markets-external-v636320.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06]


4.3 Drop Copy / Trade Reporting

Dedicated Drop Copy Service via separate OEG logical accesses
Provides execution reports, trade confirmations, and fill notifications to back-office systems
Available in both SBE and FIX 5.0 protocols
Drop Copy is not a trading segment; uses a different partition approach than the trading OEG
Separate connectivity configuration required (distinct IP addresses from trading gateway)
MiFID II trade reporting obligations supported through Euronext’s approved publication arrangement (APA) and approved reporting mechanism (ARM) services

[Source: Euronext, “Optiq Drop Copy Service – Interface Specification v5.351.0”, https://connect.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/Optiq%20Drop%20Copy%20Service%20-%20Interface%20Specification%20-%20Euronext%20Cash%20and%20Derivatives%20Markets%20-%20External%20-%20v5.351.0.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06]


4.4 Reference Data

Optiq MDG Reference Data provides instrument-level reference information
Published via MDG channels at start of trading day and available as downloadable files
Includes trading parameters, tick size tables, lot sizes, trading hours, instrument identifiers (ISIN, MIC, Symbol Index)
Reference data available for all Euronext-listed instruments across all markets
Standing Data files published on Euronext’s website and via Connect portal

[Source: Euronext, “Optiq MDG Reference Data”, https://www.euronext.com/en/products-services/optiq-mdg-reference-data, accessed 2026-04-06]

title: Optiq – Euronext
text:
5. Resilience & Business Continuity

5.1 Redundancy

Market data redundancy: Dual independent multicast feeds (Feed A and Feed B) per channel; clients expected to subscribe to both and perform arbitration
Gateway redundancy: Multiple OEG partitions per segment; clients can distribute order flow across partitions
Network redundancy: Multiple connectivity paths to the primary data center; colocation available within the Aruba campus
Platform redundancy: Modular, partitioned architecture isolates failures within individual segments/partitions



5.2 Disaster Recovery







Aspect
Details




Primary Site
DC1 – Aruba Global Cloud Data Centre (IT3), Ponte San Pietro, Bergamo, Italy (within Aruba S.p.A. campus)


DR Site
DC2 – Paris region (exact location not publicly confirmed; referred to as the “Disaster Recovery Data Centre”)


Configuration
Active/Passive – DR site is a separate physical data center maintained in standby


Failover Type
Managed failover; upon DR activation, trading resumes from the secondary site


IP Addressing
DR site uses different IP addresses (IPAddressDR field in OEG connectivity specs); clients must maintain separate DR connectivity configurations


DR Testing
Conducted at least annually on a dedicated Saturday; external participants involved; reconciliation reports automatically generated after failover to identify gaps


Regulatory Requirement
MiFID II Article 48 and RTS 7 require regulated markets to maintain business continuity arrangements including near-instantaneous switch-over capability



Previous Primary Site: - Before June 2022, Euronext’s primary data center was located in Basildon, Essex, United Kingdom (inherited from the NYSE Euronext era) - The 14-month migration to Bergamo was completed on 6 June 2022, part of Euronext’s strategic repatriation of infrastructure to continental Europe following Brexit and the Borsa Italiana acquisition
[Source: Euronext, “Euronext Data Centre”, https://www.euronext.com/en/technology/euronext-data-centre, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Euronext, “Successful completion of the migration of Euronext’s Core Data Centre”, June 2022, https://www.euronext.com/en/about/media/euronext-press-releases/successful-completion-migration-euronexts-core-data-centre, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: Euronext, “Disaster Recovery Test 25 October 2025: Guidelines for Participants”, https://connect.euronext.com/sites/default/files/it-documentation/euronext-disaster-recovery-test-25-october-2025-guidelines-participants.pdf, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: The TRADE, “Inside Europe’s new fortress: Euronext’s continental data centre and trading floor”, https://www.thetradenews.com/inside-europes-new-fortress-euronexts-continental-data-centre-and-trading-floor/, accessed 2026-04-06]


5.3 Primary Data Center: Bergamo (Aruba IT3 Campus)







Specification
Details




Location
Ponte San Pietro, Bergamo, Italy (Aruba S.p.A. Global Cloud Data Centre campus)


Campus Size
~20 hectares; capacity for up to 5 data center buildings; 200,000 sqm total potential


Current Building
~17,600 sqm with 8,000 sqm colocation space across 10 data rooms


Total Power Capacity
12 MW (initial building); campus scalable to 60 MW


Additional Buildings
DC-B (9 MW, 4,950 sqm) and DC-C (8 MW, 5,950 sqm) available on campus


Certification
Rating 4 (Tier IV equivalent); maximum safety and resilience


Power Source
100% renewable energy – hydroelectric (River Brembo dedicated plant), photovoltaic (10,258 sqm solar panels), geothermal and dynamic free cooling


Connectivity
Colocation services available for Euronext members; cross-connects to matching infrastructure


Migration Date
6 June 2022 (from Basildon, UK)



[Source: Euronext, “New, Green Data Centre: A Glimpse into the Future”, https://www.euronext.com/en/news/new-green-data-centre-bergamo, accessed 2026-04-06] [Source: DataCenterMap, “Aruba Global Cloud IT3, Bergamo”, https://www.datacentermap.com/italy/bergamo/global-cdc-it3/, accessed 2026-04-06]


5.4 Capacity Management

Partitioned architecture allows horizontal scaling by adding partitions within segments
Throttling mechanism prevents individual clients from overloading partitions
Market data distributed across multiple disaggregated multicast channels to manage bandwidth
10x capacity improvement over predecessor UTP platform
Kafka persistence layer benchmarked for 1 million messages/second sustained ingestion
Scalable infrastructure described by Euronext as able to “accommodate unlimited capacity”
