section: Retail Options Trading: The Explosion and Regulatory Response
text:
Retail Options Trading: The Explosion and Regulatory Response

Scale of the Phenomenon
NSE’s derivatives market experienced an extraordinary surge in retail options trading:

Volume growth: Equity index options volume surged ~13x, from Rs 10.8 trillion (FY20) to Rs 138 trillion (FY24)
NSE market share: NSE holds over 90% of India’s index options market
Global dominance: At peak, NSE accounted for more than 61% of all futures and options traded worldwide



SEBI Study Findings (September 2024)







Metric
Data




Percentage of individual traders incurring losses
93% (FY22–FY24)


Aggregate losses by individual traders
Rs 1.8 lakh crore (~USD 21.5 billion) over three years


Average loss per trader
~Rs 2 lakh per trader


Loss rate trend
Worsening — 89% in FY22 to 91.1% in FY24


Proprietary trader profits (FY24)
Rs 33,000 crore gross


FPI profits (FY24)
Rs 28,000 crore gross


Algo trading share of institutional profits
96–97%





Regulatory Response
SEBI’s six-point reform package (October 2024) was explicitly designed to address the retail speculation crisis:

Weekly expiry rationalization — reduced to one per exchange (effective Nov 20, 2024)
Lot size increase — minimum contract value raised to Rs 15–20 lakh (effective Nov 21, 2024)
Expiry-day ELM — 2% additional margin on short options on expiry day (effective Nov 20, 2024)
Upfront premium collection — full premium required from option buyers (effective Feb 1, 2025)
Intraday monitoring of position limits — enhanced real-time surveillance
Removal of calendar spread benefit on expiry day — reduces margin offsets for spread positions on expiry



Outcome
Post-implementation, F&O volumes declined 30–38%, smaller investor participation dropped ~49%, and NSE lost its #1 global ranking to Brazil’s B3. SEBI views this as a successful policy outcome — protecting retail investors from disproportionate losses.

Part of SGX Group, which is publicly listed on its own exchange (ticker: S68)

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)


Annual Revenue (FY2025)
Equities — Derivatives: SGD 345.9 million (+13.8% YoY); Currencies & Commodities: SGD 312.5 million (+8.6% YoY); SGX Group total: SGD 1.30 billion (record)

329 million contracts (record) across equities, FX, and commodities


Average Daily Volume (Feb 2025)
~1.4 million contracts/day (derivatives DAV +8% YoY)


Listed Instruments
Futures and options across equity indices (>15 Asian markets), FX (6+ currency pairs), commodities (iron ore, freight, rubber, coking coal, steel), interest rates (JGB, APAC bonds), and digital assets (BTC, ETH perpetual futures)


Clearing House
SGX Derivatives Clearing Limited (SGX-DC) — central counterparty



[Source: SGX Group FY2025 Annual Report; SGX Group market statistics press releases, February 2025; TipRanks, “SGX Ends 2025 With Record Derivatives Volumes”, January 2026]

Key Historical Milestones

1984: Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) established as Asia’s first financial futures exchange; launched Eurodollar futures via mutual offset with CME
1986: SIMEX launches Nikkei 225 futures — pioneering offshore access to Japanese equity markets; first offshore listing of a major Asian equity index
1999 (1 December): SGX formed through merger of Stock Exchange of Singapore (SES), SIMEX, and Securities Clearing and Computer Services Pte Ltd, enabled by the Exchanges (Demutualisation and Merger) Act 1999
2000: SGX listed on its own Mainboard (23 November); established SGX Derivatives Trading (SGX-DT) and SGX Securities Trading (SGX-ST) as separate arms
2002: Launched Japanese Government Bond (JGB) futures
2003: Technology partnership with Nasdaq for trading systems commenced
2006: Launched FTSE China A50 Index Futures — the first and only USD-denominated A-share futures contract globally
2007: Launched AsiaClear, OTC clearing service for commodities; launched iron ore swaps
2009: Launched SGX iron ore futures — now the global benchmark for seaborne iron ore derivatives
2010: Proposed merger with ASX for AUD 8.4 billion; blocked by Australian government in 2011
2013: Acquired 24.9% stake in the Baltic Exchange (full acquisition in 2017)
2014: Launched FX futures (USD/CNH, INR/USD, and other Asian currency pairs)
2015: Announced next-generation derivatives platform (Titan) using Nasdaq Genium INET technology
2016–2017: SGX Titan DT/DC derivatives trading and clearing platform goes live, replacing legacy systems
2018: Launched FTSE-SGX indices; expanded iron ore and commodity suite
2019: Upgraded securities trading engine to Nasdaq multi-matching engine
2020: Extended FX derivatives product suite; record iron ore volumes
2022: Signed GIFT Connect agreement with NSE (India) for Nifty derivatives transition
2023 (3 July): NSE IX-SGX GIFT Connect became fully operational — Nifty derivatives migrated to NSE International Exchange in GIFT City, India
2025 (November): Launched institutional-grade Bitcoin and Ethereum perpetual futures tied to iEdge-CoinDesk Cryptocurrency Indices
2025: Record annual derivatives volume of 329 million contracts; record FX futures volumes; record OTC FX ADV of USD 143 billion; record MSCI Singapore OI
2026 (April, planned): Launch of Asia Pacific Government Bond Futures covering India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines
2027 (planned): New securities trading engine “Iris-ST” expected to go live in second half of 2027

[Source: SGX website, “About SGX”; Wikipedia, “Singapore Exchange”; SGX press releases 2022–2026; SGX FY2025 Annual Report; PR Newswire, “SGX Derivatives breaks new ground with institutional-grade crypto perpetual futures”, November 2025; Markets Media, “SGX Derivatives to Launch Asia Pacific Government Bond Futures”, March 2026]

2.5 Market Maker / Liquidity Provider Programs

title: SGX Derivatives
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Opening Auction (Pre-Open / Non-Cancel): - Pre-Open phase allows order entry, amendment, and cancellation - In the final 2 minutes before session open, only new order placements are accepted (no modifications or cancellations) - At session open, accumulated orders are matched at a single equilibrium price computed by SGX’s matching algorithm - The algorithm maximizes matched volume at the equilibrium price
Closing / Settlement: - Daily settlement prices are determined based on trading activity during defined settlement windows - For equity index contracts, final settlement price is typically based on the official closing price of the underlying index on the last trading day


3.2 Continuous Trading

Primary mechanism: continuous electronic matching on the SGX Titan DT platform
Orders matched in real-time during T and T+1 sessions
Supports outright orders and spread strategies (calendar spreads, inter-commodity spreads)
T+1 sessions provide extended hours with continuous matching but typically have thinner order books



3.3 Price Discovery

Extended trading hours (up to ~22 hours/day for key products) provide continuous price discovery spanning Asian, European, and U.S. market hours
SGX’s position as the primary offshore listing venue for major Asian indices (Nikkei 225, FTSE China A50) makes it a key price discovery venue outside home market hours
Nikkei 225 futures on SGX often lead price discovery during non-Japan trading hours
FTSE China A50 futures serve as the primary price discovery mechanism for China A-share exposure when mainland markets are closed



3.4 Order Priority Rules / Matching Algorithms
All orders on SGX Derivatives are matched using Price-Time Priority (FIFO) as the default algorithm:








Algorithm
Description
Application




Price-Time Priority (FIFO)
Strict price priority, then time priority at each price level; earliest order at best price is filled first
Default for most futures products


Price Point Maker (PPM)
Alternative algorithm giving priority to resting passive orders
Selected products [unverified]


Pro-Rata
Allocation proportional to order size at each price level
Selected options markets [unverified]


Market Maker (MM)
Market maker receives priority allocation
Applicable where DMM program is in effect



Key Rules: - Price priority is absolute — better-priced orders always fill first - Within the same price, time priority determines allocation (FIFO) - During opening/closing routines, orders are matched at a single equilibrium price - Self-Trade Prevention (STP) functionality available to prevent matching of orders from the same firm
[Source: SGX Rulebook, “Practice Note 8.2.1 — Application of Market Phases and Algorithm”; SGX Rulebook, “Regulatory Notice 8.2.1 — Trading Hours, Market Phases, Application of Market Phases and Principles and Rules for Trade Matching”; Trading Technologies, “SGX Overview”]

4. Order Types

4.1 Standard Order Types







Order Type
Description




Limit
Buy/sell at a specified price or better; unfilled quantity rests on the book


Market
Executes immediately at the best available price; any unfilled portion is cancelled or rests depending on configuration


Market to Limit
Executes at the best available price; unfilled quantity converts to a limit order at the last execution price





4.2 Advanced Order Types







Order Type
Description




Stop Limit
Triggered when the stop price is reached; once triggered, becomes a limit order at the specified limit price


Stop Market
Triggered when the stop price is reached; once triggered, becomes a market order


Stop Market to Limit
Triggered when the stop price is reached; once triggered, becomes a market-to-limit order


Spread Orders
Calendar spreads and inter-commodity spread strategies


Mass Quote
Allows market makers to submit multiple two-sided quotes in a single message via OUCH protocol





4.3 Time-in-Force (TIF) Conditions







TIF
Description




Day
Valid for the current trading session only; cancelled at session end


Good Till Cancel (GTC)
Remains active until filled or explicitly cancelled


Good Till Date (GTD)
Remains active until a specified date


Fill and Kill (FAK)
Executes immediately for any available quantity; unfilled portion is cancelled


Fill or Kill (FOK)
Must be filled entirely and immediately, or the entire order is cancelled





4.4 Order Modification & Cancellation

Orders can be modified (price, quantity) or cancelled at any time during trading sessions via the OUCH protocol
Replace Order: Modifies an existing order (price/quantity change) while maintaining or updating time priority
Cancel Order: Cancels a specific order by order token
Cancel by Order ID: Alternative cancellation method using the exchange-assigned order ID
Self-Trade Prevention (STP): Enhanced in 2024/2025 to allow configurable prevention of self-matching within the same firm

[Source: Trading Technologies, “SGX Supported Order Types”; OnixS, “SGX Titan OUCH Trading Handler — EnterOrder”; SGX Titan OUCH Protocol Specifications; Trading Technologies, “SGX Self-Trade Prevention Enhancement”]

5. Trading System Technology — SGX Titan

5.1 System Overview







Item
Details




Platform Name
SGX Titan DT (Derivatives Trading) / SGX Titan DC (Derivatives Clearing)


Technology Vendor
Nasdaq (Genium INET version 4)


First Announced
December 2014

2016–2017 (phased migration from legacy platform)


Architecture
High-performance, low-latency matching engine with product-level partitioning


Primary Data Center
Co-location facility in Singapore


Order Entry Protocol
OUCH (Nasdaq native binary protocol for asynchronous order entry)


Market Data Protocol
ITCH (Nasdaq native binary multicast protocol for market data)


Recovery Protocol
GLIMPSE (order book snapshot recovery for ITCH)


Average Latency
Sub-90 microseconds (benchmark average); sub-200 microseconds round-trip in production


Throughput
>1 million messages per second





5.2 Architecture

Matching Engine: Product-partitioned matching engines running on dedicated hardware optimized for deterministic, low-latency processing
Order Entry Gateway: OUCH protocol servers providing direct, asynchronous order entry with minimal overhead
Market Data Dissemination: ITCH multicast feed providing real-time, full-depth order book data to all connected participants
Clearing Engine (Titan DC): Integrated clearing platform processing trades in near-real-time for risk management and settlement
Deterministic Processing: Designed for consistent, predictable latency with minimal jitter



5.3 Latency

Benchmark Latency: Sub-90 microseconds average (gate-to-gate) — among the fastest derivatives trading platforms globally at time of launch
Production Round-Trip: Sub-200 microseconds for co-located participants
Order Routing Latency: Approximately 100–150 microseconds via OUCH protocol
Compared to Predecessor: Significant improvement over previous SGX derivatives platform; Nasdaq marketing described Titan as “the world’s fastest trading platform” at announcement



5.4 Platform History & Evolution







Year
Milestone

SIMEX trading floor opens — open outcry for financial futures


1999
SGX formed; electronic trading introduced alongside open outcry

Nasdaq technology partnership begins for SGX trading systems

2015
Development and testing phase; originally targeted for late 2015 go-live

2017
Full production migration to Titan DT/DC completed; legacy platform decommissioned


2019
Securities trading engine upgraded to Nasdaq multi-matching engine (SGX-ST, 3 June 2019)

2027 (planned)
New securities trading engine “Iris-ST” planned; derivatives platform evolution TBD





5.5 Technology Stack

Technology

OUCH — Nasdaq native binary protocol for low-latency, asynchronous order submission; supports Enter Order, Replace Order, Cancel Order, Cancel by Order ID messages


Market Data

Order Book Recovery

Operational Support: SGX operates follow-the-sun support model given extended trading hours (up to ~22 hours/day)
System Resilience: Nasdaq Genium INET platform designed with built-in redundancy and failover capabilities
Regulatory Requirement: MAS requires all approved exchange operators to maintain robust BCP and DR capabilities under its Technology Risk Management Guidelines

title: SGX Derivatives
text:
8. Risk Controls & Circuit Breakers

8.1 Circuit Breaker Mechanism
SGX’s derivatives circuit breakers operate as dynamic price bands:

Price Band Thresholds: Upper and lower thresholds set as a prescribed percentage from a reference price
Trigger: When an incoming order seeks to match against a resting order at a price outside the threshold, a Cooling-Off Period is activated and the incoming order is rejected
Cooling-Off Period: A brief pause (typically 5 minutes) allowing the market to analyze conditions before resuming; designed to moderate the pace of large price movements without halting price discovery entirely
Reference Price Calculation:

At the start of each Trading Phase: derived from the prior session’s settlement or last traded price
After the first 5 minutes: rolling reference price based on the last traded price as of 5 minutes prior to each potential trade
If no trade in the preceding 5 minutes, the reference price at the start of the Trading Phase applies


Purpose: The circuit breaker guards against disorderly situations from rapid, unchecked market movements. It is not intended to halt price movement but rather to allow market participants and regulators a pause to assess conditions. It also helps avert contagion risk to other markets.


8.2 Price Limits (Selected Products)
Specific price limit thresholds vary by product and are published by SGX in regulatory notices. Representative thresholds include:








Product Category
Typical Price Limit
Notes




Equity Index Futures
+/- 10% to 15% from reference price
Varies by specific contract [unverified]


Commodity Futures
+/- 15% to 20% from reference price
Iron ore, rubber, etc. [unverified]


FX Futures
Product-specific bands
Wider bands for volatile EM currencies [unverified]





8.3 Pre-Trade Risk Controls







Control
Description




Price Banding
Rejects orders outside an acceptable dynamic price range around the current market price


Maximum Order Size
Limits on maximum quantity per order, configurable by clearing member


Credit Controls
Real-time credit limit monitoring by clearing members for each trading participant


Self-Trade Prevention (STP)
Configurable to prevent matching of orders from the same firm; enhanced in 2024/2025


Cancel on Disconnect
Optional feature to cancel all working orders upon connection loss





8.4 SGX-DC Clearing Financial Safeguards (Default Waterfall)







Layer
Description




1. Defaulted Member’s Resources
Margin/collateral + clearing fund contribution of the defaulted member


2. SGX-DC’s Contribution (“Skin in the Game”)
SGD 200 million (increased from SGD 150 million; represents ~25% of clearing fund — higher than all U.S. and European CCPs)


3. Clearing Fund (Non-Defaulting Members)
Mutualized fund contributions from all non-defaulting clearing members, sized based on stress testing


4. Assessments
Additional capped financial contributions from clearing members



Key Risk Management Features: - Daily mark-to-market settlement through approved Settlement Banks - Intraday margin calls to cover shortfalls in margin requirements and potential mark-to-market losses - Clearing members must meet margin calls via Settlement Banks following intraday cycles - Clearing fund contributions scaled to the risks each member brings, based on stress losses over specified periods - SGX-DC is registered as a Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO) with the U.S. CFTC, enabling access by U.S. market participants
[Source: SGX Rulebook, “Practice Note 8.10A — Circuit Breaker”; SGX Rulebook, “Regulatory Notice 8.14.1 — Circuit Breaker”; WFE, “SGX Takes a Deep Look at Circuit Breakers”; SGX website, “Risk Management”; Hong Kong Lawyer, “Singapore Exchange Eyes Increase in Skin in the Game for OTC Derivatives Clearing”; CFTC, “SGX-DC Regulatory Compliance Chart”]

title: SGX Derivatives
text:
9. Regulatory Framework

9.1 Primary Regulator

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS): Central bank and integrated financial regulator; supervises SGX as an Approved Exchange (AE) and SGX-DC as an Approved Clearing House (ACH) under the Securities and Futures Act 2001
SGX RegCo: Established in 2016 as an independent regulatory subsidiary of SGX Group; performs front-line regulatory functions including market surveillance, member regulation, listing regulation, and enforcement



9.2 Key Legislation and Regulations







Regulation
Description




Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA)
Primary legislation governing securities and derivatives markets in Singapore; covers licensing, trading, clearing, market conduct, and market abuse


Securities and Futures (Trading of Derivatives Contracts) Regulations 2019
Mandatory platform trading requirements for certain derivatives contracts


Securities and Futures (Reporting of Derivatives Contracts) Regulations 2013
OTC derivatives reporting requirements to licensed trade repositories


MAS Technology Risk Management Guidelines
Requirements for technology governance, IT security, availability, and disaster recovery for financial institutions including exchanges


SGX-DT Futures Trading Rules
Exchange-specific rules governing trading conduct, order types, market phases, and member obligations


SGX-DC Clearing Rules
Rules governing clearing membership, margin, settlement, default management, and the clearing fund





9.3 Market Surveillance

SGX RegCo conducts real-time market surveillance for manipulation, spoofing, wash trading, insider trading, and other forms of market abuse
Surveillance systems monitor trading patterns across both securities and derivatives markets
SGX RegCo has powers to investigate, discipline, and sanction members and listed companies
Cross-market surveillance capabilities spanning equity, derivatives, and OTC markets



9.4 Reporting Requirements

Large Position Reporting: Members must have automated processes to monitor positions at the firm level; must report if at risk of breaching prudential limits on exposures to a single customer and a single contract
OTC Derivatives Reporting: Under the 2013 Regulations, counterparties must report OTC derivative contracts to a licensed trade repository (exchange-traded derivatives subject to different treatment)
Clearing Member Reporting: Daily reporting of margin, collateral, and financial position to SGX-DC
Transaction Reporting: Trade details reported to MAS as required



9.5 Cross-Border Recognition

U.S. CFTC: SGX-DC is registered as a Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO), enabling U.S. FCMs and customers to clear on SGX-DC; SGX-DT has been granted “no-action” relief for direct access by certain U.S. persons
EU/EMIR: SGX-DC recognized as a third-country CCP under EMIR for EU clearing member access
GIFT Connect (India): Regulatory framework established between MAS and SEBI/IFSCA for the NSE IX-SGX GIFT Connect
Mutual Offset System (MOS): Historically maintained with CME Group for Nikkei 225 and Eurodollar futures — enables positions opened on one exchange to be transferred to the other for close-out
CPMI-IOSCO: SGX-DC publishes disclosure documents in accordance with Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI)
Multiple bilateral MOUs with regulators in Japan (JFSA), Hong Kong (SFC), Australia (ASIC), and others

[Source: MAS website, “Securities and Futures Act 2001”; SGX Rulebook, “Futures Trading Rules”; SGX Rulebook, “SGX-DC Clearing Rules”; CFTC, “Industry Filings: Derivatives Clearing Organizations”; SGX website, “Memberships”]

11. Recent Developments

11.1 System Upgrades & Technology

Titan DT Enhancements: Self-Trade Prevention (STP) enhancement deployed on Titan DT (2024/2025) — allows more granular configuration of self-match prevention
Iris-ST (Planned 2027): New securities trading engine planned for the second half of 2027; derivatives platform evolution likely to follow
SGX-Nasdaq Global Listing Board: Joint initiative announced in 2025 for companies with market cap above SGD 2 billion; dual-listing bridge between SGX and Nasdaq



11.2 New Products & Market Developments

Crypto Perpetual Futures (November 2025): Launched Bitcoin and Ethereum perpetual futures — continuous, no-expiry structure with institutional-grade clearing and margining; supported by eight clearing members; debuted with ~2,000 lots (~USD 35 million notional) on day one; tied to iEdge-CoinDesk Cryptocurrency Indices
Asia Pacific Government Bond Futures (April 2026): First exchange-listed regional government bond futures covering India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines; USD-denominated; designed for sovereign rate risk hedging; trading commences 20 April 2026
Record Derivatives Volumes (2025): 329 million contracts — record year across equities, FX, and commodities

FTSE China A50 futures: ~84 million lots in first 9 months (+20%)
FX futures: 73.6 million contracts (+49.7% YoY); February 2025 alone saw 6.1 million contracts — all-time monthly high
Commodity derivatives: 65.3 million contracts (+6.2%)
Iron ore futures: 43.6 million contracts (+15%) — global volume record
MSCI Singapore OI: record notional USD 6.1 billion (+80% YoY)
FTSE China A50 OI: USD 13.8 billion (+24% YoY as of Feb 2025)

GIFT Connect Growth: GIFT Nifty monthly turnover exceeded USD 102 billion as of May 2025, with over 2 million contracts traded in that month



11.3 Regulatory Changes

MAS Legislative Proposals (2026): MAS proposes legislative changes to facilitate dual listings on the SGX-Nasdaq Global Listing Board
SGX RegCo ETF Market Maker Streamlining (2025): Simplified designated market maker requirements for ETFs
Enhanced Default Management: SGX proposed changes to SGX-DC Clearing Rules to enhance default management capabilities, consistent with international best practices



11.4 Strategic Initiatives

Pan-Asian Gateway Strategy: SGX continues to position itself as the primary international gateway for Asian derivatives exposure, covering >80% of Asia’s economies through its equity index derivatives suite
Iron Ore Global Benchmark: SGX now clears over 90% of the world’s seaborne iron ore derivatives, firmly establishing the SGX TSI Iron Ore 62% contract as the global benchmark
Multi-Asset Expansion: Strategic expansion across all asset classes — equities, FX, commodities, interest rates, digital assets — creating a comprehensive multi-asset platform
GIFT Connect Deepening: Continued growth of the NSE IX-SGX GIFT Connect with expanding product shelf (Nifty 50, Nifty Bank, Nifty Financial Services, Nifty IT) and growing volumes
Interest Rate Product Expansion: Leveraging existing JGB futures franchise and new APAC government bond futures to build a rates franchise complementing the multi-asset platform

title: SGX Derivatives
text:
D3. Margin Framework

Methodology: SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk)
SGX-DC uses SPAN as its primary margining system — a risk-based, portfolio approach to computing margin requirements.
Key Features:







Feature
Description




Model
SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk), originally developed by CME Group


Approach
Evaluates the worst possible portfolio loss over a specified time horizon (typically 1 day for futures, 1–2 days for options) under multiple market scenarios


Risk Scenarios
16 standard scenarios combining price moves and volatility shifts


Price Scan Range
Set based on a confidence level (typically 99% or higher), calibrated using historical price data with volatility scaling


Volatility Scan Range
Scenarios include shifts in implied volatility


Portfolio Offsets
Cross-margining credits for correlated positions within the same combined commodity group





SGX-DC’s Enhanced SPAN Parameters
SGX-DC has enhanced the standard SPAN methodology with specific modifications:

Volatility Scaling: SGX replaced the legacy standard deviation approach (which gave equal weight to all price observations during the prior year) with a volatility-scaling methodology. Margins are now more responsive to the prevailing volatility regime — increasing during high-volatility periods and decreasing during calm periods.
Anti-Procyclicality Floor: A floor ensures that margins cannot dip below those that would be calculated using a 10-year lookback period, even during extended benign/low-volatility periods. This prevents the buildup of under-margined risk during calm markets.
Stress Testing: SGX-DC regularly performs stress tests beyond SPAN scenarios to ensure clearing fund adequacy under extreme but plausible market conditions.



Margin Types







Margin Type
Description




Initial Margin (Performance Bond)
Required deposit to open a position; covers the estimated maximum one-day loss under SPAN scenarios


Maintenance Margin
Minimum margin level that must be maintained; typically set at a lower level than initial margin


Variation Margin
Daily mark-to-market settlement; calculated at the end of each trading day and settled in cash through Settlement Banks


Intraday Margin
Additional margin calls during the trading day if positions incur significant unrealized losses or volatility spikes


Spread Margin
Reduced margin for spread positions (calendar, inter-commodity) that benefit from offsetting risk





Margin Call Process

End-of-Day: Settlement prices determined; variation margin and any margin shortfalls calculated
Margin Call Issued: Clearing members notified of margin obligations via SGX-DC systems
Settlement: Cash transfers through approved Settlement Banks
Intraday Cycles: Additional intraday margin calls may be issued (and must be met promptly) to cover shortfalls arising from market movements during the trading session
Accepted Collateral: Cash (multi-currency), government securities, bank guarantees, and other approved collateral forms



Industry Context
While the broader derivatives industry is migrating from SPAN to VaR-based margin models (e.g., CME SPAN 2, Eurex PRISMA), SGX-DC continues to use its enhanced SPAN framework. The anti-procyclicality measures and volatility scaling represent meaningful improvements over basic SPAN, providing margin stability while maintaining risk responsiveness.
[Source: SGX website, “Risk Management”; SGX Rulebook, “Practice Note 6A.5.2 Calculation of Amount of Clearing Member Required Margins”; Risk.net, “SGX’s Koh defends clearing methods post-Nasdaq”; CME Group, “SPAN Methodology Overview”; FIA, “Navigating a New Era in Derivatives Clearing”]

title: SGX Derivatives
section: D4. Position Limits & Large Position Reporting
text:
D4. Position Limits & Large Position Reporting

Position Limits
SGX imposes position limits on derivatives contracts to manage systemic risk and prevent excessive concentration:

Position limits are defined per contract in the SGX Rulebook (Section 18.4.2) and vary by product
Members must have automated processes in place to monitor at the firm level if they are at risk of breaching prudential limits on exposures to a single customer and a single contract
Position limits apply to speculative positions — positions held for trading/investment purposes without an underlying commercial hedging need



Hedge Exemptions

Market participants with bona fide hedging needs may apply for exemptions from speculative position limits
Applications for exemption must be submitted to SGX-DT, demonstrating the hedging rationale and underlying commercial exposure
Exempted positions must be monitored and reported on an ongoing basis



Large Position Reporting

Clearing members are required to report large positions to SGX-DC when positions exceed specified thresholds
Large position reports enable SGX to monitor concentration risk and potential market manipulation
Thresholds are set on a product-by-product basis



Accountability Levels
SGX may set accountability levels (as distinct from hard position limits) for certain contracts, requiring participants exceeding these levels to provide additional information about their positions and trading intentions upon request.
[Source: SGX Rulebook, “18.4.2 Position Limits”; SGX Rulebook, “Practice Note 7.22 — Margins of Third Parties”; SGX website, “Risk Management”]

title: SGX Derivatives
section: D5. Block Trading / Negotiated Large Trades (NLT) / EFP / EFS
text:
D5. Block Trading / Negotiated Large Trades (NLT) / EFP / EFS

Negotiated Large Trades (NLT)
SGX’s equivalent of block trades is the Negotiated Large Trade (NLT) facility:
Key Rules: - NLTs are privately negotiated transactions executed off the central order book at a price agreed between two parties - Each NLT must meet the minimum volume threshold specified per contract in Appendix A of Regulatory Notice 4.1.11 - Representative minimum thresholds: - Nikkei 225 Options: 25 lots - Other products: varies by contract (specific thresholds published in the Regulatory Notice) - A multi-leg NLT within the same underlying is deemed compliant if at least one leg meets the minimum volume threshold - Members shall not combine individual customers’ orders solely to meet the minimum volume threshold - However, individual orders that each independently exceed the threshold may be combined to match a larger NLT counter bid/offer
Reporting and Registration: - NLTs must be reported to SGX within the prescribed timeframe - Both the seller and buyer must have satisfied the credit and position thresholds prescribed by their respective clearing members - NLTs are registered with SGX-DC for clearing upon successful validation


Exchange for Physical (EFP)

EFP transactions allow the exchange of a derivatives position for a corresponding physical or cash market position
Must meet procedures prescribed by SGX
The physical leg must be a bona fide transaction in the underlying or related commodity/instrument
Clearing member credit and position thresholds must be satisfied



Exchange for Swap (EFS)

EFS transactions allow the exchange of a listed derivatives position for an equivalent OTC swap position
Subject to similar rules as EFP transactions regarding procedures, credit thresholds, and reporting



Registration Requirements
For NLT, EFP, and EFS transactions involving contracts listed on a “Relevant Market” (i.e., contracts that are also listed on another exchange), Rule 7.04A requires compliance with additional registration procedures to ensure cross-market integrity.
[Source: SGX Rulebook, “Regulatory Notice 2.1.3A(4); 4.1.11 — Negotiated Large Trades”; SGX Rulebook, “4.1.11 Negotiated Large Trades”; SGX Rulebook, “7.04A Registration of an NLT, EFP or EFS in Respect of Contracts Listed on a Relevant Market”; SGX website, “Negotiated Large Trade (NLT)”]

title: SGX Derivatives
text:
D6. Delivery & Settlement Process

Daily Settlement (Mark-to-Market)

Daily Settlement Prices: SGX-DC determines daily settlement prices for all listed derivatives contracts at the end of each trading day
Variation Margin: The difference between the current day’s settlement price and the prior day’s settlement price (or the trade price for new positions) is settled in cash
Settlement Banks: Cash transfers are effected through approved Settlement Banks; clearing members must maintain accounts with approved banks
Intraday Settlement: Intraday margin calls and mark-to-market may be triggered during volatile market conditions



Final Settlement — Cash-Settled Contracts
The majority of SGX derivatives are cash-settled:







Product
Final Settlement Price Methodology




FTSE China A50 Futures
Based on the official closing price of the FTSE China A50 Index on the last trading day


Nikkei 225 Futures
Based on the Special Quotation (SQ) of the Nikkei 225 Index


Iron Ore Futures
Arithmetic average of TSI Iron Ore CFR China 62% Fe Fines assessments during the contract month


FX Futures (USD/CNH)
Based on the USD/CNH(HK) fixing published by TMA


FX Futures (INR/USD)
Based on the RBI Reference Rate


MSCI Index Futures
Based on the official closing price of the respective MSCI Index





Final Settlement — Physically Delivered Contracts
A small number of SGX commodity contracts (e.g., rubber futures — TSR20, RSS3) settle via physical delivery:

Delivery obligations fall to the trading counterparties, not to SGX-DC
SGX-DC acts as the central counterparty for financial settlement but has no liability for the actual delivery process
Delivery locations, quality specifications, and procedures are defined in each contract’s specifications
Clearing members must ensure their customers are prepared to make or take delivery if holding positions into the delivery period



Settlement Currency

Most SGX derivatives contracts are denominated and settled in USD, making them accessible to international participants without currency conversion
Selected contracts settle in JPY (Nikkei 225 JPY), SGD (MSCI Singapore), HKD (Hang Seng products), or AUD (S&P/ASX 200)

[Source: SGX website, “Clearing Information”; CFTC, “SGX-DC Regulatory Compliance Chart”; SGX Rulebook, “SGX-DC Clearing Rules”; Capital Futures Corp., “SGX Contract Specifications”]

title: Taiwan Futures Exchange (TAIFEX)
text:
3. Trading Mechanism

3.1 Auction Mechanisms
Opening Auction (Call Auction): - Pre-open phase (08:30 – 08:45) allows order entry; simulated opening price and best 5 bid/ask prices/volumes are revealed during each simulated match cycle - During the final 2 minutes prior to opening, submitted orders cannot be deleted or modified (to prevent manipulation of the simulated matching information) - At 08:45, accumulated orders are matched at a single equilibrium price via call auction - Calendar spread orders are not accepted prior to market open and do not participate in the opening auction - IOC market orders are accepted prior to open; FOK orders are not accepted during the call auction phase
Continuous Trading: - After the opening auction, orders are executed continuously upon entry into the order book - Price-time priority (FIFO) is the standard matching algorithm
Settlement: - Daily settlement prices determined at market close - Final settlement prices for expiring contracts based on the opening prices of the underlying index on the final settlement day


3.2 Order Types
TAIFEX accepts two primary order types for direct execution: - Market Orders: Execute immediately at the best available price - Limit Orders: Execute at the specified price or better
FCMs may accept additional order types at their own discretion for client-side management, including: market-if-touched, stop, stop limit, one-cancels-the-other (OCO), market-on-close, straight cancel, and cancel-replace orders.


3.3 Order Validity

ROD (Rest of Day): Valid for the remainder of the current session
IOC (Immediate-or-Cancel): Execute immediately for available quantity; unfilled portion is cancelled
FOK (Fill-or-Kill): Must be filled entirely and immediately, or the entire order is cancelled (not available during opening auction)

[Source: TAIFEX — FAQ Trading; Trading Technologies — TAIFEX Overview]

text:
D3. Margin Framework

Margin Methodology







Item
Details




Methodology
SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk)


Margin Calculation
Risk coefficient based on price movements within certain periods, anti-procyclicality factors, and other considerations to cover 99% of two-day price volatility risk


Initial Margin
Clearing margin multiplied by a TAIFEX-determined ratio (typically ~115–135% of clearing margin) [unverified]


Maintenance Margin
Set as a percentage of initial margin (typically ~75–88% of initial margin) [unverified]


Variation Margin
Daily mark-to-market settlement of gains and losses


Margin Announcement
Initial and maintenance margin amounts are periodically announced by TAIFEX and may be adjusted during periods of high volatility





Margin Call Process

End-of-Day Settlement: TAIFEX Clearing calculates clearing margin, variation margin, and clearing fees for each clearing member after market close
Intraday Mark-to-Market: Performed at 09:30, 11:00, 12:30, and 15:00 (or more frequently during high volatility)
Margin Deficit: If a client’s equity falls below the maintenance margin level, the FCM issues a margin call requiring the client to restore equity to the initial margin level
Margin Call Deadline: Typically by market open of the next trading day; positions may be liquidated if margin calls are not met [unverified]



Acceptable Collateral

Cash (NTD and major foreign currencies)
Government bonds
Other securities approved by TAIFEX (subject to haircuts)



Day Trading Margin

Day trading positions can be included with the rest of the portfolio for SPAN margin calculations
Reduced margin rates may apply for confirmed intraday positions [unverified]

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
1. Regulatory Authorities

1.1 European Commission

Initiates and proposes legislative measures for derivatives markets (e.g., EMIR, MiFID II/MiFIR)
Adopts delegated and implementing acts (Regulatory Technical Standards, Implementing Technical Standards) based on ESMA drafts
Issues equivalence decisions for third-country regulatory regimes
Responsible for legislative reviews and impact assessments (e.g., EMIR review proposals)



1.2 ESMA (European Securities and Markets Authority)

Supervisory coordination: coordinates NCAs’ supervision of derivatives markets across the EU
Direct CCP supervision: directly supervises Tier 2 third-country CCPs under EMIR 2.2 and EMIR 3.0; monitors risk models, liquidity, and operational risk
Technical standards: drafts RTS and ITS for Commission adoption (clearing obligation, reporting formats, CCP requirements)
Third-country CCP recognition: determines tiering (Tier 1 vs Tier 2) and grants or refuses recognition
Data and transparency: oversees trade repositories, consolidated tape provider selection, and data quality
Position limits: establishes the commodity derivatives position limit framework under MiFID II
Established: 2011, headquartered in Paris



1.3 National Competent Authorities (NCAs)
Key NCAs include: | NCA | Country | Key Role | |—–|———|———-| | BaFin | Germany | Supervision of Eurex participants, German banks’ derivatives exposure | | AMF (Autorite des Marches Financiers) | France | Oversight of Euronext derivatives, French market participants | | CONSOB | Italy | Italian derivatives market supervision | | CNMV | Spain | Spanish derivatives regulation | | AFM | Netherlands | Dutch derivatives market oversight | | DNB (De Nederlandsche Bank) | Netherlands | Prudential supervision of Dutch CCPs |

NCAs authorize EU CCPs under EMIR, supported by colleges of supervisors
NCAs set and enforce position limits for commodity derivatives under MiFID II (except for critical/significant contracts where ESMA has a direct role)
NCAs enforce MAR provisions including derivatives-related market abuse



1.4 ECB / ESCB (European Central Bank / European System of Central Banks)

Systemic risk monitoring for CCPs and derivatives markets
Participates in CCP supervisory colleges (particularly for euro-denominated clearing)
Provides central bank of issue opinions on CCP authorization and recognition
EMIR 3.0 enhances ECB involvement in third-country CCP oversight for euro-denominated products



1.5 ESRB (European Systemic Risk Board)

Macro-prudential oversight of EU derivatives markets
Issues warnings and recommendations on systemic risks arising from derivatives exposures
Coordinates with ESMA on CCP stress testing and systemic risk assessment

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
2. Key Legislation

2.1 EMIR (European Market Infrastructure Regulation)

2.1.1 Original EMIR – Regulation (EU) No 648/2012

Adopted: 4 July 2012; In force: 16 August 2012
Core pillars:

Clearing obligation: mandatory central clearing for standardized OTC derivatives through authorized or recognized CCPs
Trade reporting: all derivative contracts (OTC and exchange-traded) reported to authorized trade repositories
Risk mitigation for non-cleared OTC derivatives: timely confirmation, portfolio reconciliation and compression, dispute resolution, daily mark-to-market/mark-to-model valuation, exchange of collateral (bilateral margining)
CCP authorization: comprehensive requirements for EU CCP authorization including capital, governance, risk management, default procedures

Counterparty classification:

Financial Counterparties (FC): banks, investment firms, insurers, UCITS, AIFs, pension funds, CCPs
Non-Financial Counterparties (NFC): any undertaking established in the EU not qualifying as FC
NFC+: NFCs exceeding clearing thresholds; NFC-: NFCs below thresholds




2.1.2 EMIR 2.2 – Regulation (EU) 2019/2099

Adopted: 23 October 2019
Enhanced ESMA’s direct supervisory powers over third-country CCPs
Introduced the tiering framework for third-country CCPs:

Tier 1: non-systemically important; subject to recognition with ongoing compliance monitoring
Tier 2: systemically important (or likely to become so) for EU financial stability; subject to direct ESMA supervision and compliance with EMIR requirements

Strengthened role of central banks of issue in CCP supervision
Established CCP Supervisory Committee within ESMA



2.1.3 EMIR Refit – Regulation (EU) 2019/834

Published: 28 May 2019; In force: 17 June 2019
Key simplifications:

Eliminated the frontloading requirement for the clearing obligation
Simplified clearing obligation for small financial counterparties (FCs below clearing thresholds exempt from clearing obligation but must still calculate positions)
NFCs need only calculate positions in the asset class exceeding the threshold (not all classes)
Simplified reporting: NFC- reporting delegated to FC counterparty
Suspended clearing obligation for pension scheme arrangements (extended multiple times)

Reporting enhancements (RTS/ITS applicable from 29 April 2024):

Alignment with CPMI-IOSCO global standards for data elements
Introduction of Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI), Unique Product Identifier (UPI), Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)
ISIN required for derivatives traded on regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs, and SIs under MiFIR; UPI for remaining OTC derivatives
Enhanced data quality, validation, and reconciliation at trade repositories




2.1.4 EMIR 3.0 – Regulation (EU) 2024/2987

Adopted: 27 November 2024; Published in OJ: 4 December 2024 (OJ L, 2024/2987)
In force: 24 December 2024
Objective: reduce excessive EU exposures to third-country CCPs, improve efficiency of EU clearing markets
Key provisions:

Active Account Requirement (AAR): EU counterparties must maintain an active clearing account at an EU-authorized CCP for certain derivatives of substantial systemic importance (primarily euro-denominated interest rate derivatives, short-term interest rate derivatives, CDS)
Three operational conditions to ensure accounts are genuinely active and functional, including stress testing
Representativeness obligation for the most active counterparties
Reporting obligations to assess AAR compliance (reporting commenced 25 June 2025)
ESMA required to develop RTS within six months of entry into force
ESMA published final report on AAR in June 2025; consultation on draft RTS on participation requirements in October 2025
Revised clearing thresholds: new methodology focusing on uncleared OTC derivatives activity, ensuring proportionate clearing obligation
Enhanced intragroup exemptions framework: permanent regime replacing temporary extensions
Amendments to CRR (Regulation 575/2013) and MMFR (Regulation 2017/1131) to incentivize EU clearing




2.1.5 Clearing Obligation Categories
Classes of OTC derivatives subject to mandatory clearing:

Under EMIR 3.0, ESMA consulted on revised clearing thresholds (April 2025) with a final report published in February 2026, introducing a dual-threshold approach assessing both uncleared positions and aggregate OTC exposure for FCs




2.2 MiFID II / MiFIR (Derivatives Provisions)

2.2.1 MiFID II – Directive 2014/65/EU

In force: 3 January 2018
Derivatives-specific provisions:

Organized Trading Facilities (OTFs): new venue category specifically for non-equity instruments including derivatives; operator discretion in execution
Position limits for commodity derivatives (Article 57): NCAs must establish limits on the net position a person can hold in commodity derivatives traded on trading venues and economically equivalent OTC (EEOTC) contracts

Critical/significant contracts: net open interest above 300,000 lots over one year
ESMA coordinates and can intervene on NCA-set limits

Position management controls: trading venues must apply position management controls
Position reporting: trading venues must publish weekly aggregate position reports by participant category
Hedging exemptions: NCAs can grant exemptions from position limits for bona fide hedging activities
Ancillary activity exemption: non-financial entities dealing in commodity derivatives as ancillary to their main business may be exempt from MiFID II authorization (revised methodology under MiFID II review)

MiFID II Review: transposition deadline for all changes: 29 September 2025

December 2024: ESMA proposed extending position monitoring and accountability levels to emission allowance derivatives




2.2.2 MiFIR – Regulation (EU) No 600/2014

Trading obligation: standardized OTC derivatives subject to the clearing obligation must be traded on regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs, or equivalent third-country venues
Pre-trade transparency: bid/offer prices and depth of trading interest for derivatives on trading venues (with waivers for large-in-scale orders and package orders)
Post-trade transparency: price, volume, and time of transactions in derivatives, with deferred publication regimes for large-in-scale and illiquid instruments
Systematic internalisers: transparency obligations for SIs dealing in derivatives
Transaction reporting: derivatives transactions reported to NCAs under Article 26



2.2.3 MiFIR Review – Regulation (EU) 2024/791

Adopted: 2024; amends Regulation (EU) No 600/2014
Key changes for derivatives:

Consolidated Tape Provider (CTP) for OTC derivatives: ESMA authorized to select, authorize, and supervise CTPs; selection procedure for OTC derivatives CTP launched 5 January 2026 (submission deadline: 11 February 2026)
Revised pre- and post-trade transparency requirements for derivatives: balance between transparency and liquidity provider protection
Static thresholds replacing dynamic calculations for derivatives transparency
Single application date across amended RTS for derivatives
Removal of derivatives transparency reporting to ESMA (simplification)
ESMA submitted final report on derivatives transparency and CTP input/output to Commission on 11 December 2025
Payment for Order Flow (PFOF): prohibition, with transitional period
Enhanced data quality requirements





2.3 Other Relevant Regulations

2.3.1 MAR – Market Abuse Regulation (EU) No 596/2014

Extends market abuse framework to derivatives: insider dealing and market manipulation provisions apply to derivatives whose underlying is a financial instrument admitted to trading
Explicitly bans benchmark manipulation (post-LIBOR scandal reforms)
Applies to commodity derivatives and related spot commodity contracts
Cross-market surveillance obligations: trading venues must monitor for abuse across related derivatives and underlying markets
Reinforced investigative and sanctioning powers for NCAs



2.3.2 CRR / CRD (Capital Requirements)

CRR – Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 (as amended by CRR II/III):

Counterparty credit risk framework for derivatives: SA-CCR (Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk) mandatory from June 2021
Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) risk capital charge
Favorable capital treatment for centrally cleared derivatives (lower risk weights for CCP exposures)
EMIR 3.0 amendments to CRR incentivize EU clearing through adjusted capital requirements

CRD – Directive 2013/36/EU: governance and internal control requirements applicable to banks’ derivatives activities



2.3.3 SFTR – Securities Financing Transactions Regulation (EU) 2015/2365

Reporting obligation for securities financing transactions (repos, securities lending, margin lending) to trade repositories
Transparency of re-hypothecation/reuse of collateral received under derivatives transactions
Overlaps with EMIR reporting for certain collateral-related transactions
Trade repository infrastructure shared with EMIR



2.3.4 BMR – Benchmarks Regulation (EU) 2016/1011

Regulates benchmark administrators providing reference rates used in derivatives contracts (e.g., EURIBOR, EONIA successor ESTR)
Authorization/registration of benchmark administrators
BMR Review (political agreement December 2024, published May 2025): from January 2026, scope focused on critical/significant benchmarks, EU Climate Transition and Paris-aligned benchmarks, and certain commodity benchmarks
Third-country benchmark regime applicable from 31 December 2025
Post-LIBOR transition: ESTR as EU risk-free rate; impact on derivatives referencing legacy benchmarks



2.3.5 MiCA – Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (EU) 2023/1114

Fully applicable: 30 December 2024
Relevant to derivatives where crypto-assets are the underlying
Crypto-assets qualifying as financial instruments under MiFID II Annex I Section C fall under existing derivatives regulation
Transitional period for existing crypto-asset service providers: until 1 July 2026
DAC8 tax transparency rules for crypto-asset transactions: in force 1 January 2026

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
3. Position Limits Framework

3.1 Legal Basis

MiFID II Article 57: NCAs must set position limits on commodity derivatives and emission allowance derivatives
MiFID II Article 58: position reporting obligations



3.2 Scope

Commodity derivatives traded on EU trading venues (regulated markets, MTFs, OTFs)
Economically Equivalent OTC Contracts (EEOTC): OTC derivatives economically equivalent to exchange-traded commodity derivatives
Emission allowance derivatives: derivatives on EU ETS emission allowances



3.3 Position Limit Setting

NCAs set limits based on ESMA methodology:

Spot month limit: based on deliverable supply (typically 25% of deliverable supply)
Other months limit: based on open interest (typically 25% of open interest)

Critical/significant contracts: commodity derivatives with net open interest above 300,000 lots; subject to ESMA coordination
ESMA can issue opinions on NCA-proposed limits and, in exceptional cases, directly impose or revise limits



3.4 Hedging Exemptions

NCAs may grant exemptions from position limits for positions that are objectively measurable as reducing risks directly related to commercial activity
Applicants must demonstrate that positions qualify as hedging under defined criteria
Financial entities acting on behalf of NFC hedgers may also benefit from exemptions (under revised framework)



3.5 Position Management Controls

Trading venues must apply position management controls including:

Monitoring of open positions
Obtaining information from participants about positions (including in EEOTC contracts)
Requiring participants to terminate or reduce positions
Requiring participants to provide liquidity back to the market at an agreed price and volume




3.6 Position Reporting

Trading venues must publish weekly Commitment of Traders (CoT) reports with aggregate positions by participant category
Members and participants must report daily positions to the trading venue
NCAs receive position data and can share with ESMA



3.7 December 2024 Updates

ESMA proposed extending general monitoring and accountability level requirements to derivatives on emission allowances
MiFID II review changes in position limit framework to be transposed by 29 September 2025

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
4. Clearing Obligations

4.1 Product Scope
Products subject to mandatory clearing at authorized/recognized CCPs:
Interest Rate Swaps (IRS): - Fixed-to-floating IRS (plain vanilla) - Basis swaps - Forward Rate Agreements (FRAs) - Overnight Index Swaps (OIS) - Currencies: EUR, GBP, USD, JPY, NOK, PLN, SEK - Reference rates: EURIBOR, LIBOR (legacy), SOFR, SONIA, TONA, ESTR
Credit Default Swaps (CDS): - Untranched iTraxx Europe Main (Series 17 onwards, 5-year tenor) - Untranched iTraxx Europe Crossover (Series 17 onwards, 5-year tenor)


4.2 Counterparty Categories and Phase-In
The clearing obligation was phased in based on counterparty type:









Category
Description
IRS Phase-In
CDS Phase-In




Category 1
Clearing members of at least one CCP for relevant class
21 June 2016
9 February 2017


Category 2
FCs and AIFs with aggregate notional > EUR 8 billion
21 December 2016
9 August 2017


Category 3
FCs and AIFs not in Categories 1 or 2
21 June 2017
9 February 2018


Category 4
NFC+ (non-financial counterparties above clearing thresholds)
21 December 2018
9 May 2019





4.3 Frontloading

Eliminated under EMIR Refit (Regulation 2019/834): contracts entered into after notification but before the clearing obligation takes effect are no longer required to be retrospectively cleared



4.4 Intragroup Exemptions

OTC derivative contracts between entities within the same group may be exempted from the clearing obligation (Article 3 of EMIR)
Conditions:

Both counterparties are included in the same consolidation
Both are subject to appropriate centralized risk evaluation, measurement, and control procedures
The parent undertaking is not a FC

Third-country intragroup exemptions: require equivalence decision for the third-country counterparty’s jurisdiction

Temporary exemption regime extended multiple times (ESAs proposed three-year extension during EMIR review)
EMIR 3.0 establishes a more permanent intragroup exemptions framework




4.5 Pension Scheme Arrangements

Temporary exemption from the clearing obligation for pension scheme arrangements (PSAs)
Multiple extensions granted; EMIR 3.0 addresses the long-term treatment of PSAs



4.6 EMIR 3.0 Changes to Clearing

Revised clearing thresholds with dual assessment (uncleared positions + aggregate OTC exposure for FCs)
Active Account Requirement drives additional clearing volume to EU CCPs
Enhanced proportionality for smaller counterparties

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
5. CCP Supervision & Authorization

5.1 EU CCP Authorization (Title III of EMIR)

CCPs must be authorized by their home NCA, with involvement of a college of supervisors including:

Home NCA (lead supervisor)
ESMA
Relevant central banks of issue
NCAs of the most relevant clearing members
NCAs of trading venues served by the CCP

Authorization requirements:

Minimum capital: EUR 7.5 million
Governance: independent risk committee, senior management requirements
Risk management: margining framework (initial margin, variation margin, default fund), stress testing, back testing
Default waterfall: defaulter’s margins -> defaulter’s default fund contribution -> CCP’s dedicated own resources (skin-in-the-game) -> non-defaulting members’ default fund contributions
Segregation and portability of client positions and collateral
Business continuity and disaster recovery
Interoperability arrangements (subject to NCA/ESMA approval)

Major EU CCPs: Eurex Clearing (Germany), LCH SA (France), CC&G (Italy), BME Clearing (Spain), ICE Clear Netherlands, European Commodity Clearing (Germany)



5.2 Third-Country CCP Recognition

Third-country CCPs must be recognized by ESMA to provide clearing services to EU members/venues
Prerequisites:

European Commission equivalence decision for the third country’s regulatory framework
Cooperation arrangement between ESMA and the third-country authority
CCP authorized in its home jurisdiction

Tiering determination (introduced by EMIR 2.2):

Tier 1: non-systemically important; recognized subject to ongoing compliance with home-country rules
Tier 2: systemically important (or likely to become so) for EU/Member State financial stability

Must comply with relevant EMIR requirements (or comparable compliance framework)
Subject to direct ESMA supervision: risk model review, stress testing, liquidity monitoring, annual reviews
ESMA can propose remedial actions to preserve EU financial stability


As of January 2026, ESMA has recognized CCPs from multiple jurisdictions (US, UK, Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and others)



5.3 Brexit Implications for UK CCPs

Post-Brexit (1 January 2021): UK CCPs became third-country CCPs under EMIR
Key UK CCPs recognized by ESMA:

LCH Ltd (London): Tier 2 – dominant in euro-denominated IRS clearing
ICE Clear Europe Ltd: Tier 2 – significant CDS and energy derivatives clearing
LME Clear Ltd: Tier 1 – metals derivatives

Equivalence timeline:

Initial temporary equivalence: to 30 June 2022
Extended to 30 June 2025
Latest extension (January 2025): extended to 30 June 2028 (three-year extension)
Purpose: provide implementation time for EMIR 3.0 measures to reduce reliance on UK CCPs

Central policy tension: EU firms heavily rely on LCH Ltd for euro IRS clearing, but EU policy aims to repatriate clearing to EU CCPs (Eurex, LCH SA)



5.4 EMIR 3.0 Active Account Requirement

EU counterparties subject to the clearing obligation for derivatives of substantial systemic importance must:

Open and maintain an active account at an EU-authorized CCP
Clear a representative proportion of their relevant derivatives through this account
Ensure the account is operationally functional (including participation in stress tests)

Applies primarily to: euro-denominated IRS, short-term interest rate derivatives, certain CDS classes
Phased implementation with reporting from June 2025
ESMA developing detailed RTS on operational conditions, representativeness, and reporting

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
6. Reporting Requirements

6.1 EMIR Trade Reporting (Article 9)

Scope: all derivative contracts (OTC and exchange-traded) must be reported to an EU-registered trade repository (TR)
Reporting parties:

Both counterparties must report (dual-sided reporting)
Under EMIR Refit: FC responsible for reporting on behalf of NFC- counterparty
Reporting can be delegated to the counterparty, CCP, or third-party service provider

Timeline: reported no later than T+1 (one working day after execution, modification, or termination)
Content: counterparty data, contract data, valuation data, collateral data



6.2 Key Identifiers








Identifier
Purpose
Standard




LEI (Legal Entity Identifier)
Identify counterparties
ISO 17442 (GLEIF system)


UTI (Unique Transaction Identifier)
Unique identification of each transaction
CPMI-IOSCO / ISO 23897


UPI (Unique Product Identifier)
Product classification for OTC derivatives not identified by ISIN
CPMI-IOSCO / ANNA DSB


ISIN
Identify derivatives traded on RM, MTF, OTF, SI
ISO 6166





6.3 EMIR Refit Reporting Changes (Applicable 29 April 2024)

Alignment with CPMI-IOSCO global data standards (CDE – Critical Data Elements)
Expanded reportable fields (from ~129 to ~203 fields)
XML reporting format based on ISO 20022
Enhanced data quality requirements: validation rules at TR level, reconciliation processes
Lifecycle event reporting standardized
Pairing and matching requirements between counterparties
ESMA Guidelines on EMIR Refit reporting published October 2023



6.4 Trade Repositories

Must be registered with ESMA (or recognized if third-country TR)
Responsibilities: data collection, validation, reconciliation, secure storage, access provision to authorities
EU-registered TRs include: DTCC Derivatives Repository (DDRL), Regis-TR, UnaVista (LSEG), KDPW (Poland), CME TR
TRs must provide data access to relevant authorities (NCAs, ESMA, ECB, ESRB)



6.5 EMIR 3.0 Reporting Obligations

New reporting on AAR compliance to ESMA (from 25 June 2025)
ESMA public statement on upcoming EMIR 3 reporting obligations (December 2025)
Enhanced reporting on clearing volumes at EU vs. third-country CCPs



6.6 MiFID II Position Reporting

Daily position reports from members to trading venues
Weekly aggregate Commitment of Traders reports published by trading venues
Position data shared with NCAs and ESMA



6.7 MiFIR Transaction Reporting (Article 26)

Investment firms report derivatives transactions to their NCA
Includes detailed client, decision-maker, and execution information
Data shared across NCAs and with ESMA for cross-border surveillance

title: EU Derivatives Regulation
text:
7. Cross-Border Framework

7.1 Third-Country CCP Recognition

ESMA recognition process requires:

Commission equivalence decision for the third country’s CCP regulatory framework
Cooperation arrangement (MoU) between ESMA and third-country authority
Application by the third-country CCP
ESMA tiering assessment (Tier 1 or Tier 2)

Recognized third-country CCPs listed on ESMA register (updated regularly)



7.2 Equivalence Decisions

Commission has adopted equivalence decisions for CCP frameworks of multiple jurisdictions:

Full equivalence: USA (CFTC-regulated), Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Mexico, South Korea, India, and others
UK: time-limited equivalence extended to 30 June 2028

Equivalence assessed on an outcomes-based approach (not line-by-line regulatory matching)
Commission can withdraw equivalence decisions if conditions change



7.3 Third-Country Trading Venue Recognition

Under MiFIR trading obligation, equivalence decisions allow derivatives to be traded on third-country venues deemed equivalent
Limited equivalence decisions adopted to date for trading venues



7.4 IOSCO Coordination

EU framework aligned with IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMIs)
CPMI-IOSCO standards for data harmonization (UTI, UPI, CDE) adopted in EMIR Refit
IOSCO coordination on cross-border CCP supervision and recovery/resolution



7.5 Post-Brexit UK-EU Derivatives Landscape

UK equivalence for EU venues: UK (FCA) granted equivalence to EU regulated markets for trading obligation purposes
EU equivalence for UK CCPs: time-limited to 30 June 2028
Divergence risks:

UK developed independent derivatives regulation (UK EMIR, UK MiFIR)
Differences in clearing obligation scope, reporting formats, and CCP requirements are emerging
UK onshored EU regulations with subsequent UK-specific amendments

Market impact: fragmented liquidity in some derivatives markets; dual reporting obligations for cross-border participants
Memoranda of Understanding: ESMA-FCA cooperation arrangements for CCP supervision, TR data sharing, and market surveillance

8.2 Active Account Requirement Debates

Significant industry debate on scope and calibration of the AAR
Concerns about market fragmentation and increased costs for EU participants
LCH Ltd (London) dominates euro-denominated IRS clearing (~90%+ market share historically)
EU CCPs (especially Eurex) investing in capacity and incentive programs to attract clearing volumes
Ongoing discussions on whether representativeness thresholds are set at appropriate levels
Potential impact on clearing liquidity and pricing for EU end-users



8.3 Consolidated Tape Provider (CTP)

MiFIR Review establishes framework for CTPs across asset classes
OTC derivatives CTP: ESMA launched selection procedure on 5 January 2026

Submission deadline: 11 February 2026
ESMA to select, authorize, and supervise the CTP

CTP expected to consolidate post-trade data for OTC derivatives, enhancing price transparency
Revenue-sharing model between data contributors and CTP



8.4 ESG Derivatives Regulation

Growing market for ESG-linked derivatives (sustainability-linked swaps, carbon derivatives, green bond futures)
EU ETS emission allowance derivatives subject to MiFID II position limit regime
EU Taxonomy Regulation and SFDR: increasing focus on ESG-related disclosure for derivatives portfolios
ESG Rating Regulation: application date 2 July 2026; ESMA developing supporting technical standards
Carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) may generate new derivatives products
ESMA monitoring ESG-related greenwashing risks in derivatives markets



8.5 Digital / Crypto Derivatives

MiCA (fully applicable December 2024): framework for crypto-assets; crypto-assets qualifying as financial instruments fall under MiFID II/EMIR
Derivatives on crypto-assets subject to same clearing, reporting, and transparency requirements as traditional derivatives (where underlying qualifies under MiFID II)
DLT Pilot Regime (Regulation 2022/858): sandbox for trading and settlement of DLT-based financial instruments, including derivatives (limited scope)
DAC8: tax transparency for crypto-asset transactions from 1 January 2026
ESMA guidelines on qualification of crypto-assets as financial instruments to ensure consistent NCA interpretation



8.6 CCP Recovery and Resolution

CCPRRR – CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (EU) 2021/23:

Recovery plans, resolution plans, and resolution authorities for EU CCPs
Resolution tools: position allocation, forced contract termination, write-down of equity/debt
Resolution fund contributions from clearing members

Ongoing ESMA work on CCP stress testing and resolution readiness



8.7 ESMA 2026 Work Programme (Key Derivatives Items)

Continued Tier 2 CCP supervision (risk model monitoring, stress testing, liquidity and operational risk)
EMIR 3.0 RTS development and implementation
MiFIR Review technical standards finalization
CTP selection and authorization process
Simplification of financial transaction reporting (call for evidence issued June 2025)

9.4 Key Structural Differences

Market structure: EU has a fragmented multi-venue, multi-CCP landscape vs. Korea’s centralized single-exchange model under KRX
Regulatory complexity: EU’s multi-layered framework (EU-level regulations + national transposition + NCA implementation) vs. Korea’s streamlined FSC/FSS-KRX structure
Cross-border dimension: EU framework heavily focused on third-country CCP recognition and equivalence (due to Brexit and global interconnection); Korea’s framework is primarily domestic-focused with international cooperation through IOSCO/FSB
Active account concept: EU’s EMIR 3.0 AAR has no direct Korean equivalent (KRX CCP is the domestic monopoly clearing provider)
Reporting standards: Both aligned with CPMI-IOSCO global data standards (UTI, UPI, LEI)

title: Genium INET — Nasdaq Technology
text:
2. Architecture

2.1 High-Level Design
Genium INET follows a modular, event-driven architecture designed to support multiple asset classes (derivatives, equities, fixed income, commodities) within a single integrated platform. Unlike the INET equities matching engine which is optimized for single-threaded pure speed, Genium INET balances performance with the rich functionality required for derivatives markets (implied pricing, complex strategies, pro-rata matching, clearing integration).
Design Principles: - Multi-asset, multi-market — a single platform instance can support multiple products, markets, and asset classes simultaneously - Integrated trading and clearing — designed as a combined trading + clearing solution (unlike many equities systems where clearing is separate) - Configurable matching logic — supports multiple matching algorithms (price-time priority, pro-rata, and hybrid configurations) per product - Real-time risk management — pre-trade and at-trade risk controls embedded in the order processing path - High availability — active-standby architecture with hot standby at secondary site
Data Flow (simplified): 1. Order arrives via gateway (FIX, OUCH, or OMnet API) over TCP 2. Pre-trade risk validation applied (PRM/TradeGuard: price limits, quantity limits, credit checks) 3. Order routed to the appropriate matching engine partition (by product/market) 4. Matching engine executes configured matching algorithm (price-time, pro-rata, or hybrid) 5. For derivatives: implied pricing engine evaluates potential implied orders from strategy combinations 6. Execution reports returned to participant; trade data forwarded to clearing engine (DCASS or equivalent) 7. Market data update published via ITCH (multicast/unicast) and AMD (Advanced Market Data)


2.2 Core Components








Component
Function
Details




Matching Engine
Core order matching with configurable algorithms; supports price-time priority, pro-rata, and hybrid matching; handles opening/closing auctions, continuous trading, and request-for-quote sessions
Processes new orders, modifications, cancellations; generates trades; manages order book state; supports implied pricing for derivatives strategies


Order Gateway
Accepts and validates inbound orders from participants; protocol translation; session management and authentication
Supports FIX (industry standard), OUCH (native binary for high performance), and OMnet API (Nasdaq proprietary); conformance testing required for all connecting applications


Market Data Engine
Generates and disseminates real-time market data from matching engine events
ITCH protocol (binary, order-by-order depth); AMD (Advanced Market Data) for derived/summary data; MoldUDP64 multicast delivery


Clearing Engine (DCASS/Genium INET Clearing)
Integrated post-trade clearing, position management, margin calculation
Supports real-time clearing; position netting; margin computation (typically SPAN-based at client exchanges); settlement processing


Risk Engine (PRM / TradeGuard)
Pre-trade risk management; validates orders against configurable limits before reaching matching engine
Fat-finger price checks; maximum order quantity checks; accumulated value limits; net/gross position limits; virtually zero additional latency; supports ESMA guidelines compliance


Surveillance Interface (SMARTS)
Real-time feed of all order and trade activity to Nasdaq SMARTS surveillance platform
Used by 50+ exchanges and 170+ banks/brokers globally; order book replay capability; AI-powered anomaly detection; market manipulation and insider trading detection


Implied Pricing Engine
Calculates implied bid/offer prices derived from strategy leg combinations
Generates implied-in and implied-out prices for calendar spreads, inter-commodity spreads, and other strategy types; increases liquidity by connecting outright and strategy order books


Mass Quote Handler
Efficient bulk quote management for market makers
Allows market makers to submit and update large numbers of two-sided quotes simultaneously; supports configurable quote update throttling


Strategy/Complex Order Engine
Manages multi-leg derivative strategies (spreads, straddles, strangles, etc.)
Pre-defined and user-defined strategies; strategy creation and validation; multi-leg matching; implied pricing integration


Reference Data Server
Distributes security master data, contract specifications, trading schedules
Includes derivative order book directories, product definitions, expiration dates, tick tables, margin parameters


Drop Copy Server
Provides real-time copies of executions and order status to participants
FIX Drop Copy protocol; copied messages tagged with CopyMsgIndicator (797)=“Y”; used for compliance, reconciliation, and back-office integration


Front-End Applications
GUI-based trading workstations provided as reference clients
CLICK Trade (derivatives trading GUI); TradeGuard (risk management GUI); available for exchange-branded customization

Layer
Technology




Programming Language
C/C++ (matching engine core and critical path); Java (application layer, front-end components) [unverified]


Operating System

5. Resilience & Business Continuity

5.1 Architecture







Aspect
Details




Deployment Model
Primary site (active) + secondary site (hot standby); central system components run on the primary site with real-time state replication to secondary


Failover Model
In the event of a primary site failure, the matching engine on the secondary site is promoted to primary mode; ITCH ports on secondary site become active only after matching engine assumes primary role


Heartbeat Monitoring
Primary and secondary systems exchange regular status signals; failure detection triggers predetermined failover procedures


Gateway Redundancy
Multiple order entry and market data gateways; participants maintain connections to both primary and backup infrastructure


Network Redundancy
Redundant network paths between primary and secondary sites; diverse physical cable routes


Data Integrity
Real-time state replication ensures minimal data loss during failover; order book state recoverable from replicated log





5.2 Deployment-Specific Configurations
Each exchange deploying Genium INET configures its own business continuity plan. Examples:

Nasdaq Nordic: Primary and secondary data centers with hot standby; detailed BCP published to members; periodic DR failover tests conducted
HKEX: HKATS on Genium INET operates with primary site and DR site in Hong Kong; HKEX maintains its own BCP independent of Nasdaq’s standard configuration
SGX: Singapore Exchange maintains separate primary and DR facilities with Genium INET-based systems



5.3 Operational Resilience

Conformance Testing: All applications connecting to Genium INET must pass conformance testing before production access, ensuring they handle failover scenarios, market state changes, and error conditions correctly
Test Environments: Dedicated Genium INET test systems available for participant connectivity testing, conformance certification, and disaster recovery simulation
Capacity Planning: Systems designed with significant headroom above normal operating volumes; stress testing conducted regularly
