모니터링
실시간 용량 대시보드; 포화 전 선제적 쓰로틀링

title: CME Globex — CME Group
text:
6. 주요 기술 특징 (Notable Technical Features)

내재가격 엔진 (Implied Pricing Engine)
CME Globex의 매매체결엔진은 관련 스프레드 및 아웃라이트 계약 간의 매수·매도 호가를 통합하여 유동성과 가격 발견을 극대화하기 위해 실시간으로 내재가격(implied prices)을 계산한다.

Implied-in: 아웃라이트 주문이 내재 스프레드 가격을 생성
Implied-out: 스프레드 주문이 내재 아웃라이트 가격을 생성
상품간 내재 스프레드: 관련 상품 간 비율 기반 내재가격 산출 (예: 금리 선물)
제한사항: Self-Match Prevention (SMP)은 내재 유동성이 관여하는 거래에는 적용되지 않는다



매칭 알고리즘 (Matching Algorithms)
CME Globex는 상품 그룹별로 구성 가능한 다중 매칭 알고리즘을 지원한다:








알고리즘
설명
적용 상품 예시




FIFO (가격-시간)
엄격한 가격 우선, 이후 시간 우선; 한 가격 수준에서 최초 주문이 최우선 체결
축산물 아웃라이트 선물, Black Sea 밀/옥수수 선물


Pro-Rata
해당 가격 수준의 대기 주문 수량에 비례하여 체결 배분; 큰 주문이 더 큰 체결량을 수령
Eurodollar/SOFR 옵션, 특정 금리 상품


Split FIFO / Pro-Rata (하이브리드)
구성 가능한 비율 (예: 40% FIFO / 60% Pro-Rata); 시간 우선과 광범위한 참여 간 균형
곡물 및 유지작물 선물/스프레드, 축산물 스프레드


Allocation
특정 상품 유형을 위한 전문 배분 로직
일부 OTC 형식 상품


Top Order + Pro-Rata
최우선 대기 주문이 우선 체결을 받고, 나머지는 pro-rata로 배분
일부 금리 선물


Threshold Pro-Rata
pro-rata 배분이 적용되기 전 최소 체결 수량 기준
일부 옵션 상품





Market with Protection (MKT w/ Protection)
시장가 주문에는 내장된 가격 보호가 포함되어 있다 — 시장이 설정 가능한 범위를 넘어 움직이면, 미체결 잔량은 해당 범위 경계에서의 지정가 주문으로 전환되어 과도한 슬리피지를 방지한다.


자기거래 방지 (Self-Trade Prevention, SMP)

동일 회사/트레이더(SMP ID로 식별)의 반대 주문 간 매칭을 방지
구성 가능한 조치: 대기 주문 취소, 유입 주문 취소, 또는 양쪽 모두 취소
제한사항: SMP는 내재 유동성이 관여하는 자기 매칭을 방지하지 못한다 (예: 스프레드의 내재 다리에 대한 아웃라이트 주문의 매칭)



Mass Quote 기능 (Mass Quote Functionality)

마켓 메이커가 여러 종목에 걸쳐 양방향 호가를 동시에 제출하도록 설계
대역폭의 효율적 사용 — 단일 메시지로 다수의 호가 업데이트
Mass quote에 대한 연결 해제 시 취소(cancel-on-disconnect) 보호



Globex Credit Controls (GC2)

청산회원 리스크 관리자가 관리하는 사전체결 리스크 제어
거래소별 위탁매매회원별 매수 및 매도 거래/포지션에 대한 익스포저 한도
위반 시 실시간 조치: 이메일 통보, 주문 차단, 주문 취소
위탁매매회원 ID / 거래소 그룹 수준에서 적용



Inline Credit Controls (ICC)

상품별, 계좌별 세분화된 일일 포지션 한도
Account Management Service (AMS)를 통해 관리
일말에 포지션을 평탄화(flat)로 재설정
구성 가능한 임계값 알림 (예: 80% 활용도 경고)



CME SPAN / SPAN 2

SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk): CME가 개발한 업계 표준 증거금 방법론; 포트폴리오 수준의 증거금 요건을 계산
SPAN 2: 더 세분화된 시나리오와 개선된 모델링을 통합한 차세대 리스크 방법론
사전거래 및 장중 증거금 평가를 위해 GC2와 통합



코로케이션 서비스 (Co-location Services)

매매체결엔진에 근접하기 위한 CyrusOne Aurora 시설에서의 코로케이션 이용 가능
모든 코로케이션 참가자에 대한 균등 지연시간 접근
Google Cloud 프라이빗 리전에서의 향후 코로케이션 옵션: 전통적 랙 공간, Google 인프라 서비스, 또는 하이브리드

상품별 다중 (FIFO, pro-rata, 하이브리드, allocation)

클라우드 전략
2028년까지 Google Cloud 이전
온프레미스





주요 차별화 요소 (Key Differentiators)

매칭 알고리즘의 다양성: CME Globex의 상품별 매칭 알고리즘(FIFO, pro-rata, 하이브리드)은 주요 차별화 요소이다. KRX Exture+는 주로 FIFO를 사용한다. CME의 하이브리드 알고리즘은 유동성이 낮은 상품에서 체결 우선순위와 마켓 메이커 참여 인센티브 간의 균형을 맞추기 위해 특별히 설계되었다.
내재가격 엔진: Globex의 스프레드와 아웃라이트 간 실시간 내재가격 산출은 업계에서 가장 정교한 수준이다. 관련 종목을 연결하여 합성 유동성을 창출하는데, 이는 대규모 상품 카탈로그(수천 개의 상장 종목)를 보유한 파생상품 시장에서 매우 중요하다.
프로토콜 성숙도: iLink 3의 FIX SBE와 FIXP 사용은 초저지연 주문 입력을 위해 목적에 맞게 구축된 바이너리 프로토콜을 나타낸다. MDP 3.0의 시장데이터용 SBE 인코딩도 마찬가지로 직접 메모리 접근 패턴에 최적화되어 텍스트 기반 프로토콜 대비 직렬화 오버헤드를 줄인다.
멀티에셋 vs. 파생상품 특화: KRX Exture+는 주식, 채권, 파생상품을 단일 통합 플랫폼에서 다루는 반면, CME Globex는 파생상품 전용으로 구축되었다. 이러한 전문화는 Globex가 파생상품 고유 기능(내재가격, 스프레드 거래, mass quote)에 깊이 최적화할 수 있게 하지만, 폭넓은 자산 커버리지를 희생한다.
클라우드 이전 궤적: CME Group의 프라이빗 Google Cloud 리전 이전 계획은 중대한 전략적 전환을 나타낸다. 성공할 경우 결정론적 지연시간 요건을 유지하면서 자체/임차 데이터센터에서 클라우드 기반 매칭 인프라로 이동하여 거래소 기술의 인프라 모델을 재정의할 수 있다.
상품 카탈로그의 규모: CME Globex는 수백만 개의 종목(모든 옵션 행사가격 및 만기 포함)을 상장하고 있어, 내재가격 엔진과 시장데이터 인프라가 극히 방대한 상품 유니버스에 걸쳐 수평적으로 확장되어야 한다.

3. Clearing Models

3.1 CCP Clearing (Central Clearing)

Novation and open offer
Multilateral netting
Benefits: counterparty risk reduction, netting efficiency, transparency



3.2 Bilateral Clearing

Still applies to certain OTC derivatives not subject to clearing mandates, bilateral repos, and some fixed income instruments
Trend toward central clearing: Dodd-Frank Title VII and EMIR mandated clearing for standardized OTC IRS and CDS; SEC Treasury clearing mandate (2024) requires expanded central clearing of U.S. Treasury cash (Dec 2026) and repo (Jun 2027) through FICC
CCIL (India) clears government securities, forex, and money market instruments that were historically bilateral
Muqassa (Saudi Arabia) introduced CCP clearing for equity and repo markets that previously settled bilaterally



3.3 Hybrid Models

Interoperability: SIX x-clear and LCH Ltd operate interoperable CCP links for European cash equities, allowing clearing members to choose their preferred CCP while maintaining risk management across linked CCPs. Cboe Clear Europe also participates in interoperable arrangements.
Client clearing / Sponsored access: FICC’s Sponsored Member model allows buy-side firms to access CCP clearing through sponsoring clearing members; JSCC opened client clearing for JPY IRS to U.S. participants via CFTC exemption (Sept 2025)
Cross-margining: CME-FICC cross-margining arrangement (Jan 2024) for Treasury futures vs. cash Treasuries; OCC cross-guaranty agreements with NSCC/FICC/DTC

Vertical Integration: ASX operates one of the world’s few fully vertically integrated exchange groups, spanning listings, trading (ASX Trade for cash equities, ASX 24 for derivatives), clearing (ASX Clear and ASX Clear (Futures)), settlement (ASX Settlement via CHESS), and depository services (Austraclear for debt securities). This vertical integration is a defining feature of the Australian financial market infrastructure. Unlike many global markets where trading, clearing, and settlement functions are operated by separate entities (e.g., US markets with exchanges, DTCC/NSCC, and DTC), ASX controls the entire post-trade value chain for the Australian market.
Comparison with KRX/KSD: Korea’s post-trade infrastructure is similarly concentrated but split across two entities: KRX (Korea Exchange) acts as the CCP for both securities and derivatives, while KSD (Korea Securities Depository) handles settlement and depository functions. ASX’s model consolidates both clearing and settlement under a single corporate group with separate legal entities for each function.

2. Clearing Model

Description

Traded on ASX 24

[Source: ASX Clearing and Settlement Services, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services] [Source: Clarus Financial Technology, “What’s New in AUD Swaps in 2024?”, https://www.clarusft.com/whats-new-in-aud-swaps-in-2024/]


2.2 Novation Process
Upon acceptance of a trade for clearing, the relevant ASX CCP interposes itself as the legal counterparty to both sides of every transaction through the process of novation. The original bilateral contract between buyer and seller is extinguished and replaced by two new contracts: one between the CCP and the buyer, and one between the CCP and the seller.

ASX Clear: Novation occurs automatically for all trades executed on ASX Trade and Cboe Australia that are registered with ASX Clear. Novation takes place at the point of trade registration.
ASX Clear (Futures): Novation occurs when a trade is matched on ASX 24 or when an OTC transaction is submitted through an approved affirmation platform and accepted for clearing.

Through novation, each clearing participant only faces the CCP as its counterparty, eliminating bilateral counterparty credit risk. This is the standard CCP model consistent with PFMI Principle 4 (Credit Risk).
[Source: ASX Clearing, https://www.asx.com.au/about/regulation/clearing-and-settlement-of-cash-equities-in-australia/clearing]


2.3 Netting
ASX Clear (Cash Equities): - Employs multilateral netting of settlement obligations - For each settlement participant, all buys and sells in each individual cash market product are netted into one net buy or sell obligation per security - All payment obligations (pays and collects) are netted into one net pay or collect per settlement participant - Settlement occurs in a single daily multilateral net batch via CHESS (DvP Model 3) - Netting arrangements are approved under the Payment Systems and Netting Act 1998 - Netting efficiency is high – significantly reduces the gross value of settlement obligations
ASX Clear (Futures): - Multilateral netting of variation margin across all positions within a clearing participant’s account - Portfolio-based margining via CME SPAN recognises offsets between correlated positions - OTC interest rate derivative positions are also netted within the same clearing account
Comparison with KRX: KRX similarly employs multilateral netting for both securities and derivatives, settling net obligations through KSD. However, KRX’s netting occurs within a single CCP entity, whereas ASX maintains separate netting pools for cash (ASX Clear) and derivatives (ASX Clear (Futures)).
[Source: ASX Settlement services and pricing, https://www.asx.com.au/about/regulation/clearing-and-settlement-of-cash-equities-in-australia/settlement/settlement-services-and-pricing.html]

Clears own trades and trades on behalf of third parties (NCMs); must meet same capital requirements plus additional requirements for third-party clearing

Capital Requirements (ASX Clear): - Two capital regimes: Risk-Based Capital Requirements (for participants clearing equities or options, unless an ADI eligible for Other Capital Regime) and Other Capital Regime (for authorised deposit-taking institutions / ADIs) - Risk-Based Capital Requirements calculated based on the participant’s risk exposures, including market risk, counterparty risk, and operational risk - Capital adequacy is monitored via end-of-day financial returns; intraday monitoring may apply during periods of high volatility - ASX Clear published a consultation in January 2026 on third-party clearing capital requirements
Note: Unlike many global CCPs (e.g., CME Clearing with its USD 5M minimum net capital for non-bank FCMs), ASX Clear’s capital requirements are more principles-based and risk-proportionate, reflecting the smaller number of clearing participants in the Australian market.

Payment haircutting (variation margin haircutting)
Reduces outgoing payments to allocate losses


10
Contract termination / partial tear-up
As required



Total ASX Clear (Futures) Default Fund: AUD 650 million pre-funded - ASX capital contribution: AUD 450 million (across 3 tranches) - Participant contributions: AUD 200 million (across 2 tranches, commingled across futures and OTC products)
Juniorisation mechanism: In the auction process for the defaulter’s portfolio, participants’ default fund contributions are applied in order related to the size of their auction bids – the auction winner’s contribution is applied last (best protected), while the lowest bidder’s contribution is applied first. This incentivises aggressive bidding in the default management auction.
Comparison with other CCPs:

ASX’s model is notable for the very high proportion of CCP-funded resources relative to participant contributions, reflecting the vertically integrated ownership model.
[Source: RBA Standard 12, 2016/17 Assessment, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2016-2017/asx-central-counterparties/standard-12.html] [Source: RBA Standard 12, 2015/16 Assessment of ASX Clear (Futures), https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2015-2016/asx-clear-futures/standard-12.html] [Source: FIA, “FIA supports ASX default management proposals”, https://www.fia.org/fia/articles/fia-supports-asx-default-management-proposals]


3.4 Default Fund / Guarantee Fund
ASX Clear: - Total size: AUD 250 million (100% funded by ASX) - No participant contributions to the default fund - Participants are instead subject to Recovery Assessments (up to AUD 300M) if the default fund is exhausted - Additional contingent resources: AUD 300 million available beyond the default fund [unverified – exact structure of contingent resources] - Review frequency: Reviewed periodically by ASX and assessed annually by the RBA
ASX Clear (Futures): - Total size: AUD 650 million pre-funded - ASX capital: AUD 450 million (3 tranches) - Participant contributions: AUD 200 million (2 tranches) - Contribution methodology: Participant contributions are proportional to risk brought to the CCP (based on initial margin requirements) - Contributions commingled across futures and OTC derivative products - Review frequency: Reviewed periodically; RBA assesses annually - Replenishment: After a default event and a 22-business-day cooling-off period, default funds are replenished to up to AUD 400 million for ASX Clear (Futures) and AUD 150 million for ASX Clear
[Source: RBA 2024/25 Assessment of ASX Clearing and Settlement Facilities] [Source: ASX PFMI Disclosure Framework]


3.5 Stress Testing & Back-testing
Credit Stress Testing (CST):

Both CCPs conduct daily credit stress tests to assess the adequacy of financial resources
Cover 2 standard: ASX Clear (Futures) sizes its financial resources to cover the default of the two participants with the largest exposures under extreme but plausible market conditions (consistent with PFMI Principle 4)
ASX Clear also targets a Cover 2 standard for its default fund sizing

Stress Test Methodology:







Scenario Type
Description




Historical
Based on observed market events (e.g., GFC 2008, COVID-19 March 2020)


Hypothetical
Constructed by ASX risk management to cover extreme but plausible scenarios


Theoretical
Mathematical/statistical extreme scenarios


Volatility Skew (Phase 3, Sep 2024)
Scaling factors to account for equity volatility skew on out-of-the-money index and equity options


Specific Wrong-Way Risk (Nov 2024)
Additional scenarios to address wrong-way risk exposures



Back-testing: - Regular back-testing of margin models to assess the adequacy of margin rates - Comparison of margin held against actual portfolio losses
RBA Concerns (2024/25 Assessment): - The RBA was “disappointed by the number of issues identified with ASX’s financial risk models” during the assessment period - Errors were identified in ASX’s credit stress tests, leading to the downgrade of the Credit Risk Standard to “partly observed” for both CCPs - RBA expects ASX to prioritise improving its model validation and control testing frameworks, particularly data and reporting controls
[Source: ASX Clear Credit Stress Test methodology, August 2024, https://asxonline.com/content/asxonline/public/notices/2024/august/0954.24.08.html] [Source: ASX Clear Credit Stress Test parameters, March 2024, https://www.asxonline.com/content/asxonline/public/notices/2024/march/0226.24.03.html] [Source: RBA 2024/25 Assessment Executive Summary, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2024-2025/executive-summary.html]


3.6 Recovery & Resolution
Recovery Tools:
Both ASX Clear and ASX Clear (Futures) have formal ASX Recovery Rules (effective from November 2017, amended since), which provide the following tools:








Tool
ASX Clear
ASX Clear (Futures)




Recovery Assessments
Up to AUD 300 million for one or multiple defaults
Up to AUD 200 million per default; max AUD 600 million for multiple defaults within a defined default period


Variation Margin Haircutting
Not available – variation margin is applied differently in cash equities (collected on losses but not paid out on gains in the same way as derivatives)
Available – ASX Clear (Futures) can reduce (haircut) outgoing payments to participants to allocate losses


Partial Tear-up
Available – forced termination of some open contracts to restore a matched book
Available


Complete Termination
Available – termination of all open contracts with haircutting of settlement payments
Available


Auction / Default Management
ASX can auction the defaulter’s portfolio
ASX can auction the defaulter’s portfolio; juniorisation mechanism incentivises bidding



Resolution Authority: - Australia does not currently have a dedicated CCP resolution regime comparable to the EU’s CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (CCPRRR) or the US Dodd-Frank Title II - The RBA and ASIC would coordinate any resolution actions under existing powers in the Corporations Act 2001 and the Reserve Bank Act 1959 - The Council of Financial Regulators (CFR) has considered the need for a dedicated CCP resolution framework, but as of 2026 no formal legislation has been enacted [unverified]
[Source: ASX Recovery Rules Handbook, https://www.asx.com.au/content/dam/asx/rules-guidance-notes-waivers/asx-recovery-rules/asx-recovery-rules-handbook.pdf] [Source: ASX Recovery and Resolution, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services/asx-clear/risk-management/recovery-and-resolution] [Source: RBA Special Topic on Default Management and Recovery, 2019/20, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2019-2020/special-topic-default-management-and-recovery.html] [Source: RBA Recovery and Resolution Bulletin, December 2013, https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/bulletin/2013/dec/5.html]

4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle








Product
Settlement Cycle
Notes




Cash Equities
T+2
Standard cycle since March 2016 (moved from T+3)


Equity Options (ETOs)
T+1 (premium); exercise settlement varies
Premium paid T+1; exercise settlement follows underlying equity cycle


Government Bonds (Austraclear)
T+2
Settled via Austraclear RTGS


Futures
Daily mark-to-market (variation margin); final settlement varies by contract
No physical settlement for most financial futures


OTC Derivatives
Daily variation margin; maturity settlement as per contract




T+1 Transition Plans: - ASX published an industry whitepaper in April 2024; T+1 Working Group established December 2023 - Industry consensus: T+1 is desirable but should not proceed until CHESS replacement is complete - No confirmed T+1 implementation date; earliest feasible timeline likely 2029+ (after CHESS Phase 2 delivery) - International context: US moved to T+1 in May 2024; EU targeting 2027; UK targeting 2027
[Source: ASX T+1 Settlement Cycle, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services/t1-settlement-cycle]


4.2 DVP Model
ASX Settlement (CHESS) – Cash Equities: - BIS DvP Model 3: Multilateral net batch settlement - Settlement of all transactions due on a given business day occurs in a single daily batch that completes at approximately 12:30pm AEST - Securities and cash obligations are settled simultaneously on a net basis - CHESS also has functionality for DvP Model 1 (item-by-item RTGS settlement), but this is not currently used by any settlement participant
Austraclear – Debt Securities: - BIS DvP Model 1: Simultaneous exchange of assets (cash and securities) on an item-by-item basis in real time - Interbank cash element settled via RITS (Reserve Bank Information and Transfer System) using real-time gross settlement (RTGS) across Exchange Settlement Accounts (ESAs) at the RBA - Settlement in central bank money
Comparison with KRX/KSD: KSD uses DvP Model 1 for government bonds (real-time settlement via BOK-Wire+) and a combination of DvP Model 2/3 for equities (multilateral netting with same-day settlement). ASX’s single daily batch for equities (DvP Model 3) is less granular than some Asian markets but provides high netting efficiency.
[Source: RBA Standard 10, 2017/18 Assessment, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2017-2018/asx-securities-settlement-facilities/standard-10.html] [Source: RBA Standard 7, 2017/18 Assessment, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2017-2018/asx-securities-settlement-facilities/standard-07.html]


4.3 Settlement Finality

Legal basis: Payment Systems and Netting Act 1998 (PSN Act) – provides legal protections for payments and transfers of assets through approved RTGS systems
CHESS: The RBA has declared CHESS an approved RTGS system under the PSN Act, providing protection from reversal or invalidation under insolvency law
Point of finality (CHESS): Settlement is final and irrevocable upon completion of the daily batch settlement process (~12:30pm AEST)
Austraclear: Also an approved RTGS system; settlement is final when the security record amendments are made and RITS confirms the cash transfer has been effected
Irrevocability: Once settlement is completed, it cannot be unwound, even in the event of a participant’s insolvency

[Source: RBA Standard 7: Settlement Finality, 2017/18 Assessment, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2017-2018/asx-securities-settlement-facilities/standard-07.html]


4.4 CSD / Settlement Infrastructure








System
Function
Details




CHESS (Clearing House Electronic Subregister System)
CSD and settlement system for cash equities
Launched 1996; handles settlement, subregistry, and corporate actions for all ASX-listed securities; operates as ASX Settlement Pty Limited


ASX Settlement
Settlement facility licensee
Licensed under the Corporations Act 2001; holds a CS facility licence


Austraclear
CSD for debt securities and depository for government bonds
Handles settlement and registry for fixed income instruments; uses RTGS via RITS


Cash Settlement
Central bank money (via RITS/ESAs at RBA)
Both CHESS and Austraclear settle the cash leg through ESAs at the Reserve Bank of Australia – settlement in central bank money, providing the highest level of safety



CHESS as Subregister: A unique feature of the Australian market is that CHESS acts as an electronic subregister for securities holdings. Rather than having a separate share registry system, CHESS maintains a subregister of all holdings that have been “CHESS-sponsored” (i.e., held in the CHESS system under a HIN – Holder Identification Number). This differs from most other markets where the CSD/depository function is separate from the share registry.
[Source: ASX Clearing and Settlement Services, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services]


4.5 CSD Linkages








Linked CSD/ICSD
Type of Link
Products




NZX / NZ Clearing Limited
Cross-border clearing link
NZX-traded products cleared by ASX Clear (Futures)



ASX does not maintain extensive CSD linkages with international CSDs/ICSDs such as Euroclear or Clearstream. Australian securities are primarily held domestically within CHESS. International investors typically access the Australian market through custodian banks or nominee arrangements rather than direct CSD links.
[Source: ASX PFMI Disclosure Framework]


4.6 Securities Lending & Borrowing

Facility available: Yes, through ASX Collateral
ASX Collateral provides:

Free of Payment (FoP) mechanism for collateralisation and maintenance of various exposure types, including securities lending and borrowing, CSA margining, and CCP margining with ASX Clear (Futures)
Delivery versus Delivery (DvD) mechanism for principal settlement of securities-versus-securities transactions, including securities lending and borrowing

The securities lending market in Australia is primarily an OTC bilateral market between institutional participants, facilitated by custodian banks and prime brokers
ASX’s role is primarily in providing the settlement infrastructure for securities lending transactions rather than operating a centralised lending facility

[Source: ASX Collateral, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services/collateral-services]

CHESS Replacement Project (Major)
The CHESS replacement is one of the most significant and troubled technology projects in global exchange history:
Phase 1 – DLT/Blockchain Approach (2015-2022): - 2015: ASX selected Digital Asset Holdings (DA) to explore DLT for CHESS replacement - 2017: ASX formally announced CHESS replacement using DA’s distributed ledger technology - 2018-2022: Repeated delays – go-live date pushed from 2020 to 2021, 2022, then 2023 - November 2022: ASX abandoned the DLT project after an independent Accenture review found software was only 63% complete with uncertain timeline and overly complex design - Financial impact: ~AUD 250 million write-off - August 2024: ASIC commenced Federal Court proceedings against ASX, alleging misleading statements about the DLT project’s progress (particularly the February 2022 claim that the project was “on-track” and “progressing well”)
Phase 2 – Conventional Technology with TCS (2023-present): - November 2023: ASX selected Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) as new implementation partner - Architecture: Modular, cloud-based platform using conventional technology - Release 1 (Clearing): Targeted go-live 20 April 2026; estimated cost AUD 105-125 million; replaces clearing component of CHESS; introduces more efficient netting process and FIX messaging for trade registrations - Release 2 (Settlement and Subregister): Targeted for 2029; estimated cost AUD 270-320 million; replaces remaining CHESS functionality - March 2026: ASX released the CHESS Release 1 Cutover Runbook and progress updates; appears on track


ClearStar Program
The ClearStar Program is a portfolio of projects to modernise and replace the technology underpinning ASX’s derivatives clearing services over a six-year period: - OTC Clearing (Calypso Upgrade): Upgraded from Calypso v13 to v18; delivered 26 May 2025 - Exchange-Traded Derivatives Futures Clearing: Platform upgrade planned as part of the program - Objective: Improve operational efficiency, enhance risk management capabilities, modernise clearing infrastructure
[Source: ASX CHESS Project, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services/chess-project] [Source: ASX ClearStar Program, https://www.asx.com.au/markets/clearing-and-settlement-services/clearstar-program] [Source: WatersTechnology, “ASX CHESS replacement to be delivered in phases”, https://www.waterstechnology.com/trading-tech/7951687/asx-chess-replacement-to-be-delivered-in-phases-with-clearing-first-in-2026] [Source: The Fintech Times, “Blockchain Project Gone Wrong: ASIC Takes ASX to Court”, https://thefintechtimes.com/blockchain-project-gone-wrong-asic-takes-asx-to-court-over-chess-replacement/]


5.2 Interface Protocols







Protocol
Use Case

Used for Austraclear settlement messaging

Being adopted as part of CHESS replacement and broader industry modernisation

CHESS Release 1 introduces FIX messaging for trade registrations; also used for ASX Trade order entry

Proprietary messaging protocol for CHESS – used by settlement and clearing participants

Ultra-low latency protocols for ASX Trade (trading, not clearing)





5.3 Resilience

Data Centre: Australian Liquidity Centre (ALC), Gore Hill, Sydney – purpose-built Tier III financial markets data centre
DR site: ASX operates a secondary data centre for disaster recovery [specific location not publicly disclosed]
RTO / RPO: Target RTO of 2 hours for critical systems; specific RPO not publicly disclosed
Uptime SLA: Not publicly disclosed; however, operational incidents are reported to the RBA

Critical Concern – December 2024 CHESS Incident: - On 20 December 2024, a memory allocation coding error introduced in 2014 caused the CHESS batch settlement to fail - The error went undetected for 10 years until specific conditions triggered it - All settlements were pushed to the following Monday, disrupting the entire Australian cash equities market - This incident led the RBA to downgrade ASX Clear and ASX Settlement’s Operational Risk standard to “not observed” – the lowest possible rating - The RBA noted the incident “reinforced concerns about risk management at ASX and underscored that there is still substantial work to be done”
[Source: RBA Out-of-cycle Assessment, March 2025, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2024-2025/march/]

6. Regulatory Framework

6.1 Supervising Authority







Authority
Role




ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission)
Primary regulator – market supervision, licensing of market operators and participants, enforcement of market integrity rules, consumer protection; commenced formal Inquiry into ASX Group in June 2025


RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia)
Oversees clearing and settlement facility licensees under the Financial Stability Standards (FSS); assesses ASX Clear, ASX Clear (Futures), ASX Settlement, and Austraclear annually; focuses on systemic risk and financial stability


CFR (Council of Financial Regulators)
Coordinating body comprising RBA, ASIC, APRA, and Treasury; oversees financial system stability


APRA (Australian Prudential Regulation Authority)
Regulates ADIs that are clearing participants; sets capital requirements for bank participants’ CCP exposures





6.2 Key Regulations

Corporations Act 2001 (Cth): Part 7.3 – clearing and settlement facility licences; Part 7.3A – CS facility rules
Financial Stability Standards (FSS): Set by the RBA under Section 827D of the Corporations Act; based on CPMI-IOSCO PFMI principles
Payment Systems and Netting Act 1998: Provides settlement finality protections
ASIC CS Services Rules 2025: New regulatory framework for clearing and settlement service pricing; implements revenue-capping methodology reflecting ASX’s monopoly position in cash equity clearing and settlement
ASX Clear Operating Rules / ASX Clear (Futures) Operating Rules: Govern clearing participation, margining, default management
ASX Recovery Rules: Govern recovery tools including assessment powers, haircutting, and contract termination



6.3 PFMI Compliance

Five FSS standards were rated as “partly observed” or “not observed” across the ASX clearing and settlement facilities – an unprecedented level of regulatory concern.
The RBA stated it was “disappointed by the number of issues identified with ASX’s financial risk models” and expects ASX to prioritise improving its model validation and control testing frameworks.


6.4 Reporting Requirements

PQD (Public Quantitative Disclosures): Both CCPs publish quarterly CPMI-IOSCO PQD data covering credit risk, margin, collateral, liquidity risk, default procedures, and other metrics
PFMI Disclosure Framework: Qualitative self-assessment published and periodically updated
RBA Annual Assessment: Comprehensive annual review of compliance with Financial Stability Standards
Financial Returns: Clearing participants submit regular financial returns to ASX for capital adequacy monitoring

7. Interoperability

7.1 CCP Interoperability Arrangements
ASX Clear and ASX Clear (Futures) do not participate in any CCP interoperability arrangements. This is a direct consequence of ASX’s vertically integrated monopoly model for cash equity clearing – there is no competing CCP for Australian cash equities, so interoperability has not been required.
The Australian government has periodically considered introducing competition in clearing (e.g., the 2015 Review of Competition in Clearing Australian Cash Equities by Treasury), but no competing CCP has been authorised.


7.2 Cross-border Arrangements







Arrangement
Details




ESMA Recognition
Both CCPs recognised as third-country CCPs under EU EMIR (effective 27 April 2015) – allows EU-based participants to use ASX CCPs with concessional capital treatment


APRA QCCP Recognition
Both CCPs confirmed as Qualifying CCPs under APS 112 – allows Australian ADIs to apply concessional risk weightings


NZX Clearing
ASX Clear (Futures) provides clearing services for NZX-traded products under a cross-border arrangement



Comparison with KRX: KRX also does not participate in CCP interoperability arrangements. Both ASX and KRX operate as monopoly CCPs in their respective domestic markets, reflecting the concentrated market structure of their regions.
[Source: ESMA list of recognised third-country CCPs, https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/library/third-country_ccps_recognised_under_emir.pdf]

9. Recent Developments

CHESS Replacement Saga (2015-2026)
The failed CHESS replacement project is one of the most significant technology failures in global exchange history. See Section 5.1 for full details.
Current Status (as of April 2026): - CHESS Release 1 (Clearing): Go-live planned for 20 April 2026; cutover runbook published 13 March 2026; on track - CHESS Release 2 (Settlement and Subregister): Targeted for 2029; estimated cost AUD 270-320 million - ASIC Federal Court Action: ASIC commenced proceedings against ASX in August 2024 alleging misleading statements about the DLT project; case ongoing


December 2024 CHESS Settlement Failure

20 December 2024: CHESS batch settlement failed to complete due to a memory allocation coding error introduced in 2014
Error went undetected for 10 years; all settlements pushed to the following Monday
March 2025: RBA and ASIC issued joint letter expressing “deep concerns” about ASX’s operational risk management
Led to RBA downgrading Operational Risk to “not observed”



ASIC Inquiry into ASX Group (2025-2026)

June 2025: ASIC launched formal Inquiry into ASX Group covering governance, capability, and risk management across all licensed entities
December 2025: ASIC announced a “transformational package” to safeguard financial markets based on interim report
March 2026: ASIC published the ASX Inquiry Panel Final Report with observations and recommendations for change



RBA 2024/25 Assessment (September 2025)
Five FSS standards rated as “partly observed” or “not observed” – an unprecedented level of regulatory concern: - Credit Risk Standard downgraded to partly observed (errors in credit stress tests) - Operational Risk Standard downgraded to not observed (December 2024 CHESS incident) - Governance and Framework for Comprehensive Management of Risks also rated partly observed


ClearStar Program – Technology Modernisation

Calypso OTC Upgrade: v13 to v18 delivered 26 May 2025; first major delivery under ClearStar
Futures Clearing Platform: Upgrade planned as part of multi-year program
Program to modernise derivatives clearing infrastructure over a six-year period



ASIC CS Services Rules 2025

New regulatory framework implementing revenue-capping pricing methodology for ASX’s cash equity clearing, settlement, and issuer services
Reflects ASX’s monopoly position in post-trade services for Australian cash equities
Revenue sharing scheme removed; replaced with cost-of-service-plus-reasonable-return model
Effective July 2025



Margin Model Updates (2025-2026)

ASX Clear (Futures): Changes to account for outstanding margin payments in stress test calculations; expected finalised by September 2025
ASX Clear: Similar changes expected by June 2026
ASX Clear Cash Market Margining (CMM) methodology recalibrated in August 2025; average 12% increase in HSVaR margins



Other Developments

Tokenised Government Bond Settlement: ASX launched a pilot in March 2026
T+1 Settlement: Under consideration but deferred until CHESS replacement complete; earliest feasible timeline 2029+
Third-Party Clearing Capital Requirements: ASX published consultation paper in January 2026

[Source: RBA 2024/25 Assessment, https://www.rba.gov.au/payments-and-infrastructure/financial-market-infrastructure/clearing-and-settlement-facilities/assessments/2024-2025/executive-summary.html] [Source: ASIC ASX Inquiry, https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/markets/inquiry-into-asx/] [Source: ASIC MR 26-059MR, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2026-releases/26-059mr-asic-publishes-asx-inquiry-panel-final-report-and-acknowledges-observations/]

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
1. Overview & Profile



Item
Details




Official Name
The Central Depository (Pte) Limited


Abbreviation
CDP


LEI
549300CMH3J8ASUM8N29


SWIFT Code
CDPLSGSGXXX


Country / City
Singapore


Address
SGX Centre 1, 2 Shenton Way, #02-02, Singapore 068804


Website
https://www.sgx.com/securities/depository


Year Established
1987


Parent Company
Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX Group) – wholly-owned subsidiary


Regulatory Authority
Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)


Regulatory Status
Approved Clearing House (ACH) under Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA); designated Central Depository under the Companies Act


CPMI-IOSCO PFMI Compliance
Yes – publishes PFMI disclosure (SGX RegCo PFMI Page)


Role
Provides integrated clearing, settlement, and depository services for the Singapore securities market (equities and fixed income)


Systemic Importance
Designated as systemically important FMI by MAS; value of transactions cleared as percentage of Singapore GDP was ~94% (as of 2012 IMF assessment) [Source: IMF Country Report No. 13/345]



Relationship to SGX Group:
CDP is one of two clearing houses within SGX Group: - CDP – clears and settles equities, corporate bonds, ETFs, REITs, unit trusts, warrants, depository receipts, and other listed securities traded on SGX-ST (Singapore Exchange Securities Trading) - SGX-DC (SGX Derivatives Clearing Limited) – clears derivatives products (futures, options, OTC derivatives); separate entity with its own clearing fund (~S$557 million as of Dec 2024)
Both CDP and SGX-DC are wholly-owned subsidiaries of SGX and are regulated as Designated Clearing Houses (DCHs) under the SFA. [Source: MAS – Clearing Houses]

KRX/KSD Comparison: In Korea, KRX serves as the CCP while KSD serves as the CSD, and they are separate entities. In Singapore, CDP uniquely combines both CCP and CSD functions within a single legal entity.


Key Historical Milestones



Year
Event




1987
CDP established as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Stock Exchange of Singapore (SES) to serve as the central securities depository for the Singapore market


1999
SES and SIMEX merged to form Singapore Exchange (SGX); CDP became a subsidiary of SGX


2006
CDP implemented real-time surveillance capabilities for settlement risk


2012
SGX embarked on post-trade modernisation programme to upgrade clearing, settlement, and depository systems


2016 (Jan)
Phase 1 of new Post-Trade System (PTS) went live – clearing, settlement, and payment APIs with ISO 20022 messaging [Source: SWIFT Case Study]


2018 (Dec)
Phase 2 of PTS launched – new securities settlement and depository framework, powered by LSEG Technology; settlement cycle shortened from T+3 to T+2; true DVP settlement introduced [Source: LSEG Press Release]


2019 (Jul)
Enhancements to default management capabilities implemented [Source: Allen & Gledhill]


2019 (Dec)
Securities Borrowing and Lending (SBL) programme enhanced with variable rates [Source: SGX Group Media Centre]


2022 (Jun)
SGX CDP made available Marketnode’s DLT-enabled direct-to-depository service for digital bond issuance [Source: SGX Group Media Centre]


2023 (May)
Refinements to CDP margin and clearing fund frameworks implemented [Source: Allen & Gledhill]


2024
SGX Group revised cap on clearing members’ liability for multiple defaults [Source: Mondovisione]

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services
CDP acts as the central counterparty for all securities traded on SGX-ST, providing clearing services for the following:







Product Class
Description




Equities
Ordinary shares, preference shares listed on SGX-ST


Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
All ETFs listed on SGX-ST


REITs & Business Trusts
Real Estate Investment Trusts and business trusts


Fixed Income
Listed corporate bonds, government bonds


Warrants & Structured Products
Structured warrants, daily leverage certificates


Depository Receipts
Singapore Depository Receipts


Unit Trusts
Exchange-traded unit trusts


Extended Settlement (ES) Contracts
Marginable futures-like contracts on single stocks


Rights
Rights issues during corporate actions



[Source: SGX Clearing Information]


2.2 Novation Process
CDP becomes the counterparty to each side of a transaction through novation as soon as the trade is executed or reported on SGX-ST. The novation process differs based on membership type:

Both parties are Clearing Members (CMs): The trade is directly novated to CDP, with CDP becoming the buyer to the selling CM and the seller to the buying CM.
One party is a Trading Member (TM), the other a CM: The qualifying CM assumes the rights, duties, and obligations of the counterparty TM, and the transaction is then novated to CDP.
Both parties are Trading-only Members: The respective qualifying CMs assume the rights and obligations of each TM, and the transaction is then novated to CDP.

[Source: SGX Rulebook – Rule 6.2 Clearing and Novation]

KRX Comparison: KRX follows a similar novation model – upon trade execution on the exchange, KRX interposes itself as the CCP to both sides. The key difference is that KRX operates as a single integrated exchange-CCP entity, while CDP is a separate legal subsidiary within the SGX Group.



2.3 Netting
CDP operates a multilateral netting system:

Securities Netting: Net securities obligations are calculated per Clearing Member per security. On T+2, each CM has a single net delivery or receive obligation for each security.
Cash Netting: Net cash obligations are calculated per Clearing Member. A single net pay or receive amount is determined for each settlement day.
Netting Cut-off: Netting occurs at end of trade day for trades executed that day, with settlement obligations due on T+2.



2.4 Clearing Membership
CDP has two categories of clearing membership:








Type
Minimum Capital
Key Requirements




General Clearing Member (GCM)
S$5 million base capital (or S$8 million if also a clearing member of SGX-DC)
Must be Singapore-registered corporation; hold Capital Markets Services Licence (unless exempt); register a CEO; maintain reserve fund (30% of audited net profits transferred annually until base capital less unappropriated profits reaches S$15 million)


Bank Clearing Member (BCM)
No specific minimum (subject to banking regulations)
Must be authorised to conduct banking business in Singapore; must have adequate credit rating indicating intrinsic safety and soundness



[Source: SGX Rulebook – Rule 3 Membership; SGX Rulebook – Rule 5 Financial/Capital Requirements]
Additional requirements: - CDP may prescribe additional capital, financial, and other requirements based on volume, risk exposure, risk concentration, margin policies, and nature of business conducted - GCMs can clear for their own account and for Trading Members they have qualified (sponsored) - BCMs can clear for custodial clients

KRX Comparison: KRX clearing membership requires minimum net capital of KRW 10 billion (~S$10 million) for securities clearing members, broadly comparable to CDP’s S$5 million threshold.

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
CDP employs a risk-based margining framework for its clearing members:







Parameter
Details




Margin Methodology
Risk-based margin calculated at a confidence level of at least 99% [Source: SGX CDP PFMI Disclosure]


Close-out Period
1 to 5 days depending on contract liquidity


Margin Calculation Frequency
At least twice daily (intraday and end-of-day)


Margin Types
Initial Margin, Variation Margin, Additional Margin (concentration, wrong-way risk)


Collateral Accepted
Cash (SGD), government securities, and other approved collateral with appropriate haircuts [unverified – specific collateral schedule not confirmed from public sources]



Key features of the margin framework (post-May 2023 refinements): - Initial margin is designed to cover potential losses during the close-out period at a 99% confidence level - Margin calculations incorporate both current market risk and historical stress scenarios - CDP may call for additional margin during periods of heightened volatility
[Source: Allen & Gledhill – CDP Margin and Clearing Fund Refinements]


3.2 Margin Call Schedule








Cycle
Timing
Description




Intraday Margin
During trading hours
CDP monitors positions intraday and may issue margin calls to cover shortfalls in margin requirements and potential mark-to-market losses


End-of-Day Margin
After market close
Full margin recalculation; margin calls issued for any shortfall


Margin Call Deadline
Within one Trading Day
Clearing Members must meet margin calls within one Trading Day after the event giving rise to the margin call


Customer Margin Restoration
Within two Market Days
CMs must call from customers to restore to Initial Margin level within 2 Market Days of Customer Asset Value falling below Customer Required Margins



[Source: SGX Rulebook – Rule 6A Margin Requirements; SGX Rulebook – Regulatory Notice 3.3.12]


3.3 Default Waterfall (with approximate sizes)
CDP’s default waterfall specifies the order in which financial resources are applied following a clearing member default:








Layer
Resource
Approximate Size / Notes




1
Defaulter’s Margin
Margins and collateral posted by the defaulting CM; first line of defence


2
Defaulter’s Clearing Fund Contribution
The defaulting CM’s funded contribution to the Clearing Fund


3
CDP’s Skin-in-the-Game (SITG)
CDP’s own capital contribution to the Clearing Fund – at least 25% of the total Clearing Fund [unverified – exact current CDP SITG amount not confirmed; the 25% ratio is derived from SGX Group-level statements]


4
Non-Defaulting CMs’ Funded Clearing Fund Contributions
Funded contributions from other (non-defaulting) Clearing Members


5
Non-Defaulting CMs’ Contingent Contributions
Unfunded (callable) contributions from non-defaulting CMs – utilised only after all funded resources are exhausted (per 2023 refinements)


6
CDP’s Remaining Capital
Any remaining financial resources of CDP



Clearing Fund Size: - Total CDP Clearing Fund: S$80 million (as of 30 June 2024 and 31 December 2024) [Source: SGX Group Financial Results FY2024/H1 FY2025] - For comparison, SGX-DC Clearing Fund: S$557 million (as of same dates)
Key 2023 Refinements: - Contingent contributions from non-defaulting CMs were deprioritised – funded contributions (of both CMs and CDP) are now utilised ahead of unfunded resources - A cap was placed on clearing members’ total clearing fund liability to give certainty on maximum exposure - CDP’s own contribution was structured to be at least 25% of the total clearing fund, which SGX states is proportionately higher than many other CCPs in Europe and the US
[Source: Allen & Gledhill; SGX Group Financial Results H1 FY2025]

KRX Comparison: KRX’s Joint Compensation Fund for the securities market was approximately KRW 100 billion (~S$100 million) as of 2023, broadly comparable in scale to CDP’s S$80 million. KRX also places its own contribution (skin-in-the-game) in the waterfall ahead of non-defaulting members’ contributions, consistent with CPMI-IOSCO guidance. [unverified – KRX fund size approximate]



3.4 Default Fund / Guarantee Fund
The CDP Clearing Fund is sized and managed as follows:







Parameter
Details




Total Fund Size
S$80 million (as of Dec 2024)


CDP SITG Contribution
At least 25% of the Clearing Fund


CM Funded Contribution
Based on a percentage of average daily risk margin (post-2023 methodology)


CM Contingent Contribution
Callable, capped, and used only after funded resources exhausted


Fund Sizing Methodology
Revised in 2023 – changed approach for sizing the Clearing Fund to be more risk-sensitive


Fund Review Frequency
Reviewed periodically; fund calls can be made if contributions are insufficient



[Source: SGX RegCo Consultation Paper on CDP Margining and Clearing Fund (Nov 2022)]


3.5 Stress Testing & Back-testing
CDP conducts regular stress testing and back-testing as part of its PFMI compliance:

Stress Testing: CDP performs stress tests of its financial resources to ensure adequacy under extreme but plausible market conditions. These include both historical stress scenarios and hypothetical scenarios. [unverified – specific stress scenario details not publicly disclosed]
Back-testing: Margin models are back-tested to validate that they achieve the targeted coverage level (99% confidence). Results are reviewed regularly and models are recalibrated as needed. [unverified – specific back-testing results not publicly disclosed]
MAS Oversight: MAS conducts supervisory assessments of CDP’s risk management practices, including its stress testing framework. [Source: MAS Parliamentary Reply on CDP Oversight (2024)]



3.6 Recovery & Resolution

Recovery Tools: CDP has recovery plans that include tools such as variation margin haircutting, partial tear-up, and voluntary auction mechanisms to manage residual losses beyond the default waterfall. [unverified – specific recovery plan details not publicly available]
Resolution Authority: MAS is the resolution authority for CDP as a systemically important FMI in Singapore.
Default Management Enhancements (2019): SGX implemented enhancements to the default management capabilities of both SGX-DC and CDP, including amendments to the default management process for clearing members. [Source: Allen & Gledhill (2019)]
2024 Refinements: SGX revised the cap on clearing members’ liability for multiple defaults, providing greater certainty to CMs on their maximum financial exposure. [Source: Mondovisione (2024)]

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle








Product
Settlement Cycle
Notes




Equities (shares, ETFs, REITs)
T+2
Shortened from T+3 on 10 December 2018


Listed Corporate Bonds
T+2
Aligned with equities


Singapore Government Securities (SGS)
T+1
Settled via MAS’s MEPS+ system (not CDP)


Unlisted Corporate Bonds
Negotiable
Fully negotiable settlement dates


Unit Trusts
Various
Depends on fund manager’s terms



[Source: Clearstream – Settlement Process Singapore; DBS Vickers – New Securities Settlement Framework]

KRX Comparison: KRX also settles equities on T+2 (moved from T+3 in 2024). Both markets are now aligned with the global standard. The US moved to T+1 in May 2024; Singapore has not yet announced plans for T+1 migration. [unverified – Singapore T+1 status]



4.2 DVP Model
CDP operates a true DVP (Delivery versus Payment) model since the December 2018 system upgrade:







Feature
Details




DVP Type
BIS Model 3 – gross securities settlement with net cash settlement [unverified – exact BIS model classification]


Securities Settlement
Book-entry transfer within CDP; settlement only finalised once intraday batch or RTGS is completed


Cash Settlement
Via settlement banks through MAS’s MEPS+ RTGS system for SGD; multi-currency settlement supported


Settlement Windows
Settlement from 09:00 on settlement date; multiple intraday batch settlement cycles


Simultaneous Settlement
Securities and cash settle simultaneously – securities delivery occurs only upon confirmed cash payment



[Source: DBS Vickers – New Securities Settlement Framework]


4.3 Settlement Finality
Settlement finality is clearly defined under CDP rules:

Securities Finality: Delivery of securities is effected and final upon CDP debiting the securities from the Delivering Securities Account. Receipt is final upon CDP crediting the securities into the Receiving Securities Account.
Cash Finality: Settlement of a Settlement Participant’s payment obligation is effected and final upon CDP debiting an equivalent sum of money from the Settlement Participant’s Cash Ledger Account.
Legal Basis: Settlement finality is protected under the Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA), which provides statutory protection for the irrevocability and finality of settlements effected through approved clearing houses.

[Source: SGX Rulebook – CDP Settlement Rules]


4.4 CSD / Settlement Infrastructure
CDP operates as Singapore’s sole CSD for exchange-traded securities:







Function
Details




Securities Held
All SGX-listed securities including equities, corporate bonds, ETFs, REITs, warrants, structured products, unit trusts, depository receipts


Account Types
Direct Securities Account (for individual retail investors linked directly to CDP); Sub-Account (held under a Depository Agent such as a broker or custodian bank)


Immobilisation
SGX-listed securities are immobilised – all securities are held in book-entry form at CDP


Corporate Actions
CDP processes dividends, rights issues, bonus issues, share splits, and other corporate actions on behalf of account holders


Number of Accounts
Over 1.5 million CDP Securities Accounts held by retail investors [unverified – approximate figure based on industry reports]



Key Statistics (FY2025, July 2024 – June 2025): - Securities Daily Average Traded Value (SDAV): S$1.34 billion (up 26.5% YoY) - Total Securities Traded Value: S$336.4 billion (up 27.5% YoY) - Average Net Clearing Fees: 2.59 basis points (up from 2.46 bps)
[Source: SGX Group Annual Report FY2025]


4.5 CSD Linkages
CDP maintains cross-border linkages with international CSDs and settlement systems:



Counterpart
Type
Description




Clearstream Banking Luxembourg (CBL)
CSD Link
CBL clients can settle transactions with counterparties who are direct account holders with CDP; allegements accepted via depository from domestic market counterparties [Source: Clearstream – Settlement Services Singapore]


Euroclear
Indirect Link
Access to Singapore market securities through correspondent relationships [unverified – specific link details not confirmed]


MAS MEPS+
Cash Settlement
CDP uses MAS’s MEPS+ RTGS system for SGD cash settlement; MEPS+ also handles SGS bond settlement directly


Settlement Banks
Banking Interface
CDP interfaces with designated settlement banks (e.g., DBS, OCBC, UOB, international banks) for cash settlement on behalf of clearing members




KRX/KSD Comparison: KSD maintains bilateral CSD linkages with over 50 foreign CSDs and ICSDs for cross-border settlement. CDP’s linkage network is smaller, reflecting Singapore’s different market positioning as a financial hub with strong custodial bank intermediation.



4.6 Securities Lending & Borrowing
CDP operates the SGX Securities Borrowing and Lending (SBL) programme:







Feature
Details




Role
CDP acts as principal counterparty to both lender and borrower; lenders take on counterparty risk of CDP, not the borrower


Eligibility (Lender)
Retail and institutional investors with CDP securities accounts; minimum holdings: 10,000 units for shares priced <=S$1, or S$10,000 in value for shares priced >S$1


Borrowing Rate
0.5% for index stocks, REITs, business trusts; 4.0% for other securities (as of Dec 2019 variable rate introduction)


Lending Fee
Lenders receive 70% of the borrowing fee


Title Transfer
Legal ownership temporarily transferred to borrower; voting rights suspended during lending period; economic benefits (dividends) retained by lender


Registration Fee
Free for lenders



[Source: SGX Group Media Centre – SBL Enhancement (2019); SGX Securities Lending Pool]

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
5. Technology & Infrastructure

5.1 Interface Protocols







Component
Details




Post-Trade System (PTS)
New system implemented in two phases (Phase 1: Jan 2016, Phase 2: Dec 2018); powered by LSEG Technology


Messaging Standard
ISO 20022 – adopted for settlement processing; structured XML-based messaging


Connectivity
API-based connectivity allowing members flexibility to adopt “best of breed” solutions; members can connect via SWIFT network or direct API


Web Interface
SGX-PTS WEB – single web-based system for settlement, replacing legacy systems (PSMS, Enhanced DVP, E-Hub, DCSS)


Legacy System Replacement
New PTS replaced four legacy systems as of 10 December 2018



[Source: SWIFT Case Study – SGX ISO 20022; LSEG Technology Press Release (2018)]


5.2 Resilience







Feature
Details




Business Continuity
CDP maintains business continuity and disaster recovery plans as required by MAS for systemically important FMIs [unverified – specific BCP/DR details not publicly disclosed]


Operational Uptime
Target of 99.9%+ system availability [unverified]


Cyber Security
Subject to MAS Technology Risk Management (TRM) guidelines; MAS conducts regular supervisory technology risk assessments [Source: MAS regulatory framework]


Data Centre
Primary and secondary data centre facilities [unverified – specific locations not publicly disclosed]


DLT Capabilities
Marketnode integration for DLT-enabled bond issuance – separate distributed ledger layer that connects into CDP’s core depository infrastructure

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
6. Regulatory Framework (MAS Oversight)
CDP is regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) under multiple frameworks:







Framework
Details




Securities and Futures Act 2001 (SFA)
CDP is licensed as an Approved Clearing House (ACH) and operates a central depository system. MAS has powers to regulate, inspect, investigate, and enforce compliance.


Payment Systems (Oversight) Act (PS(O)A)
MAS may designate CDP’s payment and settlement systems under PS(O)A, subjecting them to additional oversight requirements including access regime provisions.


Companies Act
CDP is additionally regulated as a central depository under the Companies Act.


PFMI Standards
CDP is expected to observe the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures and publishes periodic self-assessments.


MAS Supervisory Powers
Include power to request information, make regulations, inspect, investigate, establish access regimes, and issue directions.



Key Regulatory Requirements for CDP: - Fair and objective access criteria for participation - Safe and efficient functioning of clearing facility - Protection of the investing public - Adequate financial resources and risk management - Regular reporting and disclosure to MAS
[Source: MAS – Clearing Houses; MAS – ACH/RCH Licence]

KRX Comparison: KRX is supervised by the Financial Services Commission (FSC) and Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) of Korea. Unlike CDP which is a private company subsidiary of a listed exchange, KRX is a special-purpose corporation established under the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act.

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
7. Interoperability
CDP does not currently maintain formal CCP interoperability arrangements (CCP links) with other CCPs for cross-margining or mutual clearing. Its interoperability is primarily through:

CSD Linkages: As described in Section 4.5, CDP maintains links with Clearstream and indirect access via Euroclear for cross-border settlement
SGX Group Integration: Within SGX Group, CDP and SGX-DC operate as complementary but separate clearing entities – CDP for securities and SGX-DC for derivatives. There is no formal cross-margining between the two entities. [unverified – cross-margining status]
ASEAN Linkage: SGX has been involved in ASEAN exchange connectivity initiatives (ASEAN Trading Link, launched 2012 but discontinued), which aimed to enable cross-border trading and settlement across ASEAN exchanges. [Source: Industry reports]

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
8. Fees
CDP charges clearing and settlement fees to Clearing Members based on its published fee schedules:








Fee Type
Rate / Amount
Notes




Clearing Fee
~0.0325% of trade value
Average net clearing fee was 2.59 bps in FY2025; actual rates vary by product and volume tier [Source: SGX Group Annual Report FY2025]


Settlement Fee
Per settlement instruction
Charged to Settlement Participants [unverified – specific per-instruction fee not confirmed]


Depository Fee
Free for retail CDP accounts
No custody fees for retail investors holding securities in direct CDP accounts


Corporate Action Processing
Various
Fees for processing dividends, rights issues, etc. [unverified – specific fee schedule not confirmed]


SBL Fees
0.5% – 4.0% borrowing rate
CDP retains 30% of borrowing fee; lenders receive 70%


Account Opening
Free
No charge for opening a CDP Securities Account



Note: Specific detailed fee schedules are published in the SGX Rulebook and updated periodically.

title: Central Depository Pte Ltd (CDP)
text:
9. Recent Developments

2022 – Marketnode DLT Direct-to-Depository Service
SGX CDP made available Marketnode’s DLT-enabled direct-to-depository service for debt issuers. The platform eliminates paper trails and reduces bond settlement time by 60% (from T+5 to T+2). OCBC Bank’s US$100 million Euro Commercial Paper issuance was the first transaction on the platform. Over S$1 billion in digital bonds have been issued through the platform. [Source: SGX Group (Jun 2022); Marketnode]


2023 – Margin and Clearing Fund Framework Refinements
Effective 26 May 2023 (rules) and 12 June 2023 (margin methodology), CDP implemented significant changes: - Revised approach for sizing the Clearing Fund to be more risk-sensitive - Deprioritised contingent contributions – funded resources now utilised first - Cap on clearing members’ total clearing fund liability - CDP maintains skin-in-the-game at minimum 25% of the Clearing Fund
[Source: Allen & Gledhill (2023)]


2024 – Revised Clearing Member Liability Cap for Multiple Defaults
SGX Group refined the cap on clearing members’ liability for multiple defaults, providing CMs with greater certainty on their maximum financial exposure in tail-risk events involving sequential defaults. [Source: Mondovisione (Mar 2024)]


2025 – Strong Market Activity
FY2025 (July 2024 – June 2025) saw significantly increased activity: - Securities daily average traded value reached S$1.34 billion (up 26.5%) - Total securities traded value reached S$336.4 billion (up 27.5%)
[Source: SGX Group Annual Report FY2025]


Digital Asset and Blockchain Initiatives

SGX and Temasek established Marketnode as a joint venture for digital market infrastructure
MAS and SGX successfully piloted blockchain technology for settlement of tokenised assets (Project Ubin) [Source: MAS Media Release (2018)]
SGX Derivatives (separate from CDP) launched Bitcoin and Ethereum perpetual futures in November 2025

2. Settlement Model

2.1 Clearstream Banking S.A. (CBL – ICSD)
As one of two global ICSDs, CBL provides settlement and custody for international securities (primarily Eurobonds) and cross-border transactions:

Book-Entry Settlement: All securities held in dematerialized or immobilized form; transfers through book entries
Multi-Currency Settlement: Settles in multiple currencies with commercial bank money (CMB) via correspondent banking relationships
Internal Settlement: Transactions between two CBL participants settle internally on CBL’s books
Bridge Settlement: Transactions between CBL and Euroclear Bank participants settle via the Bridge (see Section 7)
External Settlement: Transactions involving securities held at other CSDs settle through CBL’s network of links



2.2 Clearstream Europe AG (CSD – Germany + Pan-European)
Clearstream Europe (formerly CBF) serves as: - German Domestic CSD: Settlement and custody for all German domestic securities - Pan-European CSD: Via T2S, provides access to 19 European markets through a single point of entry - T2S Settlement: Uses central bank money (EUR) via TARGET2 for the cash leg; real-time gross settlement (RTGS) - Over 50% of T2S Volume: Clearstream Europe consistently handles more than half of all T2S settlement traffic

title: Clearstream (Clearstream)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
Clearstream (as a CSD/ICSD) does not operate as a CCP and does not collect traditional margins. Risk management focuses on:

DVP Settlement: Simultaneous exchange of securities and cash eliminates principal risk
Credit Facilities: CBL provides credit extensions to participants secured by pledged collateral
Collateral Valuation: Securities used as collateral are marked-to-market daily with conservative haircuts
Exposure Limits: Participant-specific credit and exposure limits monitored in real time
Liquidity Risk Management: Cash forecasting and management of settlement liquidity across currencies



3.3 Default Waterfall
As a CSD/ICSD (not CCP), Clearstream does not maintain a mutualized default fund. Risk absorption follows:

Defaulter’s pledged collateral – CBL has the right to liquidate securities pledged by the defaulting participant
Clearstream’s own capital – capital buffers maintained under CRR/CRD requirements
No loss mutualization – non-defaulting participants are not called upon to absorb losses



3.6 Recovery & Resolution

CSDR Framework: Subject to EU CSD Recovery and Resolution requirements
Banking Resolution: CBL, as a licensed credit institution, is subject to the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD)
Resolution Authority: CSSF (Luxembourg) for CBL; BaFin/SRB for Clearstream Europe AG
Systemic Importance: Designated as systemically important financial market infrastructure
Banking License Review (2025): Deutsche Borse Group is reviewing whether Clearstream Europe AG needs to retain its banking license under the amended CSDR; CBL will continue to leverage its CRR license as the Service CSD of the group

7. Interoperability

7.1 The Bridge (Clearstream-Euroclear)
The Bridge is the critical interoperability link between the two global ICSDs:

Purpose: Enables settlement of securities transactions between Clearstream Banking Luxembourg and Euroclear Bank participants
Settlement: Both free-of-payment and delivery-versus-payment transactions
Processing: Multiple overnight batch exchanges plus Automated Daytime Bridge for real-time settlement during business hours
DVP Model: Model 1 (simultaneous, final transfer)
CSDR Status: The Bridge link is explicitly covered under CBL’s CSDR authorization
History: Operational since the 1970s; continuously modernized



7.2 CSD Links Network
Clearstream maintains an extensive global network of CSD links:

Clearstream Europe: Direct T2S links to 19 European markets; additional links to non-T2S markets

title: China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Limited (CSDC / ChinaClear)
text:
2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services
CSDC acts as the central counterparty for all exchange-traded securities in China, becoming the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer upon trade execution. Its CCP function covers:








Segment
Products
Exchange




Equities
A-shares, B-shares, CDRs
SSE, SZSE, BSE


Fixed Income
Treasury bonds, corporate bonds, convertible bonds
SSE, SZSE


Funds
ETFs, LOFs, closed-end funds
SSE, SZSE


Derivatives
Stock options (e.g., SSE 50 ETF options, CSI 300 ETF options)
SSE, SZSE


Other
Margin lending securities, asset-backed securities
SSE, SZSE



[Source: CSDC Company Profile; SSE Clearing and Settlement]

Note: CSDC does not clear financial futures or commodity derivatives – these are handled by China Financial Futures Exchange (CFFEX) and commodity exchanges (Shanghai Futures Exchange, Dalian Commodity Exchange, Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange) respectively, each with their own clearing houses. This contrasts with KRX, where a single CCP clears both equities and listed derivatives.



2.3 Netting
CSDC employs multilateral netting as its primary clearing method for exchange-traded securities:

Securities netting: Net obligations of the same security issue with the same settlement date are calculated for each clearing participant
Funds netting: Net payment obligations are computed across all transactions for each participant on a given settlement date
CSDC interposes itself as CCP, providing guaranteed settlement through multilateral netting
The netting process runs after market close, with net positions calculated for T+1 settlement

[Source: SSE Clearing and Settlement; CSDC Settlement Rules]

Comparison with KRX/KSD: Both CSDC and KRX use multilateral netting for equity trades. KRX similarly interposes as CCP and nets obligations across all participants. The netting methodology is conceptually similar, though KRX operates on a T+2 settlement cycle (since 2024) while CSDC uses T+1.



2.4 Clearing Membership
CSDC operates a tiered clearing participant structure:







Type
Description




Clearing Participants
Securities companies, banks, and other institutions that directly settle with CSDC


Settlement Banks
Designated commercial banks that provide funds settlement services (including Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, etc.)


Custodian Banks
Banks approved to provide securities custody for QFII/RQFII investors




CSDC’s Shanghai Branch handles clearing for SSE-listed securities
CSDC’s Shenzhen Branch handles clearing for SZSE-listed securities
CSDC’s Beijing Data Branch handles BSE and NEEQ (New Third Board) clearing

[Source: CSDC Company Profile]

title: China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Limited (CSDC / ChinaClear)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
CSDC employs several risk management tools to ensure settlement integrity:



Tool
Description




Settlement Reserve Fund (结算备付金)
Mandatory minimum cash reserves that clearing participants must maintain with CSDC. Minimum ratio reduced from 18% to 16% in April 2024 for stock-related business [Source: Xinhua Silk Road]


Settlement Guarantee Fund (结算保证金)
Collective fund contributed by clearing participants to cover potential default losses


Mark-to-Market
Daily marking of open positions and margin calls


DVP Linkage
Since 2022 reform, securities delivery is contingent on fund payment and vice versa, eliminating principal risk




For stock options clearing, CSDC applies initial margin, maintenance margin, and variation margin requirements similar to international practices [unverified – specific methodology details not publicly available in English]


Comparison with KRX: KRX’s risk management framework includes initial margin (KOSPI200 options use SPAN-like methodology), settlement fund contributions, and a joint compensation fund. CSDC’s settlement reserve fund ratio mechanism (percentage-based minimum) is a distinctive Chinese approach, while KRX calculates margin requirements based on portfolio risk models.



3.3 Default Waterfall
CSDC’s default management follows a general sequence [unverified – specific waterfall structure based on inferred regulatory framework]:

Defaulting member’s settlement reserve fund – first applied to cover the default
Defaulting member’s settlement guarantee fund contribution – used if reserve fund is insufficient
CSDC’s own capital (skin in the game) – CSDC contributes its own resources
Non-defaulting members’ settlement guarantee fund contributions – loss mutualization
Additional assessment powers – CSDC may call for additional contributions


Note: Detailed public quantitative disclosures of CSDC’s default waterfall with specific monetary amounts are not readily available in English-language sources. This is a significant transparency gap compared to Western CCPs that publish detailed CPMI-IOSCO PQD reports.



3.6 Recovery & Resolution

CSDC operates under Chinese securities law and CSRC regulations for recovery and resolution
The CSRC has authority over CSDC as the resolution authority
China has not adopted a formal CCP resolution regime equivalent to the EU’s CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (CCPRRR) or the US Dodd-Frank Title II framework [unverified]
DVP reform (2022) significantly reduced settlement risk by linking securities and funds delivery

title: China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Limited (CSDC / ChinaClear)
text:
4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle
CSDC’s settlement cycles vary by product type:









Product
Securities Settlement
Funds Settlement
Notes




A-shares
T+0 (securities transfer)
T+1 (funds)
Securities are available for sale on T+0 but funds settle on T+1


B-shares
T+3
T+3
Longer cycle due to foreign currency settlement


Bonds (exchange-traded)
T+0 / T+1
T+0 / T+1
Varies by bond type


ETFs
T+0 (securities)
T+1 (funds)
Similar to A-shares


Stock Options
T+0
T+0
Real-time gross settlement


Stock Connect (Northbound)
T+0 (securities)
T+1 (funds)
Follows A-share settlement rules



[Source: WFE Focus - CSDC DVP; Clearstream Settlement Process - China]
Key Feature – T+0 Securities / T+1 Funds: China’s A-share market has a unique settlement arrangement where securities ownership transfers on T+0 (trade day), but funds settlement occurs on T+1. This means investors can sell purchased shares on the same day they are bought (from a depository perspective), though China’s “T+1 trading rule” prevents same-day selling of newly purchased shares.

Comparison with KRX/KSD: Korea moved to T+2 settlement for equities in 2024 (from T+2 already in practice). CSDC’s T+0 securities / T+1 funds model is unique globally. In Korea, both securities and funds settle simultaneously on T+2, which is a more conventional DVP approach.



4.2 DVP Model
Pre-2022 (Non-DVP): - Before January 2022, A-share settlement was not true DVP – securities and funds were settled separately without a strict conditional linkage - Settlement could only occur at the end of T+1 (16:00), creating liquidity and counterparty risk
Post-2022 DVP Reform: - CSRC launched the DVP reform on 14 January 2022 - CSDC adopted DVP Model 2 (gross securities settlement against net funds settlement): - Securities are delivered on a trade-by-trade (gross) basis - Funds are settled on a net basis after multilateral netting - Securities delivery occurs if and only if funds are paid, and vice versa - After the reform, participants can provide funds earlier during T+1 to complete settlement, rather than waiting until 16:00 - This reform aligned China’s capital market closer to international PFMI standards (Principle 12: Exchange-of-value settlement systems)
[Source: WFE Focus - CSDC DVP Reform]

Comparison with KRX/KSD: KSD operates a DVP Model 3 (net securities against net funds) for equity settlement. CSDC’s adoption of DVP Model 2 (gross securities, net funds) is more conservative and provides greater settlement finality at the individual trade level, though it requires more securities to be pre-positioned.

text:
7. Interoperability

Stock Connect Clearing Arrangements
The most significant cross-border interoperability arrangement is the Stock Connect program linking Mainland China with Hong Kong:








Program
Launch
Clearing Link




Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect
Nov 2014
CSDC Shanghai Branch <-> HKSCC

Dec 2016

Jul 2017

Bond Connect (Southbound)
Sep 2021

Clearing Link Mechanism: - CSDC and HKSCC became each other’s clearing participant - For Northbound trades (international investors buying A-shares): HKSCC settles with CSDC on behalf of its clearing participants, following A-share settlement rules (T+0 securities / T+1 funds) - For Southbound trades (Mainland investors buying HK stocks): CSDC settles with HKSCC on behalf of its clearing participants, following HK settlement rules (T+2) - Each CCP bears the counterparty risk of its own members; CSDC and HKSCC do not guarantee each other’s members
[Source: SSE Stock Connect Settlement; SFC Joint Announcement]


Other Linkages

CCDC (China Central Depository & Clearing): CSDC handles exchange-traded bonds while CCDC handles interbank bonds – they are separate entities for different markets
Beijing Stock Exchange / NEEQ: CSDC provides clearing for BSE and the National Equities Exchange and Quotations system through its Beijing Data Branch


Comparison with KRX/KSD: KSD has established CSD links with numerous international CSDs (Euroclear, Clearstream, DTC) for cross-border settlement. CSDC’s cross-border links are more limited, primarily operating through the Stock Connect and Bond Connect frameworks, reflecting China’s managed capital account approach.

GC Pooling
GC Pooling is the European benchmark for standardised secured funding with central clearing. Key features:

Pre-defined baskets (e.g., GC Pooling ECB Basket covering ~3,000 ECB-eligible securities)
Automated connectivity to Eurex Clearing AG (CCP) and Clearstream Banking (settlement)
Available in EUR, USD, GBP, and CHF
More than 160 sell-side and buy-side institutions participate
Re-use of received collateral permitted for further money market transactions, Eurex Clearing margining, and ECB open market operations
Operating since 2005

Source: Eurex GC Pooling


Lending CCP
The Lending CCP provides centrally cleared securities lending with distinctive features:

Eurex Clearing acts as single counterparty to all trades, eliminating bilateral credit risk
Specific Lender License: Direct CCP access for beneficial owners (pension funds, asset managers) without requiring full clearing membership
Near-time intraday risk calculations with intraday margin calls for collateral shortfalls
Triparty collateral agents connected for non-cash collateral management
Covers international fixed income, European equities, and ETFs
Partnership with Pirum for post-trade automation; integration with EquiLend for trade sourcing

Sources: Eurex Lending CCP; Eurex Clearing Lending CCP Enhancements



2.2 Novation Process

Novation by open offer: For exchange-traded products on Eurex Exchange and Frankfurt Stock Exchange, Eurex Clearing interposes itself as the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer at the point of trade execution.
Novation for OTC products: For OTC IRS and repo transactions, the bilateral trade is replaced by two separate contracts with Eurex Clearing as CCP upon trade registration/acceptance.
Straight-through processing: GC Pooling and repo clearing provide fully automated STP from trade execution through CCP clearing to settlement at Clearstream.



2.3 Netting

Multilateral netting: Eurex Clearing performs multilateral netting across all cleared positions, reducing gross exposures to a single net obligation per clearing member per product/settlement date.
Portfolio compression: For OTC IRS, compression services reduce the number of line items and gross notional outstanding.
Prisma cross-margining netting: Within liquidation groups, Prisma provides portfolio-level netting that recognizes hedging and diversification effects across correlated products.
