3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework: Eurex Clearing Prisma
Eurex Clearing Prisma (Portfolio-based Risk management by Simulating scenario Matrices and Assessing market risks) is Eurex Clearing’s proprietary portfolio-based margin methodology, introduced in 2012.

Core Methodology







Parameter
Specification




Model Type
Filtered Historical Simulation (FHS) with Value-at-Risk (VaR)


Confidence Level
99% for listed products; 99.5% for OTC instruments


Effective Confidence Level
Exceeds target levels (verified via backtesting)


Historical Scenarios
750 filtered-historical scenarios with 3-year lookback period


Stress Scenarios
250 stress period scenarios from identified historical stress episodes


Event Risk Scenarios
Supplementary scenarios for specific risk factors (e.g., single stock dividend futures)


Holding Period – Listed Equity Derivatives
2-3 days (PEQ01 liquidation group reduced from 4 to 3 days; subsequently to 2 days for some)


Holding Period – Listed Fixed Income
2 days (PFI01_HP2 split)


Holding Period – OTC IRS
5 days (PFI01_HP5 split)


Risk Measure
Maximum of VaR from filtered historical sample and VaR from stress period sample


Procyclicality Mitigation
Stress period VaR serves as prudent margin floor during low-volatility regimes; annual recalibration of margin floors



Sources: Eurex Clearing Prisma; ECC Prisma for Commodities; Part 8: Forward Looking Margin Simulations


Margin Components
Prisma initial margin consists of multiple components:

Market Risk Initial Margin (MRIM): Core risk component based on filtered historical simulation; captures potential portfolio value changes under historical and stress scenarios
Liquidity Adjustment (LA): Accounts for the cost of liquidating concentrated positions; adjusts for bid-ask spread widening and market impact during portfolio close-out
KnockIn / Event Risk Component: Additional margin for specific risk events (e.g., barrier events for structured products, dividend event risk for single stock derivatives)

The backward-looking component (filtered historical VaR) ensures model reactivity to changing market conditions, while the forward-looking component (stress period VaR) ensures margin stability and counters procyclicality.


Liquidation Groups
Products are organized into Liquidation Groups based on shared risk characteristics. Key liquidation groups include:








Liquidation Group
Products
Holding Period




PFI01 (Fixed Income)
Listed fixed income futures/options + OTC IRS

Source: Eurex Clearing Prisma Circular on PEQ01; Prisma Bonds Circular


Cross-Margining
Cross-margining is a distinctive feature of Prisma, enabling margin offsets between products with different holding periods:

Listed-OTC Cross-Margining: Within PFI01, cross-margining is offered between OTC IRS (5-day holding period) and listed fixed income products (2-day holding period)
Algorithm: The system checks whether listed FI/MM positions are economically sensible hedges to the OTC portfolio; if so, these positions are moved to the 5-day split to lower total margin
Margin Efficiency: Potential margin savings of up to 70% depending on portfolio composition
Advantage over SPAN: Unlike CME’s SPAN methodology (which calculates margin product-by-product with limited inter-commodity spreads), Prisma assesses risk at the portfolio level using full revaluation under historical scenarios, enabling more accurate capture of hedging benefits

3.3 Stress Testing & Back-Testing







Requirement
Implementation

3.4 Recovery & Resolution
Eurex Clearing operates under the EU CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2021/23), fully applicable since 12 February 2023.
Recovery Tools: - Variation Margin Gains Haircutting (VMGH): Reduction of VM payments to non-defaulting members to cover uncovered losses - Cash calls / Assessments: Non-defaulting members can be required to contribute additional funds (up to 2x their Default Fund contribution) - Position allocation / Forced allocation: Transfer or termination of the defaulting member’s portfolio - Partial tear-up: Termination of contracts where necessary to restore matched book
Resolution Tools (BaFin as Resolution Authority): - Resolution Cash Calls: BaFin can require non-defaulting members to provide further contributions up to 2x their applicable contribution requirement - Write-down and conversion tools: Authority to write down liabilities or convert claims - Position and loss allocation tools: BaFin can allocate positions and losses - Transfer tools: Transfer of clearing member positions to a bridge CCP or another CCP
Clearing members are contractually bound by any resolution tools taken by BaFin, including those affecting their assets, rights, obligations, and liabilities.

4.3 Settlement Finality

Legal basis: German law (specifically the German implementation of the EU Settlement Finality Directive 98/26/EC)

Central bank money finality: Settlement in EUR via T2 provides central bank money finality under Eurosystem rules

8.4 Membership Fees
Membership-related fees include application fees, annual membership fees, and connectivity charges. These are separate from transaction-based clearing fees and are detailed in the applicable fee schedules.


8.5 Prisma Margin Netting Benefits
The Prisma portfolio-based margining approach provides significant economic benefits to clearing members: - Cross-margining savings: Up to 70% margin reduction for portfolios with offsetting listed FI and OTC IRS positions - Portfolio margining: Full netting within liquidation groups, recognizing hedging and correlation effects - Capital efficiency: More accurate risk assessment leads to lower capital requirements under Basel III/CRD IV compared to standardized or bilateral approaches - Single collateral pool: One margin pool across listed and OTC positions reduces operational complexity and collateral fragmentation

title: Euroclear Group (Euroclear)
text:
2. Settlement Model

2.1 Euroclear Bank (ICSD)
Euroclear Bank serves as the primary ICSD for international securities, particularly Eurobonds. Its settlement model operates as follows:

Book-Entry Settlement: All securities are held in dematerialized or immobilized form; settlement occurs through book-entry transfers in Euroclear Bank’s accounts
Batch and Real-Time Processing: Settlement occurs during overnight batch processing cycles and during the daytime real-time settlement window
Multi-Currency: Settles transactions against payment in 51 currencies
Multi-Market Access: Provides access to domestic securities of 48 markets through a single account (via links with local CSDs and agent banks)



2.2 Core CSD Services (under CSDR)
Euroclear Bank is authorized to perform three core CSD services: 1. Notary Service – initial recording of securities in book-entry form 2. Central Maintenance Service – maintaining securities accounts at the top tier level 3. Settlement Service – operating a securities settlement system


2.3 The Bridge (Euroclear-Clearstream)
The Bridge is the electronic settlement link between Euroclear Bank and Clearstream Banking Luxembourg, the two global ICSDs:

Facilitates settlement of securities transactions between counterparties holding accounts at different ICSDs
Operates on a DVP Model 1 basis (simultaneous, final transfer of securities and cash)
Multiple overnight settlement exchanges plus an Automated Daytime Bridge during business hours
Critical infrastructure for the Eurobond market, where securities may be held in either ICSD



2.4 Euroclear Group CSDs
Each national CSD operates settlement services for its domestic market: - ESES CSDs (Belgium, France, Netherlands): Shared settlement platform; connected to T2S since 2015-2016 - Euroclear Finland: Connected to T2S since September 2023 - Euroclear Sweden: Not connected to T2S (Swedish krona market) - Euroclear UK & International: Operates the CREST real-time gross settlement system; not connected to T2S (post-Brexit)
[Source: Euroclear – Settlement Services, https://www.euroclear.com/services/en/settlement.html] [Source: Euroclear – Settlement Euroclear Bank, https://www.euroclear.com/services/en/settlement/settlement-euroclear-bank.html]

title: Euroclear Group (Euroclear)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
Euroclear Bank is not a CCP and does not collect margins in the traditional CCP sense. However, it manages credit and liquidity risk through:

DVP Settlement: Simultaneous exchange of securities and cash eliminates principal risk
Credit Extensions: Euroclear Bank provides intraday and overnight credit to participants to facilitate settlement; credit is secured by pledged collateral (securities in participant accounts)
Collateral Haircuts: Securities pledged as collateral are subject to haircuts based on asset type, maturity, and market risk
Credit Limits: Each participant has defined credit limits; exposures are monitored in real time
Pre-Settlement Risk: Managed through mark-to-market valuation and collateral requirements



3.3 Default Waterfall
As a CSD/ICSD (not a CCP), Euroclear Bank does not have a traditional default waterfall. Instead:

Secured Credit: All credit extensions are backed by collateral with appropriate haircuts
Loss Absorption: In the event of a participant default, Euroclear Bank has the right to liquidate pledged collateral
Capital Buffers: Euroclear Bank maintains capital in accordance with CRR/CRD requirements as a licensed Belgian credit institution
No Mutualized Default Fund: Unlike CCPs, there is no mutualized default fund; losses are absorbed by the defaulter’s collateral first, then by Euroclear Bank’s own capital



3.6 Recovery & Resolution

CSD Recovery & Resolution: Subject to the EU CSD Recovery and Resolution framework
Banking Recovery: As a licensed credit institution, Euroclear Bank is also subject to the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD)
Supervisor: National Bank of Belgium (NBB) is the resolution authority
Systemic Importance: Euroclear Bank is designated as a systemically important FMI in Belgium and globally

[Source: Euroclear – Risk Management / Pillar 3 Disclosure, https://www.euroclear.com/dam/Brochures/Pillar3_2012.pdf] [Source: IMF – Belgium FSAP 2023]

ICE Clear Credit is the world’s largest CCP for credit default swaps, with over $2 trillion in current open interest. [Source: ICE Clear Credit; NY Fed TMPG Presentation, October 2025]
ICE Clear Europe clears approximately 5 million contracts per day across multiple asset classes and is one of the world’s most significant energy derivatives clearing houses, handling the globally benchmarked Brent Crude Oil futures contract. [Source: ICE Clear Europe]


2.2 Novation Process
Upon acceptance of a trade for clearing, each ICE clearing house interposes itself as the central counterparty through novation. The original bilateral contract between buyer and seller is extinguished and replaced by two new contracts: one between the CCP and the buyer, and one between the CCP and the seller. Each clearing member’s counterparty exposure is thereby solely to the relevant ICE clearing house rather than to any bilateral counterparty.
For CDS clearing at ICE Clear Credit, the novation process involves the submission of eligible CDS contracts by clearing participants; once accepted, ICE Clear Credit becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. [Source: ICE Clear Credit – CDS Client Clearing]


2.3 Netting
Each ICE clearing house provides multilateral netting across all positions within a clearing member’s account. Variation margin is calculated and netted across all positions, resulting in a single net pay or collect amount per settlement cycle. Initial margin benefits from portfolio-based margining under the ICE Risk Model (IRM) and IRM 2, which recognise offsets and diversification within a portfolio of correlated positions.
ICE Clear Europe provides separate netting pools by product segment (Energy, Financials & Softs). [Source: ICE Clear Europe Risk Management]

3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework
ICE uses two proprietary margin models across its clearing houses:
ICE Risk Model (IRM 1) – Legacy Model:
The original ICE Risk Model calculates initial margin on at least a daily basis for futures and options. It uses a scenario-based approach similar to SPAN, evaluating potential portfolio losses across a range of price and volatility movements. Margin parameters (scanning ranges) are calibrated to cover potential losses under normal and stressed market conditions.
ICE Risk Model 2 (IRM 2) – Next-Generation VaR Model:
IRM 2 is a Filtered Historical Simulation (FHS) Value-at-Risk (VaR) methodology that represents a significant evolution from IRM 1.








Feature
IRM 1 (Legacy)
IRM 2




Methodology
Scenario-based (parametric, similar to SPAN)
Filtered Historical Simulation VaR


Risk Perspective
Instrument-by-instrument
Portfolio-level – captures all relationships and diversifying effects


Responsiveness
Static parameter updates
Dynamic – responsive to changing market conditions through volatility filtering


Anti-Procyclicality
Limited
Built-in anti-procyclical features to avoid “big step” margin changes


Stress Resilience
Scenario add-ons
Resilient against stress events and correlation breakdown


Seasonality
Not explicitly modelled
Adjusts for seasonality where appropriate



IRM 2 Calculation Steps:

Risk Factor Transformation – Market data objects are transformed from original instruments to a coherent set of risk factors (price, rate, and volatility factors required to price all traded futures and options)
Scenario Generation – Risk factors are scaled to generate risk scenarios reflecting current market conditions via filtered historical simulation
Portfolio Repricing – Relevant pricing functions convert risk factor scenarios back to instrument-level P&L
Base Margin – Portfolio VaR is calculated from the distribution of simulated P&L outcomes

3.5 Stress Testing & Back-testing
Stress Testing:
All ICE clearing houses conduct daily stress testing to assess the adequacy of their financial resources:

ICE Clear Europe: Stress tests are designed to determine whether the Guaranty Fund is sufficient to cover the simultaneous default of the two clearing member groups with the largest aggregate credit exposure under extreme but plausible market conditions. Stress scenarios include historical scenarios (e.g., 2008 financial crisis, 2020 COVID shock) and hypothetical scenarios.
ICE Clear U.S.: Conducts daily stress testing of margin and Guaranty Fund adequacy. The ICUS Guaranty Fund is designed to provide adequate funds based on Cover-2 under extreme but plausible market conditions.
ICE Clear Credit: Conducts stress testing under extreme but plausible scenarios for the CDS portfolio and the Treasury portfolio (separately).

Back-testing:
ICE conducts daily back-testing to validate that its margin models adequately cover actual portfolio losses at the required confidence level. Back-testing compares predicted margin coverage against actual observed P&L. Results are reviewed by risk committees and model calibration is adjusted as needed.
[Source: ICE Clear Europe PFMI Disclosure Framework; ICE Clear U.S. Disclosure Framework]


3.6 Recovery & Resolution
ICE Clear Europe Recovery Plan:
ICE Clear Europe maintains a comprehensive recovery plan as required by the Bank of England and filed with the SEC (for CDS clearing). The recovery plan describes tools (Recovery Options) that ICE Clear Europe could use to recover from losses:







Recovery Tool
Description




Powers of Assessment
ICE Clear Europe can immediately collect additional resources from non-defaulting clearing members intraday and in cash. Assessments are limited to a set multiple of the non-defaulting members’ Guaranty Fund contributions


Reduced Gains Distribution (RGD)
Variation margin gains haircut – ICE Clear Europe can reduce the payout of variation margin gains to non-defaulting members to cover residual losses


Investment Loss Allocation
ICE Clear Europe contributes a fixed amount of its own capital to cover losses from issuer/counterparty default on investments of clearing members’ Guaranty Fund contributions or initial margin


Non-Default Loss Allocation
Similar framework for losses unrelated to member defaults



The Recovery Plan considers factors including speed of implementation, impact on the clearing house and clearing members, and effects on other market infrastructure.
Resolution Authority:

ICE Clear Europe: The Bank of England acts as the resolution authority under the UK Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 and the Banking Act 2009.
ICE Clear Credit: The FDIC acts as the resolution authority under Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act, with the CFTC and SEC as primary supervisors.
ICE Clear U.S.: The CFTC has primary regulatory oversight.

A Crisis Management Group (CMG) arrangement exists for ICE Clear Europe, involving the Bank of England, CFTC, SEC, and other relevant authorities to coordinate supervisory and resolution activities. [Source: ICE Clear Europe CMG Framework; Federal Register – ICE Clear Europe Recovery Plan Amendments, September 2023]

4.2 DVP Model
For physically settled transactions, ICE clearing houses use delivery-versus-payment (DVP) mechanisms to ensure simultaneous exchange of securities/commodities and cash, eliminating principal risk. Cash settlement flows are processed through approved settlement banks.
ICE Clear Europe processes cash-settled futures and options through daily pay/collect of variation margin. For physically delivered contracts (e.g., Brent Crude Oil, London Cocoa), delivery procedures are specified per contract and coordinated through approved delivery facilities and settlement banks. [Source: ICE Clear Europe Operations]


4.3 Settlement Finality
ICE Clear Europe has received settlement finality designation under the Financial Markets and Insolvency (Settlement Finality) Regulations 1999 (SFR) of the United Kingdom. Under SFR, payment instructions within ICE Clear Europe’s system are protected from administrators or liquidators of insolvent firms, enhancing systemic risk protection for clearing members. [Source: ICE Clear Europe Regulation]
ICE Clear U.S. and ICE Clear Credit achieve settlement finality under U.S. law, including protections under the Commodity Exchange Act and relevant provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act. [Source: ICE Clear U.S. Disclosure Framework]

4.5 CSD Linkages
ICE Clear Europe maintains links with national emissions registries for the settlement of EU Allowances (EUAs) and Certified Emission Reductions (CERs). For financial instruments settled in securities form, ICE clearing houses interact with the relevant CSDs through approved settlement channels. Specific CSD linkage details are governed by individual contract delivery procedures. [unverified – detailed CSD linkage information not publicly available in search results]


4.6 Securities Lending & Borrowing
ICE Clear Credit accepts a range of collateral for margin purposes, including U.S. Treasury securities and certain other eligible securities. ICE clearing houses do not operate formal securities lending programs as a core service, though clearing members may post eligible securities as collateral for margin requirements, subject to appropriate haircuts.
Eligible collateral for ICE Clear Credit includes cash (USD), U.S. Treasury securities, and other approved collateral types. [Source: ICE Clear Credit Collateral Management, November 2025]

7. Interoperability
ICE’s clearing houses do not currently maintain formal CCP interoperability arrangements (i.e., links where two CCPs clear the same instruments allowing counterparties to clear at different CCPs).
However, ICE has explored and implemented cross-margining concepts:

NYPC / DTCC Cross-Margining (Historical): ICE previously operated New York Portfolio Clearing (NYPC), which linked with DTCC to provide cross-margining between interest rate futures and U.S. Treasury cash positions. This was subsequently consolidated into ICE Clear Europe operations. [Source: Finadium – NYPC consolidated into ICE Clear Europe]
Intra-ICE Offsets: While separate legal entities, ICE’s clearing houses benefit from the common ICE parent for operational efficiencies, though each maintains its own separate default waterfall and financial resources. Cross-margining across ICE entities is not formally provided. [unverified]

9. Recent Developments

ICE Clear Credit – U.S. Treasury Clearing (2025-2026)
The most significant recent development across ICE’s clearing houses is ICE Clear Credit’s entry into U.S. Treasury clearing:

August 2025: ICE Clear Credit filed application with the SEC to register as a clearing agency for U.S. Treasury securities
November 2025: SEC instituted proceedings to evaluate the application
February 2026: SEC granted approval; ICE Clear Credit’s Treasury Clearing Service became operationally live – the first alternative venue to DTCC/FICC for clearing U.S. Treasury securities

The Treasury clearing service is established as a distinct offering from the CDS clearing service with a separate rulebook, membership, risk management framework, financial and liquidity resources, and risk committee. The SEC extended the original U.S. Treasury clearing mandate deadlines by 12 months (cash transactions to December 31, 2026; repo transactions to June 30, 2027). [Source: ICE Press Release, February 2026; Federal Register – ICE Clear Credit Order, February 2026]


IRM 2 Rollout Expansion (2025)
ICE continued the phased rollout of its next-generation margin model: - Freight products at ICE Clear Europe transitioned to IRM 2 in September 2025 - Additional energy products at ICE Clear Europe transitioned in November 2025 - Remaining product groups (interest rates, equity derivatives, agricultural) remain on IRM 1 pending future phase dates
[Source: BusinessWire – ICE Launches Latest Phase of IRM 2, November 2025]


Default Insurance Renewal (2025)
ICE renewed its default insurance programme for a three-year term commencing September 17, 2025: - ICE Clear Europe: $100 million - ICE Clear Credit: $75 million - ICE Clear U.S.: $25 million
[Source: ICE Quarterly Clearing Disclosures Q3 2025]


ICE Clear Credit – Client Volume Incentive Program (2025)
In April 2025, ICE Clear Credit introduced a Client Volume Incentive Program providing tiered discounts on client clearing fees based on annual billing volumes. [Source: Federal Register, April 2025]

text:
1. Overview & Profile



Item

Country / City
South Korea / Busan (headquarters); Seoul (market operations)


Ownership Structure
Public institution under the Financial Services Commission (FSC); not a stock corporation but a member-based self-regulatory organization established by statute


Parent Company / Group
None (independent statutory entity)


Regulatory Authority
FSC (Financial Services Commission) as primary regulator; FSS (Financial Supervisory Service) conducts examination; BOK (Bank of Korea) provides systemic oversight


Clearing Model
Integrated exchange-CCP — KRX serves as both trading venue and central counterparty for all exchange-traded products


Products Cleared
Equities (KOSPI, KOSDAQ), listed derivatives (futures & options), bonds, OTC IRS/CRS


Clearing / Settlement Agent

[Source: KRX Global Website, https://global.krx.co.kr]; [Source: IMF, “Republic of Korea FSAP”, 2014]; [Source: Capital Market Act (자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률)]

Key Historical Milestones

1956: Korea Stock Exchange (KSE) established with basic clearing function for equities.
1996: Derivatives clearing function added with the launch of KOSPI 200 futures/options — one of the world’s first index derivatives products to achieve massive retail participation.
1999: Korea Futures Exchange (KOFEX) established in Busan with dedicated derivatives clearing.
2005 (January 27): Korea Exchange (KRX) formed through merger of KSE, KOFEX, and KOSDAQ; unified clearing across all market segments under one CCP.
2009: EXTURE (Exchange Trading Using Revolutionary Engine) trading/clearing system launched.
2014: IMF FSAP assessment completed, evaluating KRX’s clearing and risk management against PFMI standards.
2016: EXTURE+ next-generation platform deployed with enhanced clearing capabilities.
2021: Split settlement system introduced for equity settlement (10 billion KRW units).
2024: Split settlement units reduced from KRW 10 billion to KRW 5 billion (15-20% deposit reduction for members); derivatives daily settlement volume up 47.9% YoY.
2025 (April): KRX clearing/settlement technology exported to Thai Stock Exchange (SET).
2025 (June): Night session clearing operational (18:00-06:00 KST) for derivatives.
2026 (February): Settlement operating hours expanded from 9:00-16:10 to 7:00-16:10.
2026 (Late April): Further split settlement reduction from KRW 5 billion to KRW 1 billion units.

[Source: KRX, https://global.krx.co.kr]; [Source: WFE, “KRX Clearing Milestone”]; [Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정_전문_20260304”]

title: KRX Clearing (Korea Exchange CCP)
text:
2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services
KRX operates as an integrated exchange-CCP, a model common among Asian exchanges (similar to pre-reform structures at HKEX, SGX, and historical structures at JPX before the JSCC spin-off):

Novation: KRX interposes itself as the counterparty to all matched trades — becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer upon trade matching.
Scope: All exchange-traded products across KOSPI Market, KOSDAQ Market, derivatives market, bond market, and mandated OTC products (IRS/CRS).
Multilateral Netting: Net obligations calculated by settlement category (equity trading, bond trading, repo, derivatives).
Guarantee Function: KRX guarantees settlement of all matched trades through its default waterfall and clearing fund structure.

[Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정_전문_20260304”]


2.2 Clearing Membership
From KRX regulations (업무규정):







Category
Description




Clearing Members (결제회원)
Securities companies and other financial institutions meeting capital requirements set by FSC regulations; directly participate in KRX clearing


Membership Tiers
Based on capital adequacy and business scope — different requirements for equity, derivatives, and bond clearing


Capital Requirements
Per FSC regulations; minimum net capital requirement varies by business scope (e.g., KRW 20 billion+ for derivatives clearing)


Non-Clearing Participants
Must clear through a clearing member; the clearing member assumes guarantee obligation for the non-clearing participant’s trades


Clearing Member Obligations
Maintain clearing deposits, contribute to Joint Compensation Fund, meet margin requirements, comply with position limits



[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정_전문_20250609”]


2.3 Netting
From 증권시장 청산결제 업무규정, Article 9:







Netting Category
Description




Equity Trading (주식매매)
Multilateral netting of all buy/sell obligations per settlement date


Government Bond Market (국채시장)
Special netting provisions with separate calculation


Repo Transactions (환매채거래)
Netted independently from outright bond trades


Bond Market (채권시장)
Separate netting cycle from equity market


Derivatives
Daily mark-to-market with cash settlement of variation margin




Settlement amounts calculated to KRW 1 precision.
Netting is legally enforceable under the Capital Market Act, providing protection against insolvency claw-back.

[Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정_전문_20260304”]

title: KRX Clearing (Korea Exchange CCP)

3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework

Listed Derivatives — KRX-SPAN (Modified SPAN)
KRX employs a modified SPAN (Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk) methodology for listed derivatives margin calculation:

Methodology: Scenario-based approach drawing on CME SPAN portfolio risk concepts, adapted for Korean market characteristics.
Calculation Frequency: Daily at market close; positions marked to settlement price.
Margin Formula: Position x Price x Multiplier x Margin Rate.
Typical Initial Margin Rate: ~8-10% for KOSPI 200 futures.
Maintenance Margin Rate: ~5-6% (lower than initial margin threshold).

[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정_전문_20250609”]


Margin Types








Type
Korean Term
Description




Initial Margin
개시증거금
Required when opening new positions; must be deposited before or at time of order


Maintenance Margin
유지증거금
Minimum balance required to maintain positions; breach triggers margin call


Trading Margin
거래증거금
Cleared by exchange; due by 11:00 next trading day for member-level settlement


Client Margin
위탁증거금
Pre-funded before order entry for retail; post-funded (due by 11:00 next day) for qualified institutional investors


Spread Margin
스프레드증거금
Reduced rate for recognized spread positions (calendar, inter-commodity)



[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정_전문_20250609”]


Options Margin

Buy Orders: Full premium must be deposited in cash.
Sell Orders: Margin is the greater of three calculations involving theoretical price + volatility scenarios.
Spread Trading: Reduced margin with substitute securities allowed within limits.



Eligible Collateral (대용증권)







Collateral Type
Haircut / Acceptance Rate




Cash (현금)
100%


Listed Stocks (meeting liquidity criteria)
70-80% of market value (quarterly adjusted)


Government Bonds (국채)
Varies by maturity; generally 95-98%


Corporate Bonds (BBB+ minimum rating)
Varies by maturity and rating; generally 80-90%


ETFs and Index Securities
Accepted with restrictions on leveraged/inverse products


Foreign Currency (10 types)
USD, JPY, EUR, GBP, HKD, AUD, SGD, CHF, CAD, CNY — haircuts vary by currency



Concentration Limits: - Individual stock: Maximum 50% of average daily trading volume. - Corporate bonds: Maximum 10% of total issuance amount. - Fund securities: Maximum 10% of fund size.
Cash Requirement: Minimum 50% of total margin must be in cash; remainder may be substitute securities.
Qualified Institutional Investor Exception: May defer margin deposit until 10:00 next trading day.
[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정 시행세칙”]



3.2 Margin Call Schedule









Type
Korean Term
Trigger
Deadline




Regular Margin Call
정규증거금
Daily mark-to-market at close
11:00 next trading day


Intraday Margin Call
장중추가증거금
KOSPI 200 index volatility >= 80% of futures margin rate, OR member’s intraday requirement >= 120% of deposit
2 hours from notification

추가증거금

1 hour after 2-hour buffer period




Intraday margin call is released if triggering conditions ease within 30 minutes of notification.
Failure to meet margin call within deadline results in position liquidation and potential clearing membership suspension.

[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정_전문_20250609”]


3.3 Default Waterfall (손해배상 체계)
The default waterfall for derivatives clearing follows a “defaulter pays first” principle:









Layer
Resource
Korean Term
Estimated Size




1
Defaulter’s margin deposits
위탁증거금
Per-position (varies)


2
Defaulter’s clearing deposit / contribution
회원증거금
Per-member (varies)


3
Joint Compensation Fund
손해배상공동기금
~KRW 100 billion (~USD 75 million) [estimated]


4
KRX’s own capital contribution (SITG)
거래소 자기자본
[data not publicly disclosed]


5
Non-defaulting members’ additional contributions
회원 추가분담금
Assessed pro-rata based on clearing activity



Key Features: - KRX places Skin-in-the-Game (SITG) before non-defaulting members’ resources, consistent with PFMI guidance. - Joint Compensation Fund contributions follow a Fixed + Variable model: fixed base contribution plus variable component based on clearing volume/risk. - Replenishment of the Joint Compensation Fund is required after usage in a default event. - Recovery tools include: asset liquidation, securities sales, netting of claims against the defaulter, and assessment powers on surviving members.
[Source: KRX, “파생상품시장 업무규정_전문_20250609”; IMF, “Republic of Korea FSAP”, 2014]


3.4 Stress Testing







Item
Details




Frequency
Quarterly stress testing per regulatory requirements; real-time position monitoring


Scenarios
Historical stress scenarios (e.g., 2008 GFC, 2020 COVID crash, 2022 LUNA/Terra incident) and hypothetical extreme-but-plausible scenarios


Coverage
Liquidity risk, credit risk, concentration risk, wrong-way risk


Back Testing
Daily back testing of margin model adequacy


FSAP Recommendations (2014)
IMF recommended enhancements to back testing methodology, sensitivity analysis, and reverse stress testing


Reporting
Results reported to FSC/FSS; BOK reviews systemic risk implications



[Source: IMF, “Republic of Korea FSAP”, 2014]

4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycles








Product
Settlement Cycle
Settlement Time




Equities (KOSPI, KOSDAQ)
T+2
9:00 AM

T+1
9:00 AM

Daily mark-to-market; margin by 11:00 next day

OTC IRS/CRS
Per payment schedule
As per swap terms



[Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정_전문_20260304”]


4.2 DVP Model

KRX/KSD employ a DVP (Delivery versus Payment) model for securities settlement.
Securities leg: KSD (Korea Securities Depository) acts as CSD, handling book-entry transfer of securities.
Cash leg: Settlement through Bank of Korea (BOK) for large-value government bond transactions; settlement banks (KEB Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, etc.) for equity and other settlement.
Central bank money: Used for government bond settlement to eliminate settlement bank credit risk.
Simultaneous exchange: Securities delivery and payment occur simultaneously to eliminate principal risk.

[Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정 시행세칙_전문_20250304”]


4.3 Settlement Finality







Item
Details




Legal Framework
Capital Market Act (자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률)


Finality Point
Transfer orders entered into KRX/KSD system are legally enforceable and irrevocable


Insolvency Protection
Netting and settlement finality provisions protect against insolvency claw-back under Korean law


Derivatives
Same-day finality for derivatives margin settlement


Regulatory Basis
Article 390 et seq. of FSCMA provides legal certainty for settlement finality



[Source: Capital Market Act; IMF, “Republic of Korea FSAP”, 2014]


4.4 Settlement System Overhaul (2021-2026)
KRX has been progressively reforming its equity settlement system through “split settlement” (분할결제):








Year
Change
Impact




2021
Split settlement introduced
Settlement obligations divided into KRW 10 billion units, settled sequentially throughout the day


2024
Units reduced from KRW 10B to KRW 5B
15-20% reduction in settlement deposit requirements for members


2026 (February)
Operating hours expanded
Settlement window extended from 9:00-16:10 to 7:00-16:10


2026 (Late April)
Units reduced from KRW 5B to KRW 1B
Further reduction in member deposit burden; more granular liquidity management



Rationale: Split settlement reduces the peak liquidity requirement for clearing members by distributing settlement obligations throughout the day, lowering systemic risk and member funding costs.
Market Context: Average daily equity trading value reached KRW 29.6 trillion (Jan-Mar 2026), up 138.7% YoY, necessitating the infrastructure upgrade.
[Source: KRX, “증권시장 청산결제 업무규정_전문_20260304”]

Item
Details




Clearing System
Integrated within EXTURE+ (Exchange Trading Using Revolutionary Engine Plus) platform

Memory-based, real-time processing on x86 Linux infrastructure

Real-time margin calculation and position monitoring; KRX-SPAN engine for derivatives

Designed to handle peak volumes exceeding 2x historical maximums



[Source: KRX Global Website, https://global.krx.co.kr; WFE, “KRX Clearing Milestone”]

title: KRX Clearing (Korea Exchange CCP)
text:
6. Regulatory Framework







Item
Details




Primary Regulator
Financial Services Commission (금융위원회, FSC) — policy-making and rule approval


Examination Authority
Financial Supervisory Service (금융감독원, FSS) — on-site examination and off-site surveillance


Systemic Oversight
Bank of Korea (한국은행, BOK) — oversight of systemically important payment and settlement systems


Governing Law
Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (자본시장과 금융투자업에 관한 법률, FSCMA)


Clearing Regulations
파생상품시장 업무규정 (Derivatives Market Business Regulations); 증권시장 청산결제 업무규정 (Securities Market Clearing & Settlement Regulations)


PFMI Compliance
IMF FSAP 2014 assessment completed; Korea assessed as largely observant of PFMI principles


CCP Recovery & Resolution
No dedicated CCP recovery and resolution regime as of 2026 (similar to Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore)


OTC Clearing Mandate
KRW-denominated IRS (Interest Rate Swap) and CRS (Currency Rate Swap) mandated for central clearing through KRX


Self-Regulatory Function
KRX has SRO status; conducts market surveillance and member supervision alongside FSS



Korea’s Dual Regulatory Structure: Korea’s FSC/FSS dual structure is distinctive — the FSC handles policy-making, licensing, and regulatory approvals while the FSS conducts day-to-day supervision, examination, and enforcement. This separation of policy from execution is unusual among major markets and provides a form of checks and balances in financial regulation.
[Source: IMF, “Republic of Korea FSAP”, 2014; Capital Market Act]

title: KRX Clearing (Korea Exchange CCP)
text:
7. Interoperability







Item
Details




CCP Interoperability Links
None — KRX operates as a domestic monopoly CCP (similar to Japan/JSCC model)


CSD Cross-Border Links
KSD maintains CSD links with Euroclear, Clearstream, and DTC for cross-border settlement


Stock Connect
None currently; KRX monitoring developments in China-Hong Kong Stock Connect and potential replication


OTC Clearing Scope
KRW IRS and KRW CRS only (narrower than JSCC which clears JGB repos, or LCH which clears multi-currency IRS)


MSCI Inclusion Considerations
Enhanced foreign investor access to clearing/settlement infrastructure is relevant to Korea’s MSCI Developed Market reclassification efforts


Mutual Recognition
KRX recognized as QCCP by major jurisdictions for bank capital treatment purposes



[Source: KRX Global Website, https://global.krx.co.kr]

Key Observations: - KRX’s default fund size is notably smaller than global peers, reflecting the domestic-only scope and integrated exchange-CCP model where exchange revenue provides an implicit backstop. - KRX’s OTC clearing scope is narrower than peers, limited to KRW-denominated products — expansion could enhance systemic risk management. - The integrated exchange-CCP model provides operational efficiency (high STP, no trade matching delays) but raises governance questions about conflicts of interest between commercial and risk management functions. - KRX’s planned transition from SPAN to VaR-based margining would align it with global best practice trends.

2.2 Novation Process

Novation by open offer: For exchange-traded products and interoperable clearing, LCH becomes the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer at the point of trade registration.
Novation for OTC derivatives: Upon trade registration/acceptance, the original bilateral contract is extinguished and replaced by two new contracts – one between the CCP and each original counterparty.
SwapClear real-time trade registration: Trades are novated within approximately 10 seconds of submission, supported by a dedicated GBP 600 million real-time trade registration (RTTR) default fund component. (RBA Assessment 2020)



2.3 Netting & Compression
Multilateral Netting: - LCH performs multilateral netting across all cleared positions, reducing gross bilateral exposures to a single net exposure to the CCP per clearing member. - RepoClear provides netting for cash bond and repo transactions, significantly reducing settlement obligations.
Portfolio Compression (SwapClear): - Compression reduces the number of line items and gross notional outstanding by combining or offsetting trades with compatible economics. - Eligible products for compression: IRS, OIS, FRAs, basis swaps, zero-coupon inflation swaps. - Techniques include blended rate compression and future cash flow netting. - In 2015 alone, SwapClear compressed $323 trillion in trades with $107 trillion net notional reduction. (LCH Compression) - LCH’s SwapClear has compressed more than $1 quadrillion of cleared notional cumulatively. (LeapRate) - Multilateral compression (via OSTTRA triReduce) generated approximately USD 1 trillion of additional gross notional reduction in a single month (September 2022). (OSTTRA)

3. Risk Management

3.1 Margin Framework

PAIRS Methodology (Portfolio Approach to Interest Rate Scenarios)
PAIRS is LCH’s proprietary margin methodology used for SwapClear, ForexClear, and Listed Rates services. (LCH Ltd Margin Methodology)







Parameter
Specification




Model Type
Expected Shortfall (ES) model based on filtered historical simulation incorporating volatility scaling


Confidence Level
99.7% (equivalent to ~2.75 standard deviations)


Holding Period (Members)
5-day close-out period


Holding Period (Clients)
7-day close-out period (5 days + 2 additional days for portfolio transfer)


Lookback Period
10 years of historical market data with volatility-scaled movements in yield curves and exchange rates


Floor Calibration
Unscaled historical 10-year lookback plus an additional 2.5-year window covering the Global Financial Crisis (2007-2009)



Source: RBA Assessment 2020 Appendix B
PAIRS Process: 1. Collects 10 years of daily market data (yield curves, FX rates, credit spreads depending on service) 2. Applies volatility scaling (EWMA-based) to historical returns to reflect current market conditions 3. Generates a distribution of simulated portfolio P&L changes 4. Calculates Expected Shortfall at 99.7% confidence over the holding period 5. Determines initial margin as the expected loss conditional on losses exceeding the 99.7% VaR threshold
Margin Add-ons: - Credit Risk Add-on: Applied where a member’s credit exposure is not fully captured in the base PAIRS model - Liquidity Risk Add-on: Accounts for potential costs of liquidating large or concentrated positions - Concentration Risk Add-on: For portfolios with disproportionately large positions in specific tenors or currencies - Stress Margin Add-on: May be applied during periods of elevated market stress

3.5 Default Management Process
LCH’s default management process follows three stages:

Risk Neutralization & Client Porting: Immediate hedging of the defaulting member’s portfolio to contain market risk; attempt to transfer (port) client positions and collateral to non-defaulting clearing members
Portfolio Auction: The defaulting member’s portfolio is divided by product and currency, then auctioned to surviving clearing members via a structured auction process
Loss Attribution: Losses from variation margin/hedging costs allocated pro-rata; auction losses allocated based on bidding outcomes

Proven Track Record: - Lehman Brothers (2008): LCH managed the default of Lehman Brothers’ $9 trillion IRS portfolio (66,390 trades) using only 35% of Lehman’s posted initial margin. No losses were imposed on non-defaulting members or the default fund. (LCH SwapClear Risk Management)

4.3 Settlement Finality
LCH Ltd: - Legal Basis: UK Financial Markets and Insolvency (Settlement Finality) Regulations 1999 (SI 1999/2979), as amended post-Brexit. LCH Ltd is designated as a “designated system” by the Bank of England. (Settlement Finality Regulations) - Point of Finality: Transfer orders entered into the system become irrevocable and cannot be unwound in the event of a participant’s insolvency proceedings. - Protection: The SF Regulations protect transfer orders and related collateral security from being invalidated by insolvency proceedings.
LCH SA: - Legal Basis: EU Settlement Finality Directive (Directive 98/26/EC) as transposed into French law; LCH SA is a designated system under French implementation. - Point of Finality: Upon entry into the system as defined by LCH SA’s rules; protected from insolvency proceedings of participants.

7.3 Post-Brexit Dynamics
The most significant interoperability and cross-border issue for LCH is the post-Brexit regulatory dynamic:

LCH Ltd (UK) lost its EU-authorised CCP status after Brexit (31 January 2020 / end of transition period 31 December 2020). ESMA granted temporary recognition under EU EMIR Article 25 as a third-country CCP.
Tier 2 Classification: ESMA designated LCH Ltd as a Tier 2 (systemically important) third-country CCP, subjecting it to enhanced ESMA supervision and potential requirements to relocate certain euro-denominated clearing activities.
Equivalence Extensions: The EU has repeatedly extended equivalence decisions for UK CCPs, most recently to 30 June 2028, acknowledging the systemic risk of a sudden withdrawal of recognition.
EU Active Account Requirement: Under EMIR 3.0 (proposed), EU clearing members may be required to maintain active accounts at EU-authorised CCPs for certain systemically important products (particularly euro-denominated IRS), potentially shifting some volume from LCH Ltd SwapClear to EU-based alternatives.
LCH SA Repositioning: Following the loss of Euronext clearing, LCH SA has pivoted to focus on CDSClear, RepoClear SA, and the new DigitalAssetClear service, maintaining its EU-authorised CCP status.

text:
1. Overview & Profile



Item
Details




Official Name
The Options Clearing Corporation


Abbreviation
OCC


Website
https://www.theocc.com


Year Established
1973


Country / City
United States / Chicago, Illinois


Ownership Structure
Jointly owned by stockholder exchanges: Cboe Global Markets, Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE Arca, NYSE American), and Nasdaq (which holds ~40% following ISE acquisition). Originally five equal shareholders; Nasdaq’s stake increased from 20% to 40% with ISE acquisition.


Parent Company / Group
None (independent market utility)


Regulatory Authority
SEC (primary regulator as a registered clearing agency), CFTC (secondary, as a registered Derivatives Clearing Organization), Federal Reserve Board (oversight under Dodd-Frank Title VIII as SIFMU)


CPMI-IOSCO PFMI Compliance
Yes — publishes PFMI Disclosure Framework and CPMI-IOSCO Public Quantitative Disclosures (PQD) quarterly


QCCP Status
Yes — recognized as a Qualifying CCP under Basel III framework for bank capital purposes


SIFMU Designation
Designated as a Systemically Important Financial Market Utility (SIFMU) by FSOC in July 2012 under Dodd-Frank Title VIII



Sources: OCC — What Is OCC?; Wikipedia — Options Clearing Corporation; OCC SIFMU Designation Press Release (2012); OCC PFMI Disclosures

Participant Exchanges and Futures Markets
OCC provides CCP clearing and settlement services to approximately 21 exchanges and trading platforms, including:
Options Exchanges: - BOX Options Exchange LLC - Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. - Cboe C2 Exchange, Inc. - Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. - Cboe Exchange, Inc. - MIAX Emerald, LLC - Miami International Securities Exchange, LLC (MIAX) - MIAX PEARL, LLC - Nasdaq BX, Inc. - Nasdaq GEMX, LLC - Nasdaq ISE, LLC - Nasdaq MRX, LLC - Nasdaq Options Market, LLC - Nasdaq PHLX, LLC - NYSE American Options, LLC - NYSE Arca, Inc.
Futures Exchanges: - Cboe Futures Exchange (CFE)
Sources: Wikipedia — Options Clearing Corporation; OCC 2024 Annual Report


Key Historical Milestones

1973: OCC founded as a clearing house for listed equity options on five exchanges, coinciding with the launch of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE).
1975: OCC began clearing put options (previously only calls were listed).
1985: OCC began clearing index options.
1993: OCC launched its Stock Loan/Hedge Program for securities lending transactions.
2000: ENCORE clearing platform launched, replacing legacy systems.
2000: Monthly volume record of 75.3 million contracts set in October.
2006: STANS (System for Theoretical Analysis and Numerical Simulations) margin methodology implemented, replacing TIMS (Theoretical Intermarket Margin System).
2011 (August): Record monthly volume of 550 million contracts; S&P lowered OCC credit rating to AA+ from AAA.
2012 (July): Designated as SIFMU by FSOC under Dodd-Frank Title VIII.
2015: OCC submitted Capital Plan to SEC for enhanced capitalization; subsequently challenged by non-shareholder exchanges.
2019 (February): SEC disapproved OCC’s Capital Plan on procedural and substantive grounds, citing insufficient information and governance concerns.
2019 (September): SEC and CFTC charged OCC with failing to establish and maintain adequate risk management policies.
2019–2021: Clearing Fund underfunding incident — OCC’s Clearing Fund was underfunded by $200 million to $588 million at various times between October 2019 and May 2021 due to errors in the Liquidation Cost Model.
2022 (October): SEC issued no-objection notice for OCC’s Renaissance Initiative cloud infrastructure proposal.
2023 (February): OCC settled with SEC ($17 million penalty) and CFTC ($5 million penalty) over Clearing Fund underfunding and operational risk management failures.
2024 (May 28): Transition to T+1 settlement cycle for underlying equity securities.
2024: Record-breaking annual volume — 12.2 billion options contracts cleared (+10.6% YoY), 60.1 million futures contracts (+7.7% YoY).
2025 (April 4): Daily volume record of 102.6 million contracts, the first time exceeding 100 million in a single day.
2025 (October 10): New daily volume record of 110 million option contracts cleared.

Sources: Wikipedia — Options Clearing Corporation; OCC 2024 Volume Release; SEC Charges OCC (2023); CFTC Penalty Order (2023); SEC Capital Plan Disapproval (2019)

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
2. Clearing Model

2.1 CCP Services
OCC serves as the sole CCP for standardized equity options listed on U.S. national securities exchanges. It also clears futures, securities lending transactions, and certain OTC products.








Product Class
Description
Volume / Scale (2024)




Equity Options
Puts and calls on individual equities, ETFs
Majority of 12.2 billion total


Index Options
Options on equity indexes (e.g., SPX, NDX, VIX)
Included in total; SPX alone ~2+ billion


Futures
Futures on CBOE Futures Exchange (VIX futures, etc.)
60.1 million contracts


Securities Lending
Stock Loan/Hedge Program and Market Loan Program
~$139 billion average daily loan balance (June 2023 peak); ~9,800 transactions/day


Single-Stock Futures
Futures on individual equities
Minimal volume (largely dormant)



Sources: OCC 2024 Volume Release; OCC Stock Loan Programs; FOW — OCC Securities Lending 30th Anniversary


2.2 Short-Dated and 0DTE Options
Short-dated options (contracts with less than one week to expiration) represent a rapidly growing segment of OCC’s cleared volume:

Short-dated options represented approximately 40% of total volume in 2024
Zero-day-to-expiry (0DTE) options represented approximately 20% of total volume in 2024
In SPX options specifically, 0DTE accounted for 48% of volume in Q1 2024 (up from 11% five years prior)
This rapid growth creates significant intraday risk management challenges, as 0DTE positions are currently uncollateralized intraday under traditional end-of-day margining

Sources: OCC 2024 Volume Release; SEC Filing SR-OCC-2024-010


2.3 Novation Process
OCC uses an open offer model for novation. When an options trade is executed on a participant exchange and reported to OCC, OCC interposes itself as the CCP:

OCC becomes the buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer
This novation occurs at the point of trade acceptance
OCC guarantees the performance of every cleared contract
Positions are maintained at the clearing member account level



2.4 Netting
OCC performs multilateral netting:

Position Netting: Long and short positions in the same series are netted at the account level
Premium Netting: Daily premiums receivable and payable are netted into a single payment per clearing member
Exercise/Assignment Netting: Delivery obligations from exercise and assignment are netted with NSCC through the “Accord” agreement



2.5 Clearing Membership







Category
Details




Number of Clearing Members
~115


Member Types
U.S. broker-dealers, futures commission merchants (FCMs), U.S. banks (newly eligible), non-U.S. securities firms


Minimum Net Capital
$10,000,000


Operational Requirements
Qualified staff, adequate facilities, ability to interface with OCC systems


Clearing Fund Contribution
Required; allocated based on risk-based methodology proportional to stress exposure



In May 2023, the SEC approved OCC’s amendment to expand eligible membership to include certain U.S. banks, in addition to the traditional broker-dealer and FCM categories.
Sources: OCC — Becoming a Clearing Member; SEC Approval of Membership Standards Amendment (2023)


2.6 Securities Lending Programs
OCC operates two distinct securities lending programs, established in 1993:








Program
Model
Description




Hedge Program
Bilateral
Supports transactions executed bilaterally between counterparties; OCC acts as CCP guarantor


Market Loan Program
Exchange-based
Supports transactions originating through participating loan markets (e.g., AQS)




Since 2012, stock loan clearing volumes have grown at a CAGR of 16%, with open interest growing at 22%
OCC is the world’s largest U.S. equities lending CCP
OCC selected Axoni (DLT platform) to modernize securities lending infrastructure

Sources: OCC Stock Loan Programs; Axoni — OCC Modernization

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
3. Risk Management

3.1 STANS Margin Methodology
OCC’s System for Theoretical Analysis and Numerical Simulations (STANS) is the primary margin methodology, implemented in August 2006 to replace TIMS (Theoretical Intermarket Margin System). OCC was the first derivatives clearinghouse in the world to use a large-scale Monte Carlo-based risk management methodology.

STANS Technical Details







Parameter
Details




Methodology
Monte Carlo simulation — full portfolio margining


Risk Measure
99% Expected Shortfall (ES) — average of all losses beyond the 99% VaR point


Enhanced Measure
99.5% ES for the two single-factor sub-portfolios with greatest exposure; 99% ES for residual portfolio


Holding Period
2-day liquidation horizon (one day longer than U.S. competitors like CME)


Simulation Paths
Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations across all risk factors


Risk Factors
Equity prices, implied volatilities (by strike/maturity), interest rates, dividend yields, correlation structures


Pricing Models
Sophisticated options pricing models for all listed derivatives


Margin Components
Base component (ES) + Stress test add-on component


Stress Add-On
Considers ES increases from especially large market moves, perfect/zero correlations replacing estimated correlations, and extreme adverse idiosyncratic movements


Calculation Frequency
Daily (end-of-day), with intraday monitoring





STANS vs. SPAN Comparison








Feature
OCC STANS
CME SPAN




Methodology
Monte Carlo simulation
Scenario-based (16 risk scenarios)


Risk Measure
Expected Shortfall (99%)
Worst-case loss across scenarios


Portfolio Approach
Full portfolio margining with correlations
Product-group scanning with inter-commodity spreads


Holding Period
2 days
1 day (typically)


Non-linearity
Fully captured through simulation
Approximated via scanning range


Correlation Treatment
Dynamically estimated from historical data
Fixed inter-commodity spread credits


Computational Intensity
High (Monte Carlo)
Lower (parametric scenarios)


Historical Context
Introduced 2006
Introduced 1988



Sources: OCC — Margin Methodology; Risk.net — Clearing House of the Year: OCC; SEC STANS Approval Order (2006)



3.2 Margin Call Schedule

End-of-Day Margin: Calculated daily after market close using STANS; margin calls issued overnight for next-morning settlement
Intraday Monitoring: OCC monitors positions and market movements intraday and may issue intraday margin calls
Intraday Risk Charge (proposed/approved 2025): New margin add-on to address uncollateralized intraday exposure, particularly from 0DTE options and overnight trading activity

Sources: SEC Approval of Intraday Risk Charge (April 2025)


3.3 Default Waterfall
OCC’s default waterfall describes the order in which financial resources are used to address losses arising from a clearing member default:








Layer
Resource
Approximate Size




1
Defaulting member’s margin deposits
Varies by member (total margin pool ~$180–232 billion)


2
Defaulting member’s Clearing Fund contribution
Proportional share of ~$19.5 billion total


3
OCC’s Skin-in-the-Game (SITG) — OCC’s own capital contribution
Persistent minimum of $69 million (capital) / ~$76 million (including deferred compensation); at least 25% of target regulatory capital


4
Non-defaulting members’ Clearing Fund contributions (mutualized loss sharing)
Remainder of ~$19.5 billion Clearing Fund


5
Assessments on non-defaulting members (powers of assessment)
Up to the amount of each member’s required Clearing Fund contribution (effectively doubling the mutualized pool)


6
Recovery tools (VMGH, partial tear-up, etc.)
See Section 3.5



Cover 2 Standard: OCC sizes its financial resources (margin + Clearing Fund) to cover the default of its two largest clearing members and their affiliates under extreme but plausible market conditions. This is consistent with CPMI-IOSCO PFMI Principle 4 for systemically important CCPs.
Sources: OCC — Default Rules & Procedures; SEC Filing on Default Waterfall Amendments (2024); Risk.net — OCC Cover 2


3.4 Stress Testing & Back-Testing
Stress Testing: - OCC performs daily stress testing of its financial resources - Two categories of scenarios: - Sizing Scenarios: Assess whether collected resources are adequate and inform the size of OCC’s financial resources - Sufficiency Scenarios: Measure potential exposures to determine whether additional margin or Clearing Fund calls are needed - Scenarios include historical (e.g., 2008 financial crisis rally/decline variations), hypothetical, and reverse stress tests - In 2024, OCC recategorized certain 2008-based Informational Scenarios as Sufficiency Scenarios after finding they consistently generated higher exposures - In January 2025, SEC approved enhancements to STANS and Comprehensive Stress Testing (CST) methodology to better capture risks from short-dated options
Back-Testing: - OCC conducts daily back-testing of its margin model - In September 2024, SEC approved OCC’s updated backtesting framework and establishment of a Resource Backtesting Margin Charge - Back-testing compares actual portfolio P&L against margin requirements to validate model coverage
Sources: SEC Approval of Stress Testing Amendments (July 2024); SEC Approval of STANS/CST Enhancements (January 2025); SEC Approval of Backtesting Framework (September 2024)


3.5 Recovery & Resolution Tools
OCC maintains a Recovery and Orderly Wind-Down (RWD) Plan that describes tools for managing losses and liquidity shortfalls beyond routine risk management:







Tool
Description




Assessments
OCC may assess non-defaulting clearing members up to their required Clearing Fund contribution amount


Variation Margin Gains Haircutting (VMGH)
OCC can allocate losses to clearing participants that experience mark-to-market gains on their positions; provides incentive for members to participate in default management


Voluntary Partial Tear-Up
Members may voluntarily extinguish contracts to help OCC return to a matched book


Mandatory Partial Tear-Up
OCC authority to extinguish remaining contracts of a defaulted clearing member at OCC’s marking price; used after other default management tools have been exhausted


Orderly Wind-Down
Planned cessation of critical services with transfer of positions to alternative clearing arrangements



The RWD Plan was most recently amended and approved by the SEC in August 2025.
Sources: OCC Recovery and Orderly Wind-Down Plan; SEC Approval of RWD Plan Modifications (August 2025); FSB OCC Questionnaire

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
4. Settlement

4.1 Settlement Cycle








Settlement Type
Cycle
Details




Premium Settlement
T+1
Payment of options premium is settled the next business day after trade date


Exercise/Assignment (Equity Options)
T+1
Following the transition on May 28, 2024; previously T+2


Exercise/Assignment (Index Options)
Cash settlement on T+1
Cash-settled index options pay/receive cash difference


Futures
Daily mark-to-market
Variation margin settled daily; final settlement at expiration


Stock Loan
Same-day or T+1
Depending on program and initiation time





4.2 DVP and Settlement Finality

Exercise/Assignment of Equity Options: When equity options are exercised/assigned, the resulting stock delivery obligation is processed through the Accord — an agreement between OCC and NSCC (National Securities Clearing Corporation)
Under the Accord, NSCC accepts “E&A/Delivery Transactions” resulting from OCC exercise and assignment for clearing and settlement through NSCC’s Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) system
Settlement of underlying shares occurs at the Depository Trust Company (DTC) on a DVP (Delivery versus Payment) basis
Settlement is considered final and irrevocable once completed through DTC’s book-entry system



4.3 Premium Settlement Process

At end of each trading day, OCC calculates net premium obligations for each clearing member
Net premiums receivable and payable are aggregated across all cleared trades
Settlement occurs on T+1 through Fedwire or commercial bank payment systems
OCC may call for intraday premium settlement during periods of high volatility



4.4 Exercise and Assignment Process

Exercise Notice: Option holder’s clearing member submits exercise notice to OCC (either by instruction or automatic exercise for in-the-money options)
Assignment: OCC uses a random assignment algorithm to distribute exercise notices fairly among clearing members with short positions in the assigned series
Delivery/Cash Settlement: For equity options, the resulting buy/sell obligations flow to NSCC via the Accord for settlement at DTC. For index options, cash settlement amounts are calculated and settled directly through OCC
Automatic Exercise: Options expiring in-the-money by $0.01 or more are automatically exercised unless contrary instructions are received

Sources: OCC Equity Options Product Specifications; OCC T+1 Info Memo #54580; SEC — OCC/NSCC Accord Modifications (2024)

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
5. Technology & Infrastructure

5.1 Core Systems








System
Function
Status




ENCORE
Core clearing, risk management, and data management platform; real-time processing engine
Legacy — operational since 2000; scheduled for replacement by Ovation


Ovation
Next-generation cloud-based clearing, settlement, risk management, and data platform
In testing; external beta testing began July 2024; launch targeted for mid-2025 [unverified if completed]


STANS
Margin calculation engine (Monte Carlo-based)
Active — continuously enhanced


CLEARS
Clearing member reporting and inquiry system
Active [unverified current status]





5.2 ENCORE Architecture

Monolithic architecture — tightly coupled components making change difficult
Runs in traditional on-premises data centers
Receives trade and post-trade data from exchanges on a transaction-by-transaction basis in real time
Maintains clearing member positions, calculates margin and Clearing Fund requirements
Provides reporting to OCC staff, regulators, and clearing members



5.3 Ovation Architecture (Renaissance Initiative)
OCC’s Renaissance Initiative is a multi-year technology modernization program to replace ENCORE with the Ovation platform:







Feature
Details




Cloud Provider
Amazon Web Services (AWS)


Architecture
Modular, cloud-native; three pillars — Clearing & Settlement, Data, Risk Management


Real-Time Processing
Stream processing using Apache Kafka and Apache Flink


Data Processing
Prices for over 2 million financial instruments per second; billions of open option positions


Disaster Recovery
Isolated Kafka + Flink infrastructure in both AWS and on-premises data center


Key Benefits
Enhanced resiliency, security, scalability; real-time risk measurement using current prices (vs. prior-day close)



Renaissance Timeline: - October 2022: SEC no-objection notice for cloud infrastructure proposal - 2023: Ovation development and internal testing - July 2024: External beta testing commenced (Beta 1) - October 2024: Beta 2 launched with expanded functionality - January 2025: Beta 3 — collateral management testing - Mid-2025: Planned Ovation launch (ENCORE-to-Ovation conversion in single processing cycle)


5.4 Processing Capacity







Metric
Value




Daily Peak Volume (record)
110 million contracts (October 10, 2025)


Data Ingestion
>2 million instrument prices per second


Open Positions Tracked
Billions of open option positions


Participant Exchanges Supported
~21 exchanges and trading platforms





5.5 Interface Protocols

FIX/FIXML: Industry-standard messaging for trade submission and reporting
Proprietary APIs: OCC-specific interfaces for clearing member connectivity
Market Data Feeds: Real-time position and margin data delivery

Sources: OCC Transformation; OCC — Clearing, Risk and Data Changes; Confluent Current 2024 — OCC Stream Processing; Built In Chicago — OCC Tech Infrastructure; Traders Magazine — OCC Ovation Testing; IBM — OCC Case Study

6. Regulatory Framework

6.1 Regulatory Structure

CFTC Core Principles: Requirements for DCOs under the Commodity Exchange Act

Year

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
7. Interoperability

7.1 Cross-Margining Programs
OCC maintains cross-margining agreements that allow hedged positions cleared at separate clearinghouses to be combined into a single portfolio for margin purposes:








Program
Counterpart CCP
Description




OCC-CME Cross-Margin Program
CME Clearing
Allows qualifying clearing members to offset equity option positions (OCC) against related equity index futures positions (CME); established after 1987 Black Monday crash; second amended and restated agreement approved in 2020



Cross-margining uses OCC’s STANS methodology to calculate the combined portfolio risk, typically resulting in lower margin requirements than if margins were calculated separately at each CCP.


7.2 Cross-Guaranty and Linkages







Arrangement
Details




OCC-NSCC Accord
Governs the processing of physically settled equity options; NSCC accepts exercise/assignment delivery transactions for settlement through its CNS system at DTC


Exchange Linkages
OCC maintains Participant Exchange Agreements with all 16+ options exchanges; the Amended and Restated Participant Exchange Agreement was approved by the SEC in July 2025





7.3 Ongoing Coordination
OCC is evaluating adjustments to existing cross-CCP agreements and exploring potential new arrangements to support aligned margin cycles and risk management, particularly in light of: - Extended trading hours initiatives - T+1 settlement transition - Growing intraday risk from 0DTE options
Sources: OCC — Cross Margin Programs; Yale SOM — Cross-Margining and Financial Stability; SEC Approval of Participant Exchange Agreement (July 2025)

title: Options Clearing Corporation (OCC)
text:
9. Recent Developments

9.1 Renaissance Initiative / Technology Modernization
OCC’s multi-year Renaissance Initiative is the most significant technology transformation in its history:

Ovation platform built on AWS cloud with modular architecture (clearing & settlement, data, risk management pillars)
Transition from batch processing (ENCORE) to real-time stream processing using Apache Kafka and Flink
Enables intraday risk calculation using current market prices rather than prior-day closing prices
External industry testing began July 2024 with progressive beta releases
Planned conversion from ENCORE to Ovation in a single processing cycle [target: mid-2025; completion status unverified as of April 2026]
SEC no-objection on cloud infrastructure received October 2022



9.2 Extended Trading Hours

Cboe and other exchanges have expanded or proposed extended trading sessions (pre-market and post-market) for equity options
Cboe extended trading includes 7:30–9:25 a.m. ET and 4:00–4:15 p.m. ET sessions for select options classes
OCC infrastructure must support clearing and risk management across extended hours
Creates challenges for margin calculation timing, intraday risk exposure, and settlement cycle alignment



9.3 0DTE Options Growth Impact
The explosive growth of zero-day-to-expiry options has driven significant risk management adaptations:

Intraday Risk Charge: SEC approved (April 2025) a new margin add-on applied to all clearing member accounts to mitigate risks from intraday and overnight trading activity
STANS Enhancements: SEC approved (January 2025) changes to STANS and CST methodology to better capture short-dated options risks; average daily margin impact estimated at +0.58%
Volatility Adjustments: OCC proposed (October 2024) a mechanism to adjust margin parameters during periods of high volatility
OCC’s intraday exposure to 0DTE options was previously uncollateralized — the new Intraday Risk Charge addresses this gap



9.4 Securities Lending Expansion

OCC selected Axoni (distributed ledger technology platform) to modernize its securities lending infrastructure
Stock loan clearing volumes have grown at a 16% CAGR since 2012
OCC is now the world’s largest U.S. equities lending CCP
Programs expanded to support broader market participation and operational efficiency



9.5 2021 Capital Plan / Governance Crisis and Resolution
This episode represents a significant chapter in OCC’s history:
Timeline: 1. 2015: OCC submitted Capital Plan to SEC proposing significant capitalization increase through dividends to stockholder exchanges, funded by clearing fee increases 2. 2017: SEC initially approved the Capital Plan 3. 2017: D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals remanded the decision back to the SEC following challenge by non-shareholder exchanges (e.g., MIAX) who argued they were denied fair notice and opportunity to present views 4. 2019 (February): SEC disapproved the Capital Plan, finding: - Insufficient evidence that the Plan was consistent with the Securities Exchange Act - Governance concerns — conflicts of interest between OCC management/board and stockholder exchanges - Failure to notify non-shareholder exchanges of the Plan’s competitive significance - Questions about whether fee-funded dividends to owner-exchanges were appropriate for a market utility 5. 2019 (September): SEC and CFTC separately charged OCC with risk management policy failures unrelated to the Capital Plan but occurring during the same period 6. 2019–2021: Errors in OCC’s Liquidation Cost Model led to Clearing Fund underfunding of $200M–$588M at various times 7. 2023 (February): OCC settled with SEC ($17M) and CFTC ($5M); total penalties of $22M 8. Post-2023: OCC implemented remedial measures including enhanced governance, improved internal controls, new Capital Management Policy with regulatory capital target of $303 million, and persistent minimum SITG of $69 million
Lessons: - Highlighted tensions in OCC’s ownership model — stockholder exchanges as both owners and competitors of non-shareholder exchanges - Led to enhanced regulatory scrutiny of OCC governance - Prompted OCC to adopt more transparent capital management and fee-setting processes - Reinforced the importance of robust internal controls at SIFMUs


9.6 Clearing Fund Methodology Reform (2025)

In October 2025, OCC filed a proposed rule change to reform its Clearing Fund allocation methodology to better align contributions with the stress risk each clearing member poses to OCC
In December 2025, SEC granted accelerated approval of the reformed methodology
The new methodology ensures that stress-based risk is “fairly allotted to market participants that expose OCC to such stress risk”



9.7 Volume Records and Market Growth

2024: 12.2 billion options contracts cleared (record; +10.6% YoY)
2025 (January): 1.16 billion monthly contracts (+17.8% YoY)
2025 (April 4): First-ever 100M+ daily volume — 102.6 million contracts
2025 (October 10): New daily record of 110 million contracts
Driven by retail participation, zero-commission trading platforms, 0DTE growth, and economic uncertainty

Sources: OCC Transformation; SEC Approval of Intraday Risk Charge (April 2025); SEC Approval of STANS/CST Enhancements (January 2025); SEC Capital Plan Disapproval (2019); SEC Charges OCC (2023); Compliance Week — OCC Penalties; FIA — OCC Capital Plan; OCC 2024 Volume Release; SEC Clearing Fund Allocation Approval (December 2025); Cboe Extended Trading Hours FAQ
