title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
1. Japan

1.1 Regulatory Authorities

FSA / JFSA (Financial Services Agency): Primary regulator for securities markets and clearing organizations. JSCC is directly regulated by JFSA under the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act. JFSA oversees licensing of Financial Instruments Obligation Assumption Services. [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure, March 2025]
Bank of Japan (BOJ): Oversees payment and settlement systems, operates BOJ-NET for JGB settlement and fund transfers. Conducts oversight assessments of FMIs under the PFMI framework. [Source: BOJ Red Book 2012]
Role Division: JFSA handles prudential regulation and licensing of clearing organizations; BOJ focuses on systemic risk oversight and payment system operation. Both coordinate on FMI supervision. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry co-regulate commodity derivatives clearing alongside JFSA. [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure, March 2025]



1.2 Key Legislation

Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (FIEA): Core statute governing securities and derivatives markets, including mandatory clearing requirements for specified OTC derivatives. JSCC is licensed under FIEA to perform Financial Instruments Obligation Assumption Services. Business Rules established under FIEA are legally binding and enforceable. [Source: Chambers Derivatives 2025 - Japan]
Act on Book-Entry Transfer of Corporate Bonds, Shares, etc.: Legal framework for dematerialized securities holding and transfer through JASDEC. [Source: BOJ Red Book]
Payment and Settlement Systems Act: Governs payment systems including BOJ-NET operations, netting arrangements, and settlement finality. [Source: BOJ Red Book]
Commodity Derivatives Act (CDA): JSCC is also licensed under the CDA to perform Business of Assuming Commodity Transaction Debts. [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure, March 2025]



1.3 CCP/CSD Framework

JSCC (Japan Securities Clearing Corporation): Sole CCP in Japan, a wholly-owned subsidiary of JPX (Japan Exchange Group). Provides clearing services for listed equities, JGBs, listed derivatives, OTC interest rate swaps (TONA), and credit default swaps (iTraxx Japan). Updated its PFMI Disclosure on April 1, 2026. [Source: JPX/JSCC website, JSCC PFMI Disclosure 2025/2026]
JASDEC (Japan Securities Depository Center, Inc.): Central securities depository for equities, corporate bonds, and other securities. Provides book-entry transfer services. DVP settlement for cash products is conducted by linking JASDEC book-entry transfer with fund settlement at Fund Settlement Banks. [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure, March 2025]
BOJ-NET: Real-time gross settlement (RTGS) system operated by BOJ for JGB settlement and interbank fund transfers. DVP for JGBs is achieved through BOJ-NET. [Source: BOJ Red Book]
OTC Derivatives Clearing Mandate: Categories subject to mandatory clearing under FIEA include Designated Cleared CDSs (iTraxx Japan) and Designated Cleared IRSs (TONA compounded in arrears). [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure, March 2025]



1.4 Settlement

Equities: T+2 settlement cycle. DVP through linkage between JASDEC (securities leg) and Fund Settlement Banks (cash leg). [Source: JSCC PFMI Disclosure]
JGBs: T+1 settlement cycle. DVP through BOJ-NET. [Source: BOJ Red Book]
T+1 Considerations for Equities: Japan has not yet announced a formal timeline for equity T+1 migration but is monitoring global developments. [unverified]



1.5 Recent Changes

JSCC Margin Methodology Migration (SPAN to VaR): JSCC migrated from SPAN to a VaR-based margin calculation method on November 6, 2023, covering JGB futures, index futures, options, and commodity futures/options. The methodology uses Historical Simulation (HS-VaR) and Alternative Simulation (AS-VaR) methods. VaR Margin Software (VMA) upgrade from v3.0 to v4.0 is planned for April 13, 2026. [Source: JPX Working Paper Vol. 45, February 2025; JSCC VaR Method page]
Listed Derivatives April 2026 Project: JSCC published outline of changes for listed derivatives scheduled for April 2026. [Source: JSCC News, 2026]
Cross-border CCP Recognition: JSCC has obtained recognition from foreign regulators including the Ontario Securities Commission (Canada) under s.147 orders. [Source: OSC decision]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
2. Hong Kong

2.1 Regulatory Authorities

SFC (Securities and Futures Commission): Primary securities regulator. Oversees recognized clearing houses, OTC derivatives regime, and market infrastructure. Jointly administers clearing rules with HKMA for OTC derivatives. [Source: SFC website; ICLG Derivatives 2025-2026 Hong Kong]
HKMA (Hong Kong Monetary Authority): Oversees designated clearing and settlement systems under the Clearing and Settlement Systems Ordinance. Co-regulator (with SFC) for OTC derivatives clearing mandate applying to authorized institutions. [Source: HKMA press releases 2025-2026]



2.2 Key Legislation

Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO): Core legislation governing securities and futures markets, including the framework for recognized clearing houses (HKSCC, HKCC, SEOCH, OTC Clear). Part IIIA governs OTC derivatives. [Source: ICLG Derivatives 2025-2026 Hong Kong]
Clearing and Settlement Systems Ordinance (CSSO): Empowers HKMA to designate and oversee clearing and settlement systems that are important to the monetary or financial stability of Hong Kong. [Source: HKMA website]



2.3 CCP/CSD Framework

HKSCC (Hong Kong Securities Clearing Company): CCP and CSD for equities and fixed income traded on SEHK. Operates CCASS (Central Clearing and Settlement System). All are subsidiaries of HKEX. [Source: HKEX PFMI Disclosure]
HKCC (HKFE Clearing Corporation): CCP for futures and options traded on HKFE. [Source: HKEX]
SEOCH (SEHK Options Clearing House): CCP for stock options. [Source: HKEX]
OTC Clear (OTC Clearing Hong Kong): CCP for OTC derivatives (IRS, NDF, cross-currency swaps). [Source: ICLG Derivatives 2025-2026 Hong Kong]
Stock Connect Clearing Arrangements: HKSCC acts as sole clearing participant in ChinaClear, holding two omnibus stock accounts (Shanghai and Shenzhen) on behalf of CCASS participants. The offshore investor faces only HKSCC as clearing house. ChinaClear settlement occurs at 6 pm Shanghai time on trade date. Bond Connect operates similarly for fixed income. [Source: HKEX Stock Connect Information Book; Dorsey & Whitney Guide]



2.4 Settlement

Equities: T+2 settlement cycle via CCASS. [Source: Citi Hong Kong Market Report]
Multi-Counter Securities: In June 2025, HKSCC adopted a single tranche multiple counter arrangement for dual counter securities and multi-counter ETFs in CCASS. [Source: Citi Hong Kong Report]
T+1 Consultation: HKEX released a consultation paper in July 2025 proposing to shorten the cash market settlement cycle from T+2 to T+1. HKEX advised that post-trade systems will be technically ready to support T+1 by end of 2025. No final implementation date announced as of April 2026. [Source: HKEX consultation paper July 2025; Broadridge insight]



2.5 Recent Changes

Uncertificated Securities Market (USM): SFC is implementing a compulsory uncertificated (paperless) securities regime. All new issues required to be paperless from early 2026. Five-year transition period (to early 2031) for existing listed companies issuing prescribed securities. HKSCC platforms connected to approved securities registrars. [Source: SFC USM page; Charltons Law update]
OTC Derivative Clearing Mandate Extensions: Clearing obligation applies to prescribed persons trading in-scope products. HKMA and SFC jointly consulting on standard calculation periods under OTC derivative Clearing Rules (effective from 1 March 2027). Comments due by 27 February 2026. [Source: HKMA press release, January 2026]
OTC Derivatives Reporting Enhancements: Mandatory implementation of UTI, UPI, and CDE reporting from 29 September 2025. [Source: EY Hong Kong FSRM Insights, March 2025]
Margin for Non-Centrally Cleared OTC Derivatives: SFC deferred effective date of margin requirements for non-centrally cleared single-stock options, equity basket options, and equity index options until 4 January 2026. [Source: ICLG Derivatives 2025-2026 Hong Kong]
Stock Connect Enhancements: Ongoing expansion of eligible securities and operational improvements for both Stock Connect and Bond Connect. [Source: HKEX]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
3. Singapore

3.1 Regulatory Authorities

MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore): Sole integrated regulator serving as central bank, financial regulator, and supervisor. Regulates clearing facilities (CDP, SGX-DC) under the Securities and Futures Act. Designates systemically important FMIs. [Source: MAS; BIS CPMI Red Book Singapore]



3.2 Key Legislation

Securities and Futures Act (SFA): Core legislation governing securities, derivatives markets, and clearing facilities. Provides framework for recognition and regulation of approved clearing houses. [Source: SGX Rulebook - CDP Clearing Rules]
Payment Services Act (PSA): Governs payment systems and services, complementing the SFA framework for settlement systems. [Source: MAS]



3.3 CCP/CSD Framework

CDP (Central Depository Pte Ltd): Wholly-owned subsidiary of SGX, providing securities clearing, settlement, and depository services for equities and fixed income traded on SGX-ST. MAS regulates CDP as a clearing house under SFA. CDP custody modernization initiative announced by MAS Deputy Chairman Chee Hong Tat. [Source: SGX Rulebook; MAS]
SGX-DC (SGX Derivatives Clearing): Wholly-owned subsidiary of SGX, CCP for all derivatives traded on SGX. Acts as CCP guaranteeing all executed trades. [Source: SGX Derivatives Clearing Information]
MAS Designation: Both CDP and SGX-DC are designated as systemically important clearing houses by MAS. [Source: BIS CPMI Red Book Singapore]



3.4 Settlement

Equities: T+2 settlement cycle. DVP model through CDP. [Source: Clearstream Singapore Market Guide]
CDP Settlement Rules: Governed by detailed CDP Settlement Rules published in SGX Rulebook. [Source: SGX Rulebook - CDP Settlement Rules]



3.5 Recent Changes

Post-trade Modernization: CDP custody modernization to facilitate wider investor adoption of broker custody accounts while retaining the option for retail investors to keep CDP direct accounts. Board lot reduction also under consideration. [Source: MAS Deputy Chairman remarks; SGX]
T+1 Considerations: MAS reached out to CDP to understand views on adopting T+1. Industry participants have requested a cautious approach citing operational challenges. No firm timeline set. [Source: BNP Paribas Securities Services T+1 APAC report]
SGX-Nasdaq Bridge: Progress toward mid-2026 SGX-Nasdaq dual-listing bridge. [Source: SGX update December 2025]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
4. Australia

4.1 Regulatory Authorities

ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission): Regulates market operators and clearing/settlement facility licensees. Has new powers under Competition in Clearing and Settlement (CiCS) reforms. Commissioned expert-led Inquiry into ASX in June 2025. Published ASX Inquiry Panel Final Report in 2026. [Source: ASIC media release 25-019MR; ASIC media release 26-059MR]
RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia): Oversees clearing and settlement facilities for financial stability. Conducts annual assessments of ASX clearing and settlement facilities against FSS (Financial Stability Standards), which implement the PFMI. Published Assessment of ASX Clearing and Settlement Facilities for 2024-2025. [Source: RBA Assessment Report September 2025]
Council of Financial Regulators (CFR): Coordinates ASIC and RBA oversight. Published regulatory expectations for conduct in cash equity clearing and settlement. [Source: ASIC CS Services Rules background]



4.2 Key Legislation

Corporations Act 2001: Core legislation governing CS facility licensing. Part 7.3 establishes the framework for clearing and settlement facility licences. [Source: ASIC Licensed CS Facilities page]
Payment Systems and Netting Act 1998: Provides legal framework for settlement finality and netting arrangements. [Source: RBA]
Financial Sector (Collection of Data) Act 2001: Enables data collection from financial market infrastructure operators. [Source: RBA]
Competition in Clearing and Settlement (CiCS) Reforms: Passed September 2023, enlivened by the Minister in May 2024. Gives ASIC new powers to promote competitive outcomes in clearing and settlement. [Source: ASIC media release 25-019MR]



4.3 CCP/CSD Framework

ASX Clear Pty Ltd: CCP for cash equities and equity-related derivatives. [Source: RBA Assessment 2024-2025]
ASX Clear (Futures) Pty Ltd: CCP for futures, options on futures, and OTC derivatives. [Source: RBA Assessment 2024-2025]
ASX Settlement Pty Ltd (CHESS): Securities settlement facility and sub-register for ASX-listed securities. Operates the CHESS system. [Source: ASX CHESS Replacement page]
Austraclear Limited: Settlement facility for debt securities and OTC derivatives. [Source: RBA Assessment 2024-2025]
Vertically Integrated Model and Competition Debate: ASX operates all four CS facilities in a vertically integrated structure. ASIC has now exercised CiCS powers to require fair and transparent provision of CS services, including publication of fee comparisons against international providers. [Source: ASIC media release 25-019MR]



4.4 Settlement

Equities: T+2 settlement cycle through CHESS. [Source: ASX]
CHESS Replacement Project: Two-phased approach:

Release 1 (Clearing): Go-live planned for 20 April 2026. Industry Test Environment (ITE) opened 28 February 2025. TCS (Tata Consultancy Services) as vendor, Accenture as solutions integrator. Budget: A$105 million. [Source: ASX CHESS Replacement page; ASX update 23 March 2026]
Release 2 (Settlement and Sub-registry): Expected during 2028 or 2029. Budget: A$125 million. [Source: ASX CHESS Project page]
The original DLT-based CHESS replacement project was abandoned; the current project uses conventional technology. [Source: Digital Finance Group analysis]

T+1 Considerations: Deferred to 2030 at earliest, essentially one year after Australia’s CHESS Release 2 migration (expected 2029). Australia and New Zealand are eyeing joint transition. [Source: BNP Paribas T+1 APAC report; EquiLend analysis]



4.5 Recent Changes

ASIC CS Services Rules 2025: First exercise of new CiCS powers. Requires ASX to provide CS services on transparent and fair basis, publish fee comparisons, ensure technical interoperability, manage intragroup conflicts of interest, and obtain external assurance on pricing and barriers to competition. Implements previously non-enforceable CFR Regulatory Expectations as binding obligations. [Source: ASIC media release 25-019MR; ASX CS Service Rules and Code of Practice page]
ASIC ASX Inquiry Panel Final Report: Published in 2026 following expert-led inquiry commissioned June 2025 into persistent operational issues. [Source: ASIC media release 26-059MR]
RBA FSS Standard Assessments: Annual assessment of ASX clearing and settlement facilities published September 2025. RBA and ASIC monitoring CHESS Release 1 cutover closely to ensure adequate planning, cutover, and rollback strategies. [Source: RBA Assessment 2024-2025]
CS Facility Resolution Regime: RBA published guidance for consultation on the Australian Clearing and Settlement Facility Resolution Regime in June 2025. [Source: RBA Consultation Paper, June 2025]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
5. China

5.1 Regulatory Authorities

CSRC (China Securities Regulatory Commission): Primary regulator for securities and futures markets, including clearing organizations. Issues administrative measures governing securities registration and settlement. Published revised Administrative Measures for Securities Registration and Settlement to support DVP reform. [Source: CSRC; Xinhua Silk Road]
PBOC (People’s Bank of China): Central bank overseeing interbank bond market clearing and settlement, payment systems. Regulates SHCH (Shanghai Clearing House) for interbank market. [Source: Chambers Derivatives 2025 - China]



5.2 Key Legislation

Securities Law of the People’s Republic of China: Core statute governing securities markets including registration, custody, clearing, and settlement. [Source: CSDC website - Legal Documents]
Measures for the Administration of Securities Registration and Settlement: Issued by CSRC, governing CSDC operations. Amended to incorporate DVP reform provisions including tagged securities protections and default procedures. [Source: CSRC; CSDC website]
Futures and Derivatives Law: Came into force on 1 August 2022, providing comprehensive regulatory framework for trading, settlement, and clearing of futures and derivatives. CSRC has issued implementing regulations. [Source: FIA; Chambers Derivatives 2025 - China]
Regulations on Administration of Securities Registration and Settlement: Detailed operational regulations for CSDC. [Source: CSDC website]



5.3 CCP/CSD Framework

CSDC (China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation / ChinaClear): Dual CCP and CSD role. Based in Beijing with Shanghai and Shenzhen branches serving the respective stock exchanges. Responsible for all securities depository, registration, clearing, settlement, and netting for SSE and SZSE. Analogous to DTCC in the US. [Source: CSDC Company Profile; Wikipedia]
Shanghai Branch: Serves Shanghai Stock Exchange. [Source: SSE website]
Shenzhen Branch: Serves Shenzhen Stock Exchange. [Source: CSDC]
SHCH (Shanghai Clearing House): CCP for interbank bond market and OTC derivatives, regulated by PBOC. [Source: Chambers Derivatives 2025 - China]
Stock Connect Cross-border Arrangements: HKSCC is a participant in ChinaClear as nominee for all CCASS clearing participants. HKSCC maintains two omnibus stock accounts with ChinaClear (one for Shanghai Connect, one for Shenzhen Connect). Settlement occurs at 6 pm Shanghai time on trade date (T+0 for securities). [Source: HKEX Stock Connect Information Book; Dorsey & Whitney Guide]



5.4 Settlement

Unique T+0 Securities / T+1 Funds Model: Securities are delivered on T+0 (trade date), while fund settlement occurs on T+1. This is a unique settlement model globally, and with DVP reform, China is described as the first market to adopt T+1 DVP. [Source: WFE Focus article by CSDC; ACG CSD article]
DVP Reform (December 2022): Implemented on December 26, 2022. The reform establishes linkage between securities delivery and funds transfer via “tagging” of securities. At end of T+0, for buyers with sufficient funds, CSDC freezes the corresponding amount in the buyer’s fund settlement account. Tagged securities in settlement are protected from enforcement. Aligned with 2016-2017 IMF/World Bank FSAP recommendation. [Source: WFE Focus - CSDC DVP; Xinhua Silk Road; CGTN]
CSDC Settlement Reserve Fund Reduction: CSDC cut the minimum ratio of stock settlement reserve funds to lower costs and better serve the real economy. [Source: Xinhua Silk Road]



5.5 Recent Changes

DVP Implementation and Stabilization: Six months after the December 2022 reform, the market reported positive feedback and stable operation. [Source: WFE Focus - CSDC]
Bond Connect and Stock Connect Expansion: Ongoing expansion of eligible securities and operational improvements. CSRC unveiled a work plan to optimize the QFI (Qualified Foreign Investor) regime. [Source: Chambers article on CSRC QFI optimization]
Programme Trading Regulations: CSRC issued new rules on programme trading in China. [Source: Simmons & Simmons]
CSRC 2025 Legislative Plan: CSRC published an active legislative plan for 2025, indicating continued regulatory evolution. [Source: UDF Space article]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
6. India

6.1 Regulatory Authorities

SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India): Primary securities market regulator. Oversees clearing corporations (NSCCL, ICCL) and depositories (NSDL, CDSL). Pioneered T+1 settlement and launched T+0 pilot. Extended clearing corporation licences. [Source: SEBI circulars; Bigul blog]
RBI (Reserve Bank of India): Central bank overseeing payment systems, government securities clearing (through CCIL), and foreign exchange settlement. [Source: RBI]



6.2 CCP/CSD Framework

NSCCL (NSE Clearing Ltd, formerly National Securities Clearing Corporation Ltd): Clearing corporation for NSE (National Stock Exchange). Licence extended by SEBI until October 2, 2026. [Source: SEBI; Bigul blog]
ICCL (Indian Clearing Corporation Ltd): Clearing corporation for BSE (formerly Bombay Stock Exchange). Licence extended by SEBI until October 2, 2026. [Source: SEBI; Bigul blog]
CCIL (Clearing Corporation of India Ltd): CCP for government securities, money market instruments, and foreign exchange. Regulated by RBI. [Source: RBI]
NSDL (National Securities Depository Ltd): Central securities depository, primarily serving NSE participants. [Source: SEBI]
CDSL (Central Depository Services Ltd): Central securities depository, primarily serving BSE participants. [Source: SEBI]



6.3 Settlement

T+1 for Equities (Pioneer): India fully implemented T+1 settlement for all equities from January 27, 2023, becoming one of the first major markets globally to do so. The migration was phased starting from the lowest-capitalization stocks and moving upward. [Source: SEBI; multiple market reports]
Instant Settlement (T+0) Pilot and Expansion:

Phase 1 (March 2024): Pilot launched on March 28, 2024, with 25 selected stocks and limited brokers. [Source: Business Today; SEBI]
Phase 2 (January-May 2025): Starting January 31, 2025, the bottom 100 of the top 500 companies by market cap migrated to T+0, with 100 more added each month. All 500 companies had T+0 option by May 2025. [Source: Tej Mandi; SEBI circular]
NSE T+0 Official Launch (February 2026): NSE officially launched T+0 same-day settlement on February 5, 2026. [Source: Global Publicist 24]
Further Expansion: Expected rollout of 50 additional mid-cap stocks in Q3 2026. [Source: Global Publicist 24]
Operational Details: Trading until 1:30 pm, obligations determined by 2:30 pm on T day, settlement completed thereafter. Investors can choose between T+0 and T+1. Brokers may charge separate brokerage for each. [Source: SEBI circular; StockGro]
QSB Implementation: SEBI extended timeline for mandatory implementation of T+0 systems by Qualified Stock Brokers (QSBs). [Source: SEBI circular October 2025]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
7. Korea (for comparison)

7.1 Regulatory Structure

FSC (Financial Services Commission): Policy and rulemaking authority for financial markets. Regulates KRX based on the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (FSCMA). KRX needs FSC approval to amend its regulations. From 2026, mandatory English disclosure requirement expands to all KOSPI-listed companies. [Source: Chambers Financial Services Regulation 2025 - South Korea; FSC press releases]
FSS (Financial Supervisory Service): Executive supervisory body under FSC. Conducts on-site examinations and enforcement. [Source: FSC/FSS]
BOK (Bank of Korea): Central bank overseeing payment and settlement systems. Operates BOK-Wire+ system. [Source: BIS CPMI Red Book Korea]
KRX (Korea Exchange): Sole exchange operator and CCP for exchange-traded products (equities, derivatives). Vertically integrated model. Regulated by FSC and overseen by BOK. [Source: Chambers 2025; BIS Red Book Korea; IMF FSAP 2014]
KSD (Korea Securities Depository): Central securities depository. Operates e-SAFE settlement system for bond institutions. [Source: FSC press release August 2025; Clearstream Market Infrastructure - South Korea]



7.2 Key Features

Vertically Integrated Model: KRX operates as combined exchange, clearing house, and CCP. KSD operates as CSD. Both are closely coordinated under FSC/FSS oversight. [Source: BIS Red Book Korea; IMF FSAP 2014]
T+2 Settlement: Current settlement cycle for equities. [Source: Clearstream Market Infrastructure - South Korea]
T+1 Working Group: On October 10, 2025, KSD and KRX announced establishment of a joint working group to explore T+1 transition, including representatives from KOFIA (Korea Financial Investment Association), major securities firms, and other market participants. Findings to be reported to financial authorities. [Source: FSC press release]
Settlement Infrastructure Enhancement: Plan to Enhance Securities Settlement Infrastructure announced August 2025. Includes extending operating hours of BOK-Wire+ and KSD’s e-SAFE system. Market participant feedback being gathered. [Source: FSC press release]
KRX as Sole CCP: KRX serves as the sole CCP for all exchange-traded products including equities, derivatives (KOSPI 200 futures/options, single stock futures, etc.). [Source: BIS Red Book Korea; IMF FSAP]

title: Asia-Pacific Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
9. Recent Trends in Asia-Pacific

9.1 T+1 Adoption Wave
The global move toward T+1 is gaining momentum in Asia-Pacific following the US/Canada migration in May 2024 and the EU’s announced transition. India pioneered T+1 (January 2023) and is already pushing toward T+0. China’s unique model already settles securities on T+0. Hong Kong issued a T+1 consultation in July 2025. Korea established a T+1 working group in October 2025. Australia has deferred T+1 to 2030 pending CHESS replacement completion. Singapore’s industry has requested a cautious approach. Pakistan announced T+1 from February 2026, and Turkey is targeting end of 2026 for preparations. [Source: BNP Paribas T+1 APAC report; EquiLend; Citi T+1 Asia report; TWSE Market Insights]


9.2 Stock Connect and Cross-Border Linkages
Stock Connect (Shanghai-Hong Kong, Shenzhen-Hong Kong) and Bond Connect continue to expand as the primary channels for cross-border investment in Chinese securities. The clearing architecture with HKSCC as ChinaClear’s nominee has proven resilient. The SGX-Nasdaq dual-listing bridge (targeted mid-2026) represents a new model of cross-border linkage. [Source: HKEX; SGX]


9.3 OTC Clearing Mandates
Jurisdictions continue to expand mandatory OTC clearing requirements. Hong Kong is refining clearing rules with new calculation period designations (effective March 2027) and implementing enhanced reporting (UTI, UPI, CDE from September 2025). Japan maintains clearing mandates for TONA IRS and iTraxx Japan CDS. China’s Futures and Derivatives Law (2022) provides the framework for further development. [Source: HKMA January 2026; JSCC; CSRC]


9.4 Technology Modernization

Australia: CHESS replacement Release 1 (clearing) go-live April 2026, after abandoning the original DLT-based approach. [Source: ASX]
Hong Kong: Uncertificated Securities Market (USM) regime launching early 2026 with five-year transition. [Source: SFC]
Singapore: CDP custody modernization and board lot reduction under consideration. [Source: MAS]
Korea: Securities settlement infrastructure enhancement plan (August 2025), including extended BOK-Wire+ and e-SAFE operating hours. [Source: FSC]
India: T+0 instant settlement infrastructure development and NSE T+0 official launch (February 2026). [Source: SEBI; NSE]



9.5 PFMI Compliance Improvements
All major Asia-Pacific jurisdictions continue to align with CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI). Japan’s JSCC updated its PFMI disclosure in April 2026. Australia’s RBA conducts annual FSS assessments (latest September 2025). China’s DVP reform directly addressed FSAP recommendations for PFMI compliance. RBA published guidance on CS facility resolution regime (June 2025). [Source: JSCC; RBA; WFE Focus - CSDC]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
1. Regulatory Authorities
The U.S. clearing and settlement regulatory framework is characterized by a multi-regulator model, with different agencies overseeing different asset classes and systemic risk. Unlike jurisdictions with a single consolidated regulator, the U.S. divides authority primarily between the SEC (securities) and CFTC (derivatives), with the Federal Reserve and FSOC providing systemic risk oversight.

1.1 SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission)
The SEC is the primary regulator for clearing agencies that clear securities, including equities, fixed income, and security-based swaps. Its Division of Trading and Markets is the key unit responsible for CCP and CSD oversight.

Jurisdiction: All clearing agencies registered under Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, including CCPs (e.g., NSCC, FICC, OCC) and CSDs (e.g., DTC)
Key Division: Division of Trading and Markets – oversees exchanges, broker-dealers, clearing agencies, transfer agents, and SROs
Core Authority:

Registration and regulation of clearing agencies under Section 17A
Rulemaking authority under Rule 17Ad-22 (standards for clearing agencies)
Approval/disapproval of clearing agency proposed rule changes (SRO filings)
Examination and enforcement against clearing agencies
Authority over security-based swap clearing agencies (Dodd-Frank Title VII)

Supervised Entities (Securities Clearing): NSCC, DTC, FICC (GSD and MBSD), OCC (jointly with CFTC), ICE Clear Credit (as SBS clearing agency)
Website: https://www.sec.gov

[Source: SEC, “About the SEC” and “Division of Trading and Markets,” accessed 2026-04-07]


1.2 CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission)
The CFTC is the primary regulator for derivatives clearing organizations (DCOs) that clear futures, options on futures, and swaps.

Jurisdiction: All DCOs registered under Section 5b of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA), including CME Clearing, ICE Clear US, ICE Clear Europe (exempt DCO), LCH Ltd (registered DCO), and others
Key Division: Division of Clearing and Risk (DCR) – responsible for oversight of DCOs and clearinghouse risk management
Core Authority:

Registration of DCOs and enforcement of 18 Core Principles (CEA Section 5b(c)(2))
Rulemaking under Part 39 of CFTC Regulations
Swap clearing mandate – determining which swaps must be centrally cleared
Review of DCO proposed rule changes
Examination and enforcement against registered DCOs
Registration of foreign DCOs under alternative compliance or exempt DCO frameworks

Supervised Entities (Key U.S. DCOs): CME Clearing (SIFMU), ICE Clear Credit (SIFMU), ICE Clear US, LCH Ltd (registered DCO), Nodal Clear, others
Website: https://www.cftc.gov

[Source: CFTC, “Derivatives Clearing Organizations,” accessed 2026-04-07; CFTC, “Division of Clearing and Risk,” accessed 2026-04-07]


1.3 Federal Reserve Board
The Federal Reserve serves as the supervisory agency for certain designated SIFMUs under Dodd-Frank Title VIII and provides systemic risk oversight.

Title VIII Role: Under Dodd-Frank Section 804, the FSOC designates SIFMUs, and the “Supervisory Agency” (the Federal Reserve for payment-related FMUs, or the SEC/CFTC for clearing-related FMUs) has primary oversight responsibility. The Fed has additional authority over all designated SIFMUs:

May prescribe risk management standards (Section 805)
Provides access to Federal Reserve discount window and payment services for designated SIFMUs in unusual or exigent circumstances (Section 806)
May examine designated FMUs (in consultation with the Supervisory Agency)

Direct Supervisory Responsibility: The Clearing House Payments Company (CHIPS) and CLS Bank International – both designated SIFMUs where the Fed is the Supervisory Agency
Indirect Authority: The Fed has backup examination and enforcement authority over all eight designated SIFMUs, including SEC-supervised (DTC, NSCC, FICC, OCC, ICE Clear Credit) and CFTC-supervised (CME Clearing) entities
Website: https://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/designated_fmu_about.htm

[Source: Federal Reserve Board, “Designated Financial Market Utilities,” accessed 2026-04-07; Dodd-Frank Act, Title VIII, Sections 803-806]


1.4 FSOC (Financial Stability Oversight Council)
The FSOC is the inter-agency body responsible for identifying and responding to threats to U.S. financial stability, including the designation of SIFMUs.

Composition: Chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury; 10 voting members (heads of SEC, CFTC, Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC, CFPB, FHFA, NCUA, and an independent insurance expert appointed by the President) plus 5 non-voting members
SIFMU Designation Authority: Under Dodd-Frank Title VIII, Section 804, the FSOC may designate an FMU as “systemically important” if the Council determines that the failure of or disruption to its functioning could create or increase the risk of significant liquidity or credit problems spreading among financial institutions or markets, thereby threatening U.S. financial stability
Designation Criteria (Consideration Factors):

The aggregate monetary value of transactions processed by the FMU
The aggregate exposure of the FMU to its counterparties
The relationship, interdependencies, and other interactions with other FMUs or payment, clearing, or settlement activities
The effect that the failure of or disruption to the FMU would have on critical markets, financial institutions, or the broader financial system
Any other factors deemed appropriate by the Council

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
2. Key Legislation & Regulations

2.1 Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (2010)
The Dodd-Frank Act is the most significant piece of financial regulatory legislation since the 1930s, enacted in response to the 2008 financial crisis. Two titles are directly relevant to clearing and settlement:

Title VII – Wall Street Transparency and Accountability (OTC Derivatives Reform)
Title VII fundamentally reformed OTC derivatives markets by mandating central clearing, trade execution on regulated platforms, and reporting to trade repositories.
Key Provisions for Clearing:

Clearing Mandate (CEA Section 2(h) / Exchange Act Section 3C): Standardized swaps and security-based swaps must be cleared through a registered DCO or clearing agency, respectively. The CFTC and SEC determine which products are subject to mandatory clearing.

CFTC has mandated clearing for certain interest rate swaps (fixed-to-floating in USD, EUR, GBP, JPY) and index CDS (CDX.NA.IG, CDX.NA.HY, iTraxx Europe, iTraxx Europe Crossover)
SEC has not yet mandated clearing for any security-based swaps as of early 2026 [unverified]

End-User Exception: Non-financial entities hedging commercial risk may elect not to clear, subject to reporting
Swap Dealer / Major Swap Participant Registration: Entities meeting certain thresholds must register with the CFTC (for swaps) or SEC (for SBS), bringing them under capital, margin, conduct, and reporting requirements
Trade Execution Requirement: Swaps subject to the clearing mandate must be executed on a designated contract market (DCM) or swap execution facility (SEF)
Reporting Requirements: All swaps (cleared and uncleared) must be reported to a swap data repository (SDR) registered with the CFTC or SEC

[Source: Dodd-Frank Act, Title VII; CFTC, “Clearing Requirement,” accessed 2026-04-07]


Title VIII – Payment, Clearing, and Settlement Supervision
Title VIII creates a framework for enhanced regulation and supervision of systemically important FMUs.
Key Provisions:

SIFMU Designation (Section 804): FSOC may designate FMUs as systemically important (see Section 1.4 above for the current list of 8 designated SIFMUs)
Risk Management Standards (Section 805): The appropriate supervisory agency (SEC, CFTC, or Federal Reserve) may prescribe risk management standards governing:

Operations of designated FMUs
The conduct of designated activities by financial institutions
Standards must be designed to promote robust risk management, promote safety and soundness, reduce systemic risks, and support the stability of the broader financial system

Federal Reserve Authority Over SIFMUs (Section 806):

Examination authority (in consultation with the Supervisory Agency)
May prescribe regulations requiring advance notice of material changes to rules, procedures, or operations
Authority to provide Federal Reserve account services and discount window access to designated FMUs in unusual or exigent circumstances

Enhanced Enforcement (Section 807): Enhanced enforcement powers including the ability to issue cease-and-desist orders
Review of Standards (Section 810): The Supervisory Agency must review SIFMU standards every five years

[Source: Dodd-Frank Act, Title VIII, Sections 803-813; Cornell Law Institute, “Dodd-Frank: Title VIII,” accessed 2026-04-07]



2.2 Securities Exchange Act of 1934

Section 17A – National System for Clearance and Settlement
Section 17A is the foundational statutory authority for SEC regulation of clearing agencies. Enacted in 1975 as part of the Securities Acts Amendments, it directs the SEC to facilitate the establishment of a national system for the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions.
Key Elements:

Registration Requirement: No clearing agency may perform the functions of a clearing agency unless registered with the SEC (or exempted)
Standards for Registration: A clearing agency must be organized and have the capacity to:

Facilitate the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions
Safeguard securities and funds in its custody or control
Comply with the provisions of the Exchange Act and SEC rules

SRO Status: Registered clearing agencies are treated as self-regulatory organizations (SROs), meaning they must file proposed rule changes with the SEC for approval
Fair Access: Clearing agencies must not unreasonably prohibit or limit access to their services
Due Process: Clearing agencies must provide fair procedures for disciplinary actions and denial of access

[Source: Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Section 17A, 15 U.S.C. Section 78q-1]


Rule 17Ad-22 – Standards for Clearing Agencies
Rule 17Ad-22 is the SEC’s primary regulation implementing standards for registered clearing agencies. It has evolved significantly since its original adoption in 2012 and was substantially expanded in 2016 to incorporate PFMI-aligned standards for SIFMUs.
[Source: SEC, Rule 17Ad-22, 17 CFR 240.17Ad-22; SEC Release No. 34-78961 (September 2016)]



2.3 SEC Rule 17Ad-22 (Detailed Breakdown)
Rule 17Ad-22 is divided into multiple sub-parts, each with distinct applicability and requirements:

Sub-Part B – General Standards (Rule 17Ad-22(b) and (c))
Applicable to all SEC-registered clearing agencies. Originally adopted in 2012.







Standard
Requirement




(b)(1)
Measurement of credit exposures to participants at least once daily


(b)(2)
Use of margin to limit credit exposures; daily mark-to-market


(b)(3)
Maintain sufficient financial resources to withstand the default of the participant family with the largest exposure (“Cover 1”)


(b)(4)
Annual model validation of margin systems


(b)(5)
Limit investments of participants’ assets to instruments with minimal credit, market, and liquidity risks


(b)(6)
Establish default procedures for participant defaults, including orderly close-out of the defaulting participant’s positions


(b)(7)
Settlement finality – ensure settlement of payment obligations occurs no later than the end of the value date, and where necessary, intraday or real-time


(c)
Governance standards, including transparent governance arrangements and fit-and-proper requirements for directors and management





Sub-Part C – Enhanced Standards for Covered Clearing Agencies (Rule 17Ad-22(e))
Applicable to covered clearing agencies, defined as clearing agencies designated as SIFMUs under Title VIII or that provide CCP services for security-based swaps, or that the SEC determines have a more complex risk profile. Adopted in September 2016, effective April 2017.
These standards are directly aligned with the PFMI and represent the most comprehensive set of requirements for major U.S. clearing agencies.

2023 Amendment – Treasury Clearing Standards (Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18)(iv)):
In December 2023, the SEC amended Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18) to add specific requirements for covered clearing agencies providing CCP services for U.S. Treasury securities (see Section 9.1 for details on the Treasury clearing mandate).
[Source: SEC Release No. 34-78961 (September 2016), “Standards for Covered Clearing Agencies”; SEC Release No. 34-99149 (December 2023), “Standards for Covered Clearing Agencies for U.S. Treasury Securities”; 17 CFR 240.17Ad-22(e)]


Sub-Part D – Standards for Security-Based Swap Clearing Agencies (Rule 17Ad-22(d))
Applicable to clearing agencies that clear security-based swaps (SBS). Includes requirements for:

Financial resources adequate to meet obligations to participants notwithstanding a default by the single participant with the largest net debit
Transparent and enforceable legal framework for netting arrangements
Participant eligibility criteria based on sufficient financial resources and operational capacity

[Source: SEC Rule 17Ad-22(d); Dodd-Frank Title VII]



2.4 Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) and CFTC Part 39 Regulations
The CEA, as amended by Dodd-Frank, establishes the framework for CFTC regulation of derivatives clearing organizations (DCOs).

DCO Registration Requirements (CEA Section 5b)

Any entity seeking to clear futures, options on futures, or swaps must register as a DCO with the CFTC
Application filed on Form DCO including organizational documents, rules, risk management framework, financial statements, and compliance plan
Registration is conditioned on compliance with 18 Core Principles

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
3. CCP Authorization & Capital Requirements

3.1 SEC-Registered Clearing Agencies

Registration Process

Application: File Form CA-1 with the SEC (Section 17A(b)(1) of the Exchange Act)
Review Period: SEC reviews for compliance with statutory standards; opportunity for public comment on the application
Approval/Denial: SEC grants registration if the clearing agency meets Section 17A requirements and rules thereunder
Ongoing SRO Obligations: Once registered, the clearing agency must file proposed rule changes with SEC (Rule 19b-4); SEC approves or disapproves within 45 days (extendable to 90 days)



Capital / Financial Resource Requirements

Covered Clearing Agencies (SIFMUs):

Credit Risk (17Ad-22(e)(4)): Maintain financial resources sufficient to cover the default of the participant family posing the largest exposure in extreme but plausible conditions (Cover 1). For CCPs that have been determined to be systemically important in more than one jurisdiction or with a complex risk profile, Cover 2 is expected.
Liquidity (17Ad-22(e)(7)): Maintain qualifying liquid resources sufficient to cover the liquidity exposure generated by the default of the single largest participant family in extreme but plausible conditions. Qualifying resources include cash at the Federal Reserve or a creditworthy commercial bank, committed lines of credit, highly marketable collateral, and other approved resources.
General Business Risk (17Ad-22(e)(3) and (e)(15)): Hold liquid net assets funded by equity equal to at least 6 months of current operating expenses for ongoing operations, plus a recovery/wind-down plan.

Non-SIFMU Clearing Agencies:

Must comply with Sub-Part B of Rule 17Ad-22 (general standards), including financial resources sufficient to withstand the default of the largest participant family


[Source: SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3), (e)(4), (e)(7), (e)(15); SEC Release No. 34-78961]



3.2 CFTC-Registered DCOs

Registration Process

Application: File Form DCO electronically via the CFTC Portal (Part 39, Appendix A)
Review Period: CFTC reviews for compliance with 18 Core Principles; may request additional information
Approval: CFTC issues order of registration if Core Principles are met
Ongoing Compliance: DCOs must file amendments to rules and procedures with the CFTC; must submit to regular examinations



Financial Resource Requirements

Standard DCOs (Part 39, Subpart B):

Core Principle B (Financial Resources): Maintain financial resources sufficient to cover the default of the participant family creating the largest financial exposure in extreme but plausible conditions (Cover 1)
Financial resources must be held in the form of cleared member contributions (default fund), the DCO’s own capital, and other approved resources
At a minimum, must hold one month of projected operating costs as general business risk capital

Systemically Important DCOs (SIDCOs) and Subpart C DCOs (Part 39, Subpart C):

Cover 2: Must maintain resources sufficient to cover the default of the two participant families posing the largest combined exposure in extreme but plausible conditions
Enhanced liquidity requirements
Must develop recovery and orderly wind-down plans
Must maintain a viable plan, approved by the board, for raising additional financial resources if the DCO’s prefunded resources are depleted


Currently CFTC-Registered DCOs (major entities): CME Clearing (SIDCO), ICE Clear Credit (SIDCO), ICE Clear US, LCH Ltd, LCH SA, Eurex Clearing, JSCC, SGX-DC, ASX Clear (Futures), Nodal Clear, and others. As of early 2026, there are approximately 15 fully registered DCOs and several exempt DCOs.
[Source: CFTC Part 39; CFTC, “Clearing Organizations,” accessed 2026-04-07]



3.3 Dual-Registered CCPs
Several U.S. CCPs are registered with both the SEC and CFTC due to the products they clear:









Entity
SEC Registration
CFTC Registration
Products Cleared




OCC
Clearing Agency (Section 17A)
DCO (Section 5b)
Listed equity options (SEC jurisdiction), futures on securities and security indices (CFTC jurisdiction)


ICE Clear Credit
Clearing Agency for SBS (Section 17A)
DCO (Section 5b)
CDS indices (CFTC jurisdiction as swaps), single-name CDS (SEC jurisdiction as SBS)


CME Clearing
Not SEC-registered for securities clearing (separate subsidiary CME Securities Clearing Inc. registered December 2025)
DCO and SIDCO
Futures, options on futures, OTC swaps; Treasury securities (via CMESC, SEC-registered)



How Dual Registration Works:

The SEC and CFTC have entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) regarding the oversight of dually-registered clearing agencies/DCOs
Each agency applies its own set of rules (Rule 17Ad-22 for SEC; Part 39 for CFTC) to the respective product categories
The agencies coordinate on examinations and rulemaking to minimize duplication and regulatory burden
For OCC specifically, SEC is the “supervisory agency” under Title VIII, but CFTC retains full DCO oversight authority for futures and options on futures cleared through OCC

[Source: SEC/CFTC MOU on Oversight of Dual-Registered Clearing Agencies; OCC PFMI Disclosure Framework, accessed 2026-04-07]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
4. PFMI Compliance

4.1 U.S. Adoption of PFMI
The Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI), issued by CPMI-IOSCO in April 2012, consist of 24 principles for FMIs and 5 responsibilities for authorities. The U.S. has adopted the PFMI through domestic regulations rather than direct transposition:
SEC Implementation: - Rule 17Ad-22(e) (Sub-Part C, adopted September 2016) – the “covered clearing agency” standards are closely aligned with PFMI Principles 1-24. The SEC stated that the standards are “designed to be consistent with the relevant PFMI” - The mapping is nearly one-to-one: each provision of 17Ad-22(e)(1) through (e)(23) corresponds to a specific PFMI Principle (see detailed table in Section 2.3)
CFTC Implementation: - Part 39 of CFTC Regulations – the CFTC has stated that compliance with Part 39, particularly the enhanced requirements in Subpart C for SIDCOs, is indicative of compliance with the PFMI - The CFTC updated Part 39 in multiple rulemakings between 2011 and 2020 to align with PFMI requirements
Joint Statement: In 2012, the SEC and CFTC issued a joint statement noting that their respective rulemakings were intended to be consistent with the PFMI and that they would coordinate to ensure a comprehensive implementation
[Source: SEC Release No. 34-78961 (September 2016); CFTC Part 39; CPMI-IOSCO, “Implementation monitoring of PFMI: Level 1 assessment – United States,” 2015]


4.2 Gaps and Differences from International Standards
While U.S. regulations are broadly consistent with the PFMI, certain differences exist:









Area
PFMI Standard
U.S. Approach
Notes




Cover 2 for CCPs
PFMI Principle 4: CCPs that are “systemically important in multiple jurisdictions” should use Cover 2
SEC 17Ad-22(e)(4): Cover 1 as baseline, with expectation of Cover 2 for more complex risk profiles; CFTC Subpart C: Cover 2 for SIDCOs
Not all covered clearing agencies explicitly required to meet Cover 2 under SEC rules


Central Bank Money Settlement
PFMI Principle 9: Conduct money settlements in central bank money where practical and available
DTC and NSCC settle through the Federal Reserve (Fedwire); FICC settles through tri-party settlement banks (primarily BNYM) for repo
FICC GSD repo settlement involves significant commercial bank money exposure


Recovery Planning
PFMI Guidance on Recovery (2017): Comprehensive recovery planning tools
SEC and CFTC require recovery and wind-down plans; implementation varies across entities
No standalone “CCP Recovery” regulation; requirements embedded in existing rules


Resolution Regime
PFMI: Authorities should have appropriate resolution frameworks
No dedicated CCP resolution legislation in the U.S. (OLA under Dodd-Frank Title II is primary framework, but not specifically designed for CCPs)
Legislative gap – various bills proposed but none enacted as of early 2026


PQD Compliance
CPMI-IOSCO Public Quantitative Disclosures
All designated SIFMUs publish quarterly PQD reports; comply with the CPMI-IOSCO PQD framework
Full compliance



[Source: CPMI-IOSCO, “Implementation monitoring of PFMI: Second update to Level 1 Assessment Report,” 2015; SEC Release No. 34-78961; industry commentary]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
5. Recovery & Resolution Framework

5.1 Recovery Plans (Living Wills for CCPs)
Under the PFMI and U.S. regulations, SIFMUs and SIDCOs are expected to maintain viable recovery and orderly wind-down plans.
SEC Requirements (Covered Clearing Agencies): - Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3)(ii) requires covered clearing agencies to maintain a viable plan, approved by the board, for raising additional financial resources if the clearing agency’s existing resources are insufficient to cover losses from clearing member defaults - Rule 17Ad-22(e)(15)(ii) requires a viable plan for recovery or orderly wind-down that considers scenarios of general business losses (as opposed to default losses) - Each covered clearing agency’s recovery tools typically include: - Assessment powers (ability to require additional contributions from clearing members) - Voluntary tear-up / partial tear-up of positions - Variation margin haircutting (VMGH) – reducing gains owed to non-defaulting members - Forced allocation of positions - Reduction of service scope
CFTC Requirements (SIDCOs and Subpart C DCOs): - Part 39.39(c) requires SIDCOs and Subpart C DCOs to maintain viable plans, approved by the board, for recovery or orderly wind-down - The plan must identify scenarios that could prevent the DCO from continuing as a going concern, including uncovered credit losses, liquidity shortfalls, and general business losses - The plan must identify tools and procedures to enable the DCO to recover and continue operations or wind down in an orderly manner
Recovery Tools Used by U.S. CCPs:

[Source: NSCC Rules & Procedures; FICC Rules; OCC Rules; CME Clearing PFMI Disclosure; ICE Clear Credit Rules; SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(3), (e)(15); CFTC Part 39.39]


5.2 Resolution Framework
Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) – Dodd-Frank Title II:

Title II of Dodd-Frank establishes the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) as a resolution framework for “financial companies” whose failure would have serious adverse effects on U.S. financial stability
The FDIC is designated as the receiver under OLA
Applicability to CCPs: Title II broadly applies to “financial companies,” and the definition could encompass clearing agencies and DCOs. However, Title II was primarily designed for bank holding companies and large financial institutions, not specifically for CCP resolution
Three-Key Determination: To invoke OLA, the Secretary of the Treasury (in consultation with the President) must determine, upon the recommendation of two-thirds of the Federal Reserve Board and two-thirds of the SEC or CFTC (depending on the entity’s primary regulator), that:

The financial company is in default or in danger of default
The failure of the company and its resolution under otherwise applicable law would have serious adverse effects on U.S. financial stability
No viable private sector alternative is available


FDIC Role: - The FDIC would serve as receiver under OLA - The FDIC has studied CCP resolution scenarios but has not published a dedicated CCP resolution framework - In 2024, the FDIC and Federal Reserve issued updated guidance on resolution planning for large financial institutions (Title I living wills), but this primarily targets bank holding companies, not CCPs
Legislative Gap: - The U.S. lacks a dedicated CCP resolution regime analogous to the EU’s CCP Recovery and Resolution Regulation (EU 2021/23) - Multiple legislative proposals have been introduced in Congress to create a CCP-specific resolution framework, but none have been enacted as of early 2026 - Industry groups (e.g., SIFMA, FIA) have advocated for tailored CCP resolution authority that accounts for the unique waterfall structure and loss-allocation tools of CCPs
[Source: Dodd-Frank Act, Title II; FDIC, “Overview of Resolution Under Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act,” April 2024; Georgetown Financial Policy Institute, “An Overview of the Dodd-Frank Act and its Evolution,” 2025]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
6. Settlement Regulation

6.1 T+1 Settlement

Background and Regulatory History
The U.S. settlement cycle has progressively shortened over several decades:








Period
Settlement Cycle
Regulatory Basis




Pre-1993
T+5
Industry practice


1993-2017
T+3
SEC Rule 15c6-1 (adopted June 1993, effective June 1995)


September 2017 - May 2024
T+2
SEC amendment to Rule 15c6-1 (adopted March 2017, effective September 5, 2017)


May 28, 2024 - present
T+1
SEC amendment to Rule 15c6-1 (adopted February 2023, effective May 28, 2024)





SEC Rule 15c6-1 (T+1 Amendment)
In February 2023, the SEC adopted final rules shortening the standard settlement cycle from T+2 to T+1:

Rule 15c6-1(a): Prohibits a broker or dealer from effecting or entering into a contract for the purchase or sale of a security that provides for payment of funds and delivery of securities later than T+1, unless otherwise expressly agreed to by the parties
Rule 15c6-1(b): Firm commitment offerings priced after 4:30 PM ET shortened from T+4 to T+2
Rule 15c6-2 (NEW): Requires broker-dealers engaged in allocation, confirmation, or affirmation to enter into written agreements or establish contractual, binding, or other arrangements with relevant parties to ensure completion of these processes as soon as technologically practicable and no later than end of trade date (T+0)
Effective Date: May 28, 2024

[Source: SEC Release No. 34-96930 (February 2023); SEC, “Shortening the Securities Transaction Settlement Cycle – Compliance Guide,” accessed 2026-04-07]


Implementation Results
The transition to T+1 was widely regarded as successful, with several measurable impacts:
Clearing Fund Reduction: - NSCC Clearing Fund decreased by an average of $2.4 billion (20%) from the prior month average of $12.2 billion (T+2) to $9.8 billion (T+1) in the immediate post-transition period - Over the first full quarter (Q3 2024), the Clearing Fund decreased by approximately $3.7 billion (29%) from the prior quarter average of $12.8 billion to $9.1 billion - This reduction represents significant capital savings for clearing members
Settlement Fail Rates: - Contrary to initial industry concerns about increased fails, settlement fail rates remained stable - First day of T+1 (May 28, 2024): CNS fail rate was 1.9% (vs. 2.01% pre-T+1); DTC non-CNS fail rate was 2.92% (vs. 3.24% pre-T+1) - July 2024 monthly average: CNS fail rate 2.12%, DTC non-CNS fail rate 3.31% – both consistent with T+2 historical averages
Affirmation Rates: - Same-day affirmation rates increased significantly from approximately 74% (pre-T+1) to over 90% in the months following implementation - Industry investment in DTCC’s CTM (Central Trade Manager) and ITP (Institutional Trade Processing) platforms drove improvements
Emerging Challenges: - Liquidity Shortfalls: NSCC reported a liquidity shortfall of $7.1 billion in Q4 2024, attributed to year-end index rebalancing activity under the compressed T+1 timeline. This raised concerns about NSCC’s liquidity resources during peak-volume periods - FX Funding: International investors, particularly in Asia-Pacific time zones, faced challenges with FX funding due to the compressed settlement window and CLS settlement cut-off times - Securities Lending Recall Timing: Compressed timelines created operational challenges for securities lending recall and return processes
[Source: SIFMA/ICI/DTCC, “T+1 After Action Report,” October 2024; DTCC, “Comments on Industry’s T+1 Progress,” May 2024; Risk.net, “NSCC liquidity shortfalls raise T+1 concerns,” 2025; Finadium, “DTCC analysis shows clearing fund drops $4bn after T+1 starts,” 2024]



6.2 DVP (Delivery-versus-Payment) Requirements
The SEC requires covered clearing agencies to eliminate principal risk through appropriate DVP mechanisms:

Rule 17Ad-22(e)(12): A covered clearing agency must establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to eliminate principal risk by conditioning the final settlement of one obligation upon the final settlement of the linked obligation
Implementation in Practice:

DTC: Operates a DVP settlement system for equities and corporate bonds. Securities movements are linked to payment obligations through the Federal Reserve’s Fedwire system. DTC’s CNS (Continuous Net Settlement) and non-CNS settlement processes both operate on a DVP basis.
FICC GSD: Settlement of U.S. Treasury transactions occurs through DVP on Fedwire Securities (for direct settlements) or through tri-party settlement (primarily at Bank of New York Mellon) for repo transactions
NSCC: Net settlement occurs through DTC on a DVP basis; NSCC’s CNS system nets all buy and sell obligations and settles the net on a delivery-versus-payment basis through DTC


[Source: SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e)(12); DTC Settlement Guide; FICC GSD Rules; NSCC Rules]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
7. Market Data & Reporting

7.1 Trade Reporting (Dodd-Frank)
Title VII of Dodd-Frank requires comprehensive trade reporting for all swap transactions:
CFTC Swap Reporting (Part 43 and Part 45): - Part 43 – Real-Time Public Reporting: All publicly reportable swap transactions must be reported to a registered SDR and disseminated to the public in real-time (as soon as technologically practicable after execution). Reports include price, size (subject to block trade delays), underlying asset, and other terms. - Part 45 – Swap Data Recordkeeping and Reporting: Detailed swap data (creation data, continuation data, termination data) must be reported to a registered SDR for regulatory purposes. The CFTC has implemented Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) and Unique Product Identifier (UPI) requirements aligned with global harmonization efforts. - Registered SDRs (CFTC): DTCC Data Repository (DDR), ICE Trade Vault, CME Global Repository Services, and others
SEC SBS Reporting (Regulation SBSR): - Security-based swap transactions must be reported to a registered SBS data repository (SBSDR) - Real-time dissemination requirements apply, similar to the CFTC regime - The SEC’s reporting regime for SBS became fully operational in 2022-2023
CCP Trade Reporting: - CCPs are themselves reporting entities for cleared transactions. When a swap is cleared, the CCP novates the trade and the resulting cleared swap must be reported to an SDR.
[Source: CFTC Part 43, Part 45; SEC Regulation SBSR; Dodd-Frank Title VII]


7.2 CPMI-IOSCO PQD Compliance
All eight designated SIFMUs in the United States publish quarterly Public Quantitative Disclosures (PQD) in accordance with the CPMI-IOSCO PQD framework:

Scope of PQD: Covers credit risk, liquidity risk, collateral, margin, default fund, back-testing results, settlement data, operational risk metrics, and other quantitative measures
Publication Frequency: Quarterly, typically with a one-quarter lag
PFMI Disclosure Framework: Each SIFMU also publishes a comprehensive qualitative PFMI Disclosure Framework document (updated periodically), describing how the entity observes each of the 24 PFMI Principles
Where Published: Typically on the entity’s website (e.g., DTCC publishes PQD for NSCC, FICC, and DTC at dtcc.com/legal/policy-and-compliance)

[Source: CPMI-IOSCO, “Public quantitative disclosure standards for central counterparties,” 2015; DTCC, OCC, CME Group respective PQD publications]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
8. Cross-Border Arrangements

8.1 SEC Equivalence / Recognition of Foreign CCPs
The SEC does not have a formal “equivalence” or “recognition” regime for foreign CCPs analogous to the EU’s EMIR equivalence framework. Instead:

Exempt Clearing Agency Status: The SEC may grant exemptions from full registration to foreign clearing agencies under Section 17A or Exchange Act Rule 3a71-6 (substituted compliance for SBS entities). This is done on a case-by-case basis.
No-Action Relief: The SEC staff may issue no-action letters permitting foreign CCPs to provide limited clearing services to U.S. persons without full registration
Substituted Compliance (SBS): Under Dodd-Frank Title VII, the SEC has adopted a substituted compliance framework for security-based swaps, allowing compliance with home-country regulation to satisfy certain SEC requirements where the SEC has found the foreign regime comparable



8.2 CFTC Foreign DCO Registration
The CFTC has a more developed framework for recognizing foreign CCPs:
Full Registration: - Foreign DCOs may register fully with the CFTC and comply with all Core Principles. Example: LCH Ltd (UK-based) is fully registered with the CFTC.
Registration with Alternative Compliance (Part 39, Subpart D): - Adopted in September 2020, this framework allows non-U.S. DCOs to register with the CFTC and comply through their home-country regulations, provided: 1. The CFTC determines that the DCO’s home-country regulatory regime is comparable to the CFTC’s Core Principles 2. The DCO is in good regulatory standing with its home-country regulator 3. A satisfactory MOU or similar arrangement exists between the CFTC and the home-country regulator - The DCO must still comply with certain CFTC requirements directly (e.g., reporting, information sharing)
Exempt DCO Status: - Under CEA Section 5b(h), the CFTC may exempt a foreign DCO from registration if the DCO is subject to comparable, comprehensive supervision in its home country - Exempt DCOs are limited to clearing for non-U.S. persons or certain institutional U.S. participants - This is a more limited form of recognition than full registration
Comparability Determinations: - The CFTC has issued comparability determinations for the EU, UK, Japan, Australia, and other jurisdictions - The EU-U.S. CCP equivalence framework was established in 2016, with the CFTC finding certain EU laws comparable to CFTC requirements for DCOs
[Source: CFTC Part 39, Subpart D; CFTC, “Comparability Determinations for Substituted Compliance Purposes,” accessed 2026-04-07; CEA Section 5b(h); SEC Rule 3a71-6]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
9. Recent Regulatory Changes (2023-2026)

9.1 Treasury Clearing Mandate
The Treasury clearing mandate is the most significant U.S. clearing regulatory development since the Dodd-Frank swap clearing mandate.

Background
The $28+ trillion U.S. Treasury market is the world’s largest and most liquid government bond market. However, a large portion of Treasury transactions – particularly in the repo market and between interdealer brokers and non-dealer participants – have historically been settled bilaterally rather than through central clearing. Stress events (the September 2019 repo spike, the March 2020 Treasury market “dash for cash”) highlighted vulnerabilities from insufficient central clearing and the concentration of settlement risk.


SEC Final Rule (December 2023)
In December 2023, the SEC adopted amendments to Rule 17Ad-22(e)(18) requiring covered clearing agencies for U.S. Treasury securities (primarily FICC) to adopt rules requiring that their direct participants centrally clear eligible secondary market transactions.
Key Requirements:

Mandatory Clearing of Eligible Secondary Market Transactions (ESMTs):

Direct participants of a covered clearing agency for U.S. Treasury securities must submit for clearance and settlement all ESMTs, including:

Cash market transactions between a direct participant and a registered broker-dealer, government securities dealer, or government securities broker
Cash market transactions between a direct participant and an interdealer broker
Repo and reverse repo transactions between a direct participant and a counterparty

Certain exemptions apply (e.g., transactions between affiliates, central bank transactions)

Separation of House and Customer Margin:

CCAs must calculate, collect, and hold margin from direct participants for proprietary positions separately from margin for customer/indirect participant positions
This is intended to protect customer collateral and enhance the portability of customer positions in a default scenario

Facilitating Access (Indirect Participation):

CCAs must establish policies designed to facilitate access to clearing for indirect participants
This includes requirements to offer “done-away” clearing (where a customer can clear through a direct participant different from the executing dealer)




Implementation Timeline (as Revised February 2025)








Milestone
Original Date
Extended Date




CCA rules for margin segregation and access effective
March 31, 2025
March 31, 2025 (with temporary exemption for margin segregation until September 30, 2025)


FICC rulebook modifications
–
September 30, 2025


Cash market ESMTs – compliance date
December 31, 2025
December 31, 2026


Repo ESMTs – compliance date
June 30, 2026
June 30, 2027



The one-year extension was adopted by the SEC in February 2025 to provide additional time for industry preparation, FICC rulebook changes, and resolution of outstanding interpretive questions.


Expansion of Clearing Infrastructure

FICC: As the incumbent CCA for U.S. Treasury securities (via its Government Securities Division), FICC has been developing expanded sponsoring member and agent clearing models to accommodate the expected increase in cleared volumes
CME Securities Clearing Inc.: On December 1, 2025, the SEC approved the registration of CME Securities Clearing Inc. as a second clearing agency for U.S. Treasury securities, breaking FICC’s monopoly. CME Securities Clearing plans to launch in Q2 2026.
ICE Clear Credit LLC: Has also applied for registration as a clearing agency for U.S. Treasury securities; application was pending as of early 2026

Expected Impact: - An estimated $4 trillion per day in U.S. Treasury market transactions will require central clearing upon full implementation - Significant increase in demand for clearing member services and collateral - Potential for increased netting efficiency and reduced bilateral settlement risk
[Source: SEC Release No. 34-99149 (December 2023); SEC Release No. 34-102487 (February 2025); SEC Press Release 2025-43; Arnold & Porter, “U.S. Treasury Clearing: Key Questions and Answers,” February 2025; Arnold & Porter, “U.S. Treasury Clearing: SEC Extends Compliance Dates,” March 2025; Federal Register, “CME Securities Clearing Inc.; Order Granting Registration,” December 2025; J.P. Morgan, “The U.S. Treasury Clearing Mandate Explained,” accessed 2026-04-07]



9.2 Other Recent Regulatory Changes

SEC Shortening of Settlement Cycle to T+1 (May 2024)

See Section 6.1 for full details
Effective May 28, 2024; resulted in significant clearing fund reductions and stable fail rates



CFTC Part 39 Reporting Amendments (2023)

The CFTC adopted amendments to DCO reporting and information requirements under Part 39.19, updating daily and event-specific reporting fields, and codifying reporting requirements in a new appendix
Effective date: 2023

[Source: CFTC Press Release 8758-23, “CFTC Approves Final DCO Reporting and Information Requirement,” 2023]


SEC Climate and ESG-Related Disclosure (2024-2025)

While primarily a corporate disclosure requirement, the SEC’s climate disclosure rules (adopted March 2024, subsequently stayed by litigation) could affect clearing agencies’ disclosure practices and risk assessment frameworks [unverified]



CFTC Governance Requirements for DCOs (2023)

The CFTC proposed amendments to Part 39 to enhance governance requirements for DCOs, including requirements for risk committees, fitness standards, and conflicts of interest procedures
Final rule status as of early 2026: adopted in part [unverified]

[Source: Federal Register, “Governance Requirements for Derivatives Clearing Organizations,” July 2023]


DTC Tokenization / Digital Asset Custody (2025-2026)

In December 2025, the SEC issued a No-Action Letter authorizing DTC to offer tokenization services on the Canton Network for DTC-custodied U.S. Treasury securities
DTCC Digital Assets Solutions launched as a new business line in 2026, with a Canton Network tokenization MVP planned for H1 2026

[Source: DTCC 2024 Annual Report; DTCC website, accessed 2026-04-07]

title: U.S. Clearing & Settlement Regulation
text:
10. Comparison with Korea

10.1 Korean Clearing & Settlement Regulatory Framework
Korea’s clearing and settlement infrastructure is governed by the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act (FSCMA), with oversight from the Financial Services Commission (FSC) and the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS).
Key Entities:








Entity
Role
Regulatory Basis




FSC (Financial Services Commission)
Primary regulator; sets policy and issues regulations for capital markets, including clearing and settlement
Government Organization Act; FSCMA


FSS (Financial Supervisory Service)
Executive arm of FSC; conducts examinations, investigations, and sanctions
Act on the Establishment of Financial Supervisory Organizations


KRX (Korea Exchange)
Operates exchange markets and serves as CCP for exchange-traded securities and derivatives
FSCMA (established as a special corporation)


KSD (Korea Securities Depository)
Sole CSD in Korea; also acts as CCP for institutional OTC settlements (since 2013)
FSCMA (established as a special corporation)


BOK (Bank of Korea)
Oversight of payment and settlement systems for financial stability purposes
Bank of Korea Act



KRX as CCP: - KRX acts as CCP for all exchange-traded transactions (equities, bonds, derivatives) on its markets - KRX assumes settlement obligations through novation, performs multilateral netting, and guarantees settlement - The KRX CCP function is embedded within the exchange organization (not a separately incorporated entity)
KSD as CSD and CCP: - KSD is the sole central securities depository for all securities in Korea - Since 2013, KSD has also acted as CCP for institutional settlements in OTC-traded stocks, bonds, repos, and securities lending - Settlement occurs through DVP on KSD’s settlement system, with funds settlement through BOK-Wire+
[Source: IMF, “Republic of Korea: Financial Sector Assessment Program – CPSS-IOSCO Assessment of KRX CCP,” 2014; BIS, “Payment, clearing and settlement systems in Korea,” 2011; KRX Clearing website, accessed 2026-04-07; Chambers, “Financial Services Regulation 2025 – South Korea,” accessed 2026-04-07]


10.2 Key Differences








Aspect
United States
Korea




Regulatory Structure
Multi-regulator: SEC (securities), CFTC (derivatives), Federal Reserve (systemic risk), FSOC (SIFMU designation)
Consolidated: FSC/FSS oversee all capital markets; BOK for payment system stability


CCP Model
Multiple independent CCPs (NSCC, FICC, OCC, CME, ICE Clear, etc.) – each separately incorporated and regulated
KRX serves as the single CCP for exchange-traded products; KSD as CCP for OTC institutional transactions – both embedded within market infrastructure entities


CSD Model
DTC is the sole CSD for equities and corporate bonds; FICC handles Treasury settlement; Fedwire Securities for government securities transfers
KSD is the sole CSD for all securities


Separation of CCP and Exchange
CCPs are generally separate legal entities from exchanges (though often within the same group, e.g., CME Group owns both the exchange and CCP)
CCP function is embedded within KRX (not separately incorporated) – this has been flagged by CPMI-IOSCO as a potential governance concern


SIFMU / Systemic Designation
8 designated SIFMUs under Dodd-Frank Title VIII; enhanced supervision by primary regulator + Federal Reserve backup authority
KRX CCP and KSD are recognized as systemically important FMIs but Korea does not have a formal “SIFMU designation” process analogous to Title VIII [unverified]


Settlement Cycle
T+1 (since May 28, 2024) for equities, corporate bonds, ETFs
T+2 for equities; KSD and KRX announced a working group in October 2025 to explore T+1 transition


Default Waterfall
Multi-layered: defaulter’s margin -> defaulter’s default fund contribution -> CCP skin-in-the-game -> non-defaulter’s default fund contributions -> CCP additional resources -> assessment powers / recovery tools
Multi-layered: defaulter’s assets (margin, settlement funds) -> defaulter’s JCF (Joint Compensation Fund) contribution -> KRX settlement reserve (skin-in-the-game) -> non-defaulter’s JCF contributions -> KRX remaining settlement reserve


Recovery / Resolution
No dedicated CCP resolution regime; OLA under Dodd-Frank Title II as fallback; covered clearing agencies must have recovery plans
No dedicated CCP resolution legislation; FSCMA provides some authority for FSC intervention; recovery planning requirements less formalized than U.S. [unverified]


PFMI Compliance
SEC Rule 17Ad-22(e) and CFTC Part 39 implement PFMI; all SIFMUs publish PFMI Disclosure Frameworks and quarterly PQDs
KRX CCP and KSD have undergone CPMI-IOSCO/FSAP assessments (2013-2014); some concerns raised about governance (CCP within exchange) and financial resources


Treasury / Government Bond Clearing
Mandatory central clearing through FICC (expanding under Treasury clearing mandate); CME Securities Clearing as second CCP from 2026
Government bond clearing through KRX CCP (exchange-traded) and KSD (OTC institutional); no specific mandate for expanded central clearing


Derivatives Clearing
Separate DCOs (CME, ICE Clear, etc.) regulated by CFTC; swap clearing mandate under Dodd-Frank
KRX is the sole CCP for exchange-traded derivatives (KOSPI 200 options/futures, etc.); no OTC derivatives clearing mandate analogous to Dodd-Frank [unverified]


Cross-Border CCP Recognition
CFTC has developed alternative compliance and exempt DCO frameworks; SEC has case-by-case approach
Korea (FSC) has entered into MOUs with foreign regulators (including CFTC-FSC-FSS MOU signed September 2025 for clearing cooperation)


Margin Methodology
Varies by CCP: NSCC uses VaR-based (NSCC Clearing Fund formula), CME uses SPAN/CME CORE, OCC uses STANS (Monte Carlo)
KRX uses KOSCOM-developed risk management system; margin methodology for derivatives is VaR-based with historical simulation [unverified]





10.3 Key Observations for KRX Benchmarking

CCP Independence: The U.S. model of legally separate CCPs (distinct from exchanges) is the international norm and is recommended by the PFMI (Principle 2 on governance). Korea’s model of embedding the CCP function within KRX has been flagged as a potential governance and conflict-of-interest concern in past FSAP assessments. Separating the CCP into an independent entity could be considered.
T+1 Transition: The U.S. experience provides a useful blueprint for Korea’s planned T+1 transition. Key lessons include the importance of same-day affirmation, the positive impact on clearing fund requirements (20-29% reduction at NSCC), and the challenges for international participants regarding FX funding and time-zone differences.
Treasury Clearing Mandate: The SEC’s expansion of mandatory central clearing for U.S. Treasuries is a significant structural change. Korea may wish to evaluate whether similar expansion of central clearing coverage for Korean government bonds (KTBs) in the OTC market would enhance market resilience.
Recovery and Resolution: Both jurisdictions lack dedicated CCP resolution legislation. The U.S. has more developed recovery planning requirements (through Rule 17Ad-22(e) and Part 39), which could serve as a reference for Korea’s development of CCP recovery frameworks.
Multi-CCP Competition: The U.S. is introducing competition in Treasury clearing (FICC + CME Securities Clearing). Korea’s single-CCP model may benefit from studying the effects of CCP competition on fees, innovation, and risk management.
